Priority revision

80 priority facts from the source

  1. Three air-quality categories: Swachh Vayu Survekshan 2026: above 10 lakh population - Lucknow; 3-10 lakh - Rourkela; below 3 lakh - Kalinganagar. Keep each winner with its population band.
    PDF p. 5Connect this with the chapter →
  2. A train needs two endpoints: The issue places the hydrogen fuel-cell train on the Jind-Sonipat section in Haryana. Water is the stated by-product of electricity generation in the fuel cell.
    PDF p. 5Connect this with the chapter →
  3. A named wetland: Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary is also called Surha Tal and is in Ballia, Uttar Pradesh. The one-liner calls it India's 100th Ramsar site in June 2026; the map gives another date, flagged below.
    PDF p. 5, 145Connect this with the chapter →
  4. Cotton mission outlay: The Mission for Cotton Productivity has a stated total outlay of ₹5,659.22 crore. Keep the programme's name and amount together.
    PDF p. 5, 6Connect this with the chapter →
  5. Two Census mascots: Census 2027 mascots: Pragati is the female enumerator and Vikas is the male enumerator. Retain both names and their roles.
    PDF p. 6Connect this with the chapter →
  6. Welfare outlay: The one-liner gives ₹53,428 crore for Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana. The detailed article links this to the renamed National Social Assistance Programme for FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31.
    PDF p. 10, 93Connect this with the chapter →
  7. Distance, event, placing: Neeraj Chopra's Lausanne Diamond League 2026 result is reported as second place with 88.05 metres on 21 August 2026. Retain the metres unit with the event and placing.
    PDF p. 17Connect this with the chapter →
  8. Venue pair: The issue places the 23rd Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, from 23 July to 2 August 2026, and lists Ahmedabad, Gujarat, as the 2030 host.
    PDF p. 17Connect this with the chapter →
  9. UDAN's purpose: RCS-UDAN means Regional Connectivity Scheme - Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik. The source dates its launch to 21 October 2016 and describes affordable connectivity to unserved and underserved regions.
    PDF p. 18Connect this with the chapter →
  10. SEMICON's value chain: SEMICON India 2026 ran at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi, on 17-19 September under Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem. Semicon 2.0 has six pillars spanning design, materials, fabrication, packaging, R&D and talent.
    PDF p. 28Connect this with the chapter →
  11. Ken to Betwa: The Ken-Betwa Link Project transfers surplus Ken basin water towards the water-deficit Betwa basin in Bundelkhand, across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. Both rivers are Yamuna tributaries; Phase I includes Daudhan Dam.
    PDF p. 38Connect this with the chapter →
  12. Modified UDAN: The issue gives an outlay of ₹28,840 crore for FY 2026-27 to FY 2035-36, with 100 airports and 200 modern helipads envisaged. Its approval and launch dates are separate milestones.
    PDF p. 18, 47Connect this with the chapter →
  13. RTI's two dates: The RTI Act received assent on 15 June 2005 and became fully operational on 12 October 2005. Its full-implementation anniversary in the issue is 12 October 2026.
    PDF p. 19Connect this with the chapter →
  14. Census: two different tasks: Census 2027 has Houselisting and Housing Census followed by Population Enumeration. The Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, conducts it; digital collection still includes house-to-house visits.
    PDF p. 49, 50Connect this with the chapter →
  15. Market access for SHGs: SARAS Melas under DAY-NRLM connect rural women entrepreneurs with buyers. The Vijayawada edition at Punnami Ghat is dated 13-31 October 2026; the issue traces the first National SARAS Mela to Delhi in 1999.
    PDF p. 19Connect this with the chapter →
  16. Access with safeguards: The issue's internet-rights article distinguishes access under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) from permissible protection against harmful content; it lists child modes, parental supervision and private-by-default accounts.
    PDF p. 18Connect this with the chapter →
  17. EFTA's four members: EFTA comprises Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. The source states that Switzerland is outside the European Economic Area.
    PDF p. 53Connect this with the chapter →
  18. TEPA dates and scale: India-EFTA TEPA was signed on 10 March 2024 and entered into force on 1 October 2025. Its stated aims are US$100 billion in investment and one million direct Indian jobs over 15 years.
    PDF p. 53Connect this with the chapter →
  19. The Swiss visit's 3Ts: Guy Parmelin's 5-7 October 2026 visit is organised around Trade, Technology and Talent. The source lists migration, young-professional exchange, transport technology, research and innovation arrangements.
    PDF p. 53Connect this with the chapter →
  20. Mobility is not unlimited exchange: The young-professionals agreement provides for 300 professionals annually from each side, expandable to 500. The migration MoU separately mentions multiple-entry visas valid up to five years.
    PDF p. 53Connect this with the chapter →
  21. BRICS host and theme: The issue places the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on 12-13 September 2026. Its theme is Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.
    PDF p. 75Connect this with the chapter →
  22. Membership versus participation: The summit account distinguishes 11 full BRICS members from 10 partner countries. It also counts 32 delegations, including regional and international organisations.
    PDF p. 75Connect this with the chapter →
  23. Payment cooperation: The BRICS article reports work on local-currency transactions and payment-system interoperability. It explicitly says no common BRICS currency was announced.
    PDF p. 75Connect this with the chapter →
  24. A complete index entry: The issue's summary lists Human Development Report 2025 - UNDP - India 130 of 193; Global Innovation Index 2025 - WIPO - India 38th. Edition labels must stay attached to the ranks.
    PDF p. 86Connect this with the chapter →
  25. IDBI: approved, not completed: The issue reports CCEA approval on 14 October 2026 for a 60.72% IDBI stake sale to 10955230 Canada Inc., a Fairfax group company, for about ₹52,878.08 crore; completion remains subject to further regulatory conditions.
    PDF p. 87Connect this with the chapter →
  26. The stake adds up: Government of India: 30.48% to be sold; LIC: 30.24%. Together these form the approved 60.72% stake. The source describes remaining stakes as approximately 15% and 19%.
    PDF p. 87Connect this with the chapter →
  27. Real versus nominal GDP: The provisional FY 2025-26 table lists real GDP ₹323.12 lakh crore with 7.7% growth and nominal GDP ₹346.36 lakh crore with 8.9% growth. They use different price bases.
    PDF p. 91Connect this with the chapter →
  28. A base-year revision: The new GDP series is described as using 2022-23 instead of 2011-12. The same page later shows revised FY 2025-26 growth of 7.8%; keep this separate from the earlier provisional 7.7%.
    PDF p. 91Connect this with the chapter →
  29. Union Budget snapshot: For FY 2026-27 BE, the issue gives a fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP, versus 4.4% in FY 2025-26 RE. It gives public capital expenditure of ₹12.2 lakh crore.
    PDF p. 113, 116Connect this with the chapter →
  30. Capital and revenue expenditure: The source describes capital expenditure as creating assets or reducing liabilities; revenue expenditure includes salaries, subsidies and interest. FY 2026-27 growth over RE is given as 11.5% and 6.6% respectively.
    PDF p. 116Connect this with the chapter →
  31. Finance Commission basics: The 16th Finance Commission is linked to Article 280, chaired by Dr Arvind Panagariya, and covers FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31. The source retains a 41% States' vertical share of the divisible tax pool.
    PDF p. 93Connect this with the chapter →
  32. Vertical share versus State weights: The issue's horizontal weights are income distance 42.5%, population 2011 17.5%, and 10% each for demographic performance, area, forest and contribution to GDP. These weights add to 100%; they are not the 41% vertical share.
    PDF p. 93Connect this with the chapter →
  33. MMX target: JAXA's MMX mission studies Phobos and Deimos and seeks to return at least 10 grams from Phobos. The issue reports an October 2026 launch, expected arrival in 2027 and sample delivery in 2031.
    PDF p. 121Connect this with the chapter →
  34. MMX instruments: TENGOO provides imaging; OROCHI takes multi-wavelength images; LIDAR measures distance. MEGANE uses gamma rays and neutrons for elemental composition, while MIRS is an infrared spectrometer.
    PDF p. 121Connect this with the chapter →
  35. An international rover: IDEFIX is the MMX rover jointly developed by CNES (France) and DLR (Germany). It assesses the surface before the spacecraft lands.
    PDF p. 121Connect this with the chapter →
  36. GAGAN's function: GAGAN means GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation. ISRO and the Airports Authority of India developed the system to improve GPS accuracy and supply integrity information for navigation.
    PDF p. 121Connect this with the chapter →
  37. Compute near the data: Pathfinder's orbital-data-centre model processes data on a satellite rather than sending all raw data to Earth. The source assigns satellite construction and hyperspectral imaging to Pixxel and the AI backbone to Sarvam.
    PDF p. 123Connect this with the chapter →
  38. Artemis II's purpose: The article describes Artemis II as a crewed lunar flyby, not a Moon landing. It tests Orion's life support, communications, navigation, manual operation and re-entry protection.
    PDF p. 123Connect this with the chapter →
  39. Criticality is a milestone: The issue reports first criticality of the 500 MWe PFBR at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, on 6 April 2026. BHAVINI built it; criticality means the start of a sustained nuclear chain reaction.
    PDF p. 129Connect this with the chapter →
  40. Three AI Summit Sutras: The India-AI Impact Summit 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, is guided by People, Planet and Progress. The source dates it to 16-21 February 2026 and separately lists seven thematic Chakras.
    PDF p. 129Connect this with the chapter →
  41. A small difference is not proof of a peak: The issue's Emissions Gap Report article gives global emissions of 58.4 GtCO₂e in 2025 against a revised 58.5 in 2024, but says uncertainty prevents confirmation of a decline or peak.
    PDF p. 144Connect this with the chapter →
  42. Absolute and per-capita emissions: The same article gives India 4.5 billion tonnes CO₂e in 2025 and 3.1 tonnes per person against a 6.4-tonne global average. Both Indian figures exclude land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF).
    PDF p. 144Connect this with the chapter →
  43. Reductions need a baseline: The source's pathway requires global reductions of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040 against 2025 levels. These are pathway requirements, not claimed achieved reductions.
    PDF p. 144Connect this with the chapter →
  44. Dated Ramsar tally: The issue reports Sauj Lake and Sukhna Wetland additions on 15 October 2026 and a total of 103 Indian Ramsar sites. This is the issue's snapshot, not a live total.
    PDF p. 144Connect this with the chapter →
  45. UP wetland pair: The map places Sauj Lake in Mainpuri and Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary (Surha Tal) in Uttar Pradesh. It lists 14 UP entries; its dates differ from the prose and are flagged.
    PDF p. 145Connect this with the chapter →
  46. Largest, smallest and first: The map's fact box identifies Sundarbans, West Bengal, as India's largest Ramsar wetland; Vembannur Wetland Complex, Tamil Nadu, as smallest; Chilika and Keoladeo as the first Indian sites in 1981.
    PDF p. 145Connect this with the chapter →
  47. COP30 setting: COP30 is placed in Belém, Brazil, on 10-22 November 2025. The article describes an implementation focus and a four-step action cycle: Coordinate, Measure, Showcase, Scale.
    PDF p. 156Connect this with the chapter →
  48. A target with two years: The Belém 4x Pledge described in the article targets quadrupling sustainable-fuel use by 2035 relative to 2024, with progress tracked by the IEA. It is a pledge, not a completed result.
    PDF p. 156Connect this with the chapter →
  49. Place-event pair: The issue places the Wings Over Ganga air show at Namo Ghat, Varanasi, on 22, 24 and 25 October 2026, and the 50th India Carpet Expo at Bhadohi on 4 October 2026.
    PDF p. 157Connect this with the chapter →
  50. Two paddy grades: UP's reported FY 2026-27 paddy procurement MSPs are ₹2,441 per quintal for common paddy and ₹2,461 for Grade A. The procurement target is 65 lakh metric tonnes.
    PDF p. 157Connect this with the chapter →
  51. Two procurement windows: The source gives western UP's paddy window as 12 October 2026-15 February 2027 and eastern UP's as 1 November 2026-28 February 2027, with payment within 48 hours.
    PDF p. 157Connect this with the chapter →

    3. Keep sports results with the event and year

    Close the notes. Explain it back.

    Why is 'Lucknow won Swachh Vayu' an incomplete revision note?

    It omits the population category. The issue names Lucknow only for cities above 10 lakh; Rourkela and Kalinganagar win the other two bands.PDF p. 5

    Reconstruct the hydrogen-train fact in three parts.

    Jind-Sonipat | Haryana | water as the fuel-cell electricity-generation by-product. Linking route, state and science prevents a place-only answer.PDF p. 5

    Match the cotton mission to its stated outlay.

    Mission for Cotton Productivity - ₹5,659.22 crore. Modified UDAN and the welfare programme have different outlays; the scheme name is part of the answer.PDF p. 5, 6

    Distinguish Pragati from Vikas.

    Both are Census 2027 mascots: Pragati represents a female enumerator and Vikas a male enumerator.PDF p. 6

    Give Neeraj Chopra's Lausanne result with its unit and context.

    88.05 metres: Neeraj Chopra's reported second-place javelin throw at the Lausanne Diamond League on 21 August 2026. A bare number is harder to check and remember.PDF p. 17

    Chapter 2 · PDF pp. 18-52

    National Affairs

    Read national news as a chain: institution → decision → intended effect → number or date. Separate the historical launch of a scheme from a later expansion, and a legal right from its safeguards.

    1. Schemes: ministry and purpose
    2. Institutions: legal basis and dates
    3. Infrastructure: route and status

    Build the chapter in eight anchors

    UDAN's purpose

    RCS-UDAN means Regional Connectivity Scheme - Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik. The source dates its launch to 21 October 2016 and describes affordable connectivity to unserved and underserved regions.

    PDF p. 18
    SEMICON's value chain

    SEMICON India 2026 ran at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi, on 17-19 September under Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem. Semicon 2.0 has six pillars spanning design, materials, fabrication, packaging, R&D and talent.

    PDF p. 28
    Ken to Betwa

    The Ken-Betwa Link Project transfers surplus Ken basin water towards the water-deficit Betwa basin in Bundelkhand, across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. Both rivers are Yamuna tributaries; Phase I includes Daudhan Dam.

    PDF p. 38
    Modified UDAN

    The issue gives an outlay of ₹28,840 crore for FY 2026-27 to FY 2035-36, with 100 airports and 200 modern helipads envisaged. Its approval and launch dates are separate milestones.

    PDF p. 18, 47
    RTI's two dates

    The RTI Act received assent on 15 June 2005 and became fully operational on 12 October 2005. Its full-implementation anniversary in the issue is 12 October 2026.

    PDF p. 19
    Census: two different tasks

    Census 2027 has Houselisting and Housing Census followed by Population Enumeration. The Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, conducts it; digital collection still includes house-to-house visits.

    PDF p. 49, 50
    Market access for SHGs

    SARAS Melas under DAY-NRLM connect rural women entrepreneurs with buyers. The Vijayawada edition at Punnami Ghat is dated 13-31 October 2026; the issue traces the first National SARAS Mela to Delhi in 1999.

    PDF p. 19
    Access with safeguards

    The issue's internet-rights article distinguishes access under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) from permissible protection against harmful content; it lists child modes, parental supervision and private-by-default accounts.

    PDF p. 18
    Do not confuse a scheme's timeline
    MilestoneSource date/detailWhat to remember
    UDAN launch21 October 2016Scheme begins
    First UDAN flightShimla-Delhi, April 2017Operational milestone
    Modified UDAN₹28,840 crore; FY 2026-27 to 2035-36Later expansion
    PDF p. 18, 47
    Learning aid - not from sourceFor each scheme write WHO does WHAT for WHOM. Add the outlay last. This editorial prompt helps reconstruct a fact instead of memorising an isolated amount.

    Close the notes. Explain it back.

    Explain UDAN in one sentence without using its outlay.

    It is the regional-connectivity scheme for affordable and viable air services to unserved and underserved regions. Purpose comes before the expansion figures.PDF p. 18

    Reconstruct the Ken-Betwa link as a direction and two States.

    Surplus Ken basin water moves towards the water-deficit Betwa basin in Bundelkhand, across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. Both rivers are tributaries of the Yamuna.PDF p. 38

    Which two RTI dates should a timeline keep?

    15 June 2005 for assent and 12 October 2005 for full operation. The 21-year anniversary is measured from full operation.PDF p. 19

    What does Silicon to Systems ask you to remember beyond a chip factory?

    The source's Semicon 2.0 ecosystem includes design, machines and materials, fabrication, advanced packaging, R&D and talent development. A complete value chain has several linked capabilities.PDF p. 28

    Distinguish the Census's two phases and its collection method.

    Houselisting and Housing Census records homes, amenities and assets; Population Enumeration records people and their characteristics. Digital collection and optional self-enumeration do not remove house-to-house visits.PDF p. 49, 50

    Source check. The issue discusses a Modified UDAN launch on 4 July 2026 and Cabinet approval on 25 March 2026. These are kept as distinct milestones; the date is not silently replaced by one undifferentiated 'launch' date.PDF p. 18, 47

    National Affairs: source readingPDF p. 18

    • Political / National AffairsPDF p. 18

    Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav Global SammelanPDF p. 18

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Sammelan on October 23, 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi.PDF p. 18
    • The 23–25 October event marks the culmination of year-long celebrations commemorating 75 years of the Chinmaya Mission.PDF p. 18
    • It was expected to bring together over 9,000 participants from India and abroad.PDF p. 18
    • The Prime Minister interacted with a holographic representation, or “Holobot,” of Swami Chinmayananda.PDF p. 18
    • He recalled their 1993 meeting in Vadodara, which focused on youth empowerment and building a strong India.PDF p. 18
    • He highlighted Swami Chinmayananda’s Gita Gyana Yagna, which brought the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita, Upanishads and Vedanta to the public.PDF p. 18
    • His address emphasised cultural preservation, social unity, self-reliance and youth participation in achieving Viksit Bharat by 2047.PDF p. 18
    • Swami Chinmayananda Saraswati was a spiritual teacher who spread the teachings of Vedanta, the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita.PDF p. 18
    • Born on May 8, 1916, as Balakrishna Menon, he passed away on August 3, 1993.PDF p. 18
    • Founded the Chinmaya Mission in 1953 to spread the timeless wisdom of Advaita Vedanta.PDF p. 18
    • He launched Gita Gyana Yagnas to make spiritual knowledge accessible to the public.PDF p. 18

    UDAN Completes 10 YearsPDF p. 18

    • RCS–UDAN completed 10 years on October 21, 2026.PDF p. 18
    • RCS-UDAN stands for Regional Connectivity Scheme -Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik.PDF p. 18
    • Launched on October 21, 2016 , it follows the National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016.PDF p. 18
    • It promotes affordable and economically viable air connectivity to unserved and underserved regions.PDF p. 18
    • The first UDAN flight connected Shimla and Delhi in April 2017.PDF p. 18
    • By October 2026, the scheme had operationalised 687 regional routes and 95 aerodromes, including 17 heliports and two water aerodromes.PDF p. 18
    • It facilitated over 3.68 lakh flights , carrying 1.72 crore passengers.PDF p. 18
    • India’s operational airports increased from 74 in 2014 to 166 in 2026. India is the world’s third-largest domestic aviation market.PDF p. 18
    • Modified UDAN , launched on 4 July 2026 , has an outlay of ₹28,840 crore for FY 2026–27 to FY 2035–36.PDF p. 18
    • It envisages developing 100 airports and 200 modern helipads.PDF p. 18
    • Its priorities include sustainable regional operations, stronger infrastructure and indigenous aircraft manufacturing.PDF p. 18

    Internet Access and Children’s RightsPDF p. 18

    • On October 15, 2026, the Supreme Court delivered its order in Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish.PDF p. 18
    • The Bench comprised Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran.PDF p. 18
    • It recognised internet access and use as a fundamental right under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a).PDF p. 18
    • Children enjoy this right irrespective of age.PDF p. 18
    • The Court rejected blanket restrictions on children’s internet access as disproportionate and unproven.PDF p. 18
    • It suggested parental supervision, dedicated child modes, private-by-default accounts and restrictions on messages from unknown adults.PDF p. 18
    • Restrictions on inherently harmful content and services remain permissible.PDF p. 18
    • The Centre must create a National Hash & URL List Database to detect and remove Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Material (CSEAM).PDF p. 18

    RTI Act Completes 21 YearsPDF p. 19

    • The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 completed 21 years of full implementation on October 12, 2026.PDF p. 19
    • It received Presidential assent on 15 June 2005 and became fully operational on 12 October 2005.PDF p. 19
    • The Right to Know derives from Article 19(1)(a), which guarantees freedom of speech and expression.PDF p. 19
    • In State of U.P . v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court recognised citizens’ right to know about public acts of government.PDF p. 19
    • In PUCL v. Union of India (2003), it upheld voters’ right to information about electoral candidates.PDF p. 19
    • The Act replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002.PDF p. 19
    • It enables citizens to obtain information held by public authorities, subject to statutory exemptions.PDF p. 19
    • It established the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions.PDF p. 19
    • Its central objectives are transparency, accountability, informed participation and prevention of corruption.PDF p. 19

    SARAS Mela 2026PDF p. 19

    • SARAS Melas, organised under the Central Government’s Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana– National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), connect rural women entrepreneurs with wider markets, buyers and business opportunities.PDF p. 19
    • The event is being held from 13 to 31 October 2026 at Punnami Ghat, Vijayawada . The Vijayawada edition is the first National SARAS Mela organised outside the Delhi–National Capital Region (Delhi-NCR).PDF p. 19

    Key FactsPDF p. 19

    • Around 1,500 women Self-Help Group (SHG) entrepreneurs and Lakhpati Didis from 34 states and Union Territories are showcasing their products through more than 650 stalls.PDF p. 19
    • Products include regional textiles, handicrafts, natural and processed foods, and other rural products.PDF p. 19
    • A major attraction is a 16-foot installation titled “SHAKTI–The Spirit of Lakhpati Didi.”PDF p. 19
    • SARAS Melas provide a practical bridge between these needs and market opportunities by bringing SHGs, consumers, institutional buyers and other stakeholders together.PDF p. 19
    • SARAS Melas began in 1999, when the first National SARAS Mela was organised in Delhi with approximately 65 beneficiaries.PDF p. 19
    • To date, 117 National SARAS Melas have been organised, with annual sales exceeding ₹200 crore.PDF p. 19

    Inauguration of a Section of Chennai Metro Rail Phase IIPDF p. 19

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Tamil Nadu on 11 October 2026 . He inaugurated the Poonamallee–Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project , built at a cost of approximately ₹4,900 crore. He also laid the foundation stones for and inaugurated key National Highway projects worth approximately ₹3,700 crore.PDF p. 19
    • A distinctive feature of this Chennai Metro corridor is its 3.7-kilometre-long double-decker structure.PDF p. 19
    • It also incorporates advanced signalling systems designed to support driverless operations.PDF p. 19
    • Among the National Highway projects, the Prime Minister inaugurated the 36-kilometre, four-lane Vadugapatti–Therkuvenganallur section of NH-744.PDF p. 19
    • He also inaugurated the 30-kilometre, four-lane Madurai Ring Road section of NH-744A.PDF p. 19
    • He laid the foundation stone for the four-lane Thiruvarur Bypass on the Nagapattinam– Thanjavur section of NH-83.PDF p. 19
    • He also inaugurated and dedicated to the nation railway infrastructure projects worth over ₹750 crore.PDF p. 19
    • These included the Karaikal–Peralam railway line, which he dedicated to the nation.PDF p. 19
    • He inaugurated five Amrit Stations , redeveloped under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme : Palani, Vellore Cantonment, Ambasamudram, Paramakkudi and Namakkal.PDF p. 19
    • At Chennai Port, he inaugurated four infrastructure projects: a Paved Storage Yard , four Export– Import (EXIM) Godowns , an upgraded Cruise Terminal and a Seafarers Club.PDF p. 19
    • He inaugurated and laid foundation stones for eight major development projects at V .O. Chidambaranar Port . He also inaugurated the Coal Berth-3 project at Kamarajar Port.PDF p. 19
    • He dedicated to the nation the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre (SGBC) at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras).PDF p. 19

    Deen Dayal Upadhyaya–Grameen Kaushalya Yojana 2.0PDF p. 19, 20

    • The Ministry of Rural Development will begin training batches under Deen Dayal Upadhyaya– Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY) 2.0 in most states and Union Territories from October 2026.PDF p. 19
    • According to the DDU-GKY 2.0 portal, 24 states and Union Territories have allocated training targets covering 5.6 lakh candidates across more than 1,200 projects to Project Implementing Agencies (PIAs).PDF p. 19
    • Approximately 2,015 training batches for around 70,000 rural youth are expected to begin across these 24 states and Union Territories during October 2026.PDF p. 20

    Key FactsPDF p. 20

    • DDU-GKY is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme that provides placement-linked skill training to poor rural youth.PDF p. 20
    • Training courses range from three to twelve months.PDF p. 20
    • Under DDU-GKY 2.0, training targets covering more than nine lakh candidates have been allocated to all 31 participating states and Union Territories for the two-year period 2026–28.PDF p. 20
    • DDU-GKY was launched on 25 September 2014 under the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM).PDF p. 20
    • Since its launch in 2014–15, more than 18.47 lakh candidates have received training for over 800 types of jobs, and more than 12.43 lakh candidates have secured employment.PDF p. 20
    • The scheme provides placement-linked skill training to youth aged 15–35 years from poor rural households.PDF p. 20
    • The Government issued revised DDU-GKY 2.0 guidelines in May 2025.PDF p. 20

    Progress in States and Union TerritoriesPDF p. 20

    • Goa has emerged as a leading state in preparations to start training batches under DDU-GKY 2.0.PDF p. 20
    • Andhra Pradesh has commenced training for more than 12,000 candidates in just three months.PDF p. 20
    • Jammu and Kashmir has allocated 100% of its assigned training targets and commenced training against 91% of the total allocation.PDF p. 20

    Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA)PDF p. 20

    • On October 6, 2026 , the Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi , approved the establishment of the Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA) as a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV).PDF p. 20
    • Its principal objective is to strengthen research, planning, project appraisal, monitoring and impact assessment across the transport and logistics sectors.PDF p. 20
    • ITLA will strengthen coordination among these sectors and promote integration across road, rail, water and air transport. This will help make transport infrastructure development more effective, economical and sustainable.PDF p. 20
    • ITLA will function as the national apex institution for integrated transport and logistics planning, research, project appraisal and monitoring, policy support and data analytics.PDF p. 20
    • It will prepare a comprehensive National Transport Master Plan with a planning horizon of ten years or more.PDF p. 20
    • It will evaluate the transport ministries’ short-term sectoral plans covering approximately five years, as well as their annual plans.PDF p. 20
    • ITLA will undertake the technical appraisal of Government of India infrastructure projects costing ₹500 crore or more.PDF p. 20
    • ITLA will develop a National Transport Data Repository (NTDR) , bringing together transport and logistics data from multiple sources.PDF p. 20
    • Major data sources will include GST Network (GSTN) e-way bills, FASTag, Vahan, GPS-based systems and urban traffic management systems.PDF p. 20

    100 Years of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)PDF p. 20

    • The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) completed 100 years on 1 October 2026. Its institutional journey began on 1 October 1926 , when India’s first Public Service Commission was established.PDF p. 20
    • At that time, it was an advisory body whose Chairman and members were appointed by the Secretary of State for India in London.PDF p. 20
    • Various programmes and activities were organised throughout the year to mark the UPSC’s centenary. The year-long celebrations began on 1 October 2025 and continued until 1 October 2026.PDF p. 20

    Key FactsPDF p. 20

    • The UPSC organised a two-day centenary event titled ‘Manthan’ at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from 30 September to 1 October 2026.PDF p. 20

    The JourneyPDF p. 20, 21

    • The Indian Civil Service (ICS) examination began in London in 1855, replacing the East India Company’s nomination system with open competition.PDF p. 20
    • In 1862, 21-year-old Satyendranath Tagore , the elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore, passed the examination in 1863 and joined the service in 1864.PDF p. 20
    • He thus became the first Indian to join the ICS . The British referred to it as the ‘heaven-born service’.PDF p. 20
    • The Government of India Act, 1919 , enacted following the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms , provided for the establishment of a Public Service Commission.PDF p. 20
    • In 1922, the ICS examination was held in India for the first time, alongside London. Its Indian examination centre was Allahabad, now Prayagraj.PDF p. 20
    • In 1924, the Lee Commission, chaired by Arthur Hamilton Lee , recommended the immediate establishment of a statutory Public Service Commission.PDF p. 20
    • The Commission was established under the Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1926 , framed under Sections 96B and 96C(2) of the Government of India Act, 1919.PDF p. 20
    • Sir Ross Barker, a member of the United Kingdom’s Home Civil Service, was its first Chairman.PDF p. 21
    • The Commission’s office was located at Metcalfe House in Delhi.PDF p. 21
    • The Indian examination centre was shifted to Delhi in 1928.PDF p. 21

    Major MilestonesPDF p. 21

    • Year Major milestone 1937 On 1 April, the Commission was renamed the Federal Public Service Commission. 1938 Combined competitive examinations were introduced for several services, marking the beginning of integrated recruitment to multiple services. 1947 Shri H. K. Kripalani became the first Indian Chairman following independence; the first examination was held in December and the IAS replaced the ICS. 1950 On 26 January , the Federal Public Service Commission was renamed the Union Public Service Commission. Shri R.N. Banerjee assumed charge on January 14, 1949, and continued as Chairman following the Institution’s Constitutional transition on January 26, 1950. 1951 The All India Services Act was enacted. 1979 The three-stage Civil Services Examination— Preliminary Examination, Main Examination and Interview—was introduced. 2011 The Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT) was introduced. A Single Window System was launched on 1 September.PDF p. 21

    Panchayat Development Planning for 2027-28PDF p. 21

    • The People’s Plan Campaign (PPC) 2026–27 began on October 2, 2026, Gandhi Jayanti, under the theme “Sabki Yojana, Sabka Vikas”.PDF p. 21
    • It initiates the preparation of Panchayat Development Plans for the financial year 2027–28 through citizen participation and evidence-based planning.PDF p. 21
    • Special Gram Sabhas brought rural residents, elected representatives, Panchayat functionaries and officials together to review schemes and identify local priorities.PDF p. 21
    • More than 2.42 lakh Special Gram Sabhas were scheduled on the GPDP and Panchayat NIRNAY portals.PDF p. 21
    • PPC, also known as Jan Yojana Abhiyan, was first launched on 2 October 2018. It is an annual exercise to strengthen participatory, transparent and accountable rural governance.PDF p. 21

    Planning framework and digital supportPDF p. 21

    • Three levels of planning: Gram Panchayats prepare Gram Panchayat Development Plans (GPDPs), Block Panchayats prepare Block Panchayat Development Plans (BPDPs) and District Panchayats prepare District Panchayat Development Plans (DPDPs). Block and district plans support coordination, convergence and the scaling of local initiatives.PDF p. 21
    • Community inputs: Village Prosperity and Resilience Plans (VPRPs), prepared by SHG federations, bring community priorities into Panchayat plans.PDF p. 21
    • Planning coverage: More than 2.55 lakh Gram Panchayats prepare participatory GPDPs and upload them on eGramSwaraj.PDF p. 21
    • As of 29 July 2025, more than 18.13 lakh Panchayat Development Plans had been uploaded for 2019–20 to 2025–26: over 17.73 lakh GPDPs, 35,755 BPDPs and 3,469 DPDPs.PDF p. 21

    National Coastal Mission 2.0PDF p. 21

    • On September 30, 2026, Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bhupender Yadav launched the implementation guidelines for National Coastal Mission 2.0 (NCM 2.0) in New Delhi.PDF p. 21
    • The Mission brings coastal conservation, climate resilience and sustainable livelihoods within a coordinated framework.PDF p. 21

    Key Facts and BackgroundPDF p. 21

    • NCM 2.0 is a Central Sector Scheme of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, with an approved outlay of ₹767 crore for 2025–26 to 2030–31.PDF p. 21
    • The earlier National Coastal Mission was subsumed into NCM 2.0 with effect from 16 May 2025. This transition preceded the launch of the implementation guidelines on 30 September 2026.PDF p. 21
    • NCM 1.0, implemented from 2021–22 to 2025–26, supported mangrove and coral-reef conservation, research on coastal and marine ecosystems, sustainable beach development and capacity building of coastal States and Union Territories.PDF p. 21
    • NCM 2.0 seeks to conserve coastal and marine ecosystems while promoting inclusive development, climate resilience and sustainable use of coastal resources.PDF p. 21

    Geographical CoveragePDF p. 21

    • Coverage or initiative Details Nine coastal States Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal. Four Union Territories Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu; Andaman and Nicobar Islands; Puducherry; and Lakshadweep. Andaman and Nicobar Islands Mangrove restoration to improve carbon storage, storm-surge buffering and shoreline stability. Gujarat A Conservation and Information Centre cum Marine Oceanarium is an envisaged outcome.PDF p. 21

    Lakshadweep and Jammu & Kashmir Declared Fully Literate StatePDF p. 22

    • Lakshadweep was declared a 100% literate Union Territory under ULLAS Scheme on October 11, 2026. Declaration was made by Administrator Praful Patel.PDF p. 22
    • The UT of Jammu and Kashmir was declared fully literate in September 2026, becoming the 10th state or Union Territory (UT) to do so since June 2024, under the Centre’s adult literacy programme ULLAS, for people aged 15 and above who missed formal schooling.PDF p. 22
    • The other states and Union Territories are Ladakh, Mizoram, Goa, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Lakshadweep.PDF p. 22
    • Under ULLAS, a state or UT is considered fully literate once at least 95% of its population aged 15 and above can read and write.PDF p. 22
    • Uttarakhand officially became India's sixth fully literate state on July 8, 2026, after achieving an adult literacy rate of 98.7%.PDF p. 22
    • Sikkim on May 27, 2026 was declared India’s fifth fully literate state after achieving the literacy benchmarks prescribed under the ‘Understanding Lifelong Learning for All in Society (ULLAS) programme.PDF p. 22
    • Himachal Pradesh was declared to be a ‘fully literate’ state (September, 2025), becoming the fifth such State/Union Territory in India (fourth among states). Himachal claims to have a literacy rate of 99.3% as per ULLAS Programme. According to the Census of India 2011, the total literacy rate for Himachal Pradesh was 82.80%.PDF p. 22
    • Earlier on May 20, 2025, Chief Minister of Mizoram, Lalduhoma, officially declared Mizoram as a fully literate state under ULLAS.PDF p. 22
    • Mizoram becomes the first state in India to attain the status of full literacy.PDF p. 22
    • Prior to Mizoram, on June 24, 2024, Ladakh became the first administrative unit (non-state) to declare full literacy.PDF p. 22
    • Sikkim Declared India’s First Paperless JudiciaryPDF p. 22
    • Sikkim marked an important milestone in India’s judicial digitalisation when it was officially declared the first paperless State judiciary in the country on May 1, 2026. The declaration was made by Justice Surya Kant, Chief Justice of India, during the Conclave on Technology and Judicial Education held in Gangtok.PDF p. 22
    • The event was held at Chintan Bhawan, Gangtok, with Chief Minister Prem Singh T amang as the Guest of Honour.PDF p. 22
    • Sikkim’s judiciary has achieved the distinction of becoming the first State judiciary in the country to move fully towards a paperless system.PDF p. 22

    Five New Entries in UNESCO Tentative List EntriesPDF p. 22

    • On September 29, 2026, the inclusion of five heritage entries in India’s UNESCO Tentative List was announced, bringing the total to 78. Four are in Madhya Pradesh; the fifth is the Sites of Satyagraha proposal linking India and South Africa.PDF p. 22
    • Bagh Cave Paintings: Nine Buddhist caves beside the Baghni River in Madhya Pradesh.PDF p. 22
    • Udayagiri Caves: This complex contains 20 caves developed mainly during the late fourth and early fifth centuries under Gupta patronage.PDF p. 22
    • Chambal Valley Temples: Bateshwar, Padavali and Kakanmath in Morena illustrate Nagara architecture under Gurjara-Pratihara and Kachchhapaghata patronage.PDF p. 22
    • Ginnorgarh Fort: This Raj Gond fortified capital lies in Sehore district.PDF p. 22
    • Sites of Satyagraha: This proposed serial, transnational property includes nine sites—seven in India and two in South Africa.PDF p. 22
    • These sites are – Pietermaritzburg Railway Station (South Africa); Phoenix Settlement (South Africa); Mahatma Gandhi Satyagraha Smarak (East Champaran, Bihar); Sabarmati Ashram (Ahmedabad, Gujarat); Mani Bhavan (Mumbai, Maharashtra); Harijan Sevak Sangh (Delhi); Sevagram Ashram (Wardha, Maharashtra); Aga Khan Palace (Pune, Maharashtra); Gandhi Smriti (Delhi). 9th Rashtriya Poshan Maah 2026PDF p. 22
    • The 9 th Rashtriya Poshan Maah was launched on September 9, 2026 at the Rudraksh International Cooperation and Convention Centre in Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh.PDF p. 22
    • The Ministry of Women and Child Development led the nationwide campaign, scheduled from 9 September to 8 October 2026. Its official theme was “Hamari Anganwadi, Hamari Jimmedari” , meaning “Our Anganwadi, Our Responsibility”.PDF p. 22
    • The campaign places Anganwadi Centres at the centre of community action for nutrition, maternal care and early childhood development.PDF p. 22
    • Rashtriya Poshan Maah, or National Nutrition Month, is traditionally observed in September under the POSHAN framework.PDF p. 22
    • The main objective is to mobilise communities against malnutrition among young children and women. The Ministry works with partner ministries and departments, states and Union Territories, districts and local institutions.PDF p. 22
    • The five priorities of the 2026 campaign are – 1. Dietary diversity and protein 2. Fresh, hot-cooked meals 3. Community ownership and accountability 4. Nutrition and early childhood development 5. Maternal nutrition and PMMVYPDF p. 22

    Cheetah Population in IndiaPDF p. 23

    • On October 5, 2026, five healthy cheetah cubs were born at Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh. The births increased India’s cheetah population to 60, including 41 Indian-born individuals.PDF p. 23
    • The announcement by Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav marked another breeding milestone under Project Cheetah but after the death of an Aasha Cub on October 12, 2026 total population is now 59.PDF p. 23

    Key Details of the New BirthsPDF p. 23

    • The mother, KJP21, is a 32-month-old Indian-born female. She became the third Indian-born female cheetah to give birth, after Mukhi and KGP12.PDF p. 23
    • The father was brought from Botswana.PDF p. 23
    • The remaining 19 animals in the reported population were born outside India, calculated as 60 minus 41. The Indian born population is now stands at 40 (59 – 19 = 40).PDF p. 23
    • Reproduction by females born in India shows that the programme is producing another generation on Indian soil.PDF p. 23

    Fact Box: Project CheetahPDF p. 23

    • Scientific name of the cheetah: Acinonyx jubatus. The subspecies native to India was the Asiatic cheetah, A. j. venaticus. Project Cheetah uses African cheetahs, identified as A. j. jubatus.PDF p. 23
    • The NTCA booklet identifies the cheetah species as Vulnerable and the Asiatic subspecies as Critically Endangered.PDF p. 23

    Key ChronologyPDF p. 23

    • Date or period Development 20 July 2022 India signed a wildlife conservation agreement with Namibia. 17 September 2022 Project Cheetah was launched at Kuno. Prime Minister Narendra Modi released eight Namibian cheetahs, five females and three males, into quarantine enclosures. 17 January 2023 India signed the cheetah cooperation agreement with South Africa. 18 February 2023 Twelve cheetahs arrived from South Africa, five females and seven males, taking cumulative imports to 20. March and April 2023 The first Indian-born litter arrived in March. By 20 April, four Namibian cheetahs were already free ranging in the wild. 2025 The programme expanded to Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh. November 2025 Botswana formally handed over eight cheetahs during President Droupadi Murmu’s visit. They remained in quarantine in Botswana before being transfer red to India. 28 February 2026 Nine cheetahs from Botswana, six females and three males, entered quarantine enclosures at Kuno. Cumulative imports from the three countries reached 29.PDF p. 23

    PRAMAAN CertificatesPDF p. 23

    • Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bhupender Yadav presented the first PRAMAAN certificates under the Indian Forest and Wood Certification Scheme (IFWCS) in New Delhi on September 29, 2026.PDF p. 23
    • The event was organised by the scheme’s operating agency, the Indian Institute of Forest Management (IIFM), Bhopal.PDF p. 23
    • PRAMAAN certificates were awarded to the Andhra Pradesh Forest Development Corporation (APFDC) for its plantations covering 33,000 hectares, and to Govind Mohapatra, a farmer associated with the Odisha Bamboo Development Agency (OBDA).PDF p. 23
    • These certificates mark the completion of the processes established following the Ministry’s launch of IFWCS in December 2023.PDF p. 23
    • They also signify the scheme’s transition from a policy framework to implementation on the ground in forest plantations and tree-based agriculture.PDF p. 23
    • PRAMAAN is an important instrument for Indian producers, exporters and forest-based enterprises.PDF p. 23
    • PRAMAAN stands for Programme for Recognition and Accreditation of Sustainable Management Practices for Agroforestry And Natural Forestry Resources.PDF p. 23

    GOBARdhan Fuelling Clean Energy and Rural GrowthPDF p. 23

    • The Union Minster of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Hardeep Puri, formally launched GOBARdhan, the Central Sector Scheme for the development of the Compressed Biogas (CBG) sector, on October 1, 2026. On 6 August 2026, the Union Cabinet approved GOBARdhan (Galvanizing Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan).PDF p. 23
    • The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas leads it, with an outlay of ₹23,731 crore for FY 2026-27 to FY 2035-36.PDF p. 23
    • It converts agricultural residue, cattle dung and municipal organic waste into clean energy, organic manure, employment and economic value.PDF p. 23

    BackgroundPDF p. 23

    • Launched in 2018 under Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen), GOBARdhan converted organic waste into biogas and bio-slurry.PDF p. 23
    • The unified scheme consolidates CBG components previously managed by four ministries and builds on SATAT and existing bioenergy programmes.PDF p. 23

    Existing Support ProgrammesPDF p. 24

    • The Biomass Aggregation Machinery Scheme has an outlay of ₹564.75 crore; by 16 March 2026, 37 proposals had received nearly ₹248 crore in approval for assistance.PDF p. 24
    • Pipeline infrastructure has an outlay of ₹994.5 crore for FY 2024-25 to FY 2028-29, with ₹56.31 crore sanctioned.PDF p. 24
    • By 4 March 2026, 120 plants were registered on the fertilizer portal and 44 MoUs had been signed. ICAR’s two-year demonstration costs ₹11.79 crore, while NITI Aayog evaluates the scheme.PDF p. 24

    Progress and RegistrationPDF p. 24

    • By 6 August 2026, the GOBARdhan portal had 1,908 registered plants, including 217 commissioned and 339 under construction.PDF p. 24
    • Commissioned capacity was 0.4 million standard cubic metres per day (MMSCMD) as of August 6, 2026.PDF p. 24

    Bharat TaxiPDF p. 24

    • Bharat Taxi is India’s first cooperative-led ride- hailing platform. It applies the principle “Driver is the Owner” to app-based transport, giving drivers a role as members and stakeholders.PDF p. 24
    • The initiative seeks to combine affordable passenger services with driver participation, transparent earnings and social-security support.PDF p. 24
    • On 23 September 2026 , Bharat Taxi was formally launched in five Uttar Pradesh cities: Lucknow, Gorakhpur, Varanasi, Kanpur and Prayagraj.PDF p. 24

    Institutional FrameworkPDF p. 24

    • Operator and legal basis: Sahakar Taxi Cooperative Limited (STCL), a multi-state cooperative society registered under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, 2002.PDF p. 24
    • Establishment and national launch: Established on 6 June 2025; officially launched on 5 February 2026. These are separate milestones.PDF p. 24
    • Capital: STCL has an authorised share capital of ₹300 crore, divided into shares of ₹100 each.PDF p. 24
    • Saarthis: Participating drivers are known as Saarthis, also spelt Sarathis in official releases.PDF p. 24
    • The platform offers cab, auto, bike and rental services. Driver and vehicle verification, trip records, an SOS facility and journey-sharing features support passenger safety.PDF p. 24

    Consumer Justice Report 2026PDF p. 24

    • In March 2026, the India Justice Report (IJR) published its inaugural Consumer Justice Report 2026 , titled “Assessing the Capacity of Redressal Commissions in India”.PDF p. 24
    • The report highlights persistent weaknesses in India’s consumer protection system, including vacancies, rising case pendency, uneven geographical coverage, limited use of mediation and inadequate data disclosure.PDF p. 24
    • Andhra Pradesh ranked first among large and mid-sized states , while Meghalaya topped the small-state category.PDF p. 24
    • The report estimates that pending cases increased by approximately 21%, from 4.27 lakh at the end of 2019 to 5.15 lakh at the end of 2024.PDF p. 24

    About the ReportPDF p. 24

    • The report assesses the capacity of consumer dispute redressal commissions through five themes: human resources, gender diversity, workload, infrastructure and budgets.PDF p. 24
    • It uses 11 equally weighted indicators to generate an overall score out of ten.PDF p. 24
    • Its rankings cover 19 large and mid-sized states and nine small states. Seven Union Territories are analysed separately but are not ranked.PDF p. 24
    • It also examines 51 selected district commissions across 27 states and Union Territories, including 23 commissions in Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru. State Rankings Category State Rank within category Score out of 10 Large and mid-sized Andhra Pradesh 1 6.28 Large and mid-sized Madhya Pradesh 2 5.92 Large and mid-sized Rajasthan 3 5.82 Large and mid-sized Karnataka 4 5.77 Large and mid-sized West Bengal 5 5.07 Large and mid-sized Uttar Pradesh 10 4.36 Large and mid-sized Telangana 19 2.20 Small Meghalaya 1 5.58 Small Sikkim 2 4.72 Small Himachal Pradesh 3 4.20 Small Manipur 9 1.70PDF p. 24

    Rising Pendency and Slow DisposalPDF p. 24, 25

    • During 2020–24, the state and district commissions covered by the national workload analysis recorded 7,64,509 filings and 6,76,964 disposals.PDF p. 24
    • Among 19 state commissions that supplied information on the age of pending cases , the report found that an average of approximately 35% of cases had been pending for more than three years.PDF p. 24
    • The share was approximately 79% in Kerala , around 71% each in Jharkhand and Jammu and Kashmir , and approximately 62% in Uttar Pradesh.PDF p. 24
    • CVC Annual Report 2025PDF p. 25
    • The Central Vigilance Commission’s 62 nd Annual Report reviews vigilance activities from 1 January to 31 December 2025. Its foreword is dated 8 June 2026.PDF p. 25
    • The report came into focus after recording 70,584 complaints received directly by Chief Vigilance Officers (CVOs) across government departments and organisations. Banks and the Railways received the highest numbers.PDF p. 25
    • During 2025, CVOs received 70,584 complaints directly. Of these, 64,905 were disposed of, and 5,679 remained under process as of December 31, 2025.PDF p. 25

    First Census of Springs 2026PDF p. 25

    • On September 25, 2026, the Ministry of Jal Shakti released the reports of the First Census of Springs at the valedictory ceremony of the ninth India International Water Week at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. The ceremony was chaired by Union Jal Shakti Minister C. R. Patil. Volume II, Part II of the First Census of Springs enumerates 14,468 springs across ten states, with Manipur recording the largest number, followed by Maharashtra. This volume forms part of the same first census.PDF p. 25

    Coverage and Reference YearPDF p. 25

    • States covered: Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Goa, Maharashtra, Manipur, Odisha, Rajasthan, Telangana, Tripura and West Bengal. The findings relate to these states and are not an all-India spring total.PDF p. 25
    • Reference year: 2023–24.PDF p. 25
    • Earlier report: Volume II covered Bihar, Karnataka, Kerala, Ladakh, Sikkim and Tamil Nadu. The Ministry released spring-census reports at the World Water Day Conclave on 23 March 2026.PDF p. 25

    Electronics Components Manufacturing SchemePDF p. 25

    • The Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) supports India’s transition from assembling finished electronic devices to manufacturing their components, materials and production equipment.PDF p. 25
    • On September 17, 2026, an update on ECMS reported 106 approved projects across 15 States, involving an expected investment of ₹69,548 crore.PDF p. 25
    • Manufacturing had begun at 38 plants, while 16 projects were at advanced stages of construction or machinery installation. These figures describe the position as of August 2026.PDF p. 25
    • India’s electronics industry has expanded rapidly over the past decade. Indicator FY 2014–15 FY 2025–26 Electronics production ₹1.9 lakh crore ₹13.11 lakh crore Electronics exports Over ₹38,000 crore ₹4.24 lakh crorePDF p. 25

    Main Features of ECMSPDF p. 25

    • The scheme was notified on 8 April 2025.PDF p. 25
    • The initial outlay was ₹22,919 crore. The Union Budget 2026–27 increased it to ₹40,000 crore.PDF p. 25
    • Turnover-linked incentives are available for six years, with an optional one-year gestation period. Capital- expenditure incentives are available for five years.PDF p. 25
    • The scheme originally envisaged an investment of ₹59,350 crore, production of ₹4,56,500 crore and 91,600 additional direct jobs during its tenure.PDF p. 25
    • India and the 2030 Electronics Manufacturing AmbitionPDF p. 25
    • India aims to build a $500 billion electronics- manufacturing ecosystem and achieve $150 billion in electronics exports by 2030.PDF p. 25
    • These national ambitions are distinct from the projected outcomes of ECMS projects.PDF p. 25

    Special Constitutional Safeguards for LadakhPDF p. 25, 26

    • At a meeting on September 9, 2026 , the Union Home Ministry reportedly proposed Article 371- K to provide special constitutional safeguards for Ladakh. Representatives of the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) participated in the discussions.PDF p. 25
    • The proposed arrangement envisages a directly elected Union Territory-level body with legislative powers over specified local matters, including land, culture, language, forests, environment and natural resources.PDF p. 25
    • It would follow a “sui generis” model, meaning a unique governance arrangement tailored to Ladakh’sPDF p. 25
    • circumstances. It would not automatically grant statehood or create a conventional Union Territory legislature.PDF p. 26
    • Ladakh became a Union Territory without a legislature on October 31, 2019 , following the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.PDF p. 26
    • Local organisations seek stronger protection for tribal identity, land, employment, culture and natural resources, alongside greater participation in governance.PDF p. 26
    • Their principal demands include statehood, Sixth Schedule protection, employment safeguards and separate Lok Sabha constituencies for Leh and Kargil.PDF p. 26
    • The Sixth Schedule, linked to Articles 244(2) and 275(1), provides special administrative arrangements for tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.PDF p. 26
    • It provides for Autonomous District and Regional Councils, with legislative, administrative, judicial and financial powers over specified subjects. Extending this framework to Ladakh would require appropriate constitutional changes.PDF p. 26
    • Article 371-K remains a proposal ; its final constitutional structure and distribution of powers require agreement and parliamentary approval.PDF p. 26

    Twin Flower Fields in LehPDF p. 26

    • On September 17, 2026, observed as Sewa Diwas, Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena inaugurated twin flower fields in Leh to mark Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 76th birthday.PDF p. 26
    • The fields are located at Choglamsar and Stakna, at an altitude of 10,600 feet, and together cover 40 acres.PDF p. 26
    • The Ladakh administration describes them as the world’s highest-altitude twin flower fields and the highest and largest flower fields in India.PDF p. 26
    • The project uses Ladakh’s climatic conditions and demand for high-value flowers in domestic and international markets to create an additional source of farm income.PDF p. 26
    • The Agriculture Department develops the flower fields and transfers them to selected self-help groups (SHGs) and cooperative societies when the flowers bloom.PDF p. 26

    Fact BoxPDF p. 26

    • Aspect Key facts Flower composition The administration reported over 25 lakh flowers in all, including approximately 24 lakh Lilium flowers and 1 lakh Gladiolus flowers. Planned crop range Lilium, Gladiolus, tulips and other ornamental species with demand in domestic and international markets. Foundation event The foundation stone for the twin projects was laid on June 22, 2026. Scientific support The Agriculture Department of the UT of Ladakh signed an MoU with the CSIR–Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (CSIR- IHBT), Palampur, Himachal Pradesh. First air consignment On 29 September 2026, the Lieutenant Governor flagged off 15,000 A-grade Lilium stems from Choglamsar at KBR Airport, Leh, for Delhi, Mumbai and Chandigarh.PDF p. 26

    Kavach 4.0PDF p. 26

    • Indian Railways has approved Kavach Version 4.0 for the identified remaining sections of the Varanasi and Izzatnagar divisions of North Eastern Railway (NER).PDF p. 26

    Recent ApprovalsPDF p. 26

    • Division Announcement date Approved cost Approved coverage Varanasi September 28, 2026 ₹223 crore 614.75 route km of identified balance sections Izzatnagar August 12, 2026 ₹295 crore (estimated) 660 route km of balance sectionsPDF p. 26
    • The Research Designs and Standards Organisation (RDSO) developed Kavach in collaboration with Indian industry.PDF p. 26
    • Its main functions are to enforce permitted speeds, help prevent Signal Passing at Danger (SPAD) - passing a stop signal without authority - and reduce collision risks.PDF p. 26
    • Kavach 4.0 ImprovementsPDF p. 26
    • RDSO approved the Kavach Version 4.0 specification on 16 July 2024. Its four major improvements are:PDF p. 26
    • Location accuracy: More accurate train-location information.PDF p. 26
    • Signal information: Improved availability of signal- aspect information in large station yards.PDF p. 26
    • Station communication: An interface between station Kavach units through optical-fibre cable (OFC).PDF p. 26
    • Electronic interlocking: A direct interface with existing electronic interlocking systems.PDF p. 26
    • These upgrades support deployment across a network with varied layouts and operating conditions.PDF p. 26

    Assam Uniform Civil Code Act, 2026PDF p. 26, 27

    • The Uniform Civil Code, Assam, Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Assam Legislative Assembly on May 25, 2026, by Parliamentary Affairs Minister Atul Bora on behalf of Chief Minister Himanta Biswa SarmaPDF p. 26
    • The Assam Legislative Assembly passed the Bill by voice vote on 27 May 2026.PDF p. 27
    • Presidential assent was given on September 29, 2026.PDF p. 27
    • With this, Assam became the first state in the North- east and the third state in India after Uttarakhand and Gujarat to adopt such UCC legislation at the state level.PDF p. 27
    • The idea of a Uniform Civil Code is linked to Article 44 of the Constitution, which directs the State to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for citizens throughout India.PDF p. 27
    • It also repeals the Assam Compulsory Registration of Muslim Marriages and Divorces Act, 2024.PDF p. 27
    • STs are excluded from the application of Assam’s UCC.PDF p. 27

    Marriage-Related ProvisionsPDF p. 27

    • The Act mandates monogamy as the legal rule for marriage.PDF p. 27
    • Bigamy and polygamy shall attract imprisonment of up to seven years.PDF p. 27
    • The act fixes the legal age of marriage at 21 years for grooms and 18 years for brides.PDF p. 27
    • Couples must submit a marriage memorandum to the Sub-Registrar within 60 days of the marriage ceremony and within 90 days outside Assam.PDF p. 27

    Divorce-Related ProvisionsPDF p. 27

    • The Act codifies uniform grounds for divorce.PDF p. 27
    • Grounds for divorce include cruelty, desertion, and mutual consent.PDF p. 27
    • The Act ensures that custody of children below five years of age remains with the mother (However, the Court remains free to consider the best interests of the child).PDF p. 27
    • Class-1 heirs will include the spouse, children, and parents of the deceased.PDF p. 27

    Live-In Relationship ProvisionsPDF p. 27

    • The Act makes registration of live-in relationships mandatory within one month, including for non- residents.PDF p. 27
    • Failure to register a live-in relationship within one month may attract imprisonment of up to three months or a fine of up to `10,000 (and continued failure may attract six months of imprisonment or `25,000 or both).PDF p. 27
    • Any child born out of a live-in relationship will be considered fully legitimate.PDF p. 27

    Penalties Under the ActPDF p. 27

    • Marriage within prohibited relationships, unless protected by valid customs, shall be punishable with imprisonment of up to six months and a fine of up to `50,000.PDF p. 27
    • Non-registration of marriage or divorce within the prescribed period shall attract a penalty of `10,000 (and `25,000 after first notice).PDF p. 27
    • Forged documents in registration matters may lead to imprisonment of up to three months, or a fine of up to `25,000, or both.PDF p. 27
    • Gujarat Uniform Civil Code 2026 President Droupadi Murmu assented to the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill on 17 September 2026. Gujar at became the second state after Uttarakhand to adopt a new UCC framework.PDF p. 27
    • The Gujarat Assembly passed the Bill on March 24, 2026.PDF p. 27
    • The committee chaired by retired Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai made recommendation for UCC.PDF p. 27
    • Scheduled Tribes and groups with constitutionally protected customary rights are exempt.PDF p. 27
    • Major provisionsPDF p. 27
    • Monogamy is compulsory: neither party may have a living spouse. The framework therefore prohibits bigamy.PDF p. 27
    • Minimum marriage age: men 21 years; women 18 years.PDF p. 27
    • Marriages covered by the Act after its commencement require a registration memorandum within 60 days; wilful non-compliance attracts monetary penalties.PDF p. 27
    • Grounds for divorce include adultery, cruelty, desertion for at least two years, etc.PDF p. 27
    • Live-in relationships: Partners living within Gujarat must declare their relationship to the Registrar.PDF p. 27

    Mukhyamantri Krishak Samriddhi YojanaPDF p. 27, 28

    • The Mukhyamantri Krishak Samriddhi Yojana is an initiative of the Uttar Pradesh Government to make long-term institutional agricultural credit more affordable for small and marginal farmers.PDF p. 27
    • Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath announced the scheme on 21 December 2025 at the Yuva Sahkar Sammelan and UP Cooperative Expo 2025.PDF p. 27
    • The Uttar Pradesh Cabinet approved the scheme on September 15, 2026.PDF p. 27
    • The Chief Minister launched it in Lucknow on 23 September 2026.PDF p. 27
    • Loan ceiling: Eligible small and marginal farmers can obtain loans of up to ₹6 lakh under the Cabinet- approved concessional framework.PDF p. 27
    • Beneficiary interest rate: 6% per annum; Akashvani reports a reduction from the earlier 11% rate.PDF p. 27
    • Interest subsidy: The State Government provides 5% interest support, available only to borrowers who pay scheduled instalments by their due dates.PDF p. 27
    • Beneficiaries : The scheme targets small and marginal farmers in Uttar Pradesh. Scheme Purpose and key facts Nandini Krishak Samriddhi Yojana Dairy development under the Nand Baba Dugdh Mission. Supports 25-cow units in the 57 districts as of FY 2025-26. The project subsidy is 50%, up to ₹31.25 lakh; the specified unit with five Gangatiri cows has a ceiling of ₹30.50 lakh.PDF p. 27
    • Mini Nandini Krishak Samriddhi Yojana Dairy development under the same mission, covering all Uttar Pradesh districts. Supports 10 indigenous cows of Sahiwal, Gir or Tharparkar breeds. Project cost: ₹23.60 lakh; subsidy: 50%, up to ₹11.80 lakh. Half the beneficiaries are to be women. Mukhyamantri Krishak Durghatna Kalyan Yojana Uttar Pradesh accident assistance scheme. Provides ₹5 lakh on the accidental death of an eligible farmer (subject to rules related with Scheme). Its coverage includes qualifying earning family members and sharecroppers.PDF p. 28

    SEMICON India 2026PDF p. 28

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the fifth edition of SEMICON India on 17 September 2026 at Yashobhoomi, the India International Convention and Expo Centre in New Delhi.PDF p. 28
    • The conference and exhibition ran from 17 to 19 September 2026 under the theme “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem”.PDF p. 28
    • It highlighted India’s effort to develop a complete semiconductor value chain, alongside the transition to Semicon 2.0. Participation and Outcomes Indicator Final reported figure Exhibitors More than 600 International companies Around 300 Countries represented 52 Speakers More than 150 Country pavilions Six — Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Singapore and Sweden State pavilions 12 Total registrations 51,656 Cumulative footfall About 40,000PDF p. 28
    • The event recorded 56 MoUs, announcements and strategic initiatives combined.PDF p. 28

    Semicon India: Progress under Phase 1.0 and the Roadmap for Phase 2.0PDF p. 28

    • Semicon 1.0 established the foundation for India’s semiconductor manufacturing and design ecosystem. Its progress includes:PDF p. 28
    • According to the July 2026 Cabinet release, 12 manufacturing units had been approved, involving a total investment of over ₹1.64 lakh crore.PDF p. 28
    • These comprised one silicon fabrication plant, one silicon-carbide fabrication plant, one integrated gallium-nitride Micro LED display fabrication plant and nine packaging units.PDF p. 28
    • Three of the approved projects had begun commercial production by August 2026.PDF p. 28

    Semicon 2.0PDF p. 28

    • The Union Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0 on 15 July 2026, with a budget outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore. Notifications covering all six pillars were issued on 31 August 2026 . Building on the first phase, the programme strengthens the capabilities needed across semiconductor design, manufacturing and supporting industries.PDF p. 28
    • Six Pillars : Design, machines and materials, more fabrication plants, advanced packaging, research and development, and talent developmentPDF p. 28
    • Under Semicon 2.0, the government aims to support 200 semiconductor design start-ups and train one lakh technicians over five years.PDF p. 28

    Status of Policing in India Report 2026PDF p. 28

    • The Status of Policing in India Report (SPIR) 2026 examines cybercrime, victims’ experiences and the response of the police and banks. Released by Common Cause and Lokniti - CSDS in New Delhi on 24 September 2026, it highlights unequal access to redressal and the association of bribery and personal influence with the recovery of lost money. Its theme is “Cybercrime—Victim Perspectives and Systemic Responses”.PDF p. 28
    • Survey Coverage: 8,306 citizens across 15 States and Delhi (a UT) examining digital exposure, victimisation, reporting, police action and financial recovery.PDF p. 28

    Cybercrime Trends and Digital ExposurePDF p. 28

    • Registered cases: NCRB data show an increase from 86,420 cybercrime cases in 2023 to 1,01,928 in 2024, a rise of 17.9%. These are registered cases, rather than the total number of incidents experienced by citizens.PDF p. 28
    • Common scam calls: 33% of respondents received calls about unordered deliveries, 31% about high-return investment opportunities and 27% from persons posing as bank officials seeking account details.PDF p. 28
    • Internet use and risk: Moderate-to-high scam exposure was reported by 46% of heavy internet users, compared with 19% of non-users.PDF p. 28
    • Overall victimisation: 13% of respondents reported experiencing cybercrime in the previous two to three years.PDF p. 28
    • Financial loss: Digital financial fraud accounted for 54% of cybercrime victims. Among digital financial fraud victims, 23% lost more than ₹20,000.PDF p. 28

    Informal channels and financial recoveryPDF p. 29

    • Informal channel Full recovery % No recovery % Paid a bribe 38 38 Did not pay a bribe 12 75 Used personal contacts 28 48 Did not use personal contacts 8 72PDF p. 29

    National Co-operative Development Corporation (Amendment) Act, 2026PDF p. 29

    • The National Co-operative Development Corporation (Amendment) Act, 2026, amends the NCDC Act, 1962, expanding its mandate and financing powers without additional Central Government budgetary assistance. The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabh a on 10 August 2026 and passed by the Lok Sabha on 11 August and the Rajya Sabha on 12 August. The President assented to the Act on 14 August 2026. Section 1(2) requires a separate commencement notification, which was not located in official sources examined up to August 22, 2026.PDF p. 29
    • The amendment provides flexible financing for diversified cooperative-sector needs and widens institutional channels for infrastructure, technology, processing and marketing.PDF p. 29
    • About National Co-operative Development CorporationPDF p. 29
    • NCDC is a statutory organisation established in 1963 under the 1962 Act and administered by the Ministry of Cooperation. It plans, promotes and finances cooperative development, including agriculture, dairy, fisheries, processing, storage and marketing.PDF p. 29

    Major Provisions of the Amended ActPDF p. 29

    • The amended Act allows direct loans and grants to any cooperative society or eligible entity engaged in cooperative development, alongside State Government financing. Share-capital investment in single-State cooperatives and other eligible entities requires prior Central Government approval.PDF p. 29
    • It expands “foodstuffs” to include processed food, other edible products and notified items, removes the rural-area restriction on eligible cooperative industrial activities, permits credit-information exchange with the Central Government, RBI, banks and notified financial institutions, and authorises activities addressing emerging technological and sectoral needs.PDF p. 29
    • The 97 th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, recognised the right to form cooperative societies under Article 19(1)(c), introduced Article 43B and added Part IXB. Article 43B promotes voluntary formation, autonomy, democratic control and professional management.PDF p. 29

    Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026PDF p. 29

    • The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026, raises the number of puisne judges from 33 to 37, excluding the Chief Justice of India (CJI).PDF p. 29
    • The total sanctioned strength increases from 34 to 38 judges. This is the first increase since 2019.PDF p. 29
    • Section 2 of the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956, initially permitted 10 judges excluding the CJI, giving a total strength of 11.PDF p. 29

    Background to the BillPDF p. 29

    • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved four additional puisne judges on 5 May 2026.PDF p. 29
    • The Lok Sabha passed the Bill by a voice vote without debate on 3 August 2026. Presidential assent was given on 11 August 2026.PDF p. 29
    • Need for Increasing Judicial StrengthPDF p. 29
    • The government cited increasing case pendency as the main reason for expansion. On 1 January 2026, the Court had 92,101 pending cases.PDF p. 29
    • During 2025, it received 75,410 cases but disposed of 65,615, leaving a gap of 9,795. By 30 April 2026, pendency had reached 92,823, according to the National Judicial Data Grid.PDF p. 29
    • This gap continued despite the Court functioning close to its sanctioned strength. The increase seeks to improve disposal capacity and deliver speedy justice.PDF p. 29

    The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026PDF p. 29

    • The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 seeks to establish an independent, transparent, efficient and professionally administered tribunal system through a judiciary-led National Tribunals Commission (NTC).PDF p. 29
    • It seeks to reduce executive discretion, establish uniform service conditions and implement the Supreme Court’s Madras Bar Association principles.PDF p. 29
    • Introduced by Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal, the Bill passed the Lok Sabha by voice vote on August 10, 2026, without detailed debate amid Opposition protests.PDF p. 29
    • It received presidential assent on August 13, 2026, and came into force on August 25, 2026.PDF p. 29
    • The Act repeals and replaces the 2021 Act and applies to 16 tribunals, appellate tribunals and authorities without altering their jurisdiction or adjudicatory powers.PDF p. 29

    Background and ObjectivesPDF p. 29, 30

    • The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasised that tribunals performing judicial functions must remain independent of the executive.PDF p. 29
    • In Madras Bar Association v. Union of India, (2026) 2 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down provisionsPDF p. 29
    • of the 2021 Act for violating judicial independence, separation of powers and earlier judicial standards.PDF p. 30
    • The new Act seeks uniform appointments, financial and administrative autonomy, expert assessment and institutional accountability.PDF p. 30
    • National Tribunals CommissionPDF p. 30
    • The Act establishes the National Tribunals Commission as the central institutional body responsible for appointments and oversight in the tribunal system.PDF p. 30
    • The Commission will replace the fragmented and predominantly executive-controlled administrative framework established under the 2021 Act.PDF p. 30
    • Its headquarters will be located in New Delhi.PDF p. 30
    • The Commission will consist of one Chairperson and four members, producing a total strength of five.PDF p. 30
    • The NTC Chairperson and members will serve for five years or until the age of 70, whichever is earlier.PDF p. 30

    Search cum Selection CommitteesPDF p. 30

    • Section 13 provides separate committees for selecting tribunal Chairpersons and members. The NTC Chairperson heads the committee for Chairpersons, which includes a retired High Court Chief Justice nominated by the NTC Chairperson.PDF p. 30
    • An NTC Judicial Member heads the committee for Members, which includes a retired High Court Judge nominated by the NTC Chairperson.PDF p. 30
    • The committee Chairperson has a casting vote when votes are equal. The Member-Secretary and empanelled experts have no voting rights. 5thPDF p. 30

    Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards 2026PDF p. 30

    • The Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) organised Swachh Vayu Diwas 2026 on 7 September 2026, coinciding with the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies. During the event, the 5th Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards were conferred on the best-performing cities and wards under the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) . The Compendium of Best Management Practices under NCAP was also released on this occasion.PDF p. 30
    • The event was presided over by Justice Prakash Shrivastava, Chairperson of the National Green Tribunal, who served as the Chief Guest.PDF p. 30
    • The Compendium of Best Management Practices under NCAP was released during Swachh Vayu Diwas 2026.PDF p. 30
    • Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards 2026PDF p. 30
    • The Ministry awarded the best-performing cities and wards covered under the National Clean Air Programme.PDF p. 30
    • These cities and wards were ranked as part of the 5th Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan.PDF p. 30
    • The Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan framework was originally introduced in 2022-23.PDF p. 30
