    Achievements under the National Clean Air ProgrammePDF p. 30, 31

    • The National Clean Air Programme is a flagship initiative for improving air quality across 130 cities in 24 States and Union Territories.PDF p. 30
    • NCAP was launched on January 10, 2019.PDF p. 30
    • A performance-linked grant of `16,425 crore has been provided to the 130 NCAP cities as critical-gap funding for implementing air pollution mitigation measures.PDF p. 30
    • In the financial year 2025-26, a total of 108 out of 130 cities recorded an improvement in their PM10 levels compared with the baseline levels of 2017-18.PDF p. 31
    • A total of 72 cities achieved a reduction of more than 20 per cent in PM10 concentrations.PDF p. 31
    • A total of 26 cities recorded a reduction of more than 40 per cent in PM10 concentrations.PDF p. 31
    • A total of 14 cities met the prescribed National Ambient Air Quality Standards in FY 2025-26.PDF p. 31
    • Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan FrameworkPDF p. 31
    • About: Introduced in 2022-23, the framework evaluates cities based on specific measures taken to curb air pollution.PDF p. 31
    • These include road dust management, solid waste management (SWM), control of vehicular and industrial emissions, management of construction and demolition (C&D) waste, and control of commercial emissions (Such as those from DG sets), alongside public outreach activities.PDF p. 31

    DAANVEER Initiative LaunchedPDF p. 31

    • On July 29, 2026, Ministry of Panchayati Raj Secretary Vivek Bharadwaj launched DAANVEER at Krishi Bhawan, New Delhi.PDF p. 31
    • It enables citizens and organisations to provide verified digital-equipment bundles directly to eligible Gram Panchayats through the Meri Panchayat application.PDF p. 31
    • DAANVEER is an entirely voluntary citizen- participation platform. Its tagline is “Give Back to Your Village.”PDF p. 31
    • The Ministry of Panchayati Raj developed DANVEER in collaboration with NIC and DigiHaat.PDF p. 31

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 31

    • DAANVEER is a platform designed not just to bridge the immediate digital infrastrcture gap in the Gram Panchayats but also to evolve into a long- term, citizen-powered ecosystem for strengthening local institutions.PDF p. 31
    • The initiative integrates the Meri Panchayat app with the DigiHaat marketplace, allowing donors to choose from pre-approved computer bundles that are mapped to State-specific technical specifications. Related Digital-Governance Platforms Platform Main Function eGramSwaraj It facilitates Panchayat planning, budgeting, accounting, progress reporting, asset management and online payments. Meri Panchayat It gives citizens access to Panchayat finances, plans, development works, public assets and participation and grievance redressal tools. SabhaSaar It uses AI to convert recordings of Gram Sabha and Panchayat meetings into reviewable, structured minutes. Gram Manchitra It uses GIS for spatial planning and decision support in preparing and implementing Gram Panchayat Development Plans.PDF p. 31

    Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp AbhiyanPDF p. 31

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the ‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan’ on 2 August 2026 to mobilise young people and communities for building a drug-free India.PDF p. 31
    • The campaign links the physical and mental well- being of India’s youth with the national objective of transforming the country into Viksit Bharat by 2047.PDF p. 31

    Key FactsPDF p. 31

    • The nationwide campaign was launched through a large video conference involving more than one crore young people from over 28,000 locations across India.PDF p. 31
    • More than 125 spiritual and public organisations, educational institutions, non-governmental organisations and industrial associations supported the programme.PDF p. 31
    • The initiative originated as a pilot project in Kashi, Uttar Pradesh, in the previous year 2025.PDF p. 31
    • The pilot initiative was supported by spiritual organ- isations and several non-governmental organisations under the Kashi Declaration before being expand- ed into a nationwide campaign.PDF p. 31
    • The Prime Minister described India’s young population as the “Amrit generation”.PDF p. 31

    Major FeaturesPDF p. 31

    • The campaign will continue for 100 weeks, covering 100 consecutive Sundays.PDF p. 31
    • Every Sunday, participating organisations and communities will conduct activities related to art, culture, sports, meditation, spirituality, community service and public awareness.PDF p. 31
    • These 100 Sundays are intended to become 100 sustained steps towards a drug-free India.PDF p. 31
    • The campaign places young people at the centre of the movement against substance abuse.PDF p. 31
    • The campaign promotes open communication between parents and children about the risks associated with substance abuse.PDF p. 31
    • The Prime Minister described those who overcome addiction as “true warriors” who deserve respect and a second opportunity in life.PDF p. 31

    Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation Amendment Act 2026PDF p. 31, 32

    • The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was passed by both Houses of Parliament on August 13, 2026. The Act amends the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. The President assented to Ac t No. 20 of 2026 on August 17, 2026. The Act came into force August 22, 2026.PDF p. 31
    • The MMDR Act, 1957, is the principal mining legislation. The Centre regulates major minerals, conservation and royalty rates.PDF p. 32
    • In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India, a nine-judge bench ruled by 8:1 in July 2024 that royalty is a contractual payment, not a tax.PDF p. 32
    • States may tax mineral rights under Entry 50, subject to parliamentary restrictions absent from the existing MMDR Act.PDF p. 32

    Major Provisions of the ActPDF p. 32

    • Union Regulation of Mineral Bearing Land: The amendment to Section 2 brings mineral- bearing land, defined as land containing minerals under Central parameters, within Central regulatory control.PDF p. 32
    • Restrictions on State Levies: Section 9D restricts State taxes, cesses and similar levies on mineral rights and mineral-bearing lands, including levies based on mineral quantity, value or royalty. States may impose them only under Central conditions or restrictions.PDF p. 32
    • Treatment of Past Dues: Unpaid or unrecovered State levies for periods before commencement will become invalid. Amounts already deposited or recovered will not be refunded.PDF p. 32
    • Central Rule Making Power: The amendment to Section 13 authorises Central rules prescribing conditions and restrictions for future State levies.PDF p. 32

    Evolution of the MMDR FrameworkPDF p. 32

    • The 2015 amendment introduced mandatory auctions, the District Mineral Foundation and the National Mineral Exploration Trust. The 2016 amendment defined the leased area and permitted certain captive lease transfers.PDF p. 32
    • The 2020 reforms opened coal and lignite auctions to companies without prior coal-mining experience. In 2021, captive mines could sell up to 50% of their annual output after meeting linked end-use requirements.PDF p. 32

    Protection for Women in Live-in RelationshipsPDF p. 32

    • In Dr. Lokesh B.H. & Others v. State of Karnataka & Another, decided on 3 August 2026, the Supreme Court held that protection against domestic cruelty under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) is not confined to women in legally valid marriages.PDF p. 32
    • The protection may extend to a woman in a live-in relationship when the relationship is “in the nature of marriage” and the parties have the intention to marry.PDF p. 32

    What Is Section 498A of the IPC?PDF p. 32

    • Section 498A of the IPC criminalised cruelty committed against a woman by her husband or a relative of her husband.PDF p. 32
    • The provision prescribed imprisonment for up to three years and a fine.PDF p. 32
    • Following the replacement of the IPC by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) , the corresponding offence is contained in Section 85 of the BNS.PDF p. 32

    Supreme Court’s RulingPDF p. 32

    • The Supreme Court held that Section 498A is not restricted exclusively to relationships based on a legally valid marriage.PDF p. 32
    • It can apply to a live-in relationship that legally qualifies as a relationship in the nature of marriage.PDF p. 32
    • However, the woman must also establish that the relationship involved a genuine intention to marry.PDF p. 32
    • The relationship must be between consenting adults and must satisfy the legal characteristics of a marriage-like domestic partnership.PDF p. 32

    Essential Conditions for Invoking Section 498APDF p. 32

    • A woman in a live-in relationship must initially establish two essential requirements:PDF p. 32
    • The live-in arrangement must constitute a relationship in the nature of marriage.PDF p. 32
    • The relationship must involve an intention to marry.PDF p. 32
    • The initial burden rests on the woman seeking protection under Section 498A.PDF p. 32
    • In Indra Sarma v. V .K.V . Sarma (2013) , the Supreme Court recognised that a live-in relationship between consenting adults is not an offence.PDF p. 32

    Samudra Manthan: National Offshore Exploration SchemePDF p. 32

    • On July 31, 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Samudra Manthan - the National Offshore Exploration Scheme - with a Phase-I outlay of ₹84,084 crore up to FY 2030–31.PDF p. 32
    • It is a Central Sector Scheme of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.PDF p. 32
    • It seeks to unlock India’s offshore oil and gas potential through better geological data, risk-sharing, deepwater drilling, shared infrastructure and indigenous manufacturing.PDF p. 32
    • The Cabinet-approved outlay remains ₹84,084 crore, and no subsequent official revision has been announced.PDF p. 32
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi articulated the vision of a modern-day “Samudra Manthan” from the Red Fort on Independence Day 2025.PDF p. 32
    • The scheme aims to accelerate oil and gas exploration in India’s deepwater, ultra-deepwater and frontier offshore basins.PDF p. 32
    • It seeks to identify and add more than 600 MMTOE (Million Metric Tonnes of Oil Equivalent) of hydrocarbon reserves.PDF p. 32
    • It aims to increase the domestic production of crude oil and natural gas.PDF p. 32

    Major ComponentsPDF p. 33

    • Accelerated Offshore Exploration: ₹43,200 crore has been allocated for 60 wells, with government assistance covering up to 50% of eligible costs, capped at ₹675 crore per well.PDF p. 33
    • Offshore Data Acquisition: ₹28,534 crore will support seismic surveys and data analysis to identify potential hydrocarbon reserves and reduce geological risks.PDF p. 33
    • Common Infrastructure Hubs: ₹10,000 crore will fund shared facilities for faster and more cost- effective offshore oil and gas production.PDF p. 33
    • Manufacturing and Services Zone: ₹2,000 crore will promote domestic equipment manufacturing, specialised services and reduced import dependence.PDF p. 33

    India’s First Telecom Manufacturing Zone in GwaliorPDF p. 33

    • The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and the Government of Madhya Pradesh signed a Memorandum of Understanding on July 30, 2026, in New Delhi to establish India’s first Telecom Manufacturing Zone (TMZ) at Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh.PDF p. 33
    • It supports the national visions of Aatmanirbhar Bharat and “Make in India, Make for the World.”PDF p. 33
    • According to government information, the bhumi pujan of the project will be held in Gwalior on October 29, 2026.PDF p. 33
    • The zone aims to transform India from a predominantly telecom services market into a major telecom-product manufacturing hub.PDF p. 33
    • It seeks to increase domestic value addition in telecom and mobile-phone manufacturing.PDF p. 33
    • The manufacturing zone is envisaged as an integrated 350-acre plug-and-play industrial cluster, designed to provide world-class infrastructure.PDF p. 33
    • The Central Government has approved ₹493 crore for Phase-I core infrastructure.PDF p. 33
    • One account places cumulative committed investment at ₹5,500 crore.PDF p. 33
    • Investment is expected to cross ₹10,000 crore in the second phase.PDF p. 33
    • The Government of Madhya Pradesh will hold 51% equity in the SPV , while the Department of Telecommunications will hold 49%.PDF p. 33
    • The zone will cover mobile phones, telecom equipment, optical fibre, semiconductors, electronic components and 5G-6G technologies.PDF p. 33
    • India’s mobile-phone production has reportedly risen from ₹18,000 crore to ₹6.2 lakh crore during FY 2014-15 to FY 2025-26.PDF p. 33
    • Mobile-phone exports have reportedly increased from ₹1,500 crore to ₹2.59 lakh crore. Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971 – Enacted on 23 December 1971, the Act extends to the whole of India and protects the National Flag, Constitution and National Anthem. Section 2 addresses insults to the Flag and Constitution in a public place or within public view. Section 3 currently protects the singing of the Nat ional Anthem.PDF p. 33

    The Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Act 2026PDF p. 33

    • The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Act, 2026, amends the 2024 Act, which came into force on June 21, 2024.PDF p. 33
    • Dr. Jitendra Singh introduced the Bill in the Lok Sabha on July 27, 2026. It passed the Lok Sabha on July 29 and the Rajya Sabha on July 30, and received presidential assent on July 31, 2026.PDF p. 33

    Public examination authorities coveredPDF p. 33

    • The Act covers examinations conducted by the Union Public Service Commission, Staff Selection Commission, Railway Recruitment Boards, Institute of Banking Personnel Selection, National Testing Agency, Central Government ministries and attached offices, and other authorities notified by the Central Government.PDF p. 33

    Major provisionsPDF p. 33

    Enhanced penaltiesPDF p. 33

    • For individuals using unfair means, imprisonment increases from 3–5 to 5–10 years, and the maximum fine increase from ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh. For service providers, the maximum fine rises from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore and debarment expands from up to four years to eight years. Proportionate examination costs shall also be recovered.PDF p. 33
    • Directors, senior managers or persons in charge who consent to or connive in an offence face 5–10 years’ imprisonment and a ₹5 crore fine, compared with 3–10 years of imprisonment and a fine of ₹1 crore earlier. Organised crime attracts 7–10 years’ imprisonment and a minimum ₹10 crore fine, compared with 5–10 years of imprisonment and a fine of a minimum ₹1 crore fine under the 2024 Act.PDF p. 33

    InvestigationPDF p. 33

    • The amendment introduces a two-month investigation period, counted from the date of recording information for police investigations, referral for central agencies, and the date of the notification constituting a Special Task Force (STF).PDF p. 33

    Special Fast Track CourtsPDF p. 33

    • Every state and Union Territory must designate one or more Courts of Session as Special Fast- Track Courts in consultation with Chief Justice of the relevant High Court. Trials must be completed within three months of filing the charge sheet, or within three months of transfer in pending cases. State governments and UT administrations must appoint Special Public Prosecutors under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023.PDF p. 33

    AppealsPDF p. 34

    • Appeals lie before a two-judge High Court bench, normally within 30 days, with an absolute 90-day limit. Appeals should be disposed of, as far as possible, within three months of admission.PDF p. 34

    Performance Grading Index 2.0 for School EducationPDF p. 34

    • The Union Ministry of Education released the Performance Grading Index 2.0 for States and Union Territories (PGI-S) and the Performance Grading Index for Districts (PGI-D) for 2025–26 on 7 July 2026. The reports assess school education performance at two administrative levels: PGI-S covers all 36 States and Union Territories, and PGI-D covers 784 districts.PDF p. 34

    Evolution and Objectives of PGIPDF p. 34

    • The concept of the Performance Grading Index was introduced in 2017. The first PGI report was published in 2019 for the reference year 2017-18.PDF p. 34
    • PGI-S evaluates the school education systems of States and Union Territories with a maximum score of 1,000. Its 70 indicators are arranged under two categories and six domains.PDF p. 34

    Inter-State DisparityPDF p. 34

    • The highest score recorded in PGI 2.0 for 2025–26 was 766.0, achieved by Chandigarh.PDF p. 34
    • The lowest score was 525.7, recorded by Meghalaya.PDF p. 34
    • The difference between the highest and lowest scores was 240.3 points.PDF p. 34
    • The inter-State Performance Gap declined from 51% in 2017-18 to 31.4% in 2025-26.     All-India Survey on Higher Education 2023–24PDF p. 34

    • The Union Ministry of Education released the reports of the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE) for the years 2022-23 and 2023-24 on July 8, 2026.PDF p. 34
    • The AISHE 2023–24 is the 14th edition of the nationwide survey conducted by the Ministry of Education.PDF p. 34
    • The reference period of the survey was the academic session 2023–24 (and the 2022-23 session in some cases).PDF p. 34
    • The AISHE report for 2021-22 was released in January 2024. The survey was initiated to collect data for the academic year 2010–11.PDF p. 34

    Key FindingPDF p. 34, 35

    • A total of 64,756 Higher Educational Institutions formed part of the AISHE 2023–24 survey frame.PDF p. 34
    • These included: 1,289 universities and university- level institutions, 48,246 colleges, 15,221 standalone institutions.PDF p. 34
    • India had 18 universities exclusively for women in 2023–24.PDF p. 34
    • There were 19 open universities in India during 2023–24.PDF p. 34
    • The number of registered colleges increased from 38,498 in 2014–15 to 48,246 in 2023–24.PDF p. 34
    • Total enrolment in higher education reached approximately 4.5 crore students in 2023–24.PDF p. 34
    • Total enrolment had increased from approximately 3.4 crore in 2014–15 to 4.5 crore in 2023–24.PDF p. 34
    • Approximately 76.8% of students were enrolled at the undergraduate level.PDF p. 34
    • Undergraduate enrolment was approximately 3.5 crore students.PDF p. 35
    • Postgraduate programmes accounted for 12.9% of total enrolment.PDF p. 35
    • Female enrolment reached approximately 2.2 crore students in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • Women accounted for around 49.7% of total higher education enrolment.PDF p. 35

    Female enrolment within Social GroupsPDF p. 35

    • Category Female enrolment Growth since 2014–15 Scheduled Castes 35.1 lakh 66.9% Scheduled Tribes 15.1 lakh 101.8% Other Backward Classes Around 90.1 lakh Around 72%PDF p. 35
    • Of the total students enrolled in 2023–24:PDF p. 35
    • 15.5% belonged to Scheduled Castes.PDF p. 35
    • 6.4% belonged to Scheduled Tribes.PDF p. 35
    • 40.1% belonged to Other Backward Classes.PDF p. 35
    • 38% belonged to other social groups.PDF p. 35
    • Scheduled Caste enrolment increased from 69.1 lakh in 2022–23 to 69.7 lakh in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • SC student enrolment increased by 23.2% between 2019–20 and 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • SC female enrolment increased from 33.9 lakh in 2022–23 to 35.1 lakh in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • Compared with 2014–15, SC female enrolment increased by 66.9%.PDF p. 35
    • Scheduled Tribe enrolment increased marginally from 28.72 lakh in 2022–23 to 28.8 lakh in 2023-24.PDF p. 35
    • Compared with 2014–15, ST student enrolment rose by 75.7%.PDF p. 35
    • ST female enrolment increased from 14.7 lakh in 2022–23 to 15.1 lakh in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • Compared with 2014–15, ST female enrolment increased by 101.8%.PDF p. 35
    • Other Backward Classes (OBC) student enrolment increased from approximately 1.74 crore in 2022–23 to around 1.8 crore in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • Compared with 2014–15, OBC student enrolment rose by 60.2%.PDF p. 35
    • OBC female enrolment increased from 85.3 lakh in 2022–23 to 90.1 lakh in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • Compared with 2014–15, OBC female enrolment increased by 72%.PDF p. 35
    • Minority student enrolment increased from 21.8 lakh in 2014–15 to 33.3 lakh in 2023–24.PDF p. 35

    States with the Highest EnrolmentPDF p. 35

    • The seven States with the highest student enrolment were: Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Bihar and Rajasthan.PDF p. 35

    Overall GER (Gross Enrolment Ratio)PDF p. 35

    • India’s higher education GER increased to 30.0 in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • It was 29.5 in 2022–23 and 23.7 in 2014–15.PDF p. 35
    • The male GER in 2023–24 was 28.9.PDF p. 35
    • The female GER was 31.2, which was higher than the male GER.PDF p. 35
    • The GER of Scheduled Caste students increased from 27.3 in 2022–23 to 27.8 in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • The GER of Scheduled Tribe students stood at 22.8 in 2023–24.PDF p. 35

    Gender Parity IndexPDF p. 35

    • The Gender Parity Index is calculated as the ratio of female GER to male GER.PDF p. 35
    • The all-India GPI in higher education stood at 1.08 in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • A GPI above one indicates that the GER of female students is higher than that of male students.PDF p. 35

    Enrolment by Academic DisciplinePDF p. 35

    Undergraduate LevelPDF p. 35

    • Based on actual institutional responses, the distribution of undergraduate enrolment was: Arts (32.1%); Science (13.5%); Engineering and Technology (12.9%).PDF p. 35

    Postgraduate LevelPDF p. 35

    • The leading postgraduate disciplines were:PDF p. 35
    • Social Sciences: 18.6%; Management: 18.2%.PDF p. 35
    • Total enrolment in universities stood at approximately 1.09 crore students in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • A total of 58,134 foreign students (from 173 countries) were enrolled in Indian higher education institutions during 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • Nepal accounted for the highest share of foreign students in India.PDF p. 35

    Teachers and FacultyPDF p. 35

    • The total number of teachers and faculty members in higher education institutions stood at approximately 17.3 lakh in 2023–24.PDF p. 35
    • Male teachers constituted 55.1% of total faculty.PDF p. 35
    • The Pupil-Teacher Ratio represents the average number of students per teacher.PDF p. 35
    • For the regular mode of study in universities and colleges, the PTR was 23 students per teacher.PDF p. 35

    UDISE+ Report 2025 - 26PDF p. 35

    • The Union Ministry of Education released the Unified District Information System for Education Plus (-UDISE+) Report 2025 - 26 on 7 July 2026.PDF p. 35

    Key Findings of the ReportPDF p. 35, 36

    • The total number of teachers increased consistently between 2022–23 and 2025–26.PDF p. 35
    • The number of teachers rose from 94,83,294 in 2022–23 to 1,02,73,020 in 2025–26 (8.3%).PDF p. 35
    • Pupil-Teacher Ratio School level 2022–23 2023–24 2024–25 2025–26 Foundational 11 10 10 10 Preparatory 14 13 13 12 Middle 18 18 17 17 Secondary 23 21 21 21PDF p. 36
    • Dropout rates declined substantially at the preparatory and secondary levels in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • The preparatory-level dropout rate declined from 2.3% in 2024–25 to 1.8% in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • The secondary-level dropout rate declined from 8.2% to 7.0% during the same period.PDF p. 36
    • Student retention improved at the middle and secondary levels in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • The middle-level retention rate increased from 82.8% in 2024–25 to 83.7% in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • The secondary-level retention rate increased significantly from 47.2% to 51.9% (from Class 1-12 standards)PDF p. 36
    • The secondary-level GER (Gross Enrolment Ratio) increased from 68.5% in 2024–25 to 71.7% in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • The middle-level GER declined marginally from 90.3% to 89.6%.PDF p. 36
    • The number of single-teacher schools declined consistently between 2022–23 and 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • Single-teacher schools decreased from 1,04,125 in 2024–25 to 1,00,843 in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • The number of zero-enrolment schools declined from 7,993 in 2024–25 to 5,663 in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • The proportion of schools with access to computers increased from 64.7% in 2024–25 to 69.9% in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • The proportion of schools with internet connectivity increased from 63.5% in 2024–25 to 67.4% in 2025–26.PDF p. 36
    • Internet access increased by 17.7 percentage points between 2022–23 and 2025–26.PDF p. 36

    Union Cabinet Approved Varanasi Highways and Urea PolicyPDF p. 36

    • On July 15, 2026, the Union Cabinet and Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved two major elevated highway corridors in Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, and the National Investment Policy for Urea-2026 (NIPU-2026) to boost self-sufficiency.PDF p. 36

    Varanasi Highway ProjectsPDF p. 36

    • Two corridors costing approximately ₹25,446 crore will be implemented by the National Highways Authority of India under the Hybrid Annuity Model.PDF p. 36
    • They form part of the Varanasi Decongestion Plan and align with the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan.PDF p. 36
    • The 43.218-kilometre corridor along the Varuna River will connect NH-31 to the Varanasi Ring Road at a cost of ₹10,998.32 crore.PDF p. 36
    • The 46.039-kilometre corridor along the Ganga River will connect NH-19 to the Varanasi Ring Road at a cost of ₹14,447.64 crore.PDF p. 36

    National Investment Policy for Urea 2026PDF p. 36

    • The National Investment Policy for Urea, 2026, updates and extends the New Investment Policy, 2012.PDF p. 36
    • It seeks to establish eight to nine new gas-based plants, adding approximately 10 million tonnes of annual capacity to achieve urea self-reliance and encourage investment.PDF p. 36
    • The policy separates fixed and variable production costs and sets returns on equity at 12%–16%. Fixed costs will be converted into Indian rupees after four years at the prevailing exchange rate to reduce foreign-exchange risk.PDF p. 36

    Delhi Electric Vehicle Policy 2.0PDF p. 36

    • The Delhi Government has notified the Delhi Electric Vehicle Policy 2.0, effective from July 1, 2026 to March 31, 2030. Chief Minister Rekha Gupta defended the decision to stop fresh registrations of petrol two- wheelers from April 2028. The policy was approved by the Cabinet on June 29, 2026.PDF p. 36

    About the Policy and Its ObjectivesPDF p. 37

    • Delhi EV Policy 2.0 promotes electric mobility in the National Capital Territory to reduce vehicular emissions, improve air quality and make Delhi a leading electric mobility hub.PDF p. 37
    • It builds on the 2020 policy, under which EVs accounted for around 14% of newly registered vehicles in 2025.PDF p. 37

    Vehicle Registration and School Bus TargetsPDF p. 37

    • From 1 January 2027, only electric three-wheelers and N1-category trucks will be registered in Delhi.PDF p. 37
    • From 1 April 2028, only electric two-wheelers will be registered. Existing petrol and other fossil-fuel vehicles may complete their full life cycle, allowing a gradual transition.PDF p. 37
    • School buses must convert at least 10% of their fleet to EVs within two years of policy notification. The target is to electrify at least 30% of the school-bus fleet by 31 March 2030.PDF p. 37
    • The government is committing a direct investment of over ₹7,000 crore for implementation.PDF p. 37
    • The overall investment plan is ₹15,000 crore, covering charging infrastructure, purchase incentives and scrapping incentives.PDF p. 37
    • EV buyers receive purchase incentives, road-tax exemptions and registration-fee waivers.PDF p. 37
    • Electric two-wheeler incentives are up to ₹30,000, ₹20,000 and ₹10,000 in the first, second and third years, respectively. Electric three-wheelers receive ₹50,000, ₹40,000 and ₹30,000, respectively (No incentive shall be given to e-autos with a battery capacity of less than 4 kWh.). N1 commercial trucks receive up to ₹1 lakh in the first year.PDF p. 37
    • The government targets 32,000 public EV charging points, with around 9,000 already operational, and has allocated around ₹1,000 crore for charging infrastructure.PDF p. 37

    Scrapping IncentivesPDF p. 37

    • Vehicles complying with BS-IV or earlier emission standardes receive scrapping incentives of around ₹10,000 for two-wheelers, ₹25,000 for three- wheelers, ₹1 lakh for new non-transport electric four-wheelers and ₹50,000 for N1 trucks.PDF p. 37

    Draft National Health Research Policy 2026PDF p. 37

    • The Department of Health Research (DHR), under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, released the draft policy in July 2026, inviting public comments until July 27, 2026. It updates the 2011 policy.PDF p. 37
    • The policy seeks to establish a trusted, inclusive, self-reliant, ethical and impact-oriented research ecosystem aligned with India’s disease burden, healthcare needs and equity concerns.PDF p. 37
    • Publicly funded health-research expenditure is approximately 0.024% of GDP in 2026–27. The draft proposes increasing it to 0.072% by 2037 and 0.15% by 2047, more than six times the present level but remaining below for the reported weighted average of 0.27% for thigh-income countries.PDF p. 37
    • The proposed National Health Research Agenda would set periodically reviewed priorities based on disease burden, scientific opportunities, health- system needs, equity, pandemic preparedness, emerging threats and national interests.PDF p. 37
    • A National Health Research Stewardship Committee would provide strategic direction and coordination.PDF p. 37

    India Ranks Ninth in Global Internet Blackout PreparednessPDF p. 37

    • India has been ranked ninth globally among nearly 100 countries considered least vulnerable to a majo r internet blackout or digital infrastructure breakdo wn, according to a study by TRG Datacenters, a United States-based colocation and digital infrastructure provider acquired by Tallvine Partners.PDF p. 37

    India’s PositionPDF p. 37

    • India recorded a digital vulnerability score of 23.4, placing it ninth among the ten countries best prepared to handle an internet blackout.PDF p. 37
    • India had:PDF p. 37
    • 22 submarine Internet cables.PDF p. 37
    • 40 Internet Exchange Points.PDF p. 37
    • An Internet usage rate of approximately 70% of the population.PDF p. 37

    Top-Ranked CountriesPDF p. 37

    • The United States emerged as the country best prepared to deal with an Internet blackout, with a vulnerability score of zero.PDF p. 37
    • It was followed by:PDF p. 37
    • Indonesia, with a vulnerability score of 10.3.PDF p. 37
    • United Kingdom , with a vulnerability score of 16.2. It is followed by Japan, Brazil and others.PDF p. 37

    NITI Aayog’s Strategic Roadmap for Making Ayurveda GlobalPDF p. 37

    • NITI Aayog’s roadmap seeks to transform Ayurveda from a wellness-oriented, product-led presence into a regulated, evidence-based global healthcare syste m, aligned with Viksit Bharat @2047 and “One Earth, One Health.”PDF p. 37

    About the ReportPDF p. 37, 38

    • NITI Aayog’s Health Division prepared the report with PricewaterhouseCoopers under its Research Scheme, using stakeholder consultations, international benchmarking and evidence-based analysis.PDF p. 37
    • India has approximately 3,55,000 trained Ayurveda practitioners, with research spanning nearly 70 countries.PDF p. 37
    • The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is in Jamnagar, Gujarat, and WHO has integrated Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani into ICD-11’s Traditional Medicine Conditions module.PDF p. 38
    • The roadmap aims to integrate Ayurveda into national health systems by 2047 through scientific evidence, quality standards and regulatory compliance.PDF p. 38
    • The proposed Global Ayurveda Register, anchored under the National Commission for Indian System of Medicine, would provide WHO-aligned digital credentials, continuous professional development and international mobility. Mutual Recognition Agreements with countries and blocs such as the G20, BRICS and ASEAN would support practitioner recognition.PDF p. 38
    • Facts at a GlancePDF p. 38
    • Ayush and herbal exports rose from USD 1.09 billion in 2014 to USD 2.16 billion in 2023. Exports reach around 150 countries. Medical tourism proposals include bundled Ayush visa packages.PDF p. 38

    Ken-Betwa River Link ProjectPDF p. 38

    • Tribal families and farmers renewed their protest on July 3, 2026 beside the Barana River near Kupi village, Chhatarpur, alleging that assurances made in April remained unfulfilled. Participants included people affected by the Ken-Betwa, Majhgawan, Runjh, Neguwan or Naiguwa, and NTPC-linked projects.PDF p. 38
    • Protesters stood in the river during the Jal Satyagraha, women lay on symbolic pyres during the Chita Andolan and wore symbolic nooses during the Faansi Satyagraha, while soil represented their attachment to ancestral land during the Mitti Satyagraha. Activists began an indefinite hunger strike.PDF p. 38

    Revision of the Rehabilitation PackagePDF p. 38

    • After the April protest, a fresh survey added around 750 families to rehabilitation plans for the Majhgaon and Runjh projects.PDF p. 38
    • The Madhya Pradesh Cabinet approved an increase of approximately ₹202.50 crore increase in the package.PDF p. 38
    • Compensation rose from ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh per affected family. Protesters were advised to raise remaining concerns with Panna’s administration.PDF p. 38

    Background of the ProjectPDF p. 38

    • Launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 25 December 2024, the Ken-Betwa Link Project is the first of 30 proposed river-linking projects under the National Perspective Plan.PDF p. 38
    • It seeks to transfer surplus Ken basin water to the water-deficit Betwa basin, addressing shortages in Bundelkhand across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.PDF p. 38
    • The Ken and Betwa rivers are tributaries of the Yamuna River.PDF p. 38

    Phase IPDF p. 38

    • Phase I proposes the 77-metre-high Daudhan Dam, two powerhouses and a 216.46-kilometre link canal, including a 2-kilometre tunnel.PDF p. 38
    • The reservoir’s dead and full reservoir levels will be 240 and 288 metres; respectively, dead and gross storage capacities will be 169 and 2,853 million cubic metres respectively.PDF p. 38
    • Annual gross water yield up to Daudhan is estimated at 6,590 million cubic metres (MCM) at 75% dependability.PDF p. 38
    • The canal will divert 1,377 million cubic metres annually. Of this, 220.77 million cubic metres will be used at the RD 18-kilometre pumping station, 1,010.51 million cubic metres for irrigating 1,93,899 hectares en route and 94.79 million cubic metres for drinking.PDF p. 38
    • The remaining 50.93 million cubic metres will enter the Betwa upstream of Parichha Weir for drinking water and irrigation in Lalitpur.PDF p. 38

    Phase IIPDF p. 38

    • Phase II includes the Lower Orr Dam, Kotha Barrage and Bina Complex. These will meet water requirements in water-deficit areas of the Betwa basin within Madhya Pradesh’s allocated share at Rajghat Dam.PDF p. 38

    Inauguration of Noida International Airport (Phase–1)PDF p. 38, 39

    • Commercial operations at Jewar Airport officially started on June 15, 2026. The first commercial flight, operated by IndiGo, arrived from Lucknow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Noida International Airport (Phase–1) on 28 March 2026 at Jewar in Gautam Buddha Nagar district. The DGCA granted the airport its aerodrome licence on March 6, 2026.PDF p. 38
    • The airport has been constructed at a cost of `11,200 crore, and along with its inauguration, the cargo terminal was also inaugurated. He also laid the foundation stone of the Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) facility.PDF p. 38
    • With the inauguration of Noida International Airport (Phase–1), Uttar Pradesh has become one of the states with the highest number of international airports in the country (5 international airports).PDF p. 38
    • It is noteworthy that recently the Central Government has approved approximately `29,000 crore (~ `28,840 crore) to further expand the UDAN Scheme.PDF p. 38
    • Under this scheme, 100 new airports and 200 new helipads will be developed in smaller cities.PDF p. 38
    • On 13 March 2026 , Noida International Airport (NIA) and Akasa Air announced a strategic partnership to establish the of Akasa Air’s first MRO facility at Noida International Airport.PDF p. 38
    • It is noteworthy that the project for this airport was approved in 2003 during the government of former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee.PDF p. 39
    • Yamuna International Airport Private Limited (YIAPL), a 100% subsidiary of Zurich Airport International AG, has been entrusted with the responsibility for the development, construction, and operation of the greenfield Noida International Airport project.PDF p. 39
    • Through close cooperation with the Government of Uttar Pradesh and the Government of India, YIAPL is responsible for implementing this public–private partnership (PPP) initiative.PDF p. 39

    Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2024 ReportPDF p. 39

    • Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2024 (ADSI 2024) is an annual report published by the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) on May 6, 2026 under the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.PDF p. 39

    Key Findings of the ReportPDF p. 39

    Accidental Deaths in IndiaPDF p. 39

    • In 2023, the total number of accidental deaths in India was 4,44,104.PDF p. 39
    • In 2024, the total number of accidental deaths in India increased to 4,67,857.PDF p. 39
    • The rate of accidental deaths was 31.9 in 2023.PDF p. 39
    • The rate of accidental deaths increased to 33.3 in 2024.PDF p. 39
    • The maximum number of accidental deaths in 2024 was reported in the age group of 30 to below 45 years.PDF p. 39
    • This age group accounted for 1,46,370 deaths, which represented 31.3% of total accidental deaths.PDF p. 39

    Major Causes of Deaths Due to Forces of NaturePDF p. 39

    • Out of the 7,903 accidental deaths attributable to forces of nature, 35.7% were due to lightning.PDF p. 39
    • Out of the 7,903 accidental deaths attributable to forces of nature, 23.2% were due to heat or sunstroke. Percentage Share of States/UTs in Accidental Deaths during in 2024 Haryana (3.9%) Madhya Pradesh (9.8%) Uttar Pradesh (9.2%) Maharashtra (16.2%) Tamil Nadu (7.2%) Rajasthan (6.6%) Gujarat (5.1%) Karnataka (6.6%) Odisha (5.0%) Bihar (4.2%) Other State/UTs (26.2%)PDF p. 39

    Cases, Deaths, and Injuries Due to Other CausesPDF p. 39

    • A total of 7,54,441 cases of under accidents due to other causes were reported.PDF p. 39
    • These cases resulted in 4,59,954 deaths.PDF p. 39
    • The male-female ratio among fatalities during 2024 was 82.4:17.6.PDF p. 39
    • Traffic accidents were the leading cause of accidental deaths due to other causes and accounted for 43.4% of such deaths.PDF p. 39

    Fire AccidentsPDF p. 39

    • A total of 5,971 fire accident case were reported in the country during 2024.PDF p. 39
    • These fire accidents resulted in 5,888 deaths.PDF p. 39
    • Drowning caused 40,044 deaths during 2024.PDF p. 39

    Total Traffic AccidentsPDF p. 39

    • A total of 4,95,256 traffic accidents were reported during 2024.PDF p. 39
    • These traffic accidents included 4,67,967 road accidents.PDF p. 39

    Deaths by Type of Traffic AccidentPDF p. 39

    • Road accidents accounted for 87.8% of deaths in traffic accidents.PDF p. 39
    • Road accidents caused 1,75,142 deaths.PDF p. 39

    Rural and Urban Road AccidentsPDF p. 39

    • Rural areas reported 59.7% of road accidents.PDF p. 39
    • Rural areas reported 2,79,412 road accident cases.PDF p. 39
    • Urban areas reported 40.3% of road accidents.PDF p. 39
    • Urban areas reported 1,88,555 road accident cases.PDF p. 39

    Total Suicides and Suicide RatePDF p. 39

    • In 2023, the total number of suicides in India was 1,71,418.PDF p. 39
    • In 2024, the total number of suicides in India decreased to 1,70,746.PDF p. 39
    • The suicide rate was 12.2 in 2024.PDF p. 39
    • The suicide rate refers to the number of suicides per lakh of the population.PDF p. 39

    Suicide Rate in CitiesPDF p. 39

    • The suicide rate in cities was 16.3.PDF p. 39
    • The suicide rate in megacities was higher than the all-India suicide rate of 12.2.PDF p. 39

    Major Causes of SuicidesPDF p. 39, 40

    • Family problems, other than marriage-related problems, accounted for 33.5% of total suicides in the country during 2024.PDF p. 39
    • Illness accounted for 18.0% (~ 17.9%) of total suicides in the country during 2024.PDF p. 39
    • Drug abuse or addiction accounted for 7.6% of total suicides in the country during 2024.PDF p. 39
    • Family problems other than marriage-related problems, illness, and drug abuse or addiction together accounted for 59.0% of total suicides in the country during 2024.PDF p. 39
    • The overall male-female ratio of suicide victims was 73.5:26.5.PDF p. 40
    • A total of 10.1% of suicide victims were illiterate.PDF p. 40
    • A total of 14.4% of suicide victims were educated up to the primary level.PDF p. 40
    • A total of 17.7% of suicide victims were educated up to the middle level.PDF p. 40
    • A total of 25.6% of suicide victims were educated up to the matriculation level.PDF p. 40
    • Only 5.6% of total suicide victims were graduates or had higher qualifications.PDF p. 40

    Election Commission Announces Special Intensive Revision Phase IIIPDF p. 40

    • The Election Commission of India announced Phase III of the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls to be conducted in a phased manner on May 14, 2026 beginning on May 30, 2026.PDF p. 40
    • As of September 2026, Special Intensive Revision (SIR) was being implemented in phases across India. Phase III covered 16 States and 3 Union Territories. Odisha, Mizoram, Sikkim and Manipur were scheduled to publish their final electoral rolls on September 6, while other regions had later deadlines extending into October, November and December 2026.PDF p. 40

    Constitutional and Legal BasisPDF p. 40

    • The SIR exercise is based on the Election Commission’s constitutional and statutory powers. Article 324 and 326 of the Constitution gives the Election Commission superintendence, direction and control over the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections. Section 16, 19, 21 and 22 of Representation of the People Act 1950 are also invoked.PDF p. 40
    • On May 27, 2026, the Supreme Court in Association for Democratic Reforms & Ors. vs. Election Commission of India & Ors. (2026) held that SIR falls within the ECI’s statutory mandate and is consistent with its constitutional responsibility to ensure free and fair elections.PDF p. 40

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 40

    • More than 3.94 lakh Booth Level Officers is participating in the revision process during Phase III.PDF p. 40
    • These Booth Level Officers visit households covering 36.73 crore electors.PDF p. 40
    • The Special Intensive Revision Phase III will not cover Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.     Progress in Earlier PhasesPDF p. 40

    • In the first two phases, the Special Intensive Revision covered 13 States and Union Territories.PDF p. 40
    • SIR Phase I: Bihar was covered from June to September 2025.PDF p. 40
    • The starting electorate was 7.89 crore, while the final electoral roll contained nearly 7.42 crore electors.PDF p. 40
    • SIR Phase II: Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, along with the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep and Puducherry, were covered during the second phase.PDF p. 40
    • The exercise covered about 50.99 crore electors.PDF p. 40
    • The final electorate was approximately 45.81 crore, representing a reduction of about 10.2%.PDF p. 40
    • Earlier revisions: Intensive revisions were conducted in 1952-56, 1957, 1961, 1965, 1966, 1983-84, 1987-89, 1992, 1993, 1995, 2002, 2003 and 2004 in different parts of India.PDF p. 40

    • The majority mark in the 30-member Assembly is 16 seats, making coalition dynamics crucial.PDF p. 42

Congress - AINRC 12 Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam - DMK 5 Bharatiya Janata Party - BJP 4 Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam - TVK 2 Indian National Congress - INC 1 Total 30PDF p. 42

    Crime in India Report 2024PDF p. 42

    • The National Crime Records Bureau released the Crime in India Report 2024 on May 6, 2026. It is also significant because 2024 was the year in which the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita was used along with the Indian Penal Code framework.PDF p. 42
    • NCRB is an attached office of the Ministry of Home Affairs. It was established in March, 1986.PDF p. 42

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 42

    • According to the report, India recorded 58,85,867 criminal cases in 2024 (a declined of ~ 6% compared with 2023).PDF p. 42
    • This was a 6 percent (~5.7%) decline from 62.41 lakh cases recorded in 2023.PDF p. 42
    • The overall crime rate declined from 448.3 cases per lakh population in 2023 to 418.9 cases per lakh population in 2024.PDF p. 42
    • Out of all criminal cases, 35,44,608 cases were registered under the Indian Penal Code/Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.PDF p. 42
    • A total of 23.41 lakh cases were registered under Special and Local Laws.PDF p. 42

    Impact of Legal ReclassificationPDF p. 42

    • Cases under the hurt category declined sharply by 30.58 percent.PDF p. 42
    • The number of cases under IPC Sections 325, 326 and 329–335 declined from 6.36 lakh in 2023 to 4.41 lakh in 2024.PDF p. 42

    Rise in CybercrimePDF p. 42

    • Cybercrime continued to rise sharply in 2024.PDF p. 42
    • India recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024.PDF p. 42
    • This was a 17.9 percent increase over 86,420 cases in 2023.PDF p. 42
    • Cybercrime cases had already increased by 31.2 percent in 2023 over 65,893 cases in 2022.PDF p. 42
    • Out of 1,01,928 cybercrime cases , 73,987 cases were related to financial fraud.PDF p. 42
    • Financial fraud accounted for 72.6 percent of all registered cybercrime cases in 2024.PDF p. 42
    • Sexual exploitation accounted for 3.1 percent, with 3,190 cases.PDF p. 42

    Economic OffencesPDF p. 42

    • Economic offences increased by 4.6 percent in 2024.PDF p. 42
    • India reported 2,14,379 economic offence cases in 2024.PDF p. 42
    • In 2023, the number of economic offence cases stood at 2,04,973.PDF p. 42
    • 1,92,382 cases were related to forgery, cheating and fraud.PDF p. 42
    • This category accounted for nearly 90 percent of total economic offences.PDF p. 42
    • Authorities seized 8,21,100 fake currency notes in 2024.PDF p. 42
    • The total face value of these seized fake currency notes was `54.61 crore.PDF p. 42

    Crimes Against WomenPDF p. 42, 43

    • Crimes against women declined slightly by 1.5 percent in 2024.PDF p. 42
    • The crime rate under this category fell from 66.2 to 64.6 per lakh female population.PDF p. 43
    • However, the total number of cases remained very high at 4.41 lakh.PDF p. 43
    • “Cruelty by the husband or his relatives” accounted for 1,20,227 cases.PDF p. 43
    • This category acconted for 27.2 percent of total crimes against women.PDF p. 43
    • Kidnapping and abduction of women accounted for 67,829 cases (15.4 percent of total crimes against women).PDF p. 43
    • Uttar Pradesh reported the highest number of crimes against women, with 66,398 cases.PDF p. 43
    • Nagaland, Sikkim and Manipur recorded the lowest numbers of such cases.PDF p. 43
    • Uttar Pradesh also recorded the highest number of dowry deaths cases (2038) with 2,057 victims.PDF p. 43

    Crimes Against ChildrenPDF p. 43

    • Crimes against children increased by 5.9 percent in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • India recorded 1,87,702 cases of crimes against children.PDF p. 43

    Atrocities Against Scheduled TribesPDF p. 43

    • Crimes against Scheduled Tribe communities declined by 23.1 percent in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • Cases fell from 12,960 in 2023 to 9,966 in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • The crime rate declined from 12.4 to 9.5.PDF p. 43
    • Madhya Pradesh recorded the highest number of crimes against ST communities with 3,165 cases.PDF p. 43

    Atrocities Against Scheduled CastesPDF p. 43

    • Crimes against Scheduled Caste communities declined by 3.6 percent in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • Cases fell from 57,789 in 2023 to 55,698 in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • The crime rate for crimes against Scheduled Castes stood at 27.7.PDF p. 43
    • Rape accounted for 7.6 percent of cases.PDF p. 43
    • Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest number of crimes against Scheduled Castes with 14,642 incidents.PDF p. 43

    Murder CasesPDF p. 43

    • India recorded 27,049 murder cases in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • This was a marginal decline of 2.4 percent from 2023.PDF p. 43
    • Murder cases had also declined by 2.8 percent in 2023 compared to 2022.PDF p. 43

    Deaths by SuicidePDF p. 43

    • The farming sector recorded 10,546 suicide deaths.PDF p. 43
    • This included 4,633 farmers or cultivators.PDF p. 43
    • It also included 5,913 agricultural labourers.PDF p. 43
    • People from the farming sector accounted for 6.2 percent of total suicide deaths.PDF p. 43

    Drug Overdose DeathsPDF p. 43

    • Deaths due to drug overdose increased sharply by 50 percent in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • The report recorded 978 deaths due to drug overdose.PDF p. 43
    • Tamil Nadu recorded the highest number of drug overdose deaths with 313 cases.PDF p. 43

    Crimes Against the StatePDF p. 43

    • Cases under offences against the State increased by 6.6 percent in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • These cases rose from 4,873 in 2023 to a higher level in 2024.PDF p. 43
    • About 84.6 percent of these cases were registered under the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act.PDF p. 43

    Charge-Sheet EfficiencyPDF p. 43

    • Kerala recorded the highest charge-sheeting rate among States.PDF p. 43
    • Kerala filed charge-sheets in 94.5 percent of cases.PDF p. 43
    • Puducherry followed with 91 percent charge- sheeting efficiency.PDF p. 43

    Arrests and ConvictionsPDF p. 43

    • More than 26.72 lakh people were arrested under the IPC and BNS.PDF p. 43
    • More than 10.71 lakh people were convicted.PDF p. 43

    The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Act, 2026PDF p. 43

    • President Droupadi Murmu on August 11, 2026 gave assent to The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026 which has become a law.PDF p. 43
    • The law making the intentional disruption or prevention of the singing of the national song ‘Vande Mataram’ a criminal offence, granting it the same legal protection as the National Anthem.PDF p. 43
    • The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on July 30, 2026 while the Rajya Sabha had cleared it earlier.PDF p. 43
    • The legislation grants Vande Mataram the same status as the National Anthem, ‘Jana Gana Mana’.PDF p. 43
    • The Union Cabinet gave approval on May 5, 2026 to amend The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971.PDF p. 43
    • Any insult to Vande Mataram or intentional obstruction to its singing is proposed to be made punishable.PDF p. 43
    • Under Section 3 of the existing Act, intentionally preventing the singing of the Indian National Anthem or disturbing an assembly engaged in such singing is punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both; it will now be legally enforceable to Vande Matram.PDF p. 43
    • The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 was enacted to prevent insults to national honour.PDF p. 43
    • The Act currently covers insults to the National Flag and the Constitution of India.PDF p. 43
    • V ande Mataram: National Song and Freedom StrugglePDF p. 43
    • Vande Mataram was composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee and first published in Bangadarshan (1875), later included in Anandamath (1882).PDF p. 43
    • The song was set to music by Rabindranath Tagore and emerged as a powerful symbol of unity, sacrifice and devotion to the motherland.PDF p. 43
    • It was sung by Rabindranath Tagore at the INC session of 1896.PDF p. 43

    Panchayat Advancement Index 2.0PDF p. 44

    • The Ministry of Panchayati Raj released the Panchayat Advancement Index (PAI) 2.0 Report for FY 2023–24 on the occasion of National Panchayati Raj Day, 24 April 2026.PDF p. 44
    • The Panchayat Advancement Index (PAI) is a nationwide framework developed by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj to measure the performance of rural local government institutions.PDF p. 44
    • It evaluates the progress of Gram Panchayats and Traditional Local Bodies through objective, measurable, and verifiable indicators.     Coverage and Participation under PAI 2.0PDF p. 44

    • PAI 2.0 recorded participation from 33 out of 36 States and Union Territories.PDF p. 44
    • It included 27 out of 28 States , with West Bengal being the only State that did not participate.PDF p. 44

    • These Panchayats represent 97.30 percent of the total 2,66,999 Panchayats (including non-participating West Bengal’s 3,339) across participating States and Union Territories.PDF p. 44

    JANANI PlatformPDF p. 44

    • The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has launched JANANI - Journey of Antenatal, Natal and Neonatal Integrated Care - to strengthen maternal and child healthcare services in India through digital tracking, interoperable health records and real-time monitoring.PDF p. 44
    • It was launched at the National Summit on Innovation and Inclusivity - Best Practices Shaping India’s Health Future.PDF p. 44
    • The platform is an upgraded version of the existing Reproductive and Child Health portal and is designed to create a longitudinal health record by capturing service delivery events across the continuum of care.PDF p. 44
    • JANANI is a service-oriented digital platform for maternal and child healthcare.PDF p. 44
    • It creates a longitudinal health record by capturing key service delivery events across the continuum of care.PDF p. 44
    • The platform covers antenatal care, delivery preparedness, delivery, postnatal care, newborn care, home-based newborn and young child care, and family planning.PDF p. 44
    • JANANI aims to improve service delivery, accountability and health outcomes for mothers and children.PDF p. 44
    • A key feature of JANANI is the introduction of QR-enabled digital Mother and Child Health cards.PDF p. 44
    • It can integrate with national platforms such as U-WIN and POSHAN.PDF p. 44
    • Achievements So FarPDF p. 44
    • JANANI has achieved 1.34 crore beneficiary registrations so far.PDF p. 44
    • More than 30 lakh pregnant women have been registered on the platform.PDF p. 44
    • More than 30 lakh digital MCH cards have been generated.PDF p. 44
    • The platform has completed more than 1 lakh biometric verifications.PDF p. 44

    The Constitution (One Hundred & Thirty-First Amendment) Bill, 2026PDF p. 45

    • The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 April 2026, but on 17 April 2026, it failed to pass in the Lok Sabha as it could not secure the required special majority.PDF p. 45
    • During the vote, 298 members voted in favour and 230 members voted against.PDF p. 45
    • A total of 528 members were present and voting, therefore 352 votes were required for its passage.PDF p. 45
    • The central idea of this Bill was to bring representation closer to population.PDF p. 45
    • If the population of a state has increased significantly, then the representation of its voters should increase proportionately.PDF p. 45
    • On the one hand, it strengthened the idea of “one person, one vote, one value” , and on the other hand, it raised concerns among those states that had made serious efforts towards population control.PDF p. 45

    Main Objectives of the BillPDF p. 45

    • The Bill was based on four major objectives:PDF p. 45
    • To increase the strength of the Lok SabhaPDF p. 45
    • To restart delimitation on a new basisPDF p. 45
    • To give Parliament the power to decide which census would be usedPDF p. 45
    • To implement one-third reservation for women at an earlier stagePDF p. 45
    • An amendment to Article 81 was proposed.PDF p. 45
    • The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha was proposed to be increased from 550 to 850.PDF p. 45
    • Of these a maximum of 815 members would be from the states and 35 members from Union Territories.PDF p. 45
    • A new definition of “population” was proposed in Articles 55, 81, 170, 330, 332 etc.PDF p. 45
    • Population would mean the census determined by Parliament through law.PDF p. 45
    • An amendment to Article 82 was proposed.PDF p. 45
    • Under the new proposal, delimitation would be done based on the census determined by Parliament.PDF p. 45
    • This work would be carried out by the Delimitation Commission.PDF p. 45
    • An amendment to Article 170 was proposed.PDF p. 45
    • The total number of seats and constituencies in State Legislative Assemblies would be re-determined.PDF p. 45

    Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026PDF p. 45

    • The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026 are an important step in India’s plastic-waste governance. They do not replace the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016; rather, they further amend them.PDF p. 45
    • The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change notified the amendment on March 31, 2026.PDF p. 45

    Revised Definitions and ScopePDF p. 45

    • The definition of End-of-Life Disposal has been expanded to include energy recovery methods such as co-processing, waste-to-energy, waste-to-oil, and road construction.PDF p. 45
    • Processes converting plastic into feedstock or new plastic are now classified strictly as recycling, not disposal.PDF p. 45
    • The definition of Plastic Waste Processors has been broadened to include both recyclers and end- of-life disposal entities.PDF p. 45
    • New terms such as Registered Environment Auditor, Reuse, and Seller have been introduced to improve regulatory clarity.PDF p. 45
    • The scope of local governance has been widened to include all relevant authorities beyond traditional local bodies.PDF p. 45
    • All recycled plastic packaging must comply with Indian Standard IS 14534:2023.PDF p. 45
    • Packaging must carry mandatory labeling indicating recycled content.PDF p. 45

    India’s First National Counter Terrorism PolicyPDF p. 45

    • The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) released India’s first national counter-terrorism policy , and strategy, PRAHAAR, on 23 February 2026.PDF p. 45
    • The policy comes after the government announced in November 2024 that a comprehensive national counter-terrorism strategy would be framed, and it follows recent security concerns including the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack.PDF p. 45
    • It seeks to provide a uniform, coordinated and technology-aware framework to deal with terrorism, terror financing, radicalisation, cyber- attacks, drone-based threats, and attacks on critical infrastructure.PDF p. 45

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 45

    • The policy states that India faces terrorist threats across land, air and water, along with growing risks in the cyber domain.PDF p. 45
    • It specifically warns that criminal hackers and nation- states are targeting India through cyber-attacks.PDF p. 45
    • The document underlines that India continues to face sponsored terrorism from across the border.PDF p. 45
    • The policy identifies groups such as Al-Qaeda and ISIS as entities trying to incite violence in India through sleeper cells and extremist propaganda.PDF p. 45
    • PRAHAAR notes the use of drones, encrypted messaging apps, social media, dark web platforms, and crypto wallets by terrorist groups for communi- cation, propaganda, recruitment and financing.PDF p. 45
    • It also flags the danger of misuse of CBRNED materials—Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, Explosive and Digital—as well as robot- ics and drone systems.PDF p. 45

    Age-Based Social Media Restrictions for ChildrenPDF p. 46

    • On March 6, 2026, Karnataka announced in its Budget speech that social media use would be banned for children below 16. On the same day, Andhra Pradesh said it would prohibit access for children below 13 within 90 days and was also considering rules for the 13–16 age group.PDF p. 46
    • At the Union level, the Economic Survey 2025–26 recommended age-based access limits and stronger platform responsibility, and an NHRC discussion on March 16, 2026 (Press release on March 18, 2026) showed that the matter is now being treated as a serious governance issue.PDF p. 46

    Global ContextPDF p. 46

    • The strongest global precedent has come from Australia.PDF p. 46
    • Australia enacted the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act, 2024.PDF p. 46
    • Under this law, from 10 December 2025 , age- restricted platforms must take reasonable steps to prevent children under 16 from creating or retaining accounts.PDF p. 46
    • The Australian eSafety regulator has indicated that platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X, YouTube, Kick and Reddit fall within the age-restricted category, though the list may change.PDF p. 46

    Defence Forces Vision 2047PDF p. 46

    • The Raksha Mantri, Rajnath Singh , released “Defence Forces Vision 2047: A Roadmap for a Future-Ready Indian Military” on 10 March 2026 in South Block, New Delhi . Prepared by the Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff (HQ IDS), the document presents a long-term blueprint for transforming India’s armed forces into a modern, integrated, technologically advanced, and self-reli ant military by the centenary of Independence.PDF p. 46
    • In 2025, the Ministry of Defence declared the year as the “Year of Reforms” to push jointness, integration and future-readiness.PDF p. 46
    • The Ministry’s Year End Review 2025 had also said that the Armed Forces Vision 2047 was prepared in two parts and that Part I would be released publicly soon.PDF p. 46

    Phased Roadmap to 2047PDF p. 46

    • One of the major strengths of the document is that it sets out a calibrated timeline for transformation. 1. Era of Transition (till 2030)PDF p. 46
    • This phase focuses on restructuring the military and strengthening deterrence.PDF p. 46
    • It gives importance to rapid adoption of indigenous technologies, especially in areas such as drones and surveillance. 2. Era of Consolidation (2030–2040)PDF p. 46
    • This phase aims to deepen integration of cyber and space capabilities.PDF p. 46
    • It seeks to operationalise layered air and missile defence systems. 3. Era of Excellence (2040–2047)PDF p. 46
    • This final phase envisions a fully integrated, self- reliant, all-domain military force.PDF p. 46
    • It aims to make India’s armed forces globally respected, technologically advanced, and combat ready.PDF p. 46

    Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0PDF p. 46

    • Under the chairmanship of Narendra Modi, the Union Cabinet approved Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 on 10 March 2026. Its objective is to transform Jal Jeevan Mission from being limited to infrastructure creation into a service-based model.PDF p. 46

    Key FactsPDF p. 46

    • The Cabinet has approved an increase in the total expenditure for this restructuring to `8.69 lakh crore , of which the central government’s contribution will be `3.59 lakh crore.PDF p. 46
    • This amount is higher than the earlier approved `2.08 lakh crore by the Centre in 2019–20, meaning that an additional `1.51 lakh crore of central assistance has been included.PDF p. 46
    • In this direction, an integrated national digital platform named “Sujalam Bharat” was developed by March, 2026.PDF p. 46
    • Under this, each village will be assigned a unique Sujal village/service area ID , through which a complete digital mapping of the supply system from water source to household tap will be prepared.PDF p. 46
    • To enhance transparency and accountability, active participation of Gram Panchayats and Village Water and Sanitation Committees will be ensured through the “Jal Arpan” initiative.PDF p. 46
    • Gram Panchayats will certify project completion only when adequate arrangements for operation and maintenance have been ensured by the state government; only thereafter will a village be declared as “Har Ghar Jal”.PDF p. 46
    • To strengthen community participation, “Jal Utsav” will be developed as an annual programme.PDF p. 46

    Progress and CoveragePDF p. 46

    • The Functionality Assessment 2024 covered 19,812 Har Ghar Jal Villages and 2,37,608 househoulds; 76% received water meeting prescribed quality standards.PDF p. 46
    • It is noteworthy that in 2019, only 3.23 crore (about 17%) rural households had tap water connections, whereas now more than 12.56 crore additional households have been provided this facility.PDF p. 46
    • At present, out of a total of 19.36 crore rural households, approximately 15.80 crore (about 81.61%) households have access to tap water (as on March, 2026).PDF p. 46

    Targets and ImplementationPDF p. 47

    • Under JJM 2.0, the target is to provide tap water connections to all 19.36 crore rural households by December 2028 and to ensure that all Gram Panchayats receive “Har Ghar Jal” certification.PDF p. 47
    • This mission is now moving beyond an infrastructure-based approach towards a utility- based service delivery model , which will ensure 24×7 rural drinking water supply and strengthen the goal of “Viksit Bharat @2047”.PDF p. 47
    • Quick FactsPDF p. 47
    • Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) was launched by Narendra Modi on 15 August 2019.PDF p. 47
    • It had an ambitious target of providing tap water supply to every rural household by 2024.PDF p. 47
    • At the time of its launch, only 3.23 crore (17%) rural households had access to tap water connections.PDF p. 47

    Regional Connectivity Scheme – Modified UDAN ApprovedPDF p. 47

    • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi approved the launch and implementation of the Regional Connectivity Scheme – Revised UDAN on March 25, 2026 for a period of ten years from FY 2026–27 to 2035–36.PDF p. 47
    • The total cost of the scheme is `28,840 crore, which will be borne through budgetary support from the Government of India.PDF p. 47
    • The major components of the scheme are as follows:PDF p. 47
    • Under the Revised UDAN scheme, it is proposed to develop 100 airports from existing unserved airstrips to enhance regional connectivity.PDF p. 47
    • A total provision of `12,159 crore has been made for this over the next eight years.PDF p. 47
    • Considering the high recurring O&M costs and limited revenue of airports operated under the Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS), the scheme proposes O&M support for three years.PDF p. 47
    • This support will be up to `3.06 crore per airport per year and `0.90 crore per heliport/water aerodrome. An estimated total of `2,577 crore is proposed for approximately 441 aerodromes.PDF p. 47
    • Major FactsPDF p. 47
    • The UDAN scheme was launched in October 2016 with the objective of making air travel affordable and strengthening connectivity to Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.PDF p. 47
    • During nine years of implementation, as of June, 2026, operations had been conducted on 665 routes across 95 airports, heliports, and water aerodromes.PDF p. 47
    • More than 3.5 lakh flights had been operated, carrying 1.64 crore passengers.PDF p. 47

    Republic Day 2026PDF p. 47

    • Republic Day is observed on 26 January to mark the day the Constitution of India came into force (January 26, 1950). In 2026, India celebrated its 77th Republic Day at Kartavya Path, New Delhi, with the theme “150 years of Vande Mataram”, blending constitutional values, cultural heritage, and a large military-civil ceremony.PDF p. 47
    • The Republic Day Parade featured 30 tableaux from States, Union Territories (17) and Union Ministries (13).PDF p. 47
    • The tableaux were organised under the sub-themes:PDF p. 47
    • Swatantrata ka Mantra – Vande Mataram, andPDF p. 47
    • Samriddhi ka Mantra – Atmanirbhar Bharat.PDF p. 47

    Supreme Court stays 2026 UGC Equity RegulationsPDF p. 47, 48

    • In a significant order affecting India’s higher education governance, the Supreme Court on 29 January 2026 has kept in abeyance the newly notified UGC (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2026.PDF p. 47
    • These Regulations were designed to create a time- bound, enforceable anti-discrimination framework on campuses. The Court raised concerns about vagueness, possible misuse, and exclusion, and has directed that the older 2012 UGC Equity Regulations would continue to operate for now.PDF p. 47
    • The UGC Equity Regulations, 2026, were framed pursuant to the Supreme Court’s directions in Abeda Salim Tadvi v. Union of India (2019).PDF p. 47
    • A Bench of Justices Surya Kant and Ujjal Bhuyan had directed the UGC to notify enforceable regulations to:PDF p. 47
    • Address caste-based discriminationPDF p. 48
    • Prevent student suicidesPDF p. 48
    • Rectify the ineffective implementation of the 2012 regulations.PDF p. 48

    Key Provisions of the UGC Regulations, 2026PDF p. 48

    • Broad Coverage of Caste-Based Discrimination: The regulations define caste-based discrimination as any unfair or biased treatment against Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and Other Backward Classes (OBCs), thereby explicitly extending legal protection to OBCs and correcting a major omission in the earlier draft framework.PDF p. 48
    • Mandatory Equal Opportunity Centres (EOCs): Every higher education institution is required to establish an Equal Opportu - nity Centre (EOC) to promote equity, social inclusion, and equal access, and to address com - plaints related to discrimination on campus.PDF p. 48
    • Each institution must form an Equity Committee under the EOC, chaired by the head of the institution, with mandatory representation from SCs, STs, OBCs, persons with disabilities, and women, ensuring inclusive decision-making.PDF p. 48
    • The Equity Committee is required to meet within 24 hours of receiving a complaint and submit its report within 15 working days , after which the head of the institution must initiate action within 7 days.PDF p. 48
    • The UGC will establish a national monitoring com - mittee comprising representatives from statutory bodies and civil society to oversee implementation, review complaints, and suggest preventive measures, with the committee meeting at least twice a year.PDF p. 48

    Water Budgeting in Aspirational BlocksPDF p. 48

    • NITI Aayog, in collaboration with GIZ India, has released a report titled “Water Budgeting in Aspirational Blocks”, aimed at enhancing water security at the local level, improving resource planning, and aligning with the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047. The report provides a comprehensive analysis of water availability, demand, and sector-specific challenges across 18 Aspirational Blocks in 10 states and a UT (11 states and UT), using a digital platform for water budgeting.PDF p. 48

    Key FindingsPDF p. 48

    • Water Deficits: Several blocks are facing severe water shortages. Notable examples include:PDF p. 48
    • Namchi (94% deficit)PDF p. 48
    • Gangiri (60% deficit)PDF p. 48
    • Baldeogarh (53% deficit)PDF p. 48
    • Over-extraction of Groundwater: Blocks like Kotri and Abu Road in Rajasthan are over-extracting groundwater beyond recharge levels, leading to unsustainable water use.PDF p. 48
    • Under-utilization of Runoff: Some regions, such as Fatehpur in Bihar, generate runoff but fail to utilize the stored water effectively.PDF p. 48

    Bihar Legislative Assembly Election Results, 2025PDF p. 48

    • The Bihar Legislative Assembly Election, 2025 was held in two phases (6 and 11 November) , the election witnessed a landslide victory for the National Democratic Alliance (NDA). In the 243-member Assembly, the NDA secured 202 seats, while the main opposition Mahagathbandhan was reduced to just 35 seats.PDF p. 48
    • On November 20, 2025, Nitish Kumar took oath as the Chief Minister of Bihar for the 10th time, becoming the longest-serving Chief Minister of the state . Along with him, Samrat Choudhary and Vijay Kumar Sinha took oath as Deputy Chief Ministers.PDF p. 48
    • Nitish Kumar officially resigned from his post as the Chief Minister of Bihar on April 14, 2026.PDF p. 48
    • Samrat Chaudhary took the oath of office on April 15, 2026, to become the first Chief Minister of Bihar from the Bhartiya Janata Party (BJP). Bihar Governor Syed Ata Hasnain administered the oath of office to Mr. Choudhary at Lok Bhawan in Patna.PDF p. 48

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 48

    • The Election Commission of India (ECI) successfully conducted the Bihar Legislative Assembly Election, 2025, with a voter turnout of 67.25%, the highest since 1951.PDF p. 48
    • This included 71.77% female turnout and 62.73% male turnout.PDF p. 48
    • The gender gap was about 9.04 percentage points in favour of women.PDF p. 48
    • It is noteworthy that during Special Intensive Revision (SIR), the final electoral roll in Bihar included a total of 74,526,858 voters (November, 2025).PDF p. 48
    • According to the election results, the National Democratic Alliance recorded a historic victory with 202 seats.PDF p. 48
    • The NDA comprised the BJP , Janata Dal (United), Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas), Hindustani Awam Morcha (Secular), and Rashtriya Lok Morcha.PDF p. 48
    • The BJP emerged as the largest party in the state by winning 89 seats, while JD(U) secured 85 seats.PDF p. 48
    • Folk singer Maithili Thakur (BJP) won from the Alinagar constituency (youngest MLA in Bihar).PDF p. 48
    • According to the election results, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) secured the highest vote share at 23%.PDF p. 48
