    India–Canada RelationsPDF p. 57

    • Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s official visit to India from February 27 to March 2, 2026 marked a major turning point in India–Canada relations.PDF p. 57
    • In 2026, India and Canada completed 79 years of diplomatic relations.PDF p. 57
    • The two leaders also linked India’s Viksit Bharat vision with Canada’s Build Canada Strong agenda.PDF p. 57
    • The most significant commercial outcome was the approximately CAD 2.6 billion Cameco– Department of Atomic Energy agreement for long- term uranium supply to India.PDF p. 57
    • Beyond uranium, the two sides discussed cooperation in LNG, LPG, crude oil, refined petroleum products, potash and heavy oil.PDF p. 57
    • Canada also reaffirmed its target of producing 50 million tonnes of LNG annually by 2030 and up to 100 million tonnes by 2040 for Indo-Pacific markets.PDF p. 57
    • The leaders also referred to India’s endorsement of the G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan and discussed support for India’s mineral stockpiling efforts.PDF p. 57
    • The two countries also agreed to hold an India– Canada Renewable Energy and Storage Summit in 2026.PDF p. 57
    • A particularly important outcome was the proposal to establish a Canada–India Pulse Protein Centre of Excellence at NIFTEM Kundli.PDF p. 57
    • The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE)–Mitacs MoU will allow around 300 Indian undergraduate students every year to undertake funded research internships at Canadian universities, beginning in 2027.PDF p. 57
    • The long-term objective is to raise bilateral trade to about CAD 70 billion / INR 4.65 lakh crore by 2030. India – South AmericaPDF p. 57

    India-BrazilPDF p. 57

    • Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva paid a State Visit to India from February 18-22, 2026. During the visit, he attended the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (19–20 February) and held bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Hyderabad House in New Delhi on 21 February 2026. This was Lula’s fifth visit to India as President and sixth visit overall, as well as his second State Visit, coming soon after Modi’s July 2025 visit to Brazil.PDF p. 57
    • They have cooperated closely in platforms such as BRICS, G20, IBSA, G-4, WTO and the United Nations.PDF p. 57
    • Their bilateral relationship was elevated to a Strategic Partnership in 2006.PDF p. 57
    • The economic outcome was the shared target to raise bilateral trade to over USD 30 billion by 2030.PDF p. 57
    • One of the outcomes was an MoU between India’s Ministry of Steel and Brazil’s Ministry of Mines and Energy to strengthen cooperation in mining and minerals required for the steel sector. India – EuropePDF p. 57

    State Visits of President Droupadi Murmu to EuropePDF p. 57, 58

    • President Droupadi Murmu undertook State Visits to Moldova, North Macedonia and Romania from July 19–25, 2026 . These were the first visits by an Indian President to Moldova and North Macedonia, and the first to Romania since President Shankar Dayal Sharma’s May 1994 visit. Visit to MoldovaPDF p. 57
    • President Murmu met President Maia Sandu and parliamentary leaders.PDF p. 57
    • Both sides agreed to expand cooperation in agriculture, healthcare, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) and Artificial Intelligence (AI).PDF p. 57
    • KEC International’s 400-kV Vulcănesti–Chisinău transmission line illustrated India’s infrastructure involvement.PDF p. 57
    • Moldova offers links to European value chains and the Black Sea region. Visit to North MacedoniaPDF p. 57
    • President Murmu met President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova and addressed the Assembly, stressing democratic values, parliamentary diplomacy and peace.PDF p. 57
    • Both sides aimed to double bilateral trade by the decade’s end. She proposed joint pharmaceutical manufacturing for Balkan and European markets.PDF p. 57
    • The healthcare cooperation MoU was renewed for five years, including traditional medicine.PDF p. 57
    • The unveiling of a Mahatma Gandhi bust in Skopje and a visit to the Mother Teresa Memorial reinforced cultural ties.PDF p. 57
    • Mother Teresa was born in Skopje and received the Bharat Ratna in 1980. Visit to RomaniaPDF p. 57
    • India and Romania agreed to work towards doubling bilateral trade over the next three years, viewing the India–EU Free Trade Agreement concluded in January 2026 as an opportunity for deeper economic ties.PDF p. 57
    • Both sides sought stronger defence cooperation through training, industrial contacts and possible joint production and co-development.PDF p. 57
    • Three documents were signed: a Science and Technology Programme for 2026–2029, an MoUPDF p. 57
    • establishing an ICCR Chair in Indian Studies at the University of Bucharest, and a sports cooperation MoU.PDF p. 58
    • The Bucharest University of Economic Studies conferred the degree of Doctor Honoris Causa on President Murmu.PDF p. 58
    • Both countries agreed to mark 2028, completing 80 years of diplomatic relations, as the “India–Romania Year of Innovation.”PDF p. 58

    India-UK CETA and DCCPDF p. 58

    • The India–United Kingdom Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and Double Contribution Convention (DCC) became operational on July 15, 2026. They aim to expand trade and investment, facilitate temporary professional mobility and eliminate duplicate social-security contributions for eligible workers.PDF p. 58
    • The Enhanced Trade Partnership and Roadmap 2030, launched in May 2021, laid their foundation.PDF p. 58
    • After 14 negotiation rounds, CETA was concluded on 6 May 2025 and signed in London on 24 July 2025. DCC was signed on 10 February 2026.PDF p. 58
    • CETA is a next-generation free trade agreement with 30 chapters covering goods, services, investment, digital trade, intellectual property, government procurement, competition, innovation, sustainability and MSMEs.PDF p. 58
    • The UK provides zero-duty access to nearly 99 per cent of Indian tariff lines, covering almost the entire value of Indian exports to the UK.PDF p. 58
    • Major beneficiary sectors include textiles, leather, footwear, gems, jewellery, marine products, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, processed food and automobile components.PDF p. 58
    • India excludes dairy products, cereals, millets, apples, edible oils and oilseeds from major tariff concessions.PDF p. 58
    • This protects small producers, domestic prices and rural livelihoods while balancing liberalisation with policy space for vulnerable sectors.PDF p. 58
    • UK commitments cover 12 service sectors and 137 sub-sectors, including IT, finance, engineering, healthcare, education and telecommunications.PDF p. 58
    • CETA facilitates temporary movement of business visitors, intra-corporate transferees, contractual service suppliers, independent professionals and investors.PDF p. 58
    • It also creates opportunities for Indian chefs, yoga instructors and classical musicians.PDF p. 58
    • DCC prevents dual social-security contributions for eligible temporarily posted or detached workers.PDF p. 58
    • Ordinary overseas employees generally contribute in their country of employment.PDF p. 58
    • It concerns contribution liability and does not automatically grant host-country pensions or other contributory benefits.PDF p. 58

    India–NorwayPDF p. 58

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s official visit to Oslo during 18–19 May 2026 marked an important stage in India–Norway relations. The visit was hosted by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre , and included bilateral talks, an audience with King Harald V .PDF p. 58
    • India and Norway established bilateral relations in February 1947.PDF p. 58
    • Norway is important for India because of its strengths in maritime industries, offshore energy, fisheries, aquaculture, clean technology, Arctic studies and sustainable development.PDF p. 58
    • Both sides elevated the relationship to a Green Strategic Partnership to combat climate change, create green industries and jobs, accelerate the green energy transition, maintain energy security, strengthen circular economy and encourage investment.PDF p. 58
    • India is expanding renewable energy on a large scale and has set targets of 500 GW of clean energy and 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen by 2030.PDF p. 58
    • The joint statement mentions the Norwegian Climate Investment Fund’s investments in renewable energy in India and the possibility of bilateral cooperation under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement.PDF p. 58
    • India also welcomed Norway joining the Indo- Pacific Oceans Initiative.PDF p. 58
    • India has a long-standing interest in Arctic and polar research, including the Himadri research station at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard.PDF p. 58
    • The joint statement also recognises the achievements of the Norway–India Partnership Initiative in maternal and child health and its support to India’s National Health Mission.PDF p. 58
    • Oslo hosted the 3rd India–Nordic Summit on May 19, 2026.PDF p. 58
    • The summit brought together India with Norway, Denmark, Finland, Iceland and Sweden, and elevated India–Nordic relations to a trusted Green Technology and Innovation Strategic Partnership.PDF p. 58
    • On September 11, 2025, India and Norway held their first Maritime Security, Disarmament, and Non- Proliferation Dialogue in Oslo, marking a milestone in their strategic engagement.PDF p. 58

    PM Modi’s Italy VisitPDF p. 58, 59

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Italy on May 19-20, 2026, meeting Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and President Sergio Mattarella in Rome.PDF p. 58
    • Both countries upgraded ties to a Special Strategic Partnership, agreed on annual leaders’ meetings and a Foreign Ministers-led review of the Joint Strategic Action Plan 2025–2029, adopted at the 2024 G20 Summit.PDF p. 58
    • They targeted €20 billion bilateral trade by 2029.PDF p. 58
    • Cooperation expanded in defence, counterterrorism, space, technology and the India–Middle East– Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC).PDF p. 58
    • Major initiatives included INNOVIT India, an innovation hub; ICI–Italy Calls India, connecting students with enterprises; and enhanced ISRO– Italian Space Agency cooperation.PDF p. 58
    • Both welcomed collaboration against terror financing and Italy’s participation in the February 2026 AI Impact Summit.PDF p. 59
    • They designated 2027 the Year of Culture and Tourism and supported Lothal’s National Maritime Heritage Complex.PDF p. 59
    • At FAO headquarters, Rome, Modi received the Agricola Medal, FAO’s highest honour, for contributions to food security, sustainable agriculture and rural development.PDF p. 59

    India-FrancePDF p. 59

    • President Emmanuel Macron visited India from 17–19 February 2026 , during which India–France relations were upgraded to a “Special Global Strategic Partnership” under the Horizon 2047 Roadmap.PDF p. 59
    • Modi and Macron inaugurated the India-France Year of Innovation 2026 in Mumbai, focusing on AI, science, healthcare, research, and education, along with promoting secure and inclusive artificial intelligence.PDF p. 59
    • The Tata-Airbus H125 Final Assembly Line at Vamagal, Karnataka, was inaugurated on February 17, 2026 as India’s first private-sector helicopter Final Assembly Line.PDF p. 59
    • BEL and Safran signed a joint-venture MoU to manufacture HAMMER missiles in India.PDF p. 59
    • Energy and climate collaboration also expanded, with France supporting India’s target of achieving 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047.PDF p. 59
    • Progress was made on the Jaitapur Nuclear Power Project, and continued cooperation in renewable energy, the International Solar Alliance, and disaster- resilient infrastructure.PDF p. 59

    India-GermanyPDF p. 59

    • German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited India on January 12–13, 2026, holding talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, to strengthen cooperation in trade, defence, technology, clean energy and migration.PDF p. 59
    • Bilateral trade in goods and services exceeded US$50 billion in 2024.PDF p. 59
    • Germany announced visa-free airport transit for Indian passport holders, effective June 3, 2026. A Joint Declaration of Intent (JDI) on Global Skills Partnership promoted ethical recruitment, particularly of healthcare professionals, alongside cooperation against irregular migration and human trafficking.PDF p. 59
    • Germany expressed interest in MILAN 2026, the Indian Ocean Naval Symposium (IONS) Conclave and Exercise Tarang Shakti.PDF p. 59
    • A renewable-energy skilling Centre of Excellence was proposed at the National Skill Training Institute, Hyderabad, alongside greater investment in manufacturing and technology. India – AfricaPDF p. 59

    India–LiberiaPDF p. 59

    • On September 25, 2026, India and Liberia launched the Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers (GoF on S4) at UN Headquarters, New York , during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). The meeting was co-chaired by Dr. S. Jaishankar and Liberia’s Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti, with representatives from approximately 25 countries. India and Liberia serve as co-chairs.PDF p. 59
    • India–Liberia Partnership: India is a major supplier of merchant seafarers, while Liberia maintains the world’s largest ship registry by Gross Tonnage (GT).PDF p. 59
    • Global Significance: Over 80% of global merchandise trade by volume moves by sea, supporting nearly two million seafarers.PDF p. 59
    • Security Concerns: Maritime attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea, Gulf region and Black Sea threaten global trade and seafarers.PDF p. 59
    • Three Priorities: Shipping safety (vessel standards and compliance), maritime security (piracy and armed attacks), and seafarers’ welfare (labour rights, medical care and repatriation).PDF p. 59
    • Nature: A voluntary cooperation platform supporting the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and International Labour Organization (ILO).PDF p. 59

    Important Legal FrameworksPDF p. 59

    • UNCLOS, Article 94: Flag-state jurisdiction and control.PDF p. 59
    • SOLAS Convention, 1974: Ship safety standards.PDF p. 59
    • Maritime Labour Convention (MLC), 2006: Seafarers’ rights, welfare and repatriation.PDF p. 59

    India–MaliPDF p. 59, 60

    • The first India–Mali Forum for the Promotion of Exports was held on June 19–20, 2026 in Bamako, Mali, under the theme “Reinforcing Trade and Strategic Partnerships.”PDF p. 59
    • Chaired by Malian Prime Minister Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, it was organised by Mali's Industry and Trade Ministry, the Indian Embassy and APEX- Mali.PDF p. 59
    • India's delegation was led by Joint Secretary Amit Kumar.PDF p. 59
    • Bilateral trade reached US$326.61 million in FY 2025–26, growing 55%. Mali's global exports stood at approximately US$4 billion, with US$3.96 billion untapped export potential in India.PDF p. 59
    • India's Duty-Free Tariff Preference (DFTP) Scheme supported trade.PDF p. 59
    • Mali exports cotton, leather, cashew, lead, gum arabic and sesame, while India supplies pharmaceuticals, textiles and vehicles.PDF p. 59
    • Cooperation prioritised mining, renewable energy, agriculture, shea processing, healthcare, education and skills.PDF p. 60

    India-EthiopiaPDF p. 60

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Addis Ababa on 16–17 December 2025 , marking his first bilateral visit to Ethiopia. He was received by Ethiopian Prime Minister Dr. Abiy Ahmed Ali and held high-level talks in Addis Ababa.PDF p. 60
    • PM Modi held wide-ranging discussions with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali.PDF p. 60
    • Prime Minister Modi also addressed a Joint Session of the Ethiopian Parliament during the visit.PDF p. 60
    • Prime Minister Modi was conferred Ethiopia’s highest award, “Great Honour Nishan of Ethiopia”, during the Addis Ababa visit.PDF p. 60
    • The two countries agreed to elevate bilateral ties to a Strategic Partnership, marking a new phase of cooperation.PDF p. 60
    • India–Ethiopia relations date back over 2,000 years: trade during the Axumite Empire via Adulis port.PDF p. 60
    • Indian soldiers participated in liberation efforts during Italy’s occupation (1936–41).PDF p. 60
    • Formal diplomatic relations were established in 1950.PDF p. 60
    • On September 28, 2026, the second Joint Defence Cooperation meeting was held in Addis Ababa.PDF p. 60
    • Addis Ababa also hosts the headquarters of the African Union, making it an important centre of African diplomacy. India – OceaniaPDF p. 60

    PM Modi’s Australia Visit 2026PDF p. 60

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Australia on July 8–10, 2026 and attended the Third Australia–India Annual Summit in Melbourne on 9 July at Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s invitation. The summit advanced the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership established in 2020.PDF p. 60
    • The new declaration expanded the 2009 security framework.PDF p. 60
    • The Maritime Security Collaboration Roadmap covers maritime-domain awareness, surveillance, information exchange, operational coordination, search and rescue, and sea-lane protection.PDF p. 60
    • An MoU between the Indian Coast Guard and Australia’s Maritime Border Command supports maritime law enforcement and border protection.PDF p. 60
    • An administrative arrangement is intended to facilitate long-term Australian uranium exports for peaceful use under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards.PDF p. 60
    • Australia supported India’s Nuclear Suppliers Group membership.PDF p. 60
    • Australia supported Gaganyaan.PDF p. 60
    • A temporary tracking terminal was commissioned on the Cocos Islands, and cooperation between the Indian Space Research Organisation and the Australian Space Agency will be strengthened.PDF p. 60
    • Maitri grants support cultural, research and economic cooperation. Australian universities proposed Bengaluru (Flinders University) and Gurugram (Victoria University) campuses.PDF p. 60
    • A mining Centre of Excellence will be established at Bhubaneswar’s National Skill Training Institute.PDF p. 60
    • The India–Australia Roadmap for Sports Collaboration was launched at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on 10 July 2026 and builds on the 2023 sports MoU.PDF p. 60
    • It covers coaching and capacity building, sports science and technology, para sport, women’s participation, high-performance sport, major-event management, and sports industry and investment.PDF p. 60
    • The roadmap links cooperation to major events, including the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad and the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Brisbane.PDF p. 60

    India-New ZealandPDF p. 60, 61

    • During Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Auckland visit on July 10–11, 2026, India and New Zealand established a Strategic Partnership, adopted the Roadmap to 2030 and concluded ten agreements and arrangements. This was the first Indian prime-ministerial visit to New Zealand in four decades.PDF p. 60
    • The partnership institutionalises cooperation, building on Christopher Luxon’s March 2025 visit to India, when Free Trade Agreement negotiations began.PDF p. 60
    • The Roadmap to 2030 guides relations during 2026– 2030.PDF p. 60
    • Its six pillars cover political and diplomatic engagement; defence and security; trade and economic cooperation; people, culture and sport; education, research, science, technology and disaster management; and regional and multilateral cooperation.PDF p. 60
    • It is not legally binding and creates no enforceable obligations or automatic financial commitments. Implementation requires political commitment, coordination, resources and regular review.PDF p. 60
    • Annual trade of approximately NZ$3.95 billion is targeted to reach NZ$7 billion by 2030. New Zealand committed to facilitating US$20 billion in investment into India over 15 years and up to 5,000 skilled visa pathways for Indian professionals.PDF p. 60
    • Kiwifruit Centres of Excellence are planned in Nagaland and Uttarakhand.PDF p. 60
    • Agreements between India’s National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research and the University of Canterbury, and between NIFTEM-Kundli and Massey University, support Antarctic research and cooperation in food technology and entrepreneurship respectively.PDF p. 60
    • B. International Events/Indices/Rankings/ReportsPDF p. 61

    WJP Rule of Law Index 2026PDF p. 61

    • The World Justice Project (WJP) released the Rule of Law Index 2026 on October 21, 2026, ranking India 88th among 143 countries and jurisdictions, with an overall score of 0.48. India slipped two positions from 86th in 2025 , when its score was 0.49. Globally, the rule of law declined in 62% of countries, marking the ninth consecutive year in which deterioration exceeded improvement.PDF p. 61

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 61

    • About WJP: The World Justice Project is an independent, nonpartisan, multidisciplinary organisation promoting the rule of law worldwide.PDF p. 61
    • Methodology: The Index uses eight factors and 44 sub-factors , drawing on household and expert surveys. Scores range from 0 (weakest) to 1 (strongest adherence to the rule of law).PDF p. 61
    • Four Fundamental Principles: Accountability, Just Law, Open Government, and Accessible and Impartial Justice.PDF p. 61
    • Regional Performance: India ranked 3rd among six South Asian countries and 6th among 33 lower-middle-income economies . Its strongest global factor ranking was in Open Government (45th), while its lowest was in Civil Justice (116th).PDF p. 61

    Global RankingsPDF p. 61

    • Top Seven Countries: Denmark (1st; 0.90), Norway (2nd; 0.89), Finland (3rd; 0.87), Sweden (4th; 0.86), Luxembourg (5th; 0.83), Germany (6th; 0.83) and New Zealand (7th; 0.83).PDF p. 61
    • Bottom Five Countries: Venezuela (143rd; 0.26), Afghanistan (142nd; 0.31), Haiti (141st; 0.31), Cambodia (140th; 0.31) and Nicaragua (139th; 0.32).PDF p. 61
    • South Asian Rankings: Nepal (71st), Sri Lanka (74th), India (88th), Bangladesh (123rd), Pakistan (131st) and Afghanistan (142nd).PDF p. 61
    • Other Major Economies: Singapore (14th), Japan (15th), United Kingdom (18th), United States (30th), South Africa (60th), Indonesia (75th), Brazil (76th), China (92nd) and Russia (121st).PDF p. 61
    • Largest Improvements: Latvia (+1.6%), Trinidad and Tobago (+1.2%) and Guatemala (+1.1%).PDF p. 61
    • Largest Declines: Haiti (−5.6%), Tanzania (−3.5%) and Sudan (−2.8%). These percentages represent annual changes in index scores.PDF p. 61

    Nobel Prizes 2026PDF p. 61

    • The 2026 Nobel Prizes were announced between October 5 and 12, 2026 in six categories—Physiology or Medicine, Physics, Chemistry, Literature, Peace and Economic Sciences.PDF p. 61

    Nobel Prize 2026: Winners at a GlancePDF p. 61

    • Category Laureate(s) Institution / Affiliation Awarded For Physiology or Medicine Karl Deisseroth Stanford University, USA; Investigator, Howard Hughes Medical Institute Discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics Peter Hegemann Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Germany – Experimental Biophysics Same Georg Nagel Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), Germany Same Physics Francis Halzen University of Wisconsin–Madison, USA Contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos Chemistry Henri B. Kagan Université Paris-Saclay, France – Professor Emeritus; research associated with Université Paris-Saclay/CNRS Non-linear effects in asymmetric organic synthesis Kenso Soai Tokyo University of Science, Japan – Professor Emeritus Asymmetric autocatalysis in organic synthesis Literature Anne Carson Canadian writer and classicist; University of Toronto alumna Innovative literary work engaging with the classical tradition Peace Navanethem “Navi” Pillay Former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights; former ICTR President and ICC judge; has served as an ad hoc ICJ judge Efforts to promote peace and international law Economic Sciences Robert E. Hall Stanford University, USA Microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation Michael Woodford Columbia University, USA – John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy SamePDF p. 61

    Medicine: Optogenetics RevolutionPDF p. 62

    • Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel received the Medicine Prize on 5 October.PDF p. 62
    • Hegemann and Nagel’s work on channelrhodopsins, light-sensitive ion channels found in microorganisms, helped provide the biological basis for optogenetics.PDF p. 62
    • Deisseroth helped develop these discoveries into a technique that allows researchers to activate or inhibit selected neurons using light.PDF p. 62
    • Optogenetics has transformed neuroscience by allowing scientists to examine how specific neural circuits influence memory, emotion and behaviour.PDF p. 62

    Physics: Opening a New Window on the UniversePDF p. 62

    • Francis Halzen received the Physics Prize for his decisive role in the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.PDF p. 62
    • IceCube uses about one cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice containing thousands of light sensors to detect extremely elusive neutrinos.PDF p. 62
    • Its observations established the detection of high- energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin, helping create the field of neutrino astronomy.PDF p. 62

    Chemistry: Understanding Molecular HandednessPDF p. 62

    • Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai jointly received the Chemistry Prize.PDF p. 62
    • Kagan pioneered understanding of non-linear effects in asymmetric catalysis , while Soai demonstrated asymmetric autocatalysis, in which a reaction product helps produce more of the same handed molecular form.PDF p. 62
    • Their discoveries improved understanding of chirality, an important concept in organic chemistry and pharmaceutical development.PDF p. 62

    Literature: Anne CarsonPDF p. 62

    • Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist Anne Carson received the Literature Prize on 8 October.PDF p. 62
    • She was honoured for a body of work that combines poetry, prose, criticism, translation and ancient Greek literature in innovative forms.PDF p. 62
    • Major works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband, Nox and Eros the Bittersweet.PDF p. 62

    Peace: Navi PillayPDF p. 62

    • South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay received the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.PDF p. 62
    • Pillay served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (2008–2014) and held judicial positions at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Court (ICC).PDF p. 62
    • Her career has focused on accountability for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.PDF p. 62
    • Pillay was born in Durban into a family of Indian Tamil origin, making her award especially noteworthy from an Indian current-affairs perspective.PDF p. 62

    Economic Sciences: Stabilising Economic FluctuationsPDF p. 62

    • Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University received the Economic Sciences Prize on 12 October.PDF p. 62
    • Their research connected the decisions of households and firms with economy-wide fluctuations in inflation, output and employment.PDF p. 62
    • Their work provided theoretical foundations for modern macroeconomic stabilisation policies , including the use of fiscal policy, interest rates and central-bank communication.PDF p. 62
    • Their models are widely used by central banks and finance ministries to analyse economic shocks.PDF p. 62

    Global Hunger Index 2026PDF p. 62

    • The Global Hunger Index (GHI) 2026 , released in October 2026 under the theme “No Security Without Food Security,” ranked India 100th among 122 countries , with a score of 24.1, placing it in the “serious” hunger category . India’s score improved from 38.1 in 2000 and 37.0 in 2006, but remained worse than the South Asian average of 23.5 and the global average of 18.1.PDF p. 62

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 62, 63

    • About GHI: First published in 2006, the Global Hunger Index is an annual, peer-reviewed assessment jointly published by Concern Worldwide, Welthungerhilfe and the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict (IFHV). The 2026 report is its 21st edition.PDF p. 62
    • Four Indicators: The Index measures hunger using undernourishment (1/3 weight), child stunting (1/6), child wasting (1/6) and under- five mortality (1/3). Scores range from 0 (best) to 100 (worst).PDF p. 62
    • Data Period: The 2026 Index combines undernourishment data (2023–2025), child wasting (2021–2025), child stunting (2024) and under- five mortality (2024), using international sources including FAO, WHO and UNICEF.PDF p. 62
    • India’s Performance:PDF p. 62
    • Undernourished population: 9.8%PDF p. 62
    • Child stunting: 29.3%PDF p. 62
    • Child wasting: 19.0%PDF p. 62
    • Under-five mortality: 2.7%PDF p. 62
    • Child wasting remains India’s major nutritional concern, while stunting declined significantly from 50% in 2000 to 29.3% in 2026.PDF p. 62
    • Top Performers: Twenty-four countries, including Armenia, Belarus, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria and Chile, recorded GHI scores below 5 and were jointly placed in ranks 1–24.PDF p. 62
    • Lowest-Ranked Countries: Somalia (122nd; 47.0) recorded the highest hunger score, followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (121st; 39.5), Chad (120th; 38.0), Madagascar (119th; 36.5) and Haiti (118th; 34.4). Somalia was classified in the “alarming” category.PDF p. 62
    • Global Findings: The global GHI score increased from 17.6 in 2018 to 18.1 in 2026, indicating stalled progress against hunger. South Asia scored 23.5 , remaining in the serious category. Burundi, South Sudan, Sudan and Yemen received provisional alarming designations because of incomplete data.PDF p. 63
    • Major Challenges: Conflict, climate shocks, economic pressures and disrupted food systems continue to undermine global food security.PDF p. 63
    • In India, inadequate dietary diversity, maternal malnutrition, poor sanitation and limited healthcare access contribute to persistent child undernutrition.PDF p. 63

    WHO–UNICEF JMP Report 2026PDF p. 63

    • On September 22, 2026 , the World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) released “Progress on Drinking Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Schools 2015–2025” under their Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP). The report assesses school Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services under Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Indicator 4.a.1 and warns that universal coverage (over 99%) is unlikely by 2030.PDF p. 63

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 63

    Global WASH Status (2025)PDF p. 63

    • Indicator Water Sanitation Hygiene Schools with basic services 78% 77% 72% Children lacking basic services 429 million 460 million 545 million Children with no service 258 million 244 million 362 million Projected 2030 coverage 84% 81% 79%PDF p. 63
    • Required Acceleration: Fourfold for drinking water and fivefold for sanitation. WHO specifies fourfold for hygiene, while parts of the JMP report specify fivefold.PDF p. 63
    • Important Distinction: Children lacking basic services include those with limited or no services.PDF p. 63

    India’s PerformancePDF p. 63

    • Basic Coverage: Drinking water 96.6% (2025) , sanitation 80.8% (2025) and hygiene 52.9% (2024).PDF p. 63
    • No-Service Categories (2025): Approximately 50 million children lacked sanitation , 12 million lacked drinking water and 20 million lacked hygiene services.PDF p. 63
    • Sanitation Gap: India accounted for nearly one- fifth of the global 244 million children without sanitation services.PDF p. 63
    • Progress: During 2015–2025, schools without sanitation declined by 14 percentage points, while basic drinking water coverage increased by over four percentage points annually.PDF p. 63
    • 2030 Outlook: India was among 28 of 62 countries on track for universal basic drinking water coverage.PDF p. 63

    Academic Freedom Index 2026PDF p. 63

    • The 12 th edition of Free to Think 2026, released by Scholars at Risk (SAR) on September 15, 2026, classified academic freedom in India as “severely restricted.” India’s Academic Freedom Index (AFI) score declined from 0.16 in 2024 to 0.14 in the latest assessment.PDF p. 63
    • The report documented 382 attacks arising from 321 verified incidents involving higher-education communities across 59 countries and territories between 1 July 2025 and 30 June 2026.PDF p. 63
    • Free to Think is an annual publication of the Scholars at Risk Academic Freedom Monitoring Project, examining threats to academic freedom, institutional autonomy and higher-education communities.PDF p. 63
    • The Index measures actual levels of academic freedom across 179 countries and territories.PDF p. 63
    • It is jointly implemented by Germany’s Friedrich- Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) and the V-Dem Institute, using assessments from 2,357 country experts.PDF p. 63
    • Five AFI Indicators: The Index evaluates: 1. Freedom to research and teach. 2. Freedom of academic exchange and dissemination. 3. Institutional autonomy. 4. Campus integrity. 5. Freedom of academic and cultural expression.PDF p. 63
    • India was placed in the “severely restricted” category alongside Hong Kong, Indonesia, Pakistan, the West Bank and Ukraine.PDF p. 63
    • SAR attributed India’s declining score partly to restrictions on research and teaching freedom.PDF p. 63
    • It also raised concerns about university governance, leadership appointments, faculty dismissals, cancellation of academic events, student expression and changes in UGC regulations.PDF p. 63
    • Afghanistan, China, Gaza, Iran, Russia, Türkiye, Syria, Venezuela and Zimbabwe were among the countries and territories identified as having completely restricted academic freedom.PDF p. 63

    Global Gender Gap Index 2026PDF p. 63

    • The World Economic Forum (WEF) released the 20 th Global Gender Gap Report on September 16, 2026, ranking India 131 st among 145 economies, with 64.5% gender parity.PDF p. 63
    • India retained its 2025 ranking, while its score improved marginally from 64.4% to 64.5%.PDF p. 63
    • Globally, 69.2% of the gender gap has been closed, with full parity estimated to take another 120 years.PDF p. 63
    • Launched by the WEF in 2006, the Global Gender Gap Index measures gender disparities rather than absolute development levels.PDF p. 63
    • Its scores range from 0 (disparity) to 1 (full parity).PDF p. 63
    • The Index assesses Economic Participation and Opportunity, Educational Attainment, Health and Survival, and Political Empowerment.PDF p. 63

    India’s PerformancePDF p. 64

    • Dimension Gender Parity Economic Participation and Opportunity 41.2% Educational Attainment 96.6% Health and Survival 95.6% Political Empowerment 24.5% Overall 64.5%PDF p. 64
    • Labour-force participation parity stood at 44.1%, while parity among professional and technical workers improved from 26.6% in 2006 to 49.9% in 2026.PDF p. 64
    • Representation among legislators, senior officials and managers remained low at 13.1%.PDF p. 64
    • India achieved full parity in secondary and tertiary enrolment, while adult literacy parity stood at 82.5%. Health and Survival parity improved to 95.6%.PDF p. 64
    • India ranked 67th globally in Political Empowerment with 24.5% parity.PDF p. 64
    • Parliamentary and ministerial representation parity stood at 16.1% and 5.9%, respectively, while the female head-of-state indicator reached 40.7%.PDF p. 64
    • Top Five Economies: Iceland (93.0%) ranked first for the 17 th consecutive year, followed by Finland (87.2%), Norway (85.7%), Namibia (84.5%) and the United Kingdom (84.2%).PDF p. 64
    • Other Top Ten Economies: New Zealand (6 th), Sweden (7 th), Australia (8 th), Germany (9 th) and Ireland (10th).PDF p. 64
    • Lowest-Ranked Economies: Chad (145 th), Iran (144th) and Pakistan (143rd).PDF p. 64
    • Global Dimension Scores: Educational Attainment (96.9%) and Health and Survival (96.2%) recorded the highest parity, followed by Economic Participation (61.7%) and Political Empowerment (22.1%).PDF p. 64
    • Southern Asia ranked 7 th among eight regions, closing 64.5% of its gender gap.PDF p. 64

    India Joins Global Initiative for 6G Leadership and SecurityPDF p. 64

    • In September 2026, India endorsed the US-led “Call to Action for 6G Leadership and Security,” joining the United States and 24 other countries to promote open, interoperable, secure, resilient and innovation-driven 6G networks.PDF p. 64
    • The announcement followed discussions during the G20 Innovation Ministers’ Meeting , held on September 1–2, 2026 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA.PDF p. 64
    • India’s participation will be coordinated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT).PDF p. 64
    • Launched in July 2026 under the leadership of the US Department of Commerce’s National Telecom- munications and Information Administration (NTIA), the initiative promotes international coop - eration on 6G development, cybersecurity, techno - logical innovation and secure telecom supply chains.PDF p. 64
    • India aims to contribute approximately 10% of global 6G standards and patents by 2030.PDF p. 64
    • By March 2026, India had contributed around 4,000 patents, while its proposal on ubiquitous connectivity received international acceptance through the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP).PDF p. 64
    • Bharat 6G Vision: Launched in March 2023, it provides a roadmap for India’s leadership in sixth- generation wireless technology.PDF p. 64
    • The Bharat 6G Alliance (B6GA) brings together telecom companies, startups, research institutions and academia.PDF p. 64
    • Its membership increased from 14 to 85 institutions by 15 March 2026.PDF p. 64
    • India was represented by Jitin Prasada, Minister of State for Commerce and Industry and Electronics and Information Technology.PDF p. 64
    • The meeting adopted the G20 Innovation Ministerial Statement, emphasising emerging technologies as drivers of productivity and economic growth.PDF p. 64
    • India and the US also discussed cooperation in semiconductors, AI and data centres.PDF p. 64

    Oxford Economics Global Cities Index 2026PDF p. 64

    • The Oxford Economics Global Cities Index 2026 ranked Delhi 268 th among 1,000 cities worldwide, making it India’s highest-ranked city.PDF p. 64
    • Bengaluru (311th) and Mumbai (330 th) secured the second and third positions among Indian cities.PDF p. 64
    • Globally, New York retained first place, followed by London and Paris. No Indian city featured among the global top 100.PDF p. 64
    • Introduced in 2024 by Oxford Economics, a global economic research and forecasting organisation, the Index assesses the economic performance, living conditions and future potential of 1,000 major cities.PDF p. 64
    • Five Assessment Pillars: Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment and Governance.PDF p. 64
    • These assess economic growth, employment, education, workforce skills, living standards, environmental sustainability and institutional performance.PDF p. 64
    • Delhi’s Performance: Delhi received an overall score of 57.6 out of 100, with its strongest performance in Human Capital (13th globally), reflecting its large talent pool and educational institutions.PDF p. 64
    • Top 10 Indian Cities: Delhi (268), Bengaluru (311), Mumbai (330), Chennai (381), Hyderabad (421), Pune (427), Thrissur (477), Kochi (489), Kolkata (496) and Kozhikode (499).PDF p. 64
    • Global Top 10: New York ( 1st), London (2 nd), Paris (3rd), Seattle (4 th), San Francisco (5 th), Dublin (6 th), Boston (7 th), San Jose (8 th), Tokyo (9 th) and Zurich (10th). European and North American cities occupied 78 of the top 100 positions.PDF p. 64

    US–Denmark–Greenland Arctic Defense Agreement 2026PDF p. 65

    • On September 22, 2026, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new Arctic Defense Agreement at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, strengthening military cooperation and security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.PDF p. 65
    • The agreement, signed by US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, expands US military access while recognising Denmark’s sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self-determination.PDF p. 65
    • The agreement amends the 1951 Defense Agreement concerning Greenland and will enter into force after the necessary parliamentary procedures in Denmark and Greenland are completed.PDF p. 65
    • The original US–Denmark Defense Agreement was signed on 27 April 1951 under the framework of the North Atlantic Treaty.PDF p. 65
    • It was subsequently supplemented by the 1991 Memorandum of Understanding and the 2004 Igaliku Agreement.PDF p. 65
    • The agreement permits the expansion and modernisation of US military activities at Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, in north-western Greenland.PDF p. 65
    • The facility supports ballistic missile early warning, missile defence, satellite tracking and space surveillance.PDF p. 65
    • The agreement also refers to the proposed US Golden Dome missile-defence system.PDF p. 65
    • The agreement promotes greater North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) involvement in Arctic military planning, exercises, intelligence gathering, surveillance and interoperability.PDF p. 65
    • It generally prohibits non-NATO countries from establishing military installations or maintaining a persistent military presence in Greenland without the parties’ agreement. 26th SCO Summit 2026 Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic, on August 31–September 1, 2026. Chaired by President Sadyr Japarov, it marked the SCO’s 25th anniversary.PDF p. 65
    • Leaders adopted the Bishkek Declaration and approved 28 documents covering security, emergencies, climate, energy and institutional cooperation.PDF p. 65
    • Measures for a Universal Centre for Countering Challenges and Threats and an SCO Anti-Drug Centre will complement the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) in Tashkent.PDF p. 65
    • India’s approach centred on Security, Connectivity and Opportunity.PDF p. 65
    • Modi called for dismantling the terrorist ecosystem, opposed double standards in counter-terrorism and stressed dialogue and diplomacy.PDF p. 65
    • India linked Eurasian security with peace in Afghanistan and highlighted its humanitarian and development assistance.PDF p. 65
    • It supported connectivity that promotes trade while respecting sovereignty and territorial integrity.PDF p. 65
    • India supported English as an official SCO language alongside Russian and Chinese.PDF p. 65
    • It announced that it would host the first SCO Civilisation Dialogue Forum later in 2026 and supported the Young Scientists Forum, Young Authors’ Conclave and youth cooperation.PDF p. 65
    • Originating from the Shanghai Five of 1996, the SCO was established on June 15, 2001.PDF p. 65
    • It has 10 full members. India and Pakistan joined in 2017, Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024.PDF p. 65
    • Its Secretariat is in Beijing. Members cover approximately 36 million square kilometres, have over 3.4 billion people, and account for about one- fourth of global GDP and over 15% of international trade.PDF p. 65
    • It provides India a platform for engagement with Central Asia, Russia, China, Iran and Pakistan.PDF p. 65

    Lahore as SCO Tourism and Cultural CapitalPDF p. 65

    • Kyrgyzstan transferred the 2026–27 presidency to Pakistan under the theme “Turning Vision into Action: Connectivity, Innovation and Shared Prosperity.”PDF p. 65
    • Pakistan will host the next summit in 2027. Lahore was designated the SCO Tourism and Cultural Capital for 2026–27. Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh addressed the 25th Meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (CHG) of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on October 20, 2026 .PDF p. 65

    Global Passport Index 2026PDF p. 65

    • India ranks 125 th among 197 countries and territories in Global Citizen Solutions’ Global Passport Index 2026, compared with 124th in 2025 and 127th during 2021–2023.PDF p. 65
    • Developed by a private international residency and citizenship advisory organisation, the index uses 14 indicators to assess nationality’s attractiveness.PDF p. 65
    • Enhanced Mobility carries 50% weight; Investment and Quality of Living carry 25% each. These pillars cover travel access, destination attractiveness, economic and business conditions, taxation, development, freedom, environment, well-being and migrant acceptance.PDF p. 65

    India’s PerformancePDF p. 65, 66

    • India’s overall score is 45.1. Its component ranks and scores are 135th and 41.1 for Enhanced Mobility, 94th and 40.0 for Investment, and 118th and 58.2 for Quality of Living.PDF p. 65
    • Mobility has the greatest effect on the final rank because of its 50% weight.PDF p. 65
    • Among 194 destinations, Indian passport holders have free access to 6, limited-day free access to 20, visa-on-arrival access to 10 and electronic travel authorisation access to 6.PDF p. 66
    • Electronic visas requiring prior approval cover 64 destinations, while conventional visas are required for 88.PDF p. 66

    Top and Bottom PerformersPDF p. 66

    • Sweden leads with 96.05, followed by Switzerland, Finland and Germany.PDF p. 66
    • Denmark and the Netherlands share fifth place; Ireland, the United Kingdom, Norway and Singapore occupy seventh to tenth positions.PDF p. 66
    • Afghanistan ranks last with 23.10.PDF p. 66

    FAO Food Price IndexPDF p. 66

    • The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) reported that the FAO Food Price Index (FFPI) averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, increasing by 0.7 points (0.6%) from June and 1.0% from July 2025. It reached its highest level since early 2023 but remained 29.1 points (18.2%) below its March 2022 peak. The increase was driven by higher cereal, vegetable oil and sugar prices, partly offset by declines in meat and dairy prices.PDF p. 66
    • The FFPI measures monthly changes in international prices of five globally traded commodity groups— cereals, vegetable oils, meat, dairy products and sugar—weighted by their average export shares during the 2014–2016 base period.PDF p. 66
    • It reflects international commodity prices rather than domestic retail food prices.PDF p. 66
    • The Cereal Price Index averaged 113.8 points, rising 3.4% monthly and 6.9% annually.PDF p. 66
    • Wheat prices increased 5.8% due to Black Sea export disruptions, infrastructure damage and heatwaves affecting production.PDF p. 66
    • Maize prices also rose amid hot, dry weather in parts of the United States and higher energy costs.PDF p. 66
    • The Vegetable Oil Price Index increased 2.0%, reaching its highest level since June 2022.PDF p. 66
    • Higher palm and soybean oil prices reflected strong biodiesel demand, rising crude-oil prices and increased consumption.PDF p. 66
    • The Sugar Price Index rose 5.6%, driven by adverse weather in Europe and Asia and expectations of increased sugarcane diversion towards ethanol production in Brazil.PDF p. 66
    • Meat prices declined 2.8% from their June record high, while dairy prices fell 0.7%, reflecting greater export availability and weaker demand for certain products.PDF p. 66
    • Higher international food prices can contribute to domestic inflation and complicate the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) monetary policy management.PDF p. 66

    World Investment Report 2026PDF p. 66, 67

    • The World Investment Report 2026, titled International Investment in a Turbulent Era, was released on July 7, 2026. Global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 6% to approximately US$1.6 trillion in 2025, ending two consecutive years of decline.PDF p. 66
    • The report is the principal annual publication of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), published since 1991.PDF p. 66
    • UNCTAD is now publicly known as UN Trade and Development.PDF p. 66
    • It examines investment flows, multinational enterprises, investment policies and sustainable development.PDF p. 66
    • FDI is cross-border investment intended to establish a lasting interest and significant managerial influence. At least 10% of voting power generally indicates this relationship.PDF p. 66
    • Unlike portfolio investment, it normally involves long-term influence, technology and capital transfers, and productive assets.PDF p. 66
    • India’s inward FDI rose nearly 44%, from approximately US$27.1 billion in 2024 to US$38.9 billion in 2025, improving its rank from 13th to 11th.PDF p. 66
    • Outward FDI increased from approximately US$24.3 billion to US$35.7 billion, improving its rank from 20th to 18th.PDF p. 66
    • At the end of 2025, inward and outward FDI stocks were approximately US$559 billion and US$296.4 billion.PDF p. 66
    • Outward growth indicates Indian companies’ international expansion.PDF p. 66
    • Inward inflows remained below 2021 and 2022 levels.PDF p. 66
    • UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report, Trade and Development Report, Digital Economy Report, Technology and Innovation Report, Least Developed Countries Report, Economic Development in Africa Report, Review of Maritime Transport, and Commodities and Development Report.PDF p. 66
    • The top five destination economies by FDI inflows are: Rank Economy FDI Inflows (2025) 1 United States $277 billion 2 Singapore $151 billion 3 Hong Kong, China $116 billion 4 China $105 billion 5 Brazil $77 billionPDF p. 66
    • The top five investing nations driving India's FDI inflows: Rank Country of Origin Key Share & Characteristics 1 Singapore Dominates both cumulative inflows (~25%) and recent cycles, contributing up to 34%–37% of recent periodic equity.PDF p. 66
    • 2 Mauritius Historically the top source, holding ~23% of cumulative FDI, though newer fiscal rules have slightly adjusted its routing dominance. 3 United States Represents roughly 10% of total inflows, with concentrated investments in technology, IT, and startup ecosystems. 4 Japan Stays highly active, frequently combining with Singapore to supply substantial portions of quarterly capital for automotive and infrastructure. 5 Netherlands / UAE Trade places dynamically around the fifth spot, driven by heavy routing into manufacturing, green energy, and logistics channels.PDF p. 67

    US–Saudi Arabia Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement 2026PDF p. 67

    • The United States and Saudi Arabia signed a Section 123 Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement in July 2026. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed on 20 July (Washington) and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman on 22 July (Riyadh).PDF p. 67

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 67

    • Legal Basis: Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954. Preliminary cooperation began in 2008, with negotiations concluding on 18 November 2025.PDF p. 67
    • Duration: 30 years after entry into force, following completion of domestic procedures and exchange of diplomatic notes (Article 16).PDF p. 67
    • Nuclear Safeguards: Restricts military use, unauthorised transfers, enrichment and reprocessing.PDF p. 67
    • Uranium Enrichment: Article 7 provides for a two-year joint study ; subsequent enrichment requires written consent and safeguards.PDF p. 67
    • Gold Standard: Unlike the 2009 US–United Arab Emirates agreement , Saudi Arabia has not renounced enrichment and reprocessing.PDF p. 67
    • IAEA Protocol: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Additional Protocol is not mandatory. A separate bilateral safeguards agreement was signed. Saudi Arabia withdrew its Small Quantities Protocol on December 31, 2024.PDF p. 67
    • Congressional Review: Trump submitted the agreement on 24 August 2026, triggering statutory 30- and 60-day review periods . Senators Jeff Merkley and Edward Markey introduced S.J. Res. 221 on 15 October seeking disapproval.PDF p. 67
    • Abraham Accords: Trump publicly linked the agreement to Saudi participation, but the published text contains no such condition. Two confidential side letters remain undisclosed.PDF p. 67

    US and Iranian Initial Peace AgreementPDF p. 67

    • On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a historic initial peace agreement—formalised via a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)— aimed at ending the four-month West Asia war.PDF p. 67
    • The agreement was signed electronically by US President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian; the interim pact serves primarily as a comprehensive ceasefire to halt active military operations and stave off global economic depression.PDF p. 67
    • However, the agreement is facing immense strain, highlighted by Iran’s declaration that it is closing the Strait of Hormuz due to ongoing Israeli strikes in Lebanon.PDF p. 67

    Key Terms of the 14-Point MoUPDF p. 67, 68

    • Termination of Hostilities : An immediate and permanent end to military operations on all fronts, explicitly including the conflict in LebanonPDF p. 67
    • Strait of Hormuz Reopening : Free, toll-free passage through the crucial energy shipping corridor is restored to full capacity within 30 days.PDF p. 67
    • Sanctions Relief : The US Department of the Treasury must immediately issue waivers allowing Iran to export crude oil, petroleum products, and access associated banking and transportation services.PDF p. 67
    • Reconstruction Fund: A framework with regional partners to develop an economic development plan for Iran worth at least $300 billion. White House officials noted that Gulf Arab nations are expected to finance the fund, and the US will not contribute directly.PDF p. 67
    • Unfreezing Assets: The US commits to unblocking restricted Iranian funds and assets abroad, with Tehran seeking the return of approximately $24 billion.PDF p. 67
    • Nuclear Constraints : Iran is required to halt further enrichment and “down-blend” (dilute) its existing highly enriched uranium stocks to 3.67% under IAEA monitoring.PDF p. 67
    • The 60-Day Window: The initial arrangement sets up a 60-day technical negotiation period to secure a final, legally binding nuclear pact endorsed by the UN Security Council. IRan–ISRael ConflICTPDF p. 67
    • On February 28, 2026 , joint U.S.-Israeli attacks pushed the conflict into a new phase.PDF p. 67
    • The United States called it Operation Epic Fury, while Israel called it Operation Roaring Lion.PDF p. 67
    • After these strikes, Iran presented its missile and drone attacks as successive waves of “Operation True Promise.”PDF p. 67
    • Earlier, in June 2025, Israel had carried out a 12-day campaign called Operation Rising Lion targeting Iranian nuclear and military infrastructures including Tehran, Natanz, Tabriz, and Kermanshah.PDF p. 67
    • The most inhuman face of the war was seen in the attack on Shajarah Tayyibeh Girls’ School in Minab, southern Iran, where a large number of girls were killed.PDF p. 68
    • Iran targeted over 17 key U.S. sites in the Gulf region, including the 5th Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain.PDF p. 68

    Ali KhameneiPDF p. 68

    • Ali Khamenei, Iran’s Supreme Leader since 1989, was assassinated in Tehran on February 28, 2026, during a joint US-Israeli strike.PDF p. 68
    • Following this, his son, Mojtaba Khamenei , was announced as the new Supreme Leader on March 9, 2026, selected by the Assembly of Experts.PDF p. 68
    • High-level U.S.–Iran talks took place in Islamabad on April 11–12, 2026, and ended without a deal.PDF p. 68

    Strait of Hormuz and Strait of Malacca:PDF p. 68

    • The Strait of Hormuz, located between Iran and Oman, connects the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea.PDF p. 68
    • It is the world’s most important oil transit chokepoint.PDF p. 68
    • The Strait of Malacca, located between Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore , connects the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.PDF p. 68
    • It is the shortest sea route between the Middle East and East Asia.PDF p. 68

    Kharg IslandPDF p. 68

    • Another important dimension is Kharg Island , Iran’s principal oil export terminal in the Persian Gulf.PDF p. 68
    • Handles nearly 90% of Iran’s crude oil exports.PDF p. 68
    • On 17 April 2026 , the UK and France co-chaired an international meeting on the S trait of Hormuz Maritime Navigation / Freedom of Navigation Initiative, with 51 countries participating to support free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.PDF p. 68

    U.S. Joins the FrayPDF p. 68

    • In June 2025, in a dramatic escalation of hostilities, Israel launched Operation Rising Lion , a series of coordinated airstrikes and drone attacks targeting Iran’s nuclear and military infrastructure.PDF p. 68
    • Key targets included in this operation were the Natanz uranium enrichment facility, a nuclear research center in Tehran; military bases in Tabriz; and an underground missile storage site in Kermanshah.PDF p. 68
    • This pre-emptive operation aimed to halt Iran’s progress toward acquiring nuclear weapons.PDF p. 68
    • In response, Iran launched Operation True Promise 3, firing ballistic missiles at Israeli targets, with explosions reported in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, marking a major regional escalation.PDF p. 68
    • The United States formally entered the conflict with precision airstrikes on Iran’s major nuclear installations—Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan — using B-2 stealth bombers armed with bunker- buster bombs.PDF p. 68
    • The official U.S. name for the strike on Iranian nuclear sites was Operation Midnight Hammer.PDF p. 68
    • In response to growing tensions, the Government of India launched Operation Sindhu.PDF p. 68
    • India has a strong track record in such operations, as seen during the 1990–91 Gulf War , the Libya crisis, and Operation Ganga in Ukraine (2022).PDF p. 68
    • Modi Becomes First Leader Honoured by Israel and PalestinePDF p. 68
    • PM Narendra Modi became the first leader to receive top honours from both Israel and Palestine.PDF p. 68
    • He was awarded the Speaker of the Knesset Medal (Israel’s highest parliamentary honour) on February 25, 2026.PDF p. 68
    • The award was presented by Amir Ohana at the Knesset in Jerusalem.PDF p. 68
    • Earlier, in 2018, he received the Grand Collar of the State of Palestine from Mahmoud Abbas.PDF p. 68

    World Press Freedom Index 2026PDF p. 69, 70

    • India has been ranked 157th out of 180 countries in the World Press Freedom Index 2026, released by Reporters Without Borders, also known as Reporters Sans Frontières, or RSF.PDF p. 69
    • RSF is an international non-profit organization that works to defend press freedom and the rights of journalists.PDF p. 69
    • The index compares the level of press freedom enjoyed by journalists and media organizations in 180 countries and territories.PDF p. 69
    • RSF assesses press freedom through five broad indicators: Political context; Legal framework; Economic context; Sociocultural context; SafetyPDF p. 70
    • The top five countries are: Norway (1 st); Netherlands (2 nd); Estonia (3 rd); Denmark (4 th); Sweden (5th)PDF p. 70
    • The bottom five countries are: Saudi Arabia (176th); Iran (177 th); China (178 th); North Korea (179th); Eritrea (180th)PDF p. 70
    • These countries are associated with severe restrictions on independent reporting, imprisonment of journalists, censorship and state control over information.PDF p. 70

    • India’s rank in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index is 157th (Score : 31.96) out of 180 countries.PDF p. 70
    • In 2025, India was ranked 151st, which means the country dropped by six positions in the latest index.PDF p. 70
    • RSF has placed India in the “very serious” category.PDF p. 70

    World Happiness Report 2026PDF p. 70

    • The World Happiness Report 2026 (14th edition) was released on March 19, 2026, ahead of the International Day of Happiness.PDF p. 70
    • The World Happiness Report has been published annually since 2012.PDF p. 70
    • It is published by the Wellbeing Research Centre at the University of Oxford , in partnership with Gallup, the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network, and an independent editorial board.PDF p. 70
    • Its global rankings are based primarily on a life- evaluation question —often called the Cantril Ladder—which asks respondents to rate their lives on a 0 to 10 scale.PDF p. 70
    • These six explanatory variables are used to help explain differences across countries:PDF p. 70
    • GDP per capitaPDF p. 70
    • Social supportPDF p. 70
    • Healthy life expectancyPDF p. 70
    • Freedom to make life choicesPDF p. 70
    • GenerosityPDF p. 70
    • Perceptions of corruptionPDF p. 70
    • The World Happiness Report 2026 focuses on the intersection of Social Media and Wellbeing.PDF p. 70
    • It examines how digital connectivity, screen time intensity, and platform usage affect global life satisfaction, with a major focus on the decline of youth happiness in Western nations.PDF p. 70
    • Finland ranked 1st in the world in 2026 with a life- evaluation score of 7.764, remaining the world’s happiest country for the ninth consecutive year.PDF p. 70
    • It was followed by Iceland (2nd) and Denmark (3rd).PDF p. 70
    • The top 5 in the 2026 rankings were: Finland (1st); Iceland (2nd); Denmark (3rd); Costa Rica (4th); Sweden (5th).PDF p. 70
    • A notable feature was Costa Rica’s rise to 4th , making it a standout performer outside the usual Nordic cluster.PDF p. 70
    • Bottom 5 countries in 2026 – Botswana (143 rd); Zimbabwe (144 th); Malawi (145 th); Sierra Leone (146th); Afghanistan (147th);PDF p. 70
    • India ranked 116 th out of 147 countries in the 2026 report, a slight improvement from its position in 2025 as reflected in public reporting around this year’s release.PDF p. 70
    • Among major emerging powers, China ranked 65th, Russia 79th, and Iran 97th, while India stood at 116th in the 2026 ranking table.PDF p. 70
    • The International Day of Happiness is observed every year on 20 March.PDF p. 70

    • The NRI is a global index that measures a country’s readiness to leverage information and communi - cation technologies (ICTs) for economic growth, governance, and societal transformation.PDF p. 70
    • The 2025 edition assesses 127 economies using 53 indicators grouped into four broad pillars: Technology, People, Governance, and Impact.PDF p. 70
    • Global Top 5 – United States (Score: 79.13); Finland (Score: 75.82); Singapore (Score: 75.46); Denmark (Score: 75.14); Sweden (Score: 75.09)PDF p. 70

    • India’s performance in NRI 2025 marks a significant improvement in digital readiness.PDF p. 70

    The Global Risks Report 2026PDF p. 70, 71

    • The Global Risks Report 2026 is the 21st edition of the World Economic Forum’s annual report and was published on January 14, 2026, warns that the world is entering an “Age of Competition”—a phase wherePDF p. 70
    • geopolitical rivalry, economic weaponization, technology disruption and climate stress are interacting and creating cascading crises.PDF p. 71
    • The World Economic Forum defines a global risk as an event or condition that can cause a significant negative impact on:PDF p. 71

    • Executive Opinion Survey (EOS) for country- level “national risk perceptions”.PDF p. 71

    The World Inequality Report 2026PDF p. 71, 72

    • In December 2025 , the World Inequality Report 2026 (3rd edition), published by the World Inequali ty Lab and edited by economists like Thomas Piketty and Lucas Chancel, revealed that global economic and environmental disparities remain at an extreme and persistent level.PDF p. 71
    • The report highlights unprecedented concentration of wealth at the global level:PDF p. 71
    • The top 10% of the global population controls nearly 75% of total wealth, while the bottom 50% owns only 2%.PDF p. 71
    • The top 1% holds around 37% of global wealth, exceeding the combined wealth of the bottom half of the world.PDF p. 71
    • The wealthiest 0.001% (about 60,000 individuals) possess three times more wealth than the poorest 50% globally.PDF p. 71
    • The report identifies India as one of the most unequal countries globally.PDF p. 71
    • The top 10% earns 58% of national income.PDF p. 71
    • The bottom 50% receives only 15% of income.PDF p. 71
    • The disparity has widened compared to earlier assessments.PDF p. 71
    • The richest 10% owns about 65% of national wealth.PDF p. 71
    • The top 1% alone holds around 40% of total wealth.PDF p. 71
    • Average annual income per capita: €6,200 (PPP).PDF p. 71
    • Average wealth per capita: €28,000 (PPP).PDF p. 71
    • These figures highlight that while India has witnessed economic growth, wealth creation remains highly concentrated.PDF p. 71
    • Globally, women earn 61% of men’s wages when unpaid work hours are excluded.PDF p. 71
    • When unpaid care work is included, women earn only 32% of male income.PDF p. 71
    • Women receive just 28.2% of global labour income, showing minimal progress over decades.PDF p. 71
    • India’s female labour income share was 15.7% in both 2014 and 2024, reflecting structural barriers such as social norms, skill gaps, and unpaid care responsibilities.PDF p. 71
    • The report introduces climate inequality as a major global concern:PDF p. 71
    • The top 10% contributes 77% of emissions linked to private capital ownership.PDF p. 71
    • The poorest 50% contributes only 3% of such emissions.PDF p. 71
    • The wealthiest 1% is responsible for 41% of emissions, almost double that of the bottom 90%.PDF p. 71
    • This indicates that those contributing least to climate change face the highest vulnerability, raising issues of climate justice and equity.PDF p. 71
    • C. International Conferences/Summits/OrganisationsPDF p. 72
    • The report highlights systemic financial imbalances:PDF p. 72
    • Approximately 1% of global GDP annually flows from poorer to richer nations through financial and investment mechanisms.PDF p. 72
    • Developed countries benefit from lower borrowing costs and higher investment returns, reinforcing global economic hierarchy.PDF p. 72

    Commitment to Development Index (CDI) 2025PDF p. 72

    • The Commitment to Development Index (CDI) 2025, released by the Center for Global Development on November 20, 2025, measures how major economies support or hinder development in poorer countries through policies that go beyond foreign aid.PDF p. 72
    • Top performers: Sweden (1 st), Germany (2 nd), Norway (3rd), followed by Finland and the UK.PDF p. 72
    • Major economies underperform: The U.S. ranks 28th and China 34th, showing limited development- friendly policies.PDF p. 72
    • India ranks 36 th overall and 30 th on the income- adjusted rank, not 29th.PDF p. 72
    • This indicates that India’s development policies are more progressive relative to its resource base.PDF p. 72
    • India ranks 8th in Environment among the 38 CDI economies, and in both Trade and Development Finance, it ranked 38th.PDF p. 72

    UN World Urbanization Prospects 2025PDF p. 72

    • The United Nations (UN) released the World Urbanization Prospects (WUP) 2025 Revision in November 2025, published by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA):PDF p. 72
    • Jakarta (Indonesia) ranks first with an estimated population of 42 million.PDF p. 72
    • Dhaka (Bangladesh) follows with 37 million , while Tokyo (Japan) slips to third place with 33 million.PDF p. 72
    • Nine of the world’s ten most populous cities are located in Asia, including Jakarta, Dhaka, Tokyo, New Delhi, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Manila, Kolkata and Seoul.PDF p. 72

    EU Signs Association Agreement with Andorra and San MarinoPDF p. 72

    • On October 19, 2026, the European Commission, on behalf of the European Union (EU) , signed an Association Agreement with Andorra and San Marino in Brussels, Belgium . It aims to integrate these European microstates into the EU Single Market without granting EU membership.PDF p. 72

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 72

    • Nature and Scope: The Mixed Agreement involves the EU, its member states, Andorra and San Marino. It provides for the free movement of goods, services, capital and persons , subject to agreed conditions.PDF p. 72
    • Financial Services: Market access will be phased in after regulatory assessments by the European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs) . Cooperation also covers research, education, environment and consumer protection.PDF p. 72
    • Negotiation Timeline: Talks began in 2015 under December 2014 Council directives. Negotiations with Monaco were suspended in September 2023, while those with Andorra and San Marino concluded in December 2023.PDF p. 72
    • Approval Process: The European Commission submitted proposals on 26 April 2024. The Council of the EU authorised signing and provisional application on 16 July 2026.PDF p. 72
    • Legal Status: Under Article 112(3) , provisional application may begin separately with either country after prescribed procedures. Full implementation requires necessary approvals, including European Parliament consent . Provisional application remained unconfirmed as of 21 October 2026.PDF p. 72
    • Monetary Agreements: Andorra ( 2011) and San Marino ( 2012) use the euro through monetary agreements without euro-area membership. They may issue limited national-design euro coins but not banknotes. Updated agreements were also signed.PDF p. 72
    • EEA Plus: European Commission Executive Vice- President Maroš Šefčovič informally described the arrangement as “EEA Plus” in December 2023. EEA means European Economic Area; its official legal designation remains Association Agreement.PDF p. 72

    India Approves Accession to SIOFA 2026PDF p. 72, 73

    • On October 14, 2026, India approved accession to the Southern Indian Ocean Fisheries Agreement (SIOFA) to promote sustainable high-seas fishing.PDF p. 72
    • India has been a Cooperating Non-Contracting Party (CNCP) since 2022; full membership remained pending as of October 21, 2026.PDF p. 72
    • Under Articles 23–25, accession takes effect 30 days after depositing the instrument with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Director-General.PDF p. 72
    • Signed in Rome on July 7, 2006 and effective from June 21, 2012, SIOFA is a Regional Fisheries Management Organisation (RFMO) headquartered in Le Port, Réunion (France).PDF p. 72
    • It covers squid, toothfish and alfonsino, excluding tuna and certain sedentary species.PDF p. 73
    • SIOFA promotes scientific cooperation and action against Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) fishing.PDF p. 73
    • Its boarding-and-inspection measures became effective in October 2019. Article 8 generally requires consensus for substantive decisions.PDF p. 73
    • India's 2025 guidelines mandate vessel-specific fishing authorisations. Unlike SIOFA, the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) regulates tuna.PDF p. 73
    • India accepted its agreement on March 13, 1995, effective March 27, 1996.PDF p. 73

    First BIMSTEC Home Ministers’ Meeting 2026PDF p. 73

    • The first Home Ministers’ Meeting of the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) was held in New Delhi on October 13, 2026, chaired by Union Home Minister Amit Shah. All seven member countries participated and adopted the Delhi Declaration. The meeting followed the Senior Officials’ Meeting on 12 October. The ministerial mechanism was proposed at the 4th BIMSTEC Summit (Kathmandu, 2018) and welcomed at the 6th Summit (Bangkok, 2025).PDF p. 73

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 73

    • Delhi Declaration: Called for cooperation against terrorism, organised crime, drug and human trafficking, cybercrime, money laundering and terror financing. It emphasised United Nations Security Council (UNSC) Resolution 1267 sanctions , intelligence sharing, extradition, mutual legal assistance and victim-centred protection.PDF p. 73
    • Five Major Approvals: (1) Draft Convention Against Human Trafficking; (2) Drug Control Action Plan; (3) Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on combating Money Laundering and Terror Financing; (4) Action Plan against Illicit Financial Flows; and (5) Disaster Preparedness and Coordination Action Plan.PDF p. 73
    • Additional Approval: Human Trafficking Action Plan and Implementation Matrix. The trafficking convention and anti-money-laundering MoU await formal signing.PDF p. 73
    • Disaster Management: A BIMSTEC Centre of Excellence is proposed at Jamnagar, Gujarat.PDF p. 73
    • India’s Role: India leads the Security Sector , covering counter-terrorism and transnational crime, energy and disaster management.PDF p. 73
    • About BIMSTECPDF p. 73
    • Established: 6 June 1997, through the Bangkok Declaration; initially called BIST-EC.PDF p. 73
    • Members (7): Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand. The founding members were Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka and Thailand; Myanmar joined in 1997, and Nepal and Bhutan in 2004.PDF p. 73
    • Secretariat: Dhaka, Bangladesh.PDF p. 73
    • Charter: Signed on 30 March 2022 (Colombo) ; effective 20 May 2024.PDF p. 73
    • 6th Summit: 4 April 2025, Bangkok ; adopted BIMSTEC Bangkok Vision 2030.PDF p. 73
    • Current Chair (2026): Bangladesh.PDF p. 73
    • Secretary-General: Indra Mani Pandey (India) , since 4 January 2024. FAO’s 28th Committee on Forestry Session 2026 The 28th Session of the Committee on Forestry (COFO) of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) was held from 28 September to 2 October 2026 in Rome, Italy , under the theme “Forests for Food, Resilience and Prosperity.” The 10th World Forest Week was organised alongside it.PDF p. 73

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 73

    • About COFO: Established in 1971 at the 16th FAO Conference, it is FAO’s highest intergovernmental forestry body, comprising 128 members, including the European Union. It meets biennially and reports to the FAO Council on budgetary matters and FAO Conference on policy matters.PDF p. 73
    • State of the World’s Forests (SOFO) 2026: Released on 28 September, titled “Restoring Forests and Landscapes: The Way Forward for a Sustainable Future.” It estimated 1.56 billion hectares of degraded land globally, with potential restoration returns of up to US$30 per US$1 invested.PDF p. 73
    • Four Restoration Pathways: Community empowerment and rights, landscape-level restoration, sustainable financing and coherent policies, institutions and laws.PDF p. 73

    India’s Performance and InitiativesPDF p. 73, 74

    • Forest and Tree Cover: As per the India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2023 , India’s combined cover is 8,27,357 sq. km (25.17%) , comprising forest cover of 7,15,343 sq. km (21.76%) and tree cover of 1,12,014 sq. km (3.41%).PDF p. 73
    • Global Ranking: India ranks 9th in total forest area and 3rd in net annual forest area gain , according to FAO’s Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025.PDF p. 73
    • Carbon Sink: India created an additional 2.29 billion tonnes of CO 2 equivalent during 2005–2021, increasing to 2.44 billion tonnes during 2005–2022. Its enhanced Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets 3.5–4.0 billion tonnes by 2035.PDF p. 73
    • Bonn Challenge: India targets restoration of 26 million hectares by 2030, with 21.76 million hectares brought under restoration during 2011–2020.PDF p. 73
    • Aravalli Green Wall: Covers Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi , with approximately 6.45 million hectares identified for restoration in India’s COFO statement.PDF p. 73
    • MISHTI Initiative: The Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes (MISHTI), launched on 5 June 2023 , targets restoration of 54,000 hectares of mangroves by 2028.PDF p. 74
    • Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam: Over 3.5 billion saplings had been planted by September 2026.PDF p. 74
    • Ramsar Sites: India reported 101 sites during COFO 28. The addition of Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh) and Sauj Jheel (Uttar Pradesh) on 15 October 2026 increased the total to 103.PDF p. 74
    • UN Afforestation Decade: India reaffirmed support for the United Nations Decade for Afforestation and Reforestation (2027–2036) , proclaimed under UN General Assembly Resolution 79/283 on 16 April 2025.PDF p. 74

    Global Call for Control of Frontier AI Models 2026PDF p. 74

    • On September 21, 2026, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre launched “ A Call for Control of Frontier AI Models” in New York, during the High-Level Week of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) . The initiative seeks to ensure that advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) remains under human oversight and control.PDF p. 74
    • Frontier AI: Refers to highly advanced AI models possessing capabilities comparable to or exceeding leading existing systems.PDF p. 74
    • Global Support: Initially endorsed by 22 leaders from 20 countries and the European Commission. By 21 October 2026 , participation had expanded to 31 leaders representing 29 countries and the European Commission.PDF p. 74
    • Major Supporters: Australia, Canada, Germany, Finland, Norway, Singapore, South Africa, Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates.PDF p. 74
    • European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also endorsed the appeal. France joined on 23 September 2026.PDF p. 74
    • India’s Status: India, the United States, China, United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea were not among the listed supporters as of 21 October. Singapore was the only Southeast Asian participant.PDF p. 74

    TIME100 Next 2026: Indian Personalities RecognisedPDF p. 74

    • On September 30, 2026 , TIME magazine released its TIME100 Next 2026 list, recognising 100 emerging global leaders. Launched in 2019, it has five categories—Phenoms, Artists, Leaders, Innovators and Advocates—with no fixed age limit. Raye, Ashley Padilla and Druski appeared on its three global covers.PDF p. 74
