    Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) Initiative 2026PDF p. 74

    • The Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) initiative was launched on September 21, 2026 in New York , during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) . The inaugural summit was co-chaired by India’s External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar and European Council President António Costa to strengthen UN-centred multilateral cooperation.PDF p. 74

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 74, 75

    • Founding Partners: Six countries— India, Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada and Kenya—along with the European Union (EU).PDF p. 74
    • Other Signatories: Albania, Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Cyprus, Finland, Guatemala, Ireland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Moldova, Norway, San Marino, Slovakia, Spain, Türkiye, Uruguay and the Council of Europe.PDF p. 74
    • Nature: An open, voluntary platform promoting international law, peace, cooperation and institutional reform.PDF p. 75
    • Core Priorities: Protecting international rules and institutions, addressing global challenges and making multilateral institutions more effective, representative and inclusive.PDF p. 75
    • Key Principles: Sovereign equality, territorial integrity, peaceful dispute settlement, human rights and prohibition of the threat or use of force.PDF p. 75
    • Global Cooperation: Supports the Paris Agreement, 2030 Agenda , resilient supply chains, trade reforms, climate action, Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance and global health.PDF p. 75
    • India’s Position: Advocated reformed multilateralism, transparent decision-making and solutions to the 4F crisis—Food, Fuel, Fertiliser and Finance.PDF p. 75
    • UN80 Initiative: Launched by UN Secretary- General António Guterres in March 2025 , focusing on administrative efficiency, mandate review and structural reforms.PDF p. 75
    • Coordination: Senior officials will identify cooperation priorities, with EU High Representative Kaja Kallas coordinating EU efforts. 18th BRICS Summit 2026 The 18 th BRICS Summit was held on 12–13 September 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, under India’s Presidency. Its theme was “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.” Leaders unanimously adopted the New Delhi BRICS Leaders’ Declaration on 12 September, covering cooperation and the interests of the Global South.PDF p. 75

    Key Highlights of the SummitPDF p. 75

    • India assumed its fourth BRICS Presidency on 1 January 2026, after chairing the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021.PDF p. 75
    • Its 11 full members account for approximately 49.5% of the global population, approximately 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade.PDF p. 75
    • The 10 Partner Countries engage through a structured framework without full membership.PDF p. 75
    • Summit-related engagements involved 32 delegations: 11 member states, 10 partner states, four regional organisations and seven international organisations.PDF p. 75

    New Delhi BRICS Leaders, Declaration 2026PDF p. 75

    • It condemned the 22 April 2025 Jammu and Kashmir terrorist attack that killed 26 people.PDF p. 75
    • China and Russia supported India’s and Brazil’s aspirations for a greater UN role, including the Security Council.PDF p. 75
    • Prime Minister Modi proposed a BRICS Continuity and Implementation Mechanism to follow up decisions across Presidencies.PDF p. 75
    • BRICS supported an open, transparent, fair and rules-based trading system centred on the World Trade Organization (WTO).PDF p. 75
    • It expressed concern over unilateral tariff and non- tariff measures that could disrupt trade and supply chains, and supported restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.PDF p. 75
    • BRICS encouraged local currencies in cross-border trade, investment and financial transactions among member countries.PDF p. 75
    • The BRICS Payment Task Force continued work on interoperability among payment and financial messaging systems. No common BRICS currency was announced.PDF p. 75
    • It recognised fossil fuels’ continued role in emerging and developing economies while supporting renewable and nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen and other low-carbon technologies.PDF p. 75
    • BRICS emphasised women-led development and women’s participation in governance, decision- making, entrepreneurship, economic development, peace-building, climate action, and food and nutrition security.PDF p. 75
    • Key initiatives included the BRICS Centres of Excellence on Agro-Ecology and Regenerative Agriculture, BRICS Network on Digital Agriculture, BRICS Mission for Healthy Lifestyle, BRICS CONNECT for Skilling, BRICS MSME Cooperation Portal, BRICS Incubator Network and BRICS Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework.PDF p. 75

    BRICS 2026: Major Sectoral MeetingsPDF p. 76

    • The Second Meeting of the BRICS Anti-Corruption Working Group (ACWG) and the Expert Network on Asset Recovery took place in Hyderabad, Telangana, from August 4–5, 2026.PDF p. 76
    • Host: Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), Government of India.PDF p. 76

    • Asset Recovery: Strengthening international cooperation to trace and recover stolen assets.PDF p. 76
    • Fugitive Offenders: Discussing the BRICS Repository on Informal Cooperation to stop the cross-border movement of corruption offenders and support extradition.PDF p. 76
    • Side Event: A dedicated session was held on August 5, 2026, titled “Ethical Governance through Innovation and Tech-Driven Systems,” focusing on digital public procurement and transparency. 13th BRICS Education Ministers’ Meeting in OdishaPDF p. 76

    • Priority Discussions: Leaders focused on strengthening Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE), enhancing skill development via the BRICS TVET Cooperation Alliance, and promoting joint research, innovation, and start-ups.PDF p. 76
    • Key Frameworks: Delegations worked on the Mutual Recognition of Qualifications (MRQ), academic leadership capacity building, and new guiding principles on Traditional and Indigenous Knowledge Systems. Meeting of Heads of National Statistical Offices of BRICS CountriesPDF p. 76
    • India successfully hosted the Meeting of Heads of National Statistical Offices (NSO) of BRICS Countries in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh , from August 3–4, 2026, under its BRICS Chairship.PDF p. 76
    • Organized by the National Statistical Office and the Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI), the high-level gathering brought together over 350 delegates, including statistical leaders, policymakers, and technical experts.PDF p. 76
    • India’s Specific Theme: “Quality Statistics as Driver of Change,” which highlights data quality, innovation, and people-centric systems.PDF p. 76
    • India’s 2026 BRICS chairship followed the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”. 11th BRICS Energy Ministers MeetingPDF p. 76
    • India hosted the meeting in Gurugram, Haryana, on June 25–26, 2026, with the energy track theme “Energy for All”.PDF p. 76
    • Its three priorities were energy security and sustainability, energy access and equity, and technology and innovation.PDF p. 76
    • Members adopted a Joint Communiqué supporting resilient infrastructure and capacity building and launched the BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.PDF p. 76
    • Discussions covered universal access, green cooperation and energy transitions, with participation from the International Solar Alliance and Global Biofuels Alliance. Guwahati Declaration on Drug ControlPDF p. 76
    • At the two-day BRICS Heads of Anti-Drug Agencies Meeting in Guwahati, Assam, members adopted the Guwahati Declaration on July 7, 2026.PDF p. 76
    • It strengthens cooperation against illicit drug trafficking, synthetic drugs and transnational organized crime.PDF p. 76
    • Commitments include real-time intelligence sharing, cross-border networks, AI and technology for enforcement, monitoring darknet and virtual asset transactions, and control of precursor chemicals and synthetic drug laboratories.PDF p. 76
    • Demand reduction emphasizes rehabilitation, education and youth protection. 16th BRICS National Security Advisers, MeetingPDF p. 76
    • Held in New Delhi on June 22–23, 2026, under National Security Adviser Ajit Doval’s leadership, the meeting addressed energy, food and supply chain security, climate-induced instability and cybersecurity.PDF p. 76
    • It focused on preventing terrorist use of emerging technologies and AI and reviewed BRICS working group reports on counter-terrorism and ICT security.PDF p. 76
    • Discussions also covered West Asia, Ukraine and supply chain relief through the opening of the Strait of Hormuz. BRICS Agriculture Conference and Indore DeclarationPDF p. 76
    • Indore hosted the conference on June 9–13, 2026, with participants from 21 countries representing nearly half the global population.PDF p. 76
    • The unanimously adopted Indore Declaration targets sustainable farming, digital agriculture and farmers’ welfare.PDF p. 76
    • Discussions addressed food and nutrition security, global supply chains, AI and machine learning, eco- friendly and climate-resilient farming, and smallholders’ access to modern technology and fair markets.PDF p. 76
    • BRICS Foreign Ministers, Meeting 2026PDF p. 77
    • India hosted the BRICS Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in New Delhi from May 14–15, 2026, under its national chairship of the bloc.PDF p. 77
    • Chaired by External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar, the gathering brought together foreign ministers and heads of delegations from BRICS member and partner countries.PDF p. 77
    • 17th BRICS Summit, 2025 The 17th BRICS Summit was held from July 6-7, 2025, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.PDF p. 77
    • The previous 16th BRICS Summit was held in October 2024 in Kazan, Russia , while the 18th BRICS Summit will be held in India in 2026. 27th World Knowledge Forum 2026 The 27 th World Knowledge Forum (WKF) was held from September 8–10, 2026 at Jangchung Arena and The Shilla Seoul, South Korea, under the theme “The Promethean Moment: Architecting the Co-Intelligence Order.”PDF p. 77
    • The forum brought together global leaders, economists, academics and technology experts to discuss artificial intelligence (AI), geopolitical changes, economic transformation and emerging technologies.PDF p. 77
    • Established in 2000 by South Korea’s Maekyung Media Group, the World Knowledge Forum is an annual international platform promoting global prosperity through knowledge sharing. Its founder is Chang Dae-whan.PDF p. 77
    • Theme: Inspired by the Greek myth of Prometheus, who gave fire to humanity, the theme presents AI as the “fire of the 21st century”, highlighting its transformative potential and associated risks.PDF p. 77
    • Co-intelligence emphasises responsible cooperation between human intelligence and AI.PDF p. 77
    • The forum’s discussions were organised around five pillars: 1. Power: Geopolitics, national security and global order. 2. Capital: Financial markets, investment and economic transformation. 3. Intelligence: AI, quantum computing and disruptive technologies. 4. Planet: Climate change, resources and sustainability. 5. Humanity: Employment, ethics and the social impact of technology. President of the 81st UNGA Session Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister and veteran diplomat Khalilur Rahman has been elected President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) and began his one-year term on September 8, 2026.PDF p. 77
    • Khalilur Rahman was elected after a closely contested secret ballot against Andreas Kakouris of Cyprus.PDF p. 77
    • The presidency for the 81st session fell to the Asia- Pacific Group under the UN’s regional rotation practice, which made Bangladesh eligible to field its candidate.PDF p. 77

    Italy leads in the Number of UNESCO World Heritage SitesPDF p. 77

    • The 48th UNESCO World Heritage Committee session, chaired by Mr LEE Byong Hyun, was held in Busan, Republic of Korea, from July 19 to 29, 2026, and added 25 sites.PDF p. 77
    • The inscription of the Funerary Tradition in the Prehistory of Sardinia - Domus de Janas raised Italy’s total to 62 sites, comprising 56 cultural and 6 natural sites. Italy leads China (61), France (56), Germany (55), Spain (50) and India (45).PDF p. 77
    • Italy’s position reflects over three thousand years of continuous civilization.PDF p. 77
    • The Roman Empire influenced law, governance, engineering and architecture, while the Renaissance transformed art and scientific thought.PDF p. 77
    • Italy also preserves medieval towns, religious buildings, archaeological remains and cultural landscapes.PDF p. 77
    • Its natural heritage includes the Dolomites, Mount Etna, Aeolian Islands and ancient beech forests.PDF p. 77
    • The 1972 World Heritage Convention protects cultural and natural heritage possessing Outstanding Universal Value as humanity’s common heritage.PDF p. 77
    • India ranks sixth with 45 sites: 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed. Recent additions include Sarnath (2026), Maratha Military Landscapes (2025) and Moidams (2024).PDF p. 77

    India at UNESCO 2025PDF p. 77, 78

    • In 2025, India was re-elected to UNESCO’s Executive Board for the 2025–29 term and Deepavali was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.PDF p. 77
    • UNESCO stands for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization.PDF p. 77
    • Deepavali was inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) list on December 10, 2025.PDF p. 77
    • The inscription happened during the 20th session of the Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in New Delhi.PDF p. 77
    • The session was held from December 8–13, 2025 at the Red Fort, New Delhi.PDF p. 77
    • Deepavali was inscribed under the domain of social practices, rituals and festive events.PDF p. 78

    UN Scientific Panel Releases First Global AI Assessment 2026PDF p. 78

    • On July 1, 2026, the United Nations-established Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence (AI) released its first Preliminary Report: Evidence-based Assessment of Opportunities, Risks and Impacts of AI.PDF p. 78
    • The assessment informed the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, held in Geneva, Switzerland, on 6–7 July 2026.PDF p. 78
    • The report warns that AI capabilities are advancing faster than scientific understanding, independent evaluation and governance safeguards.PDF p. 78
    • Created under UN General Assembly Resolution A/RES/79/325 of 26 August 2025, following the Global Digital Compact, the Panel comprises 40 independent experts from all five UN regional groups, appointed for three-year terms.PDF p. 78
    • Co-Chairs: Yoshua Bengio (Canada), recipient of the 2018 Turing Award, and Maria Ressa (Philippines), recipient of the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize.PDF p. 78
    • The Panel provides independent, non-prescriptive scientific assessments of non-military AI applications; it has no regulatory or enforcement powers.PDF p. 78
    • In 2025, US institutions produced 59 notable AI models, China 35 and the rest of the world 13.PDF p. 78
    • The private sector accounted for 91% of notable models.PDF p. 78
    • Among the 500 largest known AI computing clusters, the US controlled approximately 75% of computing capacity, China 15% and other countries 10%.PDF p. 78
    • India’s IndiaAI Mission, approved in March 2024 with an outlay of ₹10,371.92 crore, has onboarded over 38,000 GPUs to expand affordable computing access.PDF p. 78

    Second Pax Silica Summit 2026PDF p. 78

    • The Second Pax Silica Summit was held in Washington, D.C., on 25–26 June 2026, bringing together governments and industry leaders to strengthen artificial intelligence (AI), economic security and trusted technology supply chains.PDF p. 78
    • Thirty-five countries, including India, signed the separate Joint Statement on AI Opportunity Partnership, promoting innovation, private investment and secure AI ecosystems.PDF p. 78
    • India’s delegation was led by S. Krishnan, Secretary, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), and included K. Nagaraj Naidu of the Ministry of External Affairs.PDF p. 78
    • Launched by the United States in December 2025, Pax Silica Initiative aims to secure the entire AI technology supply chain, including critical minerals, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, energy, computing infrastructure, data centres and logistics.PDF p. 78
    • India joined Pax Silica on 20 February 2026, becoming its 10th signatory, during the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi.PDF p. 78
    • India also signed the bilateral India–U.S. AI Opportunity Partnership, focusing on innovation- friendly regulation, physical AI infrastructure and private-sector investment.PDF p. 78
    • Pax Pass Initiative: A proposed technology- enabled logistics platform will facilitate the secure movement of high-value AI-related goods through cargo verification, supply-chain traceability, AI- based risk assessment and expedited customs processing. Its initial pilot is planned for Panama.PDF p. 78

    • The Quad comprises India, the United States, Japan and Australia. India hosted the 11th Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in New Delhi on May 26, 2026.PDF p. 79

    • The Summit focused on energy and food security, strengthening the ASEAN Petroleum Security Agreement and ASEAN Power Grid (APG) amid Middle Eastern instability.PDF p. 79

    India–EU Summit 2026PDF p. 80

    • The 16th India–European Union (EU) Summit was held on January 27, 2026 in New Delhi, attended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Its major outcomes included the conclusion of Free Trade Agreement (FTA) negotiations, the first India–EU Security and Defence Partnership, and the “Towards 2030” Strategic Agenda.PDF p. 80
    • The FTA negotiations began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and resumed in 2022.PDF p. 80
    • The EU offered preferential access across 97% of tariff lines, covering 99.5% of Indian exports by value.PDF p. 80
    • Labour-intensive sectors worth approximately US$33 billion will benefit from duty-free access.PDF p. 80
    • India offered concessions on 92.1% of tariff lines, covering 97.5% of EU exports, while protecting sensitive agricultural products and phasing in automobile and alcohol tariff reductions.PDF p. 80
    • The EU opened 144 services subsectors, while India offered 102, alongside provisions for professional mobility, digital trade and regulatory cooperation.PDF p. 80
    • The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and other non-tariff barriers remain concerns.PDF p. 80
    • The FTA had not entered into force by October 2026, pending formal approvals.PDF p. 80
    • The Security and Defence Partnership covers maritime security, cybersecurity, counterterrorism and defence cooperation, with opportunities under the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme, subject to applicable conditions.PDF p. 80
    • Other outcomes included a Comprehensive Mobility Framework, proposed EU Legal Gateway Office in India, Green Hydrogen Task Force, renewed scientific cooperation for 2025–2030, exploratory talks on Horizon Europe, and disaster-management cooperation.PDF p. 80
    • About the EU: Established through the Maastricht Treaty (1992), it has 27 members. The eurozone expanded to 21 countries following Bulgaria's accession on January 1, 2026.PDF p. 80

    • The Johannesburg Leaders’ Declaration, reflecting the African philosophy of Ubuntu (shared humanity), emphasised debt relief, climate finance, food security, energy transition and multilateral reforms.PDF p. 80

    • The first G20 Global Inequality Report, released in November 2025 by a committee chaired by Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz, found that 83% of countries, representing 90% of humanity, had high income inequality (Gini coefficient above 0.4).PDF p. 80
    • During 2000–2024, the richest 1% captured 41% of new global wealth, against just 1% for the bottom 50%.PDF p. 80

    Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri Becomes Morocco’s First Woman Head of GovernmentPDF p. 81

    • On September 29, 2026, Morocco’s King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the country’s first woman Head of Government, entrusting her with forming a new government.PDF p. 81
    • She became the third woman to be appointed head of government in the Arab world, after Tunisia’s Najla Bouden and Sarru Zaafrani Zenzri.PDF p. 81
    • The appointment was made under Article 47 of Morocco’s 2011 Constitution.PDF p. 81
    • Morocco held elections for its 395-member House of Representatives on 23 September 2026, recording 38.08% voter turnout.PDF p. 81
    • The Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) emerged as the largest party with 97 seats, followed by the National Rally of Independents (66), Istiqlal Party (65) and Justice and Development Party (54).PDF p. 81
    • El Mansouri is a lawyer and coordinator of PAM’s collective leadership.PDF p. 81
    • She previously served as Minister of National Territory Planning, Urban Planning, Housing and City Policy and Mayor of Marrakech.PDF p. 81

    Military Mutiny in Niger 2026 and Coups in AfricaPDF p. 81

    • On August 28–29, 2026, a military mutiny occurred in Niamey, Niger, targeting the government of President Abdourahamane Tiani. Niger’s Defence Ministry and the Confederation of Sahel States (AES) reported that the attempt had been suppressed.PDF p. 81

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 81

    • Mutiny: Began around 12:20 a.m. on 29 August at Air Base 101 , where dissident soldiers detained fellow personnel and attacked sensitive installations near Diori Hamani International Airport , the presidential complex and state broadcaster.PDF p. 81
    • Response: On 30 August , Russia reported assistance from its Africa Corps. On 4 September, Niger’s government attributed the incident to elements of a special intelligence battalion.PDF p. 81
    • Niger’s Background: A landlocked West African country, independent from France since 3 August 1960; capital Niamey. It experienced five successful coups in 1974, 1996, 1999, 2010 and 2023.PDF p. 81
    • 2023 Coup: On 26 July , President Mohamed Bazoum was removed by the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland (CNSP) . The 26 March 2025 Charter designated Tiani as President for a modifiable 60-month transition.PDF p. 81
    • AES: Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) through the Liptako-Gourma Charter (16 September 2023) and established a confederation on 6 July 2024 . They formally withdrew from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) on 29 January 2025.PDF p. 81

Under Article 30 of the African Union (AU) Constitutive Act , governments attaining power through unconstitutional means cannot participate in AU activities.PDF p. 81

    Balendra Shah Becomes Nepal’s Youngest PMPDF p. 82

    • On March 27, 2026, Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen, became Nepal’s youngest democratically elected Prime Minister after the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) secured a strong mandate in the 2026 parliamentary election.PDF p. 82
    • Balendra Shah is a rapper, engineer and former Mayor of Kathmandu.PDF p. 82
    • He later joined the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).PDF p. 82
    • The 2026 election followed the 2025 youth-led protests against corruption and poor governance.PDF p. 82
    • The protests led to the fall of the K. P . Sharma Oli- led government.PDF p. 82
    • Shah’s rise reflected the growing role of young voters, anti-corruption politics and anti-establishment sentiment in Nepal.PDF p. 82

    Nepal Gen Z MovementPDF p. 82

    • The Nepal Gen Z movement erupted in September 2025 after the government banned 26 social media platforms (including Facebook, X, YouTube), a step widely seen as silencing dissent.PDF p. 82
    • The protests drew strength from anger over systemic corruption and nepotism , with “ Nepo Kids” symbolism highlighting elite impunity.PDF p. 82
    • The upheaval led to the resignation of PM K.P . Sharma Oli, restoration of social media access, and the creation of a political vacuum.PDF p. 82
    • Sushila Karki, a former Chief Justice, was sworn in as the interim Prime Minister of Nepal.PDF p. 82
    • She is the first woman to hold the position of Prime Minister in Nepal. E. International DisastersPDF p. 82

    Nepal’s Rasuwa Flash Flood 2026PDF p. 82

    • On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic flash flood struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Nepal–China border, sweeping through the Lhende Khola–Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system.PDF p. 82
    • The debris-laden flood damaged settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and communication networks.PDF p. 82
    • According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), a slope failure on Langtang Lirung triggered a massive rock–ice avalanche that entered the Lhende Khola catchment.PDF p. 82
    • The avalanche generated a debris-rich flood, potentially involving temporary river obstruction or displacement followed by sudden water release.PDF p. 82
    • At Galchhi, the Trishuli River reportedly rose approximately nine metres within 30 minutes. Several monitoring stations were damaged or destroyed.PDF p. 82
    • Initially considered a possible Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) or earthquake-related disaster, the event was subsequently identified primarily as a rock–ice avalanche-induced cascading hazard, rather than a conventional GLOF.PDF p. 82
    • India deployed NDRF teams in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh and provided specialised tunnel-rescue personnel and a 19-member forensic team for DNA identification, strengthening bilateral Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) cooperation.PDF p. 82
    • A GLOF occurs when a glacial lake suddenly releases water following the failure of its natural ice or moraine dam.PDF p. 82

    Colombia Declares Emergency After 7.4-Magnitude EarthquakePDF p. 82

    • On August 10, 2026, a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, at a depth of approximately 103 km.PDF p. 82
    • The Colombian Geological Service (SGC) described it as the country’s largest-magnitude earthquake of the 21st century.PDF p. 82
    • Colombia lies in north-western South America, bordering both the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.PDF p. 82
    • Its seismic activity is influenced by the interaction of the Nazca, South American and Caribbean tectonic plates.PDF p. 82
    • Along Colombia’s Pacific margin, the oceanic Nazca Plate subducts beneath the continental South American Plate.PDF p. 82
    • This convergence generates tectonic stress, causing earthquakes, crustal deformation and volcanic activity.PDF p. 82
    • Colombia is part of the Circum-Pacific Belt, extending approximately 40,000 km around the Pacific Ocean.PDF p. 82
    • This tectonically active region experiences frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions due to convergent plate boundaries and subduction zones.PDF p. 82
    • The subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate produces compression, crustal folding and uplift, contributing to the formation of the Andes Mountains.PDF p. 82
    • Fluids released from the descending plate also promote magma formation and volcanism.PDF p. 82

    Operation Amistad 2026PDF p. 83

    • On 26 June 2026, India launched Operation Amistad, a Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) mission to support Venezuela following two devastating earthquakes measuring of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 on 24 June 2026.PDF p. 83

    • Amistad, meaning “Friendship” in Spanish, symbolises India’s solidarity with Venezuela.PDF p. 83

    • Airborne Assistance: The Indian Air Force (IAF) deployed two C-17 Globemaster III aircraft carrying medical personnel, equipment and relief materials.PDF p. 83
    • BHISHM Cubes: India deployed two indigenously developed portable medical units under Project BHISHM (Bharat Health Initiative for Sahyog, Hita and Maitri).PDF p. 83
    • These rapidly deployable modular hospitals support emergency surgery, trauma care and disaster response. They form part of India’s Aarogya Maitri Initiative.PDF p. 83

    • The conference was inaugurated by PM Narendra Modi at Samvidhan Sadan and chaired by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.PDF p. 85

    CEC Gyanesh Kumar to Chair International IDEA Council for 2026PDF p. 85

    • On December 3, 2025 , India assumed the Chairship of the Council of Member States of International IDEA for 2026, with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar representing India as Chair in Stockholm, Sweden.PDF p. 85
    • International IDEA stands for the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance.PDF p. 85
    • It is an intergovernmental organisation working to support democracy and electoral processes.PDF p. 85
    • India is a founding member of International IDEA.PDF p. 85
    • Gyanesh Kumar will chair the Council of Member States for 2026.PDF p. 85
    • Mauritius and Mexico will serve as Vice-Chairs along with India.PDF p. 85
    • The 2026 chairship theme is “Democracy for an Inclusive, Peaceful, Resilient and Sustainable World.”PDF p. 85
    • International IDEA ’s Council has 35 Member States and two Observers.PDF p. 85
    • Gyanesh Kumar is the 26 th Chief Election Commissioner of India.PDF p. 85

    UN Cybercrime Convention SignedPDF p. 85

    • At Hanoi, countries signed the first-ever UN Cybercrime Convention , creating a global legal framework to combat ransomware, online fraud, and digital exploitation.PDF p. 85
    • It defines and criminalizes hacking, online fraud, and child exploitation.PDF p. 85
    • Enables real-time evidence sharing and 24/7 law enforcement cooperation.PDF p. 85
    • Managed by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).PDF p. 85

    China’s CR450: World’s Fastest Bullet Train UnveiledPDF p. 85

    • China has unveiled the CR450, the world’s fastest bullet train, reaching a record speed of 453 km/h during testing.PDF p. 85
    • With this, China surpassed all global competitors in both speed and efficiency.PDF p. 85
    • China operates the world’s largest high-speed rail network, spanning 50,000 km , linking almost all major cities.PDF p. 85
    • The CR450 strengthens China’s leadership in rail innovation and export, supporting global projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).PDF p. 85

    Bulgaria Joins the EurozonePDF p. 85

    • Bulgaria officially joined the eurozone on January 1, 2026, replacing the Bulgarian lev and becoming the 21st member of the euro area.PDF p. 85

    Chapter 4 · PDF pp. 87-120

    Economic Affairs

    Economic numbers need labels. Before learning a percentage, ask: GDP or GSDP, real or nominal, which financial year, and provisional estimate or budget estimate? Approval of a transaction is also different from its completion.

    1. Banking and monetary institutions
    2. GDP, base year and estimate status
    3. Budget and Centre-State transfers

    Build the chapter in eight anchors

    IDBI: approved, not completed

    The issue reports CCEA approval on 14 October 2026 for a 60.72% IDBI stake sale to 10955230 Canada Inc., a Fairfax group company, for about ₹52,878.08 crore; completion remains subject to further regulatory conditions.

    PDF p. 87
    The stake adds up

    Government of India: 30.48% to be sold; LIC: 30.24%. Together these form the approved 60.72% stake. The source describes remaining stakes as approximately 15% and 19%.

    PDF p. 87
    Real versus nominal GDP

    The provisional FY 2025-26 table lists real GDP ₹323.12 lakh crore with 7.7% growth and nominal GDP ₹346.36 lakh crore with 8.9% growth. They use different price bases.

    PDF p. 91
    A base-year revision

    The new GDP series is described as using 2022-23 instead of 2011-12. The same page later shows revised FY 2025-26 growth of 7.8%; keep this separate from the earlier provisional 7.7%.

    PDF p. 91
    Union Budget snapshot

    For FY 2026-27 BE, the issue gives a fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP, versus 4.4% in FY 2025-26 RE. It gives public capital expenditure of ₹12.2 lakh crore.

    PDF p. 113, 116
    Capital and revenue expenditure

    The source describes capital expenditure as creating assets or reducing liabilities; revenue expenditure includes salaries, subsidies and interest. FY 2026-27 growth over RE is given as 11.5% and 6.6% respectively.

    PDF p. 116
    Finance Commission basics

    The 16th Finance Commission is linked to Article 280, chaired by Dr Arvind Panagariya, and covers FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31. The source retains a 41% States' vertical share of the divisible tax pool.

    PDF p. 93
    Vertical share versus State weights

    The issue's horizontal weights are income distance 42.5%, population 2011 17.5%, and 10% each for demographic performance, area, forest and contribution to GDP. These weights add to 100%; they are not the 41% vertical share.

    PDF p. 93
    Four labels that change an economic number
    PairFirst meaningSecond meaning
    Real / nominalConstant pricesCurrent prices
    BE / REBudget EstimateRevised Estimate
    Vertical / horizontal devolutionCentre-States share of the poolDistribution across States
    Approval / completionTransaction authorisedRegulatory conditions still matter
    PDF p. 87, 91, 93, 113
    Learning aid - not from sourceWrite every economic figure as measure + period + unit + status. '4.3%' becomes 'Centre fiscal deficit, FY 2026-27 BE, % of GDP'. This is an editorial learning aid.

    Close the notes. Explain it back.

    Reconstruct the IDBI stake from the two sellers.

    30.48% from the Government plus 30.24% from LIC equals 60.72%. The issue reports approval, not unconditional completion.PDF p. 87

    Why should the 7.7% and 7.8% GDP figures not be merged?

    The page labels the first as the provisional annual estimate and later shows a revised figure under a new-series discussion. Preserve each label instead of choosing one silently.PDF p. 91

    Compare real and nominal GDP using the page's own terms.

    Real GDP uses constant prices; nominal GDP uses current prices. Therefore the two rupee totals and growth rates are not interchangeable.PDF p. 91

    Explain 41% versus 100% in the Finance Commission notes.

    41% is the States' vertical share of the divisible pool. The horizontal criteria weights describe distribution across States and sum to 100%.PDF p. 93

    What makes a fiscal-deficit answer precise?

    Specify the government, financial year, estimate status and denominator: the issue's Centre FY 2026-27 BE is 4.3% of GDP, versus FY 2025-26 RE at 4.4%.PDF p. 113

    Source check. The same page carries 7.7% provisional FY 2025-26 real GDP growth and 7.8% in a revised-estimates table under the new GDP series. Both are retained with their labels; no latest official estimate is asserted.PDF p. 91

    Economic Affairs: source readingPDF p. 87

    • A. Fiscal & Monetary AffairsPDF p. 87

    Strategic Restructuring of IDBI BankPDF p. 87

    • On October 14, 2026 , the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) , chaired by the Prime Minister, approved 10955230 Canada Inc., whose parent company is Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited, as the buyer for the strategic sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank Limited. The approved purchase consideration is approximately ₹52,878.08 crore. This decision marks an important stage in the transfer of the bank’s ownership and management control; completion of the transaction remains subject to compliance with further regulatory conditions.PDF p. 87

    Background of the BankPDF p. 87

    • IDBI was originally known as the Industrial Development Bank of India . It came into existence as a development finance institution on 1 July 1964, and its undertaking was transferred to a banking company with effect from 1 October 2004.PDF p. 87
    • IDBI Bank is a scheduled commercial bank regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) . Following LIC’s acquisition of 51% of its paid-up equity capital , the RBI classified it as a private sector bank for regulatory purposes with effect from 21 January 2019. Indicative Shareholding Based on the Approved Main Transaction Shareholder Before the sale Stake to be sold After the main sale Government of India 45.48% 30.48% Approximately 15% LIC 49.24% 30.24% Approximately 19%PDF p. 87

    Key Features of the Approved TransactionPDF p. 87

    • The strategic buyer is 10955230 Canada Inc., whose parent company is Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited.PDF p. 87
    • The total approved stake is 60.72%, and the purchase consideration is ₹52,878.08 crore.PDF p. 87
    • The Government of India will sell a 30.48% stake, while LIC will sell a 30.24% stake. The sale proceeds will be distributed in the corresponding proportion.PDF p. 87
    • The approved bid is ₹81 per share, compared with the benchmark of ₹75.99 per share , calculated as the average of two independent valuations. 57th GST Council Meeting The 57th meeting of the GST Council was held in New Delhi on October 8, 2026 , chaired by Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman.PDF p. 87
    • The Council recommended simplifying the registration application, FORM GST REG-01 , issuing clear guidelines on the documents required and making the portal more user-friendly.PDF p. 87
    • Automatic approval of amendments to registration particulars, other than the Principal Place of Business (PPoB), has been proposed.PDF p. 87
    • A simplified registration mechanism for small e-commerce sellers has been proposed under Rule 14B.PDF p. 87
    • Reforms have been proposed to improve the reconciliation of tax liability and Input Tax Credit (ITC) across GSTR-1, GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B.PDF p. 87
    • The Council recommended automating refunds of excess balances in the electronic cash ledger and reducing the time limit for issuing an acknowledgement or deficiency memo for refund applications from 15 days to 10 days.PDF p. 87
    • The inclusion of ITC on input services received on or after 1 November 2026 has been recommended for eligible inverted duty structure refunds.PDF p. 87
    • ITC on eligible capital goods received on or after 1 April 2027 is proposed to be included in the calculation of refunds of unutilised ITC arising from.PDF p. 87
    • A minimum tax amount of ₹10,000 has been recommended for issuing a show-cause notice.PDF p. 87

    Reserve Bank of India’s Monetary Policy (October, 2026)PDF p. 87, 88

    • The 63rd meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) was held from October 5 to 7, 2026, chaired by RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra.PDF p. 87
    • The Committee unanimously decided to increase the repo rate under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) by 25 basis points, raising it from 5.25% to 5.50%. Policy rate Rate effective from 7 October, 2026 Policy repo rate 5.50% Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) rate 5.25% Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate 5.75% Bank Rate 5.75%PDF p. 88
    • According to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), real GDP grew by 7.8% in the first quarter of FY 2026–27, covering April–June 2026.PDF p. 88
    • In its October review, the RBI projected real GDP growth of 7.1% for FY 2026–27. This is a forecast for the full financial year. The base year of the current GDP series is 2022–23.PDF p. 88

    Inflation and Major RisksPDF p. 88

    • According to the data used in the policy review, CPI inflation rose from 4.5% in July 2026 to 4.8% in August.PDF p. 88
    • The Committee projected CPI inflation at 5.2% and core inflation at 4.4% for FY 2026–27.PDF p. 88
    • In a subsequent update, MoSPI released September CPI inflation data on 12 October 2026, reporting headline inflation of 5.54% and food inflation of 7.74%. Both figures are provisional. The CPI base year is 2024=100. This release came after the October monetary policy decision.PDF p. 88
    • For the period from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031, the inflation target is 4%, with a lower tolerance limit of 2% and an upper tolerance limit of 6%. The target was notified by the Government in consultation with the RBI.PDF p. 88
    • The next MPC meeting is scheduled for 2–4 December 2026.PDF p. 88

    Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026PDF p. 88

    • The Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026 amended Section 13 of the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, specifying the competent authorities for cases reported more than one year after the event. The amendment came into force on October 1, 2026.PDF p. 88

    Key Details of the ActPDF p. 88

    • It received presidential assent on August 6, 2026.PDF p. 88
    • Section 2 of the Amendment Act substituted the existing Section 13(3) of the principal Act with new subsections 13(3) and 13(3A).PDF p. 88
    • The Office of the Registrar General, India , under the Ministry of Home Affairs, appointed 1 October 2026 as the commencement date through Notification S.O. 5081(E), dated 16 September 2026. The notification was issued under Section 1(2) of the Amendment Act.PDF p. 88

    New Framework for Delayed RegistrationPDF p. 88

    • Information reported after one year but within two years: Under Section 13(3) , registration may take place only on an order of the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or an Executive Magistrate authorised by the District Magistrate.PDF p. 88
    • Information reported after more than two years: Under Section 13(3A) , registration requires an order of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.PDF p. 88
    • Jurisdiction: The Magistrate issuing the order must have jurisdiction over the place where the birth or death occurred.PDF p. 88

    Previous Framework and the ChangePDF p. 88

    • Following the 2023 amendment , registration of all births and deaths reported more than one year after the event required an order of the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or an authorised Executive Magistrate. The 2026 amendment specifies different authorities for delays of more than one year but within two years, and more than two years.PDF p. 88

    Other ProvisionsPDF p. 88

    • Births and deaths are ordinarily required to be reported within 21 days . Registration after the ordinary reporting period but within 30 days attracts a late fee.PDF p. 88

    PMJDY Completes 12 YearsPDF p. 88

    • The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) completed 12 years on August 28, 2026, expanding access to formal banking and financial services among underserved and economically disadvantaged sections.PDF p. 88

    Key Facts and BackgroundPDF p. 88

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched PMJDY on 28 August 2014 as India’s National Mission for Financial Inclusion.PDF p. 88
    • India’s Financial Inclusion Index increased from 53.9 in 2021 to 67 in March 2025.PDF p. 88
    • In January 2015, Guinness World Records recognised 18,096,130 bank accounts opened in a single week (from August 23-29, 2014) under the Department of Financial Services campaign.PDF p. 88

    Major Features and BenefitsPDF p. 88

    • Eligible account holders receive a RuPay debit card, accepted at ATMs and most Point-of-Sale terminals. Banks had issued 41.29 crore cards by 19 August 2026, promoting digital payments.PDF p. 88
    • Accident insurance cover increased from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh for new accounts opened after August 28, 2018.PDF p. 88
    • An overdraft of up to ₹10,000 is available to one eligible account holder per household, ordinarily after six months of satisfactory account operation and subject to prescribed conditions.PDF p. 88

    Progress so FarPDF p. 89

    • Accounts increased approximately fourfold from 14.72 crore in 2015 to 59.09 crore by 19 August 2026. Rural and semi-urban areas held 45.95 crore accounts, or 77.8%, while urban and metropolitan areas held 13.14 crore.PDF p. 89
    • Women held 32.92 crore accounts, or approximately 55.7% of the total, as of 19 August 2026, reflecting greater gender equality in formal financial access.PDF p. 89
    • Deposits increased approximately twentyfold from ₹15,670 crore in March 2015 to ₹3,16,514 crore in August 2026. Average deposits reached ₹5,356 per account on 19 August 2026.PDF p. 89

    CBDC-Based Food Subsidy Distribution under PMGKAYPDF p. 89

    • The Government of India has introduced a Central Bank Digital Currency-based Direct Benefit Transfer (CBDC-based DBT) system under the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY) . Under this model, eligible beneficiaries receive food subsidies as programmable Digital Rupee tokens in their CBDC wallets instead of receiving the subsidy through conventional bank-account transfers.PDF p. 89

    BackgroundPDF p. 89

    • The Digital Rupee , also known as the e₹ or e-rupee, is a tokenised digital form of the Indian rupee issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as a Central Bank Digital Currency.PDF p. 89
    • Chandigarh was among the early adopters of food- subsidy DBT in September 2015 , when it shifted from physical distribution of subsidised foodgrains to direct subsidy transfers into beneficiaries’ Aadhaar-linked bank accounts.PDF p. 89
    • CBDC based food subsidy was initiated on a pilot basis on February 15, 2026 by Home Minister Amit Shah in Gujarat and later on February 26, 2026 by Prahlad Joshi in Pducherry as a pilot initiative.PDF p. 89
    • The Government launched CBDC-based DBT for PMGKAY beneficiaries in Chandigarh and Dadra & Nagar Haveli on August 14, 2026.PDF p. 89
    • The initiative was launched by Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare Shivraj Singh Chouhan.PDF p. 89

    20 Polymer BanknotesPDF p. 89

    • The Government of India has approved a proposal by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for field trials of ₹10 and ₹20 polymer banknotes.PDF p. 89

    Key FactsPDF p. 89

    • The RBI proposed one billion notes of each denomination, totalling 200 crore notes with a face value of approximately ₹3,000 crore. The Government informed Parliament of the approval in 2026, when procurement remained at an initial stage. Regular issuance may be considered only after successful trials.PDF p. 89
    • The RBI submitted the proposal under Sections 24 and 25 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, following its Central Board’s recommendation. Section 24 covers the banknote denominations whereas Section 25 covers design, form and materials. Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL), an RBI subsidiary, initiated polymer-substrate procurement.PDF p. 89
    • Polymer banknotes use a non-fibrous, non-porous plastic film. Existing Indian paper banknotes use long cotton fibres from cotton comber and cotton linter.PDF p. 89
    • Polymer notes will circulate alongside existing ₹10 and ₹20 paper notes, which will remain legal tender. Trials will assess cleanliness, security, handling and suitability for India’s cash economy.PDF p. 89

    Global ExperiencePDF p. 89

    • Australia first issued a polymer banknote in 1988. More than 60 countries reportedly use polymer currency, including Canada, the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Singapore.PDF p. 89
    • Currency in CirculationPDF p. 89
    • According to the supplied RBI figures, currency in circulation rose 12% year-on-year to ₹41.23 lakh crore (banknotes alone excluding coins) at the end of March 2026 ( ₹40,814 coins in circulation). ₹500 notes represented approximately 86% of banknotes’ total value. Printing expenditure reportedly fell nearly 24% to ₹4,875 crore in 2025–26, mainly because of lower printing requirements.PDF p. 89

    Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026PDF p. 89

    • The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 came into force on October 1, 2026. The Act replaces the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 with a technology-neutral framework recognising physical, electronic and digi tal banking records as evidence. The definition of bankers’ books includes records at off site, virtual, cloud, backup and disaster recovery locations. Banks and bankers also include post office savings bank and money order offices.PDF p. 89

    Legislative BackgroundPDF p. 89

    • The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on 5 August 2026 and the Rajya Sabha on 10 August. Presidential assent followed on 13 August 2026.PDF p. 89

    Major ProvisionsPDF p. 89, 90

    • The first schedule applies to copies of books maintained in written or physical form. The second schedule applies to copies of books maintained electronically, digitally or through other data storage mechanism.PDF p. 89
    • Certification of Banking Records – Certificates must confirm accuracy and be authenticated manually, digitally or electronically by an authorised bank officer.PDF p. 89
    • Conditions for Digital Records – Digital records are admissible if created and stored in the ordinary course of banking through regularly used, properly functioning systems.PDF p. 89
    • Evidentiary Value – Certified copies are prima facie, not conclusive, evidence where original entries are legally admissible.PDF p. 90
    • Extension to Financial-Sector Entities – The Central Government may extend coverage by notification. NBFCs, payment aggregators and fintech firms are covered only if notified or under another law.PDF p. 90
    • Legal Proceedings and Production of Records – Proceedings include court cases, arbitration, investigations and inquiries.PDF p. 90

    Indian Statistical Institute Bill 2026PDF p. 90

    • Introduced in the Lok Sabha on 3 August 2026, the Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026 seeks to replace the 1959 Act (came into force on April 1, 1960). It would convert ISI into a statutory body corporate while retaining its status as an institution of national importance.PDF p. 90

    Change in Legal StatusPDF p. 90

    • Body-corporate status would provide clearer legal authority and institutional continuity. ISI would remain under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.PDF p. 90

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 90

    • The President of India would be the Visitor, empowered to order reviews or inquiries and issue binding directions. The Visitor would nominate the Board’s Chairperson on the Centre’s recommendation.PDF p. 90
    • Admission and Reservation – Admissions would follow transparent, merit-based criteria without discrimination.PDF p. 90
    • An 11-member Board would replace the 33-member Council as the principal policy-making and executive body, accountable to the Centre. It would comprise the Chairperson, government representatives, four external experts and four ISI representatives.PDF p. 90
    • The Board would approve budgets, plans, fees and regulations, reorganise academic units and award degrees on the Academic Council’s recommendation.PDF p. 90
    • The Director-led Academic Council would include Centre-Directors, all full-time Professors, selected faculty and the Dean of Academic Affairs.PDF p. 90
    • Director – The Director would be the Chief Executive Officer, managing daily administration and implementing institutional decisions.PDF p. 90
    • ISI may receive government grants after parliamentary appropriation, earn revenue, accept donations and maintain funds.PDF p. 90

    VB – G RAM G Act, 2025PDF p. 90

    • The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, or VB-G RAM G Act, is India’s statutory framework for rural wag e employment and village development. It came into force across rural India on July 1, 2026, repealing the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA).PDF p. 90

    About the NewsPDF p. 90

    • Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan released over ₹25,000 crore as the first installment, called the Mother Sanction, to support timely wage payments. A total ₹7.5 lakh crore (as on July, 2026) will be invested in 2.86 lakh Panchayats over the next five years. Wage rates have increased by around 10 percent on average.PDF p. 90
    • The Act guarantees wage employment, strengthens village economies and promotes sustainable livelihoods. It links employment with productive public assets, transparency, convergence, climate resilience and local economic development, following “Rozgar Bhi, Samman Bhi”, or employment with dignity.PDF p. 90

    Key Features of the VB-G RAM G ActPDF p. 90

    • The Act increases the employment guarantee from 100 to 125 days per financial year for rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work.PDF p. 90
    • The notified minimum wage floor for 2026–27 is ₹300 per day.PDF p. 90
    • Wages should be paid weekly or within fifteen days of work and muster-roll closure measures delayed compensation.PDF p. 90
    • Delays attract compensation of 0.05 percent of unpaid wages per day beyond the sixteenth day after closure.PDF p. 90
    • Existing e-KYC-verified job cards remain valid until Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards are issued. Workers may register at Gram Panchayats, and pending e-KYC cannot justify denial of employment.PDF p. 90
    • Work may be demanded orally, through Form-6 or digitally.PDF p. 90
    • Failure to provide employment within the prescribed timeframe entitles workers to unemployment allowance of at least one-fourth of the notified wage for the first thirty days of the financial year and one-half for the remaining period.PDF p. 90
    • Four Priority Areas – Water security; Rural infrastructure; Livelihood infrastructure; Climate resilience.PDF p. 90
    • Funding Pattern – The Act operates as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, with a 90:10 funding ratio for Northeastern and Himalayan States (like Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir); and it is 60 : 40 for other States and UTs with legislatures.PDF p. 90
    • UTs without legislatures receive full Central funding. Central allocations follow objective, rule- based parameters. States bear expenditure beyond normative allocations and must distribute funds transparently according to local needs.PDF p. 90
    • Budgetary Commitment – For FY 2026–27, the Central share is ₹95,692.31 crore, described as the largest Budget Estimate allocation for a rural employment programme. Including the estimated State share, total outlay is expected to exceed ₹1.51 lakh crore.PDF p. 90

    Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code Completes 10 YearsPDF p. 92

    • The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 completed ten year milestone in 2026 (It was enacted on May 28, 2016 ). Over the last decade, the IBC has moved India’s insolvency regime away from delay-based liquidation towards corporate revival and preservation of enterprise value. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India was established on October 1, 2016.PDF p. 92

    Resolution and Recovery PerformancePDF p. 92

    • As of March 31, 2026, a total of 1,419 cases had resulted in approved resolution plans under the IBC.PDF p. 92
    • The IBC resolution process has facilitated realisation of more than `4 lakh crore for creditors.PDF p. 92
    • The amount realised by creditors was around 95 percent of the fair value of the assets.PDF p. 92
    • The amount realised was also around 167 percent of the liquidation value, showing that resolution under the IBC helped preserve enterprise value.PDF p. 92
    • Till March 31, 2026, a total of 8,987 cases had been admitted under the IBC framework.PDF p. 92
    • Out of these admitted cases, 7,102 cases had reached closure.PDF p. 92
    • Among the closed cases, 4,099 companies were successfully rescued.PDF p. 92
    • For Domestic Operations gross NPA ratio of the Scheduled Commercial Banks stood at 2.15 percent as of September 30, 2025.PDF p. 92
    • Scheduled Commercial Banks recovered a total of `1.04 lakh crore through various recovery channels for FY 2024-25.PDF p. 92
    • Out of this, nearly `0.54 lakh crore was realised through the IBC process.PDF p. 92
    • This means that about 52.4 percent of total recoveries by Scheduled Commercial Banks came through the IBC route.PDF p. 92

    10 Years of UPIPDF p. 92

    • On April 11, 2026, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) completed 10 years since its pilot launch in 2016. UPI has evolved from a digital payment experiment into the backbone of India’s digital economy. It recorded an all-time high of 22.64 billion transactions in March 2026 (It accounted for more than 81% of India’s volume of total retail payment transaction in FY 2024-25).PDF p. 92
    • UPI recorded 24.51 billion transactions in August, 2026.     Income-Tax Act, 2025PDF p. 92

    • The Income-tax Act, 2025 has come into force from 1 April 2026 , replacing the six-decade-old Income- tax Act, 1961. The reform aims to modernise India’s tax system and make it more aligned with current economic realities. It simplifies language, structure and tax compliance while improving the efficiency of ta x administration.PDF p. 92

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 92

    Operational and Structural ChangesPDF p. 92, 93

    • The Central Board of Direct Taxes has notified the Income-tax Rules, 2026 to implement the provisions of the new Act.PDF p. 92
    • A major procedural reform is the introduction of Form 130, which replaces the traditional Form 16 (TDS certificate issued by employers).PDF p. 92
    • The act replaces the concepts of ‘Assessment Year (AY)’ and ‘Previous Year’ with ‘Tax Year’. The Financial Year (FY) continues to remain relevant in the Act.PDF p. 92
    • A single unified concept called the “Tax Year” has been introduced for simplification. Income Tax Act 2025 vs Income Tax Act 1961 Feature Income Tax Act, 1961 Income Tax Act, 2025 Complexity 819+ sections and 298 Chapters 536 Sections, 23 Chapters, 16 SchedulesPDF p. 92
    • Language Archaic, legalistic and dense Modern, plain English and simplified Timeline Concept Dual concept of ‘Previous Year and ‘Assessment Year Only a Single ‘Tax Year’ TDS/TCS Structure Scattered across dozens of sections Consolidated sections 392, 393 and 394 Effective Zero Tax Up to `7 Lakh (For AY - 2025-26) Up to `12 Lakh as per new regime (For AY 2026-27) Standard Deduction `50,000 (For AY 2025-26) `75,000 (For AY 2026-27) Digital Powers Limited statutory definitions Statutory access to cloud, email and social mediaPDF p. 93

    Revenue DataPDF p. 93

    • According to the Central Board of Direct Taxes, India’s gross direct tax collection for 2025–26 stood at `7.99 lakh crore. Report of the 16th Finance Commission (2026–31) The Finance Commission is a constitutional body under Article 280 of the Constitution, constituted by the President every five years (or earlier) to recommend the principles governing Centre–State fiscal relations.PDF p. 93
    • The 16 th Finance Commission was constituted on December 31, 2023 under the Chairmanship of Dr. Arvind Panagariya (Article 280).PDF p. 93

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 93

    • The 16 th Finance Commission covers the period 2026–27 to 2030–31 . It submitted its report on 17 November 2025, and it was tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2026.PDF p. 93
    • The Commission has not recommended three grant categories recommended by the 15th Finance Commission, namely revenue deficit grants, sector- specific grants, and state-specific grants.PDF p. 93
    • The Commission has recommended that the States’ vertical share remain 41% of the divisible pool of Union taxes.PDF p. 93
    • The weights are 42.5% for per-capita income distance (GSDP), 17.5% for population (2011), 10% for demographic performance, 10% for area, 10% for forest, and 10% for contribution to GDP .PDF p. 93
    • The Commission has recommended total grants of about `9.47 lakh crore for 2026–31. Of this, about `7.91 lakh crore is for local bodies and `1.56 lakh crore is the Union share for disaster management grants.PDF p. 93
    • The Commission has recommended a Special Infrastructure Component of `56,100 crore for selected urban local bodies for comprehensive wastewater management in urban growth centres.PDF p. 93
    • It has also recommended an Urbanisation Premium of `10,000 crore for the full award period.PDF p. 93
    • The Commission has recommended a total disaster management corpus of `2,04,401 crore for SDRF and SDMF together for 2026–31.PDF p. 93
    • The Commission has recommended that the Centre reduce its fiscal deficit to 3.5% of GDP by 2030–31.PDF p. 93
    • It has recommended that the States’ annual fiscal deficit ceiling remain 3% of GSDP excluding loans under Special Assistane to States for Capital Investment (SASCI).PDF p. 93
    • The Commission projects that combined debt of the Centre and States will decline from 77.3% of GDP in 2026–27 to 73.1% in 2030–31.PDF p. 93

    • State 15 th FC 16 th FC Uttar Pradesh 17.94 17.62 Bihar 10.06 9.95 Maharashtra 6.32 6.44 Rajasthan 6.03 5.93 B. Key Policy Documents/EventsPDF p. 93

    National Social Assistance ProgrammePDF p. 93

    • On October 14, 2026 , the Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi , approved the continuation of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) from FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31, with a total outlay of ₹53,428 crore over five years.PDF p. 93
    • The programme provides basic assistance to elderly persons, widows and persons with disabilities from poor households, as well as families affected by the death of their primary breadwinner. It was launched on 15 August 1995.PDF p. 93

    Approved ChangesPDF p. 93, 94

    • The following new names have been approved for the programme and its four sub-schemes: Previous name Approved name National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS) Pradhan Mantri Vriddhavastha Pension Yojana Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS) Pradhan Mantri Vidhwa Pension YojanaPDF p. 93
    • Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS) Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana National Family Benefit Scheme Pradhan Mantri Parivar Labh YojanaPDF p. 94
    • Under the disability pension scheme, monthly central assistance of ₹375 for beneficiaries aged 0–79 years and ₹625 for those aged 80 years and above has been approved.PDF p. 94
    • The disability eligibility threshold will be reduced from the previous 80% to benchmark disability of at least 40%. Eligibility will begin from birth.PDF p. 94
    • The old age pension, widow pension and family benefit schemes have been approved for continuation in their existing form. The announcement states that 3.20 crore beneficiaries across 36 states and Union Territories will benefit.PDF p. 94

    Vital Statistics of India Based on the Civil Registration System 2024PDF p. 94

    • India recorded an estimated 99.1% of births and 99.4% of deaths in 2024, marking a major improvement in the coverage of its Civil Registration System (CRS). The report covers events registered between 1 Janu ary and 31 December 2024. It compiles information received from the Chief Registrars of Births and Deaths of the States and Union Territories. The report covers all states except Sikkim due to partial supply of information.PDF p. 94

    Sample Registration System (SRS) Bulletin 2024PDF p. 96

    • The Sample Registration System (SRS) Bulletin for 2024 (Volume 59-I) and the Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality (2022-24) were officially released by the Registrar General of India on May 20, 2026. The SRS Bulletin 2024 was released by the Office of the Registrar General of India.PDF p. 96
    • SRS provides annual estimates of important demographic indicators in India.PDF p. 96
    • It gives data on Birth Rate, Death Rate, Natural Growth Rate and Infant Mortality Rate.PDF p. 96

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 96, 97

    • Birth Rate means the number of live births per thousand population in a year.PDF p. 96
    • Birth Rate is an important indicator of fertility and population growth.PDF p. 96
    • India’s Birth Rate declined from 36.9 in 1971 to 18.3 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • During the last decade, India’s Birth Rate declined from 21.0 in 2014 to 18.3 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • This shows a decline of about 13% in the last ten years.PDF p. 97
    • The rural Birth Rate declined from 22.7 in 2014 to 20.2 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • The urban Birth Rate declined from 17.4 in 2014 to 14.7 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • In 2024, the Birth Rate was 20.2 in rural areas and 14.7 in urban areas.PDF p. 97
    • Bihar had the highest Birth Rate at 26.8.PDF p. 97
    • Andaman and Nicobar Islands had the lowest Birth Rate at 9.9.PDF p. 97
    • Death Rate means the number of deaths per thousand population in a year.PDF p. 97
    • India’s Death Rate declined from 14.9 in 1971 to 6.4 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • In 2024, India’s total Death Rate was 6.4.PDF p. 97
    • The rural Death Rate was 6.8 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • The urban Death Rate was 5.6 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • The rural Death Rate remained the same in 2023 and 2024 at 6.8.PDF p. 97
    • The urban Death Rate declined slightly from 5.7 in 2023 to 5.6 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • Chhattisgarh recorded the highest Death Rate at 8.4.PDF p. 97
    • Chandigarh recorded the lowest Death Rate at 3.9.PDF p. 97
    • The male Death Rate was 7.1.PDF p. 97
    • The female Death Rate was 5.6.PDF p. 97
    • The data shows that the male Death Rate was higher than the female Death Rate.PDF p. 97
    • Male IMR was 24 and female IMR was 25.PDF p. 97
    • Rural IMR was 27 and urban IMR was 17.PDF p. 97
    • In rural areas, male IMR was 27 and female IMR was 28.PDF p. 97
    • In urban areas, male IMR was 17 and female IMR was 16.PDF p. 97
    • Natural Growth Rate is the difference between Birth Rate and Death Rate.PDF p. 97
    • India’s Natural Growth Rate in 2024 was 11.9.PDF p. 97
    • The rural Natural Growth Rate was 13.5.PDF p. 97
    • The urban Natural Growth Rate was 9.0.PDF p. 97
    • Bihar had a high Natural Growth Rate of 20.8.PDF p. 97
    • Kerala had a low Natural Growth Rate of 3.9.PDF p. 97
    • Infant Mortality Rate is commonly called IMR.PDF p. 97
    • India’s IMR in 2024 was 24 infant deaths per thousand live births.PDF p. 97
    • India’s IMR declined from 129 in 1971 to 24 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • India’s IMR declined from 39 in 2014 to 24 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • This shows a decline of about 38% in the last decade.PDF p. 97
    • Rural IMR declined from 43 in 2014 to 27 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • Urban IMR declined from 26 in 2014 to 17 in 2024.PDF p. 97
    • In 2024, rural IMR was 27 and urban IMR was 17.PDF p. 97
    • Chhattisgarh recorded the highest IMR at 36.PDF p. 97
    • Manipur recorded the lowest IMR at 2 (estimate covers 2022-24).PDF p. 97
    • At the national level, about one in every 42 infants died before completing one year of life.PDF p. 97
    • India’s maternal mortality ratio was 87 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in SRS 2022-24, compared with 130 in 2014-16.PDF p. 97

    Sample CoveragePDF p. 97

    • The SRS Bulletin 2024 covered 8,839 sample units across India.PDF p. 97
    • Out of these, 4,960 sample units were rural and 3,879 were urban.PDF p. 97
    • The total population covered was about 8.981 million.PDF p. 97

    MoSPI Launches New Logo and MascotPDF p. 97

    • The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) unveiled its new logo and new mascot on 1 January 2026 to modernise its institutional identity, strengthen public outreach, and reinforce the role of official statistics in nation- building.PDF p. 97
    • The Ashoka Chakra in the logo represents truth, transparency, and good governance.PDF p. 97
    • The Rupee symbol ( `) at the centre underlines the role of statistics in economic planning, policy design, and national growth.PDF p. 97
    • The design uses numbers and statistical symbols to indicate modern data systems and statistical science.PDF p. 97
    • The upward growth bar conveys progress and explains how credible data supports sustainable economic growth.PDF p. 97
    • The colour scheme–saffron, white, green, and deep blue–is used to represent national values such as growth, truth, sustainability, stability, and knowledge, strengthening the credibility of official statistics.PDF p. 97
    • The logo carries the message “Data for Development”.PDF p. 97

    New MascotPDF p. 97, 98

    • MoSPI introduced a mascot named “सांख्य⼿की” as a citizen-centric character to make statistics simple, relatable, and engaging for the public.PDF p. 97
    • “सांख्य⼿की” will be used across National Sample Surveys in the NSS wing of NSO (earlier called NSSO) for its outreach, awareness campaigns, educational content, digital platforms, and public events to encourage participation and trust in official data.PDF p. 97
    • New Logo for Regional Rural BanksPDF p. 97
    • The Ministry of Finance (Government of India) unveiled a new common logo for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) on 18 December 2025. The main purpose is to create a single, unified brand identity for all RRBs across the country, especially after the recent restructuring of the RRB system.PDF p. 97
    • A single unified logo has been introduced to reinforce the common identity of Regional Rural Banks nationwide.PDF p. 97
    • The design of the new logo uses specific colours to symbolically represent the objectives of RRBs.PDF p. 97
    • The dark blue colour in the logo represents finance, and trust.PDF p. 97
    • The green colour in the logo symbolizes life and growth.PDF p. 97

    Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics (BAHS) 2025PDF p. 99

    • On November 26, 2025, in celebration of National Milk Day, the Minister of State for Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying and Panchayati Raj, Prof. S.P . Singh Baghel, ceremoniously released the Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics 2025.PDF p. 99

    Key Highlights of the EventPDF p. 100

    • The Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics (BAHS) 2025 is based on the results of the Integrated Sample Survey (ISS) conducted from March 1, 2024, to February 28, 2025.PDF p. 100
    • The estimated number of animals involved in milk production , egg-laying birds , animals slaughtered, and sheep shorn.PDF p. 100

    Key Facts and Data from BAHS 2025PDF p. 100

    • The livestock sector’s Gross Value Added (GVA) increased by nearly 195% (at current prices) from 2014–15 to 2023–24, and it contributed 31% of total Agricultural GVA in 2023–24 and 5.5% of national GVA (current prices).PDF p. 100
    • The total value of livestock product exports reached `66,249 crore in 2024–25, with exports driven largely by the meat industry (including bovine meat and edible offal). 1. Milk Production:PDF p. 100
    • India ranks 1st globally in milk production, with an estimated 247.87 million tonnes for 2024-25, showing a 3.58% increase from the previous year (239.30 million tonnes in 2023-24). The data is based on FAO 2023 rankings.PDF p. 100
    • Per Capita Availability : The availability has risen from 319 g/day in 2014-15 to 485 g/day in 2024-25.PDF p. 100
    • Top 5 states together contribute 54.09% of India’s total milk production. 2. Egg Production:PDF p. 100
    • India ranks 2nd globally in egg production, with an estimated 149.11 billion eggs for 2024-25, showing a 4.44% increase from the previous year.PDF p. 100
    • Per Capita Availability: Eggs have increased from 62 eggs/annum in 2014-15 to 106 eggs/annum in 2024-25.PDF p. 100
    • Commercial poultry contributes 84.49% of the total egg production. 3. Meat Production:PDF p. 100
    • India ranks 4th globally in meat production, with an estimated 10.50 million tonnes for 2024-25, reflecting a 2.46% increase.PDF p. 100
    • Poultry accounts for about 50% of total meat production. 4. Wool Production:PDF p. 100
    • Total wool production in India is estimated at 34.57 million kg for 2024-25, showing a 2.63% increase.PDF p. 100
    • These states together contribute 85.98% of the country’s wool output.
