    Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Act, 2026PDF p. 100

    • The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Act, 2026 modernises the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006. It seeks to address delayed payments, improve MSME liquidity, simplify digital registration, strengthen dispute-resolution institutions and rationalise compliance-related penalties.PDF p. 100

    Legislative Background and Present StatusPDF p. 100

    • The measure was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 28 July 2026 by Union Minister for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Jitan Ram Manjhi.PDF p. 100
    • Rajya Sabha passed it on 3 August 2026.PDF p. 100
    • Lok Sabha passed it on 7 August 2026.PDF p. 100
    • It received Presidential assent on 13 August 2026.PDF p. 100
    • It was published as Act No. 16 of 2026 in the Gazette of India.PDF p. 100
    • The act seeks to address delayed payments, improve MSME liquidity, accelerate dispute resolution, simplify registration and compliance, and promote the Ease of Doing Business.PDF p. 100
    • It amends specific provisions of the MSMED Act, 2006 rather than replacing the entire principal legislation.PDF p. 100

    Key Provisions of the MSMED (Amendment) Bill, 2026PDF p. 100, 101

    • Filing of the memorandum will be free and voluntary for all MSMEs.PDF p. 100
    • CPSEs must settle MSME invoices through TReDS, while States may impose the same requirement on their public enterprises and authorities.PDF p. 100
    • TReDS, regulated by the RBI, enables MSMEs to obtain funds against unpaid invoices.PDF p. 100
    • Discounted invoices increased from ₹40,000 crore in 2021–22 to ₹3.47 lakh crore in 2025–26.PDF p. 100
    • States may establish multiple MSEFCs and provide them with adequate infrastructure, digital systems and trained personnel.PDF p. 100
    • Mediation must be completed within 90 days of the first appearance.PDF p. 100
    • Failed mediation must be referred to arbitration within 30 days.PDF p. 101
    • A buyer challenging an award must deposit 75% of the awarded amount.PDF p. 101
    • If the case remains pending beyond six months , the court must release at least 50% of the award to the MSME supplier. Current MSME classification, effective from 1 April 2025 Category Investment limit Turnover limit Micro Up to `2.5 crore Up to `10 crore Small Up to `25 crore Up to `100 crore Medium Up to `125 crore Up to `500 crorePDF p. 101

    Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS)PDF p. 101

    • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) on July 15, 2026. MeiTY announced the notification of MPMS on August 21, 2026 after the Cabinet approval. The scheme has a budgetary outlay of ₹62,500 crore and seeks to strengthen India’s mobile phone manufacturing ecosystem.PDF p. 101

    About the SchemePDF p. 101

    • MPMS aims to expand mobile phone production, deepen domestic value addition, strengthen supply- chain resilience and improve global competitiveness.PDF p. 101
    • The scheme will operate for five years, from FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31.PDF p. 101
    • It succeeds the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Large-Scale Electronics Manufacturing (PLI-LSEM), which ended on 31 March 2026.PDF p. 101
    • Manufacturers will receive incentives ranging from 2.25% to 5% on eligible sales of mobile phones manufactured in India.PDF p. 101
    • An additional incentive of up to 1.5% will be provided for domestic sourcing of key components and sub-assemblies.PDF p. 101
    • Indian brands will receive an additional 3% incentive on eligible sales for product design and research and development.PDF p. 101

    Growth of Electronics ManufacturingPDF p. 101

    • India’s electronics production increased from ₹1.90 lakh crore in 2014–15 to an estimated ₹13.11 lakh crore in 2025–26, representing nearly seven-fold growth.PDF p. 101
    • Electronics exports increased from ₹38,263 crore to ₹4.24 lakh crore during the same period, registering an eleven-fold rise.PDF p. 101
    • Electronic goods became India’s third-largest export category, reaching USD 47.96 billion in FY 2025–26.PDF p. 101
    • Domestic value addition in electronics increased from 15% to 23%.PDF p. 101

    Startup India Completes 10 YearsPDF p. 101

    • Startup India completed 10 years on 16 January 2026. The initiative was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 16 January 2016.PDF p. 101
    • India is now the world’s third-largest startup ecosystem.PDF p. 101
    • The number of startups increased from fewer than 500 in 2014 to more than 2 lakh in 2026.PDF p. 101
    • The number of unicorns increased from 4 to nearly 125. In 2025, a total of 49,429 entities were recognised as startups.PDF p. 101
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi declared 16 January as National Startup Day in 2022.PDF p. 101

    National Startup Awards 5.0PDF p. 101

    • DPIIT announced the results of the fifth National Startup Awards.PDF p. 101
    • The fifth edition included 20 award categories.PDF p. 101
    • The awards also recognised startups from Tier- II and Tier-III cities, deep-tech innovation and emerging sectors.PDF p. 101

    States’ Startup Ranking Framework 5.0PDF p. 101

    • DPIIT also announced the results of the fifth States’ Startup Ranking Framework.PDF p. 101
    • The framework evaluates how States and Union Territories support startup growth.PDF p. 101
    • A total of 34 States and Union Territories participated.PDF p. 101

    SRF 5.0 Key ResultsPDF p. 101

    • Gujarat was the Best Performer in Category A.PDF p. 101
    • Arunachal Pradesh and Goa were the Best Performers in Category B.PDF p. 101
    • Karnataka, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh were Top Performers in Category A.PDF p. 101
    • Himachal Pradesh was a Top Performer in Category B.PDF p. 101
    • Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Telangana and Uttarakhand were Leaders in Category A.PDF p. 101
    • Manipur, Meghalaya and Nagaland were Leaders in Category B.PDF p. 101

    Semiconductor Manufacturing UnitsPDF p. 101, 102

    • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved two more semiconductor projects under the India Semiconductor Mission on 5 May 2026. These projects will be set up in Gujara t with a cumulative investment of around `3,936 crore and are expected to generate employment for 2,230 skilled professionals. The approval includes India’s first commercial Mini/Micro-LED display facility based on Gallium Nitride technology and a semiconductor packaging facility.PDF p. 101
    • The projects have been approved under the India Semiconductor Mission.PDF p. 101
    • The other project will focus on semiconductor assembly and testing for discrete semiconductors.PDF p. 101
    • With these approvals, the total number of approved projects under the India Semiconductor Mission has reached 12.PDF p. 101
    • The cumulative investment under approved semi- conductor projects has reached around `1.64 lakh crore.PDF p. 101
    • S. No. Company Location Type of Facility 1 Crystal Matrix Limited Dholera, Gujarat Integrated compound semiconductor fabrica- tion and ATMP facility 2 Suchi Semicon Private Limited Surat, Gujarat Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test facilityPDF p. 102

    India’s First Chip Fabrication Plant at Commercial Dholera SEZPDF p. 102

    • Tata Semiconductor Manufacturing Private Limited’s SEZ at Dholera, Gujarat is a major milestone, as PIB described it as India’s first chip fabrication plant/ first commercial fab. The Union Cabinet approved the Dholera fab project on February 29, 2024. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry issued the notification on April 9, 2026.PDF p. 102
    • The SEZ will be spread over 66.166 hectares of land.PDF p. 102
    • Its planned capacity is 50,000 wafer starts per month.PDF p. 102
    • It will support electronic hardware, software, and IT/ITES services.PDF p. 102
    • The project is expected to generate employment for about 21,000 persons.PDF p. 102
    • It will be an AI-enabled semiconductor fabrication facility, marking a major step in India’s semiconductor manufacturing capability.     Global Financial Centres Index 2026PDF p. 102

    • The 40th edition of the Global Financial Centres Index (GFCI) was released on September 16, 2026. New York ranked first, London second, Hong Kong third and Singapore fourth.PDF p. 102
    • The index assesses the competitiveness of major financial centres and provides a reference for policy and investment decisions.PDF p. 102

    Basis of the IndexPDF p. 102, 103

    • The index is produced jointly by London-based Z/Yen Partners and the Shenzhen-based China Development Institute.PDF p. 102
    • It is published twice a year, in March and September. The first edition was published in 2007.PDF p. 102
    • For this edition, 139 financial centres were studied. The main index included 117 centres, while another 22 remained on the list of associate centres.PDF p. 102
    • The methodology combined 144 instrumental factors with assessments provided by financial services professionals. It used 39,531 assessments from 6,147 respondents.PDF p. 102
    • The five principal areas of competitiveness are business environment, human capital, infrastructure, financial sector development and reputation.PDF p. 102
    • Shanghai rose one place to fifth, while Tokyo climbed four places to sixth. Seoul and Shenzhen each rose one place, ranking seventh and eighth, respectively.PDF p. 102
    • India’s GIFT City, Mumbai and New Delhi featured in the main index. GIFT City was India’s highest-ranked centre. Indian centre GFCI 39 rank GFCI 40 rank Current rating Change in rank GIFT City, Gujarat 46 37 722 Up 9 places Mumbai 52 49 710 Up 3 places New Delhi 54 56 703 Down 2 placesPDF p. 102
    • Under the financial centre profile classification, GIFT City and Mumbai were categorised as “International Specialists”, while New Delhi was classified as “International Diversified.”PDF p. 103
    • GIFT City stands for Gujarat International Finance Tec-City. It houses India’s first operational International Financial Services Centre (IFSC).PDF p. 103
    • The International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) was established on 27 April 2020 under the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019.PDF p. 103

    India Electric Mobility Index 2025PDF p. 103

    • The India Electric Mobility Index (IEMI) is a composite index that measures the progress of electric mobility across states and Union Territories. Developed by NITI Aayog in collaboration with WRI India , it assesses policy frameworks related to e-mobility and the outcomes of their implementation.PDF p. 103

    Introduction and ObjectivesPDF p. 103

    • IEMI 2025 is the second edition of the index. It was released on 16 September 2026 , covering the assessment period from January to December 2025. The first edition, IEMI 2024, was released on 4 August 2025.PDF p. 103
    • The index has four principal objectives:PDF p. 103
    • To identify states and Union Territories performing well in e-mobility.PDF p. 103
    • To identify the key success factors influencing progress in e-mobility.PDF p. 103
    • To encourage states to adopt a more proactive and ambitious approach towards e-mobility.PDF p. 103
    • To support evidence-based policymaking for sustainable EV growth.PDF p. 103

    Structure of the IndexPDF p. 103

    • IEMI 2025 comprises 16 indicators , classified as Outcome Indicators and Enabler Indicators, across three principal thematic areas. Thematic area Weight What it assesses Progress in transport electrification 50% EV adoption and initiatives supporting it Charging infrastructure readiness 30% Availability of charging facilities and conditions supporting their development Status of EV research and innovation 20% The research and innovation ecosystem for electric mobilityPDF p. 103
    • Scores for individual indicators, thematic areas and the overall index are calculated on a 0–100 scale.PDF p. 103
    • Four performance categories have been defined: Performance category Score Top Performer 65 or above Front Runner 50–64 Emerging Performer 35–49 Aspirant Below 35PDF p. 103

    Overall and Group-wise PerformancePDF p. 103

    • Delhi ran ked first nati onally with 84 poin ts, followed by Mah arashtra with 78, Karnata ka with 73, Chandigarh with 71, and Goa with 65. All five were classified as Top Performers.PDF p. 103
    • Among the large states, Maharashtra ranked first and Karnataka second. They were the only two states in this group classified as Top Performers.PDF p. 103
    • Among the other large states, Tamil Nadu scored 61, Madhya Pradesh 59, Odisha 55, and Andhra Pradesh 52. Telangana, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh scored 51 each. All were classified as Front Runners.PDF p. 103
    • Among the hilly and northeastern states, Manipur led with 46 points, followed by Tripura with 36 and Assam with 35. All three were classified as Emerging Performers.PDF p. 103
    • In the Union Territories and city-states group, Delhi, Chandigarh and Goa were classified as Top Performers.PDF p. 103
    • Between 2024 and 2025, the country’s highest score increased from 77 to 84, while the median score rose from 36 to 40.PDF p. 103
    • Uttar Pradesh scored 51 overall, placing it in the Front Runner category. It scored 58 in the thematic area of progress in transport electrification, also qualifying as a Front Runner in this thematic area.PDF p. 103

    World Economic Outlook Report (October 2026)PDF p. 103

    • The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released the October edition of its World Economic Outlook (WEO) on 13 October 2026 . Titled “Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices,” the report highlights economic resilience under pressure and the need for urgent policy decisions.PDF p. 103

    Global Growth and the Medium-Term OutlookPDF p. 103, 104

    • Global real GDP grew by 3.5% in 2025 . Growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027 . Compared with April 2026, the forecast for 2026 remains unchanged, while the forecast for 2027 has been raised by 0.2 percentage points.PDF p. 103
    • Average annual global growth during 2028–2031 is projected at 3.2%, below the pre-pandemic historical average of 3.7% during 2000–2019. Economy 2025 2026 2027 World 3.5 3.1 3.4 Advanced economies 2.0 2.1 1.8 United States 2.3 2.3 2.3 France 0.9 0.4 0.7 China 5.0 4.5 4.0 India—corresponding financial years 7.8 7.0 7.0 Russia 1.0 0.9 0.9PDF p. 103
    • For India, the 2025, 2026 and 2027 columns refer to FY 2025–26, FY 2026–27 and FY 2027–28 , respectively.PDF p. 103
    • India remains among the fastest-growing major economies. Its real GDP growth is projected at 7.0% in both FY 2026–27 and FY 2027–28 . Compared with April 2026, the forecasts for both years have been raised by 0.5 percentage points.PDF p. 104
    • India’s growth is projected at 7.4% for calendar year 2026 and 7.0% for calendar year 2027. These figures must be distinguished from the financial- year estimates. Real GDP growth is calculated using national accounts with 2022–23 as the base year.PDF p. 104
    • Global headline inflation is projected to rise to 4.7% in 2026 before declining to 4.1% in 2027 . Rising energy and food prices are the principal drivers of inflation in 2026.PDF p. 104

    Global Multidimensional Poverty Index 2026PDF p. 104

    • The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index, 2026, released on October 12, 2026, is jointly published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP) and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI).PDF p. 104

    Key Highlights of the ReportPDF p. 104

    • The 2026 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) report provides a statistical update of the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index, covering 108 countries.PDF p. 104
    • The report highlights that, of the 6.3 billion people living in these countries, 1.2 billion people - or 18.9 per cent - are living in acute multidimensional poverty.PDF p. 104
    • The number of people living in multidimensional poverty has risen for the first time since the index was launched in 2010.PDF p. 104
    • This year’s update of the global MPI database includes new surveys from 13 countries.PDF p. 104
    • The report identifies 33 countries that halved their MPI over the observed periods, including India.PDF p. 104
    • China achieved the fastest halving in the available data–in four years, between 2010 and 2014.PDF p. 104
    • The publication of the 2026 Multidimensional Poverty Index Report was supported by a financial contribution from the Republic of Korea.PDF p. 104
    • Severe poverty: 534 million people , representing 44.6% of multidimensionally poor people , experience severe multidimensional poverty. Another 952 million people are vulnerable to multidimensional poverty.PDF p. 104
    • A total of 617 million children under 18 years of age constitute 51.5% of all multidimensionally poor people. Approximately one in three children is poor, compared with one in seven adults.PDF p. 104
    • 83.3% of poor people (998 million) live in rural areas, compared with 16.7% (200 million) in urban areas. Poverty incidence is 28.7% in rural areas, against 7.0% in urban areas.PDF p. 104
    • Sub-Saharan Africa has both the highest poverty incidence (51.4%) and the largest poor population (616 million). South Asia follows with approximately 393 million poor people, with poverty incidence of 19.9%.PDF p. 104
    • Approximately 65.1% of multidimensionally poor people–779 million–live in middle-income countries.PDF p. 104
    • In 21 countries, more than half the population is multidimensionally poor; 18 of these countries are in Sub-Saharan Africa.PDF p. 104

    Countries at the top and bottomPDF p. 104

    • Lowest poverty: Serbia, with a reported MPI of 0.000 and poverty incidence of 0.1%. The rounded MPI value does not mean poverty is entirely absent.PDF p. 104
    • Highest poverty: Chad, with an MPI of 0.517 and a poverty incidence of 84.2%.PDF p. 104
    • The five countries with the highest MPI values , arranged from highest to lowest, are: Country MPI value Poverty incidence Chad 0.517 84.2% Niger 0.470 79.9% Central African Republic 0.461 80.4% Burundi 0.409 75.1% Madagascar 0.386 68.4%PDF p. 104

    India Specific HighlightsPDF p. 104, 105

    • Based on its 2019–2021 survey, India’s MPI is 0.069, poverty incidence 16.4%, and deprivation intensity 42.0%; 4.2% of the population is severely poor and 18.7% vulnerable.PDF p. 104
    • Between 2005–2006 and 2019–2021 , its MPI declined from 0.283 to 0.069 , while poverty incidence fell from 55.1% to 16.4%.PDF p. 104
    • The report estimates that 237.849 million people (approximately 23.78 crore) as multidimensi- onally poor based on the 2024 population , the largest absolute number among the countries covered.PDF p. 104
    • This is a population-based projection using the older survey poverty rate, not a new 2024 or 2026 poverty survey. About Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) Aspect Description About The MPI is a comprehensive measure that goes beyond income to capture the multiple and overlapping deprivations faced by individuals. It complements income-based poverty measures (like the USD 3.00/day threshold) by including non-monetary dimensions of poverty for better policy targeting. Structure 3 Dimensions → 10 Indicators (covering health, education, and living standards). Weighting System - Each dimension has equal weight (1/3 each). - Health (2 indicators) → 1/6 weight each. - Education (2 indicators) → 1/6 weight each. - Standard of Living (6 indicators) → 1/18 weight each.PDF p. 104
    • Range MPI values range from 0 to 1 . Higher values indicate greater poverty. Identification of the Poor A person is considered multi- dimensionally poor if their deprivation scores ≥ 33.3% (1/3).PDF p. 105

    India’s Foreign Exchange Reserves Scale Record HighPDF p. 105

    • India’s foreign exchange reserves reached an all-time high of $729.328 billion in the week ended August 21, 2026, according to data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).PDF p. 105
    • The reserves increased by $12.422 billion during the week , surpassing the previous record of $728.494 billion , registered in the week ended February 27, 2026.PDF p. 105
    • This was the eighth consecutive weekly increase in India’s reserves. Over these eight weeks, the country’s foreign exchange reserves expanded by approximately $63 billion.PDF p. 105

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 105

    • India’s foreign exchange reserves reached a record $729.328 billion as of August 21, 2026. The foreign exchange reaches to $785.706 billion as of September 4, 2026.PDF p. 105
    • FCNR(B) deposits accounted for the largest share, attracting $65.40 billion.PDF p. 105
    • The scheme exceeded the scale of the RBI’s 2013 FCNR(B) initiative, which had mobilised about $26 billion in roughly three months.PDF p. 105
    • India’s gold reserves increased by $2.801 billion to $114.218 billion . Special Drawing Rights rose by $112 million to $18.852 billion , while India’s reserve position with the International Monetary Fund increased by $26 million to $4.925 billion.     Index of Services Production (ISP)PDF p. 105

    • On July 14, 2026, the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) released India’s first Trial Index of Services Production for April 2026.PDF p. 105

    IntroductionPDF p. 105

    • The ISP is India’s first high-frequency macroeconomic indicator measuring short-term changes in the volume of formal services output relative to a base year. It fills a statistical gap because the Index of Industrial Production does not capture changes in services activity.PDF p. 105

    First Trial ReleasePDF p. 105

    • As of July 24, 2026, the trial covered 19 sub-sectors representing about 60% of the services economy, without a single overall ISP .PDF p. 105
    • Fourteen sub-sectors recorded double-digit year- on-year growth in April 2026 compared with April 2025.PDF p. 105

    Top-Performing Sub-sectors in April 2026PDF p. 105

    • Accommodation and food services led year-on-year growth at 37.2%, followed by retail trade (30.8%), administrative and support services (28.7%), real estate (27.7%) and telecommunications (22.8%).PDF p. 105

    Top-Performing Sub-sectors in 2025–26PDF p. 105

    • During 2025–26, annual growth was 35.6% in accommodation and food services, 30.5% in retail trade, 25.1% in repair services, 23.6% in wholesale trade and 22.6% in road transport.PDF p. 105

    Base YearPDF p. 105

    • The base year is 2024–25, aligning the ISP with revised economic indicators and broadly with the new Consumer Price Index series, whose reference year is 2024.PDF p. 105

    Investment Friendliness IndexPDF p. 105

    • During NITI Aayog’s Ninth Governing Council meeting in July 2024, the Prime Minister called for an “Investment-Friendly Charter” covering the policies , programmes and processes required to attract investment.PDF p. 105
    • The index covers all 28 States and eight Union Territories of India.PDF p. 105
    • It uses a 100-point scale to assess the investment environment of States and Union Territories.PDF p. 105
    • The index serves as a benchmark that can help states identify weaknesses and improve their investment ecosystems.PDF p. 105

    Initial Selection of IndicatorsPDF p. 105

    • An initial list of 953 indicators was prepared across the eight pillars. Pillar Weight Indicators Infrastructure 25% 24 Business climate 20% 18 Resources 15% 17 Regulatory ease 12% 8 Government policy 10% 4 Financial health 7% 3 Institutional environment 6% 6 Environmental resilience 5% 4 Total 100% 84PDF p. 105

    • The five top performers were Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Goa, and Odisha.PDF p. 106

    Export Preparedness Index (EPI) 2024PDF p. 108

    • NITI Aayog released the Export Preparedness Index (EPI) 2024 on 14 January 2026 to assess export readiness across India’s States and Union Territories (UTs).PDF p. 108
    • The EPI 2024 is a composite, evidence-based as - sessment that evaluates how prepared States/UTs are to build competitive export ecosystems through infrastructure, business conditions, governance sup- port, and export outcomes.PDF p. 108
    • The first EPI was published in August 2020, and EPI 2024 is the 4th edition.PDF p. 108
    • The index is aligned with India’s objective of achieving USD 1 trillion in merchandise exports by 2030 and the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.PDF p. 108
    • The four pillars and 13 Sub-pillars are follows – Export Infrastructure (20%) Utilities; Logistics Business Ecosystem (40%) Macro-economy; Cost competitiveness; Human capital; Finance and credit accessibility; MSME ecosystem; Industrial and innovation environment Policy & Governance (20%) State-level policy support and governance; Regulatory environment & compliance Export Performance (20%) State-level exports and trends; Export promotion and facilitation; Export portfolio and market accessPDF p. 108

    Hurun Global Rich List 2026PDF p. 109

    • The Hurun Global Rich List 2026 was released by the Hurun Research Institute in March, 2026. The report highlights a sharp rise in the number of billionaires in India.PDF p. 109

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 109, 110

    • The report shows that India added 57 new billionaires during the year (2025–26).PDF p. 109
    • With this, the total number of Indian billionaires increased to 308.PDF p. 109
    • India remains the third-largest billionaire hub in the world.PDF p. 109
    • The United States and China are ahead of India in the global billionaire ranking.PDF p. 109
    • India is now one of the fastest-growing hubs of wealth creation globally.PDF p. 109
    • The combined wealth of Indian billionaires rose by 10%.PDF p. 109
    • The total wealth of Indian billionaires reached around `112.6 trillion.PDF p. 109
    • The average wealth of Indian billionaires stood at `36,570 crore.PDF p. 109
    • The average wealth of Indian billionaires is now higher than the average wealth of billionaires in China.PDF p. 109
    • Mumbai remains India’s top billionaire hub (95 billionaires).PDF p. 109
    • Mumbai added 15 new billionaires during the year.PDF p. 109
    • This growth was higher than that of New York, which added 14 new billionaires.PDF p. 109
    • Shenzhen became Asia’s billionaire capital with 132 billionaires.PDF p. 109
    • Mukesh Ambani (Chairman of Reliance Industries) remains the richest person in India.PDF p. 109
    • G. MiscellaneousPDF p. 110

    Women Towards Better Livelihoods Through Work and EnterprisePDF p. 110

    • The expansion of women’s economic participation in India is evident across employment, entrepreneurship, manufacturing and research. The government presented key figures on women’s employment and entrepreneurship on October 15, 2026.PDF p. 110

    Women’s EmploymentPDF p. 110

    • For women aged 15 years and above, LFPR based on usual status—principal and subsidiary activities—was 23.3% in 2017–18 . It stood at 40.0% in 2025 . The corresponding female WPR figures for the same age group were 22.0% and 38.8%, respectively.PDF p. 110
    • During 2025, an average of approximately 20 crore women aged 15 years and above were employed.PDF p. 110

    Women’s Role in EntrepreneurshipPDF p. 110

    • Approximately 3.69 crore registered women- owned MSMEs as of October 2026, representing a share of approximately 38% (October 15, 2026).PDF p. 110
    • The MSME dashboard dated 17 October 2026 recorded 3,71,97,598 registrations in the women’s category, including those under Udyam Registration and the Udyam Assist Platform . Their calculated share of the total 9,89,02,198 registrations was approximately 37.61%.PDF p. 110
    • As of 31 March 2026 , more than 1.07 lakh recognised startups had at least one woman director or partner , accounting for approximately 48% of all recognised startups.PDF p. 110
    • Participation in Technical and Highly Skilled FieldsPDF p. 110
    • As of July 2026, women accounted for approximately 70% of the direct workforce in mobile phone manufacturing.PDF p. 110
    • In civil aviation, women were reported to constitute approximately 15% of India’s pilots , one of the highest proportions globally. According to figures reported in June 2025 , women accounted for 15% of air traffic controllers , 11% of flight dispatchers and 33% of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation’s (DGCA) Flight Operations Inspectors.PDF p. 110
    • According to Research and Development Statistics 2025–26 , women’s share in research careers in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) was 13% in 2000–01 , 18.6% in 2020–21 and 29% in 2023–24 . These figures relate to the research workforce.PDF p. 110

    NITI Aayog Report on Regulatory Reforms in Professional ServicesPDF p. 110

    • On August 10, 2026 , NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri launched India’s Services Sector: Insights on Regulatory Regime in Professional Services . It is the third report under the Services Thematic Series; the related PIB release was published on August 14, 2026. It identifies reforms that could improve regulatory clarity, professional mobility, recognition of qualifications and international competitiveness.PDF p. 110

    Four-Pronged StrategyPDF p. 110

    • 1. Continuous Professional Development for Professionals: Structured CPD and lifelong learning can maintain professional competence as technology and industry practices change. 2. Adoption of Best Practices in Professional Services: Regulators should publish clear eligibility rules, contact details, processing timelines, decisions and review mechanisms and should hold regular consultations. 3. Elevate Professional Services within the Services Value Chain: India should move from routine, cost-based delivery towards research, engineering design, legal analytics, advanced financial modelling and strategic consulting. 4. Advance Emerging Trends in Professional Services: Professionals should build capabilities in artificial intelligence, automation, ESG reporting, carbon accounting, climate-risk assessment, sustainable finance and supply-chain advisory. The report cautions that adopting best practices d oes not mean mechanically copying foreign laws.PDF p. 110

    IIHT SUTRA 2026PDF p. 110

    • Union Textiles Minister Giriraj Singh inaugurated IIHT SUTRA 2026, the first national conclave of the Indian Institutes of Handloom Technology (IIHTs), on 12 August 2026 in New Delhi . The conclave sought to strengthen technical education, research, entrepreneurship, innovation and industry collaboration in India’s handloom sector.PDF p. 110

    Organisation and ThemePDF p. 110

    • The Office of the Development Commissioner (Handlooms) under the Ministry of Textiles organised the conclave at the Dr Ambedkar International Centre, New Delhi.PDF p. 110
    • The event was held under the theme “IIHTs: Weaving the Future of the Indian Handloom Sector–Educate. Innovate. Transform.”PDF p. 110
    • Development Commissioner (Handlooms) Beena M. described IIHT SUTRA as a long-term institutional initiative for creating a collaborative national platform for IIHTs.PDF p. 110
    • The sector supports nearly 3.5 million weavers and allied workers, of whom more than 72% are women.PDF p. 110
    • India’s textile and apparel exports, including handicrafts, reached approximately ₹3.25 trillion in 2025–26.PDF p. 110

    Institutional Network of IIHTsPDF p. 110, 111

    • India has six Central IIHTs and five State IIHTs.PDF p. 110
    • These institutes possess nearly seven decades of experience in handloom-related technical education and skill development.PDF p. 111
    • IIHT alumni contribute to the textile industry, entrepreneurship, exports, research, public institutions and other professional fields.PDF p. 111

    SUMAN Roadmap 2030PDF p. 111

    • Union Health Minister Jagat Prakash Nadda launched the roadmap on June 29, 2026, at the 16 th Conference of the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare.PDF p. 111
    • The roadmap is an evidence-driven framework of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, led by its Maternal Health Division under RMNCHA+N, integrating reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health and nutrition.PDF p. 111
    • It aims to achieve the SDG target of an MMR below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030, reduce neonatal and infant mortality, ensure full service coverage across all States and Union Territories, and achieve zero preventable maternal and newborn deaths.PDF p. 111
    • The SUMAN package promotes early registration, complete antenatal care, quality assessment and adequate institutional stay after delivery. Interventions target 130 districts across 13 States.PDF p. 111
    • SUMAN Panchayats promote antenatal care, institutional delivery, immunisation and zero maternal and infant deaths. “Mothers’ Picnic” promotes awareness.PDF p. 111
    • Digital measures include AI-enabled labour rooms, the JANANI portal and a centralised SUMAN Call Centre.PDF p. 111
    • The roadmap strengthens maternal death surveillance, near-miss reviews, emergency obstetric care and referrals, including the use of Non-Pneumatic Anti- Shock Garment.PDF p. 111

    Income Mobility in India (2014–2025)PDF p. 111

    • The study is based on real per capita income data from the CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey, using a balanced panel of households observed from 2014 to 2025.PDF p. 111
    • The analysis classifies households according to their 2014 per capita income rank, into three groups: Top 10%; Next 40%; and Bottom 50%.PDF p. 111
    • A household is considered:PDF p. 111
    • Upwardly mobile if it moves to a higher group,PDF p. 111
    • Downwardly mobile if it moves to a lower group,PDF p. 111
    • Stable if it remains in the same group.PDF p. 111
    • The share of households facing downward mobility rose from 14% in 2015 to 26.8% in 2025.PDF p. 111
    • The share of households with no change fell sharply from over 70% to below 50%.PDF p. 111
    • Upward mobility also increased, from 14.1% to 23.5%, but this improvement is gradual and trail in rise in downward movement.PDF p. 111
    • Rural India shows the sharpest stress. By 2025, nearly 29% of rural households were worse off than in 2014.PDF p. 111
    • By 2025, around one-fourth or more of households in these groups were worse off than in 2014.PDF p. 111

    India's FDI Inflow in FY 2024–25PDF p. 111

    • According to government estimates, FDI inflows have seen a steady rise from USD 36.05 billion in FY 2013–14 to USD 81.04 billion (provisional) in FY 2024–25, marking a 14% increase from USD 71.28 billion in FY 2023–24.PDF p. 111
    • The services sector emerged as the top recipient of FDI equity in FY 2024–25, attracting 19% of total inflows, followed by computer software and hardware (16%) and trading (8%).PDF p. 111
    • FDI into the services sector rose by 40.77% to USD 9.35 billion from USD 6.64 billion in the previous year.PDF p. 111
    • India is also becoming a hub for manufacturing FDI, which grew by 18% in FY 2024–25, reaching USD 19.04 billion compared with USD 16.12 billion in FY 2023–24.PDF p. 111
    • Maharashtra accounted for the highest share (39%) of total FDI equity inflows in FY 2024–25, followed by Karnataka (13%) and Delhi (12%).PDF p. 111
    • Among source countries, Singapore led with a 30% share, followed by Mauritius (17%) and the United States (11%).PDF p. 111
    • Over the last eleven financial years (2014–25), India attracted FDI worth USD 748.78 billion, reflecting a 143% increase over the previous eleven years (2003– 14), which saw USD 308.38 billion in inflows.PDF p. 111

    News in ShortsPDF p. 111

    First Soil Carbon Payments to Farmers in IndiaPDF p. 111

    • An initiative in India has linked soil carbon sequestration and reductions in greenhouse gas emissions with additional income for farmers. Payments based on verified carbon credits have begun for farmers in Punjab and Haryana.PDF p. 111
    • A payment event was held at Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana, on 14 September 2026. Dr M. L. Jat , Secretary, Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE), and Director General, Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), initiated the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT). Arrangements for digital payments totalling more than ₹2.9 crore to 2,550 farmers in Punjab and Haryana were announced.PDF p. 111
    • Grow Indigo launched the ‘Aadi’ farmer carbon programme in 2019 under ICAR’s technical guidance. During 2019–2022, participating farmers adopted practices such as direct-seeded rice, reduced tillage and crop residue management.PDF p. 111

    India Bans Sugar ExportsPDF p. 111, 112

    • India has prohibited the export of sugar with immediate effect until September 30, 2026, or until further orders, whichever was earlier. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade’s officially notified an “Amendment in Export Policy of Sugar” on May 13, 2026.PDF p. 111
    • The decision changed sugar exports from the “Restricted” category to the “Prohibited” category.PDF p. 112
    • The latest order remained effective till September 30, 2026, or until the government issued further directions.PDF p. 112
    • India’s First Mega Greenfield ShipyardPDF p. 112
    • India has taken an important step towards becoming a major global shipbuilding nation with the proposed development of India’s first mega Greenfield shipyard at Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu. A tripartite Memorandum of Understanding was signed on 20 April 2026 for this project among HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co. Ltd., National Shipbuilding & Heavy Industries Park, Tamil Nadu Limited, and Sagarmala Finance Corporation Limited under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways.PDF p. 112

    India Adopts “One Nation, One Time” FrameworkPDF p. 112

    • The Department of Consumer Affairs notified the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026 on August 27, 2026.PDF p. 112
    • IST will become the standard time reference for official documents, commercial operations, legal contracts, transport and financial activities.PDF p. 112

    Basic Facts About Indian Standard TimePDF p. 112

    • IST is 5 hours and 30 minutes ahead of Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC+5:30.PDF p. 112
    • Its conventional geographical basis is the 82°30′ east longitude, also written as 82.5° E.PDF p. 112
    • The Standard Meridian passes through Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.PDF p. 112

    NABL Accreditation Scheme for Mobile Food Testing LaboratoriesPDF p. 112

    • On August 10, 2026, the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) launched what the government described as India’s first accreditation scheme specifically for Mobile Food Testing Laboratories.PDF p. 112
    • It was launched under the Integrated Assessment Programme at the “Gunvatta Samanvaya” event in New Delhi.PDF p. 112

    India’s First Digital Grievance Redressal System for Gig WorkersPDF p. 112

    • Karnataka has become the first State in India to launch a government-backed digital grievance redressal system for gig workers (Karnataka Platform Based Gig Workers Welfare Board).PDF p. 112
    • Gig workers can now lodge complaints through the Integrated Public Grievance Redressal System portal.PDF p. 112

    Cabinet Approves Technology-Driven SARTHAK-PDS SchemePDF p. 112

    • The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the continuation and integration of the SARTHAK- PDS Scheme on May 27, 2026. The scheme has a central outlay of `25,530 crore and will be implemented during the 16 th Finance Commission award cycle, up to 31 March 2031.PDF p. 112

    Government Notifies Two New SEZs in PuducherryPDF p. 112

    • The Government of India has notified two new Special Economic Zones in the Union Territory of Puducherry. The notification was issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on May 27, 2026, after the proposals were approved by the Board of Approval for SEZs under the Department of Commerce in its 137th meeting held on February 27, 2026. These two SEZs are aimed at accelerating investment, manufacturing activity and job creation in Puducherry. Details of the Two SEZs S. No. Developer Entity Location 1 M/s Oulgaret Municipality (`725 crore) Thattanchavady village, Oulgaret Taluk, Puducherry 2 M/s Pondicherry Industrial Promotion Development and Investment Corporation (`1,250 crore) Karasur village, Villianur Taluk, PuducherryPDF p. 112

    M S Sahoo Committee for NPS ReformsPDF p. 112

    • On 13 January 2026, the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) has constituted a high-level committee to formulate guidelines and regulations to enable a framework for assured payouts under the National Pension System (NPS).PDF p. 112
    • The committee will be chaired by Dr. M. S. Sahoo, founder of Dr. Sahoo Regulatory Chambers and former Chairperson of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI).PDF p. 112
    • The 15-member panel includes a diverse group of experts.PDF p. 112

    Kerala: Declared an ‘Extreme Poverty–Free’ StatePDF p. 112

    • Kerala Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan , on 1 November 2025 , on the occasion of ‘Kerala Piravi’, declared the state ‘extreme poverty–free’ in a special session of the Legislative Assembly. With this declaration, Kerala became the first state in India to achieve this status. Pinarayi Vijayan described this year’s Kerala Piravi as “the birth of a new era” for Kerala.PDF p. 112

    Union Budget 2026–27PDF p. 113

    • Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs, Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman, tabled the Union Budget 2026-27 in the Parliament on February 01, 2026. The highlights of the budget are as follows:PDF p. 113

    Core Theme: 3 KartavyasPDF p. 113

    • The Budget targets faster and more resilient growth by raising productivity and competitiveness amid global volatility.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget aims to build people’s capacities so citizens become partners in prosperity.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget seeks inclusive access to resources and opportunities for every region and section under Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas.PDF p. 113

    Macro & Fiscal Snapshot (BE 2026–27)PDF p. 113

    • Non-debt receipts are estimated at `36.5 lakh crore, and total expenditure is estimated at `53.5 lakh crore.PDF p. 113
    • Centre’s net tax receipts are estimated at `28.7 lakh crore.PDF p. 113
    • Gross market borrowings are estimated at `17.2 lakh crore, and net borrowings (dated securities) are estimated at `11.7 lakh crore.PDF p. 113
    • Fiscal deficit is estimated at 4.3% of GDP, while RE 2025–26 keeps fiscal deficit at 4.4% of GDP.PDF p. 113
    • Debt-to-GDP is estimated at 55.6% (BE 2026–27) versus 56.1% (RE 2025–26).PDF p. 113

    PART-A: InterventionsPDF p. 113

    Kartavya 1: Growth Push (6 Interventions)PDF p. 113

    • (1) Scale manufacturing in 7 strategic/frontier sectorsPDF p. 113
    • The Budget launches Biopharma SHAKTI with `10,000 crore (5 years) to build India as a global biopharma hub.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget expands biopharma capacity via 3 new NIPERs, upgrading 7 NIPERs , and 1,000+ accredited clinical trial sites.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget announces India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 for equipment/materials, full-stack IP , and supply-chain strengthening with industry-led R&D and training.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget raises Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme outlay to `40,000 crore.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget proposes Rare Earth Corridors in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu for activities ranging from mining to manufacturing.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget supports 3 Chemical Parks through a challenge-mode, cluster-based plug-and-play model.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget strengthens capital goods manufacturing through Hi-Tech Tool Rooms, CIE equipment scheme, and a Container Manufacturing scheme with `10,000+ crore (5 years).PDF p. 113
    • The Budget announces an Integrated Textile Programme, including the National Fibre Scheme, cluster modernisation, challenge-mode Mega Textile Parks, and Mahatma Gandhi Gram Swaraj for khadi/handloom/handicrafts. (2) Rejuvenate legacy industrial sectorsPDF p. 113
    • The Budget announces a scheme to revive 200 legacy industrial clusters through tech and infrastructure upgrades. (3) Create “Champion SMEs”PDF p. 113
    • The Budget introduces an SME Growth Fund of `10,000 crore to build future champion firms.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget tops up the Self-Reliant India Fund by `2,000 crore for micro-enterprise risk capital.PDF p. 113
    • The Budget proposes training ‘Corporate Mitras’ through professional institutes to provide support in Tier-II/III areas. (4) Infrastructure pushPDF p. 113
    • Public capex is raised to `12.2 lakh crore in FY 2026–27.PDF p. 113
    • An Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund is proposed to improve private developer confidence.PDF p. 113
    • CPSE real-estate recycling is proposed through dedicated REITs.PDF p. 113
    • A new Dedicated Freight Corridor is proposed from Dankuni to Surat.PDF p. 113
    • 20 new National Waterways are to be operationalised in 5 years, starting with NW-5 (Odisha).PDF p. 113
    • Regional training centres and ship repair ecosystems at Varanasi and Patna are proposed.PDF p. 113
    • A Coastal Cargo Promotion Scheme targets raising waterways/coastal shipping share from 6% to 12% by 2047.PDF p. 113
    • A Seaplane VGF Scheme is proposed for tourism and remote connectivity. (5) Energy securityPDF p. 113
    • `20,000 crore (5 years) is allocated for Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) technologies. (6) City Economic Regions (CERs)PDF p. 113
    • `5,000 crore per CER (5 years) is announced through challenge-mode, reform-cum-results based financing.PDF p. 113
    • Seven High-Speed Rail corridors are proposed: Mumbai–Pune, Pune–Hyderabad, Hyderabad– Bengaluru, Hyderabad–Chennai, Chennai– Bengaluru, Delhi–Varanasi and Varanasi–Siliguri.PDF p. 113

    Banking & Investment EcosystemPDF p. 114

    • A High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat is proposed.PDF p. 114
    • The restructuring PFC and REC is proposed to improve scale and efficiency.PDF p. 114
    • A review of FEMA (Non-debt Instruments) Rules is proposed for a user-friendly FDI framework.PDF p. 114
    • An incentive of `100 crore is announced for a single municipal bond issuance above `1,000 crore.PDF p. 114

    Kartavya 2: Aspirations and CapacityPDF p. 114

    • A high-powered Education to Employment and Enterprise Standing Committee is proposed with a services-sector focus.PDF p. 114
    • Allied health capacity is expanded through new/ upgraded institutions and 1,00,000 Allied Health Professionals (AHP) in 5 years.PDF p. 114
    • Five Regional Medical Hubs are proposed for medical tourism.PDF p. 114
    • Three All India Institutes of Ayurveda are proposed.PDF p. 114
    • Veterinary capacity is expanded by over 20,000 professionals, and a loan-linked subsidy supports private veterinary colleges/hospitals/labs.PDF p. 114
    • AVGC labs are planned through IICT Mumbai in 15,000 schools and 500 colleges.PDF p. 114
    • Five University Townships are proposed near industrial/logistics corridors.PDF p. 114
    • A girls’ hostel in every district is proposed through VGF and capital support.PDF p. 114
    • Tourism measures include upgrading NCHMCT, training 10,000 guides, and establishing a National Destination Digital Knowledge Grid.PDF p. 114
    • 15 archaeological sites are proposed for experiential cultural tourism, and the Khelo India Mission is proposed for sports transformation.PDF p. 114

    Kartavya 3: Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas (Targeted Areas)PDF p. 114

    • The budget aims to enhance farmer’s through 500 reservoirs/Amrit Sarovars and support for high- value crops including coconut, sandalwood, cocoa and cashew, along with a Coconut Promotion Scheme.PDF p. 114
    • Bharat-VISTAAR is proposed as a multilingual AI tool integrating AgriStack and ICAR practice packages.PDF p. 114
    • Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana is proposed for job- ready roles in IT, AVGC, hospitality, and Food & Beverage services.PDF p. 114
    • NIMHANS-2 is proposed in North India, and mental health institutes in Ranchi and Tezpur are to be upgraded.PDF p. 114
    • The Purvodaya/NER focus includes an East Coast Industrial Corridor, 5 tourism destinations, 4,000 e-buses, and a Buddhist Circuit Scheme in NE states.PDF p. 114
    • `1.4 lakh crore is provided as Finance Commission grants for states in FY 2026–27 (as per 16th FC). PART –B : Overall Fiscal FrameworkPDF p. 114
    • The Union Government is estimated to spend `53.47 lakh crore in 2026–27, representing a 7.7% increase over the Revised Estimates (RE) of 2025– 26.PDF p. 114
    • Interest payments constitute about 26% of total expenditure and absorb nearly 40% of revenue receipts, highlighting persistent debt-servicing pressures.PDF p. 114
    • Total receipts (excluding borrowings) are estimated at `36.51 lakh crore , marking a 7.2% increase over the RE of 2025–26, with tax revenue expected to grow by 8%.PDF p. 114
    • The government has projected nominal GDP growth at 10% for 2026–27, reflecting expectations of sustained real growth and moderate inflation.PDF p. 114

    Deficit and Debt TargetsPDF p. 114

    • The revenue deficit is targeted at 1.5% of GDP, unchanged from the revised estimate of 2025–26, indicating continued emphasis on fiscal consolidation.PDF p. 114
    • The fiscal deficit is targeted at 4.3% of GDP , marginally lower than 4.4% of GDP in 2025–26 (RE).PDF p. 114
    • The Centre has reiterated its commitment to reducing outstanding liabilities to around 50% of GDP by March 2031 , with liabilities estimated at 55.6% of GDP in 2026–27.PDF p. 114

    Taxation ProposalsPDF p. 114, 115

    • Income tax slabs remain unchanged for Assessment Year 2026–27, maintaining stability in the personal tax regime.PDF p. 114
    • A tax holiday until 2047 has been granted to foreign companies providing global cloud services using Indian data centres , subject to routing services to Indian customers through Indian resellers.PDF p. 114
    • The tax holiday for IFSC units and Offshore Banking Units has been extended from 10 years to 20 years, with income taxed at 15% thereafter.PDF p. 114
    • All share buybacks are proposed to be taxed as capital gains , with an additional buyback tax on promoters, raising the effective tax rate to 22% for corporate promoters and 30% for non-corporate promoters.PDF p. 114
    • Securities Transaction Tax (STT) rates have been increased for options and futures , signalling a calibrated tightening in capital market taxation.PDF p. 115
    • Interest expenditure deductions against dividend income or mutual fund income have been withdrawn.PDF p. 115
    • Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate has been reduced from 15% to 14% , while MAT credit accumulation is discontinued from April 2026.PDF p. 115
    • A Foreign Assets Disclosure Scheme, 2026 has been introduced for small taxpayers, offering graded relief and immunity subject to compliance.PDF p. 115
    • TCS rates on education and medical remittances, and overseas tour packages have been reduced to 2%, easing the burden on households.PDF p. 115

    Finance and Financial Sector ReformsPDF p. 115

    • A High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat will be constituted to review the banking sector.PDF p. 115
    • The FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules will be simplified to facilitate foreign investment.PDF p. 115
    • Persons Resident Outside India (PROI) will be allowed to invest up to 10% in listed Indian companies under the Portfolio Investment Scheme.PDF p. 115
    • A market-making framework for corporate bonds and incentives for municipal bond issuance have been announced to deepen debt markets.PDF p. 115

    Industry, MSMEs, and CommercePDF p. 115, 116

    • A scheme will be launched to revive 200 legacy industrial clusters through modern technology and infrastructure.     • To create Champion SMEs , the government announced a `10,000 crore SME Growth Fund , top-up of the Self-Reliant India Fund , and liquidity support.PDF p. 116

    Infrastructure and ConnectivityPDF p. 116

    • Public capital expenditure has been increased to `12.2 lakh crore , up from `11.2 lakh crore in 2025–26.PDF p. 116
    • An Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund will be established to crowd in private investment.PDF p. 116
    • New initiatives include five tourism destinations in Purvodaya States , 4,000 electric buses , 20 new National Waterways, and a Surat–Dankuni freight corridor.PDF p. 116
    • Seven high-speed rail corridors and City Economic Regions (CERs) will be developed to support urban-industrial growth.PDF p. 116

    Education, Labour, and Human CapitalPDF p. 116

    • Five university townships will be created along industrial and logistics corridors.PDF p. 116
    • A Standing Committee on Education to Employment and Enterprise will assess skill gaps and the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs.PDF p. 116
    • Support will be extended to creative technologies through AVGC labs in 15,000 schools and 500 colleges.PDF p. 116

    Energy, Technology, and Strategic SectorsPDF p. 116

    • The Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme outlay has been increased to `40,000 crore.PDF p. 116
    • Rare Earth Corridors will be established in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu.PDF p. 116
    • `20,000 crore has been allocated over five years for carbon capture, utilisation, and storage , and Semiconductor Mission 2.0 will be launched.PDF p. 116

    Health, Pharmaceuticals, and AgriculturePDF p. 116

    • New Allied Health Professional institutions , five medical tourism hubs , and three All India Institutes of Ayurveda will be established.PDF p. 116
    • The Biopharma SHAKTI Scheme, with an outlay of `10,000 crore will promote domestic production of biologics and biosimilars.PDF p. 116
    • Agricultural measures include incentives for cooperative members , support for animal husbandry, and a Coconut Promotion Scheme.PDF p. 116

    Federal Transfers and Expenditure CompositionPDF p. 116

    • Transfers to States will increase to `26.21 lakh crore, including `15.26 lakh crore as tax devolution and `10.94 lakh crore as grants and loans.PDF p. 116
    • Capital expenditure loans to States amount to `1.85 lakh crore.PDF p. 116

    Overall AssessmentPDF p. 116

    • The Union Budget 2026–27 reflects a continuation of fiscal consolidation , capex-led growth , and structural reforms , while aligning macroeconomic stability with the long-term vision of Viksit Bharat.PDF p. 116

    Expenditure Pattern: Revenue vs CapitalPDF p. 116

    • Capital expenditure , which creates government assets or reduces liabilities, is projected to grow by 11.5% in 2026–27 over the Revised Estimates (RE) of 2025–26, reinforcing the capex-led growth strategy.PDF p. 116
    • Revenue expenditure , which includes salaries, subsidies, and interest payments, is expected to rise by 6.6%, indicating relatively tighter control over consumption-oriented spending.PDF p. 116
    • Interest payments alone account for 26% of total expenditure, underlining the structural challenge of high debt servicing costs. Growth in Expenditure Components (2026–27) Component Growth over 2025–26 (RE) Capital Expenditure 11.5% Revenue Expenditure 6.6% Interest Payments ~10%PDF p. 116

    Receipts Structure for 2026–27PDF p. 116

    • Total receipts, excluding borrowings, are estimated at `36.51 lakh crore , reflecting a 7.2% increase over 2025–26 (RE) , mainly driven by higher net tax revenue.PDF p. 116
    • Gross tax revenue is budgeted to grow by 8%, which is lower than the nominal GDP growth estimate of 10% , suggesting conservative tax buoyancy assumptions.PDF p. 116

    Tax Revenue TrendsPDF p. 116

    • Corporation tax collections are expected to grow by 11%, reflecting stable corporate profitability.PDF p. 116
    • Income tax collections are projected to grow by 11.7%, despite a revenue shortfall in 2025–26, following tax rate rationalisation.PDF p. 116
    • CGST revenue is expected to grow by 6.3%, lower than overall tax growth, indicating moderate consumption expansion.PDF p. 116

    Expenditure Composition for 2026–27PDF p. 116

    • Total expenditure is estimated at `53.47 lakh crore, an increase of 7.7% over 2025–26 (RE).PDF p. 116
    • Central Sector Schemes account for `17.72 lakh crore, while Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) account for `9.90 lakh crore , with CSS showing a higher growth rate of 17.1%.PDF p. 116

    Committed Expenditure and TransfersPDF p. 117

    • Pension expenditure in 2026–27 is estimated at `2.96 lakh crore, rising modestly by 3%.PDF p. 117
    • Interest payments are projected at `14.04 lakh crore, consuming over one-fourth of total expenditure.PDF p. 117
    • Special loans to States for capital expenditure amount to `1.85 lakh crore , supporting state-level capex.PDF p. 117
    • Finance Commission grants for 2026–27 are estimated at `1.29 lakh crore, about 15% lower than 2025–26 (RE), as per 16th Finance Commission recommendations.PDF p. 117

    Expenditure by Major MinistriesPDF p. 117

    • The top 13 ministries account for 54% of total Union expenditure in 2026–27.PDF p. 117
    • The Ministry of Defence has the highest allocation at `7.85 lakh crore , constituting 15% of total expenditure.PDF p. 117
    • Other major allocations include Road Transport and Highways , Railways, and Home Affairs , reflecting emphasis on infrastructure, logistics, and internal security. Major Ministerial Allocations (2026–27) Ministry Share of Total Expenditure Defence 15% Road Transport & Highways 6% Railways 5% Home Affairs 5%PDF p. 117

    Ministry-wise Expenditure PrioritiesPDF p. 117

    • The Ministry of Defence allocation increases by `52,166 crore (7%) in 2026–27 over 2025–26 (RE), reflecting a sustained focus on national security.PDF p. 117
    • Capital outlay for defence services rises sharply to `2,19,306 crore , marking a 17.6% increase , reinforcing indigenisation and modernisation of the armed forces.PDF p. 117

    Subsidy ExpenditurePDF p. 117

    • Total subsidy expenditure in 2026–27 is estimated at `4,54,773 crore , representing a 3.1% decline from 2025–26 (RE).PDF p. 117
    • Food subsidy ( `2,27,629 crore) and fertiliser subsidy (`1,70,799 crore) together constitute 87% of the total subsidy bill.PDF p. 117

    Flagship Schemes and Sectoral AllocationsPDF p. 117

    • VB-G RAM G receives the highest allocation of `95,692 crore in 2026–27, following the replacement of MGNREGA by the VB-G RAM G Act in December 2025.PDF p. 117
    • Despite replacement, MGNREGS is also allocated `30,000 crore in 2026–27, indicating a transition phase.PDF p. 117

    Loans to States for Capital ExpenditurePDF p. 117

    • `1,85,000 crore has been budgeted as interest-free loans to States for capital expenditure in 2026– 27, up from `1,44,000 crore (RE) in 2025–26.PDF p. 117

    Deficits and Public DebtPDF p. 117

    • The fiscal deficit for 2026–27 is estimated at 4.3% of GDP, marginally lower than 4.4% in 2025–26 , signalling continued fiscal consolidation.PDF p. 117
    • The revenue deficit remains unchanged at 1.5% of GDP, indicating continued borrowing for recurring expenditure.PDF p. 117
    • Outstanding liabilities of the Centre are estimated at 55.6% of GDP, down from the pandemic peak of 61% in 2020–21.PDF p. 117
    • The government aims to reduce liabilities to around 50% ±1% of GDP by March 2031.     Economic Survey 2025–26PDF p. 117, 118

    • The Economic Survey 2025–26 urges a shift to entrepreneurial policymaking under uncertainty, where the State acts early, structures risk, learns through experimentation, and adapts without paralysis.PDF p. 117
    • The Survey says governance is moving from compliance-driven regulation to capability- driven state capacity , signalling an emerging entrepreneurial State.PDF p. 117
    • Despite post-COVID shocks, including global trade disruption and US tariffs in April 2025, the Indian economy has shown strong macroeconomic resilience.PDF p. 117
    • The Survey anticipates real GDP growth abovePDF p. 117
    • 7% in FY 2025–26 and expects growth to stay near this level in the following year.PDF p. 118
    • It highlights a paradox in which India’s best macro performance in decades comes amid a global system that no longer reliably rewards discipline with currency stability, capital inflows, or insulation.PDF p. 118
    • The Survey argues that India’s scale population of 145 crore, and democracy make it unrealistic to copy external development templates in a geopolitically uncertain world.PDF p. 118
    • It states that global headwinds can become tailwinds if the State, private sector, and households align and sustain a national effort.PDF p. 118
    • The Survey outlines three global scenarios for 2026: managed disorder, disorderly multipolar breakdown, and a low-probability, high-impact shock cascade worse that of 2008.PDF p. 118
    • Across scenarios, it says India is relatively better placed due to a large domestic market, a less financialised growth model, strong reserves, and credible strategic autonomy, though insulation is not complete.PDF p. 118
    • It warns of a common risk of disrupted capital flows and sustained rupee pressure that could last beyond one year.PDF p. 118
    • The Survey says India must strengthen foreign currency earnings through exports and investor confidence to finance a rising import bill with rising incomes.PDF p. 118
    • It recommends supply stability, strategic buffers, diversified trade routes, and alternative payment systems, calling for strategic sobriety over defensive pessimism.PDF p. 118
    • It stresses that India must balance long-term growth with short-term shock absorption, captured in its “marathon and sprint” framing.PDF p. 118
    • The Survey emphasises process reforms alongside policy reforms because administrative processes shape citizen-state interaction and reform outcomes.PDF p. 118
    • It notes that recent deregulation and smart regulation by States show the State can shift from controller to enabler of growth.PDF p. 118
    • It links State capacity, society, and deregulation as key pillars for Viksit Bharat and greater global influence.PDF p. 118
    • It urges the State to upskill and mentally prepare for a harsher global environment where rules are changing.PDF p. 118
    • It concludes that long-term success requires resilience, innovation, and delayed gratification rather than quick fixes.PDF p. 118
    • The Survey has been reorganised into 17 chapters based on depth and time-relevance, making it broader and longer than earlier editions.PDF p. 118
    • It includes special essays on AI, quality of life in Indian cities , and how State capacity and the private sector can build strategic resilience and indispensability.PDF p. 118

    Key Highlights of Economic Survey 2025–26PDF p. 118

    State of the EconomyPDF p. 118

    • The global economic environment remains fragile, with elevated risks from geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation , and financial vulnerabilities, and some shocks may appear with a time lag.PDF p. 118
    • The First Advance Estimates project real GDP growth at 7.4% and GVA growth at 7.3% for FY26, sustaining India’s position as the fastest-growing major economy for the fourth consecutive year.PDF p. 118
    • Potential growth for India is assessed at around 7%, while FY27 real GDP growth is projected at 6.8%–7.2%.PDF p. 118
    • Private Final Consumption Expenditure rises by 7.0% in FY26 and reaches 61.5% of GDP , the highest share since 2012 (also seen in FY23), supported by low inflation , stable employment, and rising real purchasing power.PDF p. 118
    • Gross Fixed Capital Formation grows by 7.8% in FY26, with investment’s share steady at about 30% of GDP, aided by sustained public capex and revival in private investment signals.PDF p. 118
    • The services sector remains the main growth engine, with services GVA rising 9.3% in H1 FY26 and estimated at 9.1% for the full year.PDF p. 118

    Fiscal DevelopmentsPDF p. 118, 119

    • The Survey states that credible fiscal consolidation has reinforced macro-fiscal confidence and is linked with three sovereign credit rating upgrades in 2025 by Morningstar DBRS, S&P Global Ratings, and R&I.PDF p. 118
    • The Centre’s revenue receipts strengthen to 9.2% of GDP in FY25 (PA) , up from an average of about 8.5% of GDP during FY16–FY20.PDF p. 118
    • Non-corporate tax collections have risen structurally, from about 2.4% of GDP in the pre-pandemic period to around 3.3% in the post- pandemic period.PDF p. 118
    • The direct tax base expands, with income tax returns filed increasing from 6.9 crore (FY22) to 9.2 crore (FY25), reflecting higher compliance and technology-enabled administration.PDF p. 118
    • Gross GST collections during April–December 2025 stand at `17.4 lakh crore, recording 6.7% YoY growth, while e-way bill volumes grow 21% YoY in the same period, indicating robust transactions.PDF p. 118
    • The Centre’s effective capital expenditure increases to about 4.0% of GDP in FY25, up from a pre-pandemic average of 2.7% and post-pandemic level of about 3.9%.PDF p. 119
    • Through Special Assistance to States for Capital Expenditure (SASCI) , states are incentivised to maintain capital spending at around 2.4% of GDP in FY25.PDF p. 119
    • The combined State fiscal deficit edges up to 3.2% of GDP in FY25 , from about 2.8% in the post- pandemic period, reflecting emerging pressures.PDF p. 119
    • India reduces its general government debt-to- GDP ratio by about 7.1 percentage points since 2020, while maintaining high public investment.PDF p. 119

    Monetary Management and Financial IntermediationPDF p. 119

    • The Survey reports robust monetary-financial performance in FY26 (April–December 2025) , supported by policy actions and structural resilience.PDF p. 119
    • Scheduled commercial banks’ asset quality has improved sharply, with GNPA at 2.2% (September 2025) and net NPA at 0.5% (September 2025) , both at multi-decadal/record-low levels.PDF p. 119
    • Outstanding credit growth of SCBs rises to 14.5% YoY (as of 31 December 2025) compared with 11.2% (December 2024).PDF p. 119

    Financial Inclusion and Market DeepeningPDF p. 119

    • Under PMJDY, 55.02 crore bank accounts are opened as of March 2025, including 36.63 crore in rural and semi-urban areas.PDF p. 119
    • Financial participation broadened as unique investors crossed 12 crore in September 2025 , with nearly 25% being women.PDF p. 119
    • During FY26 (till December 2025) , 235 lakh demat accounts are added, taking total demat accounts beyond 21.6 crore.PDF p. 119
    • The mutual fund investor base expanded to 5.9 crore unique investors (December 2025) , with significant participation from non-Tier I and Tier II locations.PDF p. 119
    • The Survey highlights the role of GIFT City as an enabling ecosystem to attract and channel global capital.PDF p. 119
    • The Survey notes international validation of regulatory quality through the IMF–World Bank FSAP (2025) , which found the system resilient and diversified, with adequate buffers under stress scenarios.PDF p. 119

    External SectorPDF p. 119

    • India’s share of global merchandise exports nearly doubled from 1.0% (2005) to 1.8% (2024) , while its share of global commercial services exports rose from 2.0% to 4.3% over the same period.PDF p. 119
    • India’s total exports reached a record USD 825.3 billion in FY25 , growing by 6.1% YoY , driven mainly by services.PDF p. 119
    • Services exports touched an all-time high of USD 387.6 billion in FY25 , growing by 13.6%, reinforcing India’s strength in technology and business services.PDF p. 119
    • India remained the world’s largest recipient of remittances, with inflows of USD 135.4 billion in FY25, helping offset the merchandise trade deficit.PDF p. 119
    • The current account deficit remained moderate, with CAD at around 1.3% of GDP in Q2 FY26 , supported by services and remittances.PDF p. 119
    • Forex reserves rose to USD 701.4 billion (as of 16 January 2026) , providing about 11 months of import cover and covering over 94% of external debt.PDF p. 119
    • Gross FDI inflows reached USD 64.7 billion (April–November 2025) despite subdued global investment conditions.PDF p. 119
    • India rank 4th globally in Greenfield investment announcements (2024) and emerges as the largest destination for Greenfield digital investments (2020–24).PDF p. 119

    Inflation: Tamed and AnchoredPDF p. 119

    • India recorded the lowest headline CPI inflation since the inception of the CPI series, with average inflation at 1.7% during April–December 2025.PDF p. 119
    • The moderation in inflation was primarily driven by declining food and fuel prices, which together constitute 52.7% of the CPI basket.PDF p. 119
    • Among major Emerging Markets and Developing Economies, India achieved one of the sharpest disinflations, with headline inflation declining by 1.8 percentage points in 2025 over 2024.PDF p. 119

    Agriculture and Food ManagementPDF p. 119, 120

    • The livestock sector recorded strong structural growth, with its GVA rising by nearly 195% between FY15 and FY24 , while fish production, increased by over 140% during 2014–2024.PDF p. 119
    • Benefiting from a good monsoon , India’s foodgrain production was estimated at 3,577.3 LMT in AY 2024–25 , an increase of 254.3 LMT over the previous year, led by rice, wheat, maize, and coarse cereals.PDF p. 119
    • Horticulture, contributing about 33% of agricultural GVA , emerged as a major growth driver, with production reaching 362.08 MT in 2024–25, surpassing foodgrain output.PDF p. 119
    • Agricultural marketing efficiency improved through AMI under ISAM and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund , while e-NAM enhanced price discovery by onboarding 1.79 crore farmers , 2.72 crore traders , and 4,698 FPOs across 1,522 mandis by December 31, 2025.PDF p. 119
    • Farmers’ incomes were supported through assured MSP, PM-KISAN, and PM-Kisan Maandhan Yojana, with `4.09 lakh crore disbursed under PM-KISAN and 24.92 lakh farmers enrolled in PMKMY.PDF p. 120

    Services Sector: From Stability to New FrontiersPDF p. 120

    • The services sector’s share rose to 53.6% of GDP in H1 FY26, while its share in GVA reached a record 56.4%, reflecting the rising role of modern and digitally delivered services.PDF p. 120
    • India became the world’s seventh-largest services exporter, with its share in global services trade rising from 2% in 2005 to 4.3% in 2024.PDF p. 120
    • Services accounted for over 80% of total FDI inflows during FY23–FY25 , reinforcing India’s attractiveness in globally tradable services.PDF p. 120

    Industry: Structural Transformation and Global IntegrationPDF p. 120

    • Industrial GVA grew by 7.0% in H1 FY26, despite persistent global headwinds.PDF p. 120
    • Manufacturing GVA growth accelerated to 7.72% in Q1 and 9.13% in Q2 FY26, indicating a structural recovery.PDF p. 120
    • PLI Schemes across 14 sectors attracted over `2.0 lakh crore investment, generated `18.7 lakh crore of incremental production, and created over 12.6 lakh jobs.PDF p. 120
    • India’s Global Innovation Index rank improved to 38th in 2025, up from 66th in 2019.PDF p. 120
    • The India Semiconductor Mission advanced domestic capabilities with 10 approved projects involving `1.60 lakh crore investment across 6 States.PDF p. 120

    Investment and InfrastructurePDF p. 120

    • Central government capital expenditure increased 4.2 times, from `2.63 lakh crore in FY18 to `11.21 lakh crore in FY26 (BE) , with effective capex at `15.48 lakh crore.PDF p. 120
    • The national highway network expanded by about 60%, while high-speed corridors increased nearly ten-fold since FY14.PDF p. 120
    • The rail network reached 69,439 route km , achieved 99.1% electrification, and targeted 3,500 km addition in FY26.PDF p. 120
    • India emerged as the world’s third-largest domestic aviation market, with airports increasing from 74 (2014) to 164 (2025).PDF p. 120
    • Power sector reforms delivered a historic turnaround, with DISCOMs posting a positive PAT of `2,701 crore in FY25, while renewable energy accounts for nearly 50% of installed capacity.PDF p. 120
    • 5G services now cover 99.9% of districts , tele- density reached 86.76%, and over 81% of rural households have tap water under Jal Jeevan Mission.PDF p. 120
    • India became the fourth nation to achieve autonomous satellite docking (SpaDeX) , strengthening space infrastructure.PDF p. 120

    Environment and Climate ActionPDF p. 120

    • During FY26 (till December 2025) , India added 38.61 GW of renewable energy capacity , led by 30.16 GW of solar power , reinforcing climate- aligned growth.PDF p. 120

    Education and HealthPDF p. 120

    • India operates one of the world’s largest school systems, serving 24.69 crore students across 14.71 lakh schools.PDF p. 120
    • Gross Enrolment Ratios improved across stages, with 90.9% at primary , 90.3% at upper primary , and 78.7% at secondary level.PDF p. 120
    • Higher education expanded to 70,018 institutions, including 23 IITs, 21 IIMs, and 20 AIIMS , with international IIT campuses in Zanzibar and Abu Dhabi.PDF p. 120
    • Under NEP, reforms such as NCrF, Academic Bank of Credit , and flexible entry-exit systems were widely adopted.PDF p. 120
    • India achieved an 86% reduction in maternal mortality (since 1990) , a 78% decline in under- five mortality (since 1990) , and a 37% fall in infant mortality over the past decade (40 deaths per thousands live birth in 2013 to 25 in 2023).PDF p. 120

    Employment and Skill DevelopmentPDF p. 120

    • Total employment reached 56.2 crore in Q2 FY26, with net job creation continuing.PDF p. 120
    • Organised manufacturing employment increased by 6% in FY24, adding over 10 lakh jobs.PDF p. 120
    • Gig and platform workers were formally recognised under Labour Codes, while e-Shram registered over 31 crore workers , 54% of them women.PDF p. 120
    • The National Career Service platform mobilised around 80 million vacancies, strengthening labour market matching.PDF p. 120
    • The government proposed upgrading 1,000 ITIs to align skilling with industry needs.PDF p. 120

    Rural Development and Social ProgressPDF p. 120

    • As per the revised World Bank poverty line, India’s extreme poverty declined to 5.3% in 2022–23.PDF p. 120
    • Social services expenditure rose to 7.9% of GDP in FY26 (BE).PDF p. 120
    • SVAMITVA completed drone surveys in 3.28 lakh villages, and Drone Didis strengthened rural livelihoods.PDF p. 120

    Chapter 5 · PDF pp. 121-143

    Science & Technology Affairs

    Make each technology story answer four questions: who built it, what it does, how it works, and what stage it reached. A flyby is different from a landing, and reactor criticality is different from commercial operation.

    1. Space missions: target and payload
    2. AI: data, compute and use
    3. Energy and defence: capability and stage

    Build the chapter in eight anchors

    MMX target

    JAXA's MMX mission studies Phobos and Deimos and seeks to return at least 10 grams from Phobos. The issue reports an October 2026 launch, expected arrival in 2027 and sample delivery in 2031.

    PDF p. 121
    MMX instruments

    TENGOO provides imaging; OROCHI takes multi-wavelength images; LIDAR measures distance. MEGANE uses gamma rays and neutrons for elemental composition, while MIRS is an infrared spectrometer.

    PDF p. 121
    An international rover

    IDEFIX is the MMX rover jointly developed by CNES (France) and DLR (Germany). It assesses the surface before the spacecraft lands.

    PDF p. 121
    GAGAN's function

    GAGAN means GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation. ISRO and the Airports Authority of India developed the system to improve GPS accuracy and supply integrity information for navigation.

    PDF p. 121
    Compute near the data

    Pathfinder's orbital-data-centre model processes data on a satellite rather than sending all raw data to Earth. The source assigns satellite construction and hyperspectral imaging to Pixxel and the AI backbone to Sarvam.

    PDF p. 123
    Artemis II's purpose

    The article describes Artemis II as a crewed lunar flyby, not a Moon landing. It tests Orion's life support, communications, navigation, manual operation and re-entry protection.

    PDF p. 123
    Criticality is a milestone

    The issue reports first criticality of the 500 MWe PFBR at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, on 6 April 2026. BHAVINI built it; criticality means the start of a sustained nuclear chain reaction.

    PDF p. 129
    Three AI Summit Sutras

    The India-AI Impact Summit 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, is guided by People, Planet and Progress. The source dates it to 16-21 February 2026 and separately lists seven thematic Chakras.

    PDF p. 129
    Different missions, different success conditions
    Mission/systemPurposeDistinction to retain
    MMXStudy Martian moons and return Phobos materialSample return, not crewed exploration
    Artemis IICrewed lunar flyby and system testingFlyby, not landing
    PFBRFast-breeder nuclear-energy programmeFirst criticality, not full commercial operation
    GAGANAugment GPS navigationNavigation system, not a sample-return mission
    PDF p. 121, 123, 129
    Learning aid - not from sourceUse a mission passport: agency | target | payload | milestone. Draw separate boxes for demonstration, launch, criticality and full operation so the verbs do not blur together.

    Close the notes. Explain it back.

    Give MMX's agency, two targets and sample target.

    JAXA; Phobos and Deimos; at least 10 grams returned from Phobos. The sampling moon must not be confused with the two moons being studied.PDF p. 121

    Distinguish LIDAR from MEGANE in this mission.

    LIDAR measures surface distance using laser pulses. MEGANE measures gamma rays and neutrons to infer elemental composition. They answer different scientific questions.PDF p. 121

    Explain an orbital data centre using the source's edge-computing analogy.

    Processing happens near the data's source on a satellite instead of sending all raw data to a distant Earth-based server. Pixxel supplies the satellite and imaging; Sarvam supplies the AI layer.PDF p. 123

    Why is 'Artemis II landed on the Moon' wrong for this article?

    The source describes a crewed lunar flyby to test systems and return safely. A mission toward and around the Moon is not a surface landing.PDF p. 123

    What can you infer from PFBR first criticality, and what should you not infer?

    A sustained chain reaction has begun. The article treats full operation as a later condition, so criticality alone does not establish commercial operation.PDF p. 129
