    JAXA Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) missionPDF p. 121

    • The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission on 20 October 2026 aboard H3 Flight No. 10 from Tanegashima Space Center, Japan . It aims to achieve the world’s first sample return from the Martian system. Its planned duration is approximately five years.PDF p. 121

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 121

    • Mission objectives: Study Phobos and Deimos, Mars’s two moons, and return at least 10 grams of material from Phobos.PDF p. 121
    • Timeline: Arrival at Mars is expected in 2027, and sample delivery to Earth in 2031.PDF p. 121
    • Scientific significance: Determine whether the moons are captured asteroids or debris from a giant impact on Mars , improving understanding of planetary formation and the delivery of water and organic compounds.PDF p. 121

    Technical FeaturesPDF p. 121

    • Spacecraft: Three modules—propulsion, exploration and return—use solar panels for electricity and chemical propulsion for manoeuvres.PDF p. 121
    • Orbit: A quasi-satellite orbit around Mars near Phobos supports surface mapping and landing-site selection.PDF p. 121
    • Instruments: The spacecraft carries 13 mission instruments. TENGOO provides approximately 40 cm imaging resolution ; OROCHI captures images at multiple wavelengths; LIDAR measures surface distance using laser pulses.PDF p. 121
    • Spectrometers: NASA ’s MEGANE (Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons) measures gamma rays and neutrons to determine elemental composition. MIRS (MMX InfraRed Spectrometer) operates at 0.9–3.6 micrometres , investigating minerals, water-related substances and organic matter.PDF p. 121
    • Rover: IDEFIX, jointly developed by France’s CNES and Germany’s DLR, will assess surface conditions before the spacecraft lands.PDF p. 121
    • Sampling: JAXA ’s C-Sampler collects subsurface material, while NASA ’s P-Sampler uses high- pressure nitrogen gas to gather surface particles.PDF p. 121
    • Communication and return: NASA ’s Deep Space Network supports communication and navigation. A Sample Return Capsule will bring samples through Earth’s atmosphere; NASA will receive about 15% for research and curation.PDF p. 121

    First GAGAN-Based SatellitePDF p. 121

    • In late June 2026, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) supervised India’s first Satellite-Based Landing System (SLS) approach by a commercial jet using the indigenous GAGAN system. An IndiGo Airbus A321 conducted the demonstration using satellite-derived guidance instead of relying on a conventional Instrument Landing System (ILS).PDF p. 121

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 121

    • GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation) is India’s indigenous Satellite-Based Augmentation System developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Airports Authority of India.PDF p. 121
    • It enhances GPS accuracy and provides integrity information for safer aircraft navigation. Certified to international standards, GAGAN supports satellite- based landing and serves sectors beyond aviation.PDF p. 121

    Key Elements of GAGANPDF p. 121, 122

    • GAGAN operates through an integrated network of ground stations, communication systems, and geostationary satellites. These elements monitor GPS signals in real-time, calculate corrections, and broadcast enhanced navigation information to aircraft. Key Elements No. of Elements Deployed Role Indian Reference Stations (INRES) 15 Continuously monitor GPS signals across the country and detect any errors. A. Recent Astronomical ActivitiesPDF p. 121
    • Indian Master Control Centres (INMCC) 2 Process data received from all reference stations, calculate signal corrections, and generate integrity information. Indian Land Uplink Stations (INLUS) 3 Transmit correction and integrity information from the ground to GAGAN satellites. Communication Networks 4 Connect all GAGAN stations and enable secure, real-time transmission of navigation data. Geostationary Satellites with GAGAN Payloads 3 Broadcast corrected navigation signals across the service area.PDF p. 122
    • By enhancing navigation accuracy and seamless operations across the region, it continues to reinforce India’s leadership in satellite-enabled aviation services.PDF p. 122

    India’s Indigenous Navigation EcosystemPDF p. 122

    • The integrated architecture of GAGAN forms an important part of India’s broader satellite navigation programme.PDF p. 122
    • Alongside GAGAN, India has developed the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), its indigenous regional navigation satellite system. While NavIC provides positioning, navigation and timing services, GAGAN enhances GPS signals to support precise aircraft navigation and landing.PDF p. 122

    SOLAR-1PDF p. 122

    • Space weather refers to changes in the space environment caused mainly by activity on the Sun. Powerful solar events can affect technological infrastructure and space missions. To strengthen it s forecasting and early-warning system, the United States made SOLAR-1 operational on June 10, 2026. It is the first U.S. satellite designed exclusively for continuous and operational space-weather observations. The satellite is operated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) . Its observations are transmitted to NOAA ’s Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC), which uses them to issue forecasts, watches, warnings and alerts.PDF p. 122

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 122

    • SOLAR-1 stands for Space Weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness–1 . It was previously known as Space Weather Follow On–Lagrange 1, or SWFO-L1.PDF p. 122
    • It was renamed SOLAR-1 after reaching its intended orbit around the Sun–Earth Lagrange Point 1.PDF p. 122

    Launch and Journey to Deep SpacePDF p. 122

    • The spacecraft was launched on September 24, 2025, at 7:30 a.m. EDT from Launch Complex 39A at NASA ’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.PDF p. 122
    • It travelled aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. NASA ’s Launch Services Program managed the launch.PDF p. 122
    • After travelling for about four months and covering nearly one million miles, the spacecraft performed its final engine burn on January 23, 2026.PDF p. 122
    • It then entered its planned orbit around L1 and was formally renamed SOLAR-1.PDF p. 122

    Chandrayaan-3 Hop ExperimentPDF p. 122

    • A team of scientists from the Indian Space Researc h Organisation (ISRO) on May 18, 2026 shared a report of the findings of the ‘Hop’ experiment conducted by the Vikram Lander of Chandrayaan-3 and the Chandra’s Surface Thermophysical Experiment (ChaSTE) on the Moon.PDF p. 122
    • A new study conducted during the final phase of the Chandrayaan-3 missions when the Vikram lander performed a successful hop experiment, has offered fresh insights into the Moon surface.PDF p. 122
    • During the final phase of its mission, Chandrayaan- 3’s Vikram lander reignited its engines to perform a controlled “hop” experiment (primarily to test ascent capabilities for future sample-return missions) and landed nearby , nearly 50 cm away from its initial position.PDF p. 122
    • ChaSTE (Chandra’s Surface Thermophysical Experiment), a lunar thermometer was re-penetrated into the lunar regolith (soil) at the new location.PDF p. 122
    • By analysing the ChaSTE data following this historic “hop” monoeuvre by the Vikram lander, scientists have discovered that the post-hop location at the Moon’s southern polar region possesses a complex, layered soil structure that was significantly altered by the lander’s brief flight.PDF p. 122

    Key findings from the study have emerged, which include:PDF p. 122

    • Layered Stratigraphy: analysis revealed a distinct two-layer structure within the top 6.5 cm of the post- hop site which means that the top few centimetres of the Moon’s surface aren’t just a uniform pile of dust; they are made of distinct layers with different properties,PDF p. 122
    • Geotechnical Variability: the soil’s cohesion and density were found to increase significantly with depth which means that the Moon’s soil at the surface becomes more packed and sticky as we go deeper and Twilight Thermal Profiles: the data highlighted a “shadowing effect” where local craters and depressions caused temperatures to plunge faster than global models predicted.PDF p. 122
    • Surface Erosion and Compaction: The engine firing blew away the top 3 cm of regolith, exposing and slightly compacting the material underneath.PDF p. 122

    India’s First Orbital Data Centre Satellite PathfinderPDF p. 122, 123

    • Recently on 4 May 2026 , Pixxel announced a strategic partnership with Sarvam to develop and build Pathfinder , described as India’s first orbital data centre satellite . Pixxel will design, build, launch andPDF p. 122
    • operate the satellite, while Sarvam will provide th e AI backbone for running full-stack language models, training and inference directly in orbit. The mission is important because it brings together remote sensing, high-performance computing and India-built AI on a single satellite platform.PDF p. 123

    Orbital Data CentrePDF p. 123

    • An orbital data centre is a space-based computing system in which satellites carry high-performance processors such as data-centre-class GPUs.PDF p. 123
    • These processors can run AI models in orbit, rather than depending entirely on ground-based data centres.PDF p. 123
    • In ordinary satellite missions, satellites collect images or signals and send large volumes of raw data to Earth.PDF p. 123
    • In an orbital data centre model, computation happens closer to where the data is generated. This is similar to edge computing, where data is processed near its source instead of being sent to a distant cloud server.PDF p. 123
    • Pathfinder is a single-satellite demonstrator . Its purpose is to test whether powerful computing hardware, similar to that used in ground data centres, can work reliably in the space environment.PDF p. 123

    Role of Pixxel and SarvamPDF p. 123

    • Pixxel’s role:PDF p. 123
    • Pixxel will design, build, launch and operate Pathfinder. It will also provide the hyperspectral imaging payload.PDF p. 123
    • The satellite will be developed at Gigapixxel, Pixxel’s upcoming facility designed to scale satellite production to up to 100 units.PDF p. 123
    • Sarvam’s role:PDF p. 123
    • Sarvam will provide the AI backbone. Its full- stack sovereign AI platform, including models and inference infrastructure developed and governed in India, will run directly on the satellite’s GPU layer.PDF p. 123

    Artemis II MissionPDF p. 123

    • Artemis II was not a Moon-landing mission; it was a crewed lunar flyby mission meant to prove that NASA ’s Space Launch System, Orion spacecraft, ground systems, recovery teams and mission procedures can safely carry humans beyond low Earth orbit and bring them back. NASA describes it as the first crewed Artemis flight and a key step toward long-term human return to the Moon and future crewed missions to Mars.PDF p. 123
    • Artemis II lifted off from the Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026, sending the first humans to the Moon since 1972. (Note: The Apollo 17 mission in 1972 sent humans to land on the Moon, whereas Artemis II sent humans toward the Moon.)PDF p. 123
    • During the mission, the crew completed a lunar flyby, returning humans to the Moon’s vicinity for the first time in 53 years after the final Apollo Mission to the Moon.PDF p. 123

    Engineering Focus of the MissionPDF p. 123

    • The Artemis II Orion heat shield is the critical thermal protection system on the base of Orion Spacecraft. Orion heat shield protect the Capsule and Astronauts from searing temperatures and Extreme friction during high speed atmospheric re-entry.PDF p. 123
    • During the flight, the astronauts tested Orion’s life- support, communications, control, navigation and manual operation systems in a deep-space environment.PDF p. 123
    • The mission also tested how well astronauts could live and work inside Orion during a lunar-return flight.PDF p. 123
    • This is important because Artemis is not only about reaching the Moon; it is about building the systems needed for repeated journeys, lunar surface work, and eventually Mars missions.PDF p. 123
    • The Orion Spacecraft used in Artemis II was named Integrity by the crew.PDF p. 123

    Orion’s Heat Shield and Re-entry LessonPDF p. 123

    • One of the most important engineering lessons came from Orion’s heat shield. During Artemis I, NASA found unexpected cracking and shedding of heat-shield material.PDF p. 123
    • NASA later explained that heat and gases had accumulated inside the Avcoat material, creating internal pressure and uneven shedding during re- entry, although the spacecraft would still have kept a crew safe.PDF p. 123
    • For Artemis II, NASA closely monitored re-entry and the thermal protection system.PDF p. 123
    • The spacecraft returned at extremely high lunar- return speed, and NASA ’s initial inspection found that the heat shield performed as expected and that heat-shield char loss was significantly reduced compared with Artemis I.PDF p. 123
    • This result is important for astronaut safety in future Moon-landing missions.PDF p. 123
    • Artemis III is now listed by NASA as a 2027 low- Earth orbit demonstration, mission to test one or both commerical landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin.PDF p. 123

    International Conference on Spacecraft Mission Operations, 2026PDF p. 123

    • The second edition of the International Conference on Spacecraft Mission Operations — SMOPS-2026 was held from 8 to 10 April 2026 in Bengaluru/Bangalore, India.PDF p. 123
    • Its theme was “Innovative Operations for Smart and Sustainable Space Mission Management – Next Generation.” The conference was jointly organised by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), the Astronautical Society of India (ASI) and the International Academy of Astronautics (IAA).PDF p. 123
    • The conference was inaugurated on 8 April 2026 by Shri A. S. Kiran Kumar, former Chairman of ISRO and former Secretary, Department of Space.PDF p. 123

    New Telescopes in LadakhPDF p. 124

    • The Union Budget 2026-27 has given a major push to India’s astronomy programme. As per Budget 2026-27 four Telescope infrastructure facilities would be setup or upgraded. 1. National Large Solar Telescope (NLST)PDF p. 124
    • The NLST will be built at Merak near Pangong Lake Ladakh. It is a 2-metre-class ground-based telescope that will observe the Sun in optical and near-infrared wavelengths.PDF p. 124
    • It is designed to study the origin and behaviour of solar magnetic fields at very high resolution. 2. National Large Optical–Infrared Telescope (NLOT)PDF p. 124
    • NLOT will come up at Hanle (Ladakh) and is officially described as India’s next-generation flagship ground-based optical–infrared telescope.PDF p. 124
    • It will have a 13.7-metre segmented primary mirror, advanced adaptive optics for sharper infrared imaging, and instruments such as spectrographs and imagers. 3. Upgrade of the Himalayan Chandra T elescope (HCT)PDF p. 124
    • The Indian Astronomical Observatory at Hanle is a high-altitude observatory in Ladakh. The Himalayan Chandra Telescope is the 2-M optical-infrared Telescope installed there.PDF p. 124
    • It obtained first light on 26 September 2000, began regular science observations in May 2003, and is a 2-metre optical–infrared telescope remotely operated from CREST near Bengaluru through a dedicated satellite link.PDF p. 124
    • The upgraded HCT is planned as a 3.7-metre segmented optical–infrared telescope, which would make it more useful for transient and multi- messenger astronomy. 4. COSMOS-2 PlanetariumPDF p. 124
    • It will be constructed at Amaravati and it will be implemented by Indian Institute of Astrophysics.PDF p. 124

    India’s first Private EO Satellite ConstellationPDF p. 124

    • Earth Observation (EO) data is critical for day-to- day governance (agriculture, infrastructure plannin g), climate monitoring, and disaster response. Recently, in January 21, 2026, the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) formalised its agreement with a Pixxel-led consortium called “Allied Orbits” to establish India’s first indigenous commercial Earth Observation satellite constellation under the Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership (EO-PPP) programme.PDF p. 124
    • The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) announced the selection of the Pixxel Space India-led consortium to design, build, and operate India’s first fully indigenous commercial earth observation (EO) satellite constellation under the public-private partnership (PPP) model.PDF p. 124
    • The Bengaluru-based Pixxel Space India consortium comprises Piersight Space, SatSure Analytics India, and Dhruva Space.PDF p. 124
    • It is for the first time in the history of the Indian space sector that a private consortium would invest more than `1,200 crore over the next five years (from January, 2026) to launch a constellation of 12 state-of-the-art EO satellites equipped with panchromatic, multispectral, hyperspectral, and microwave Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors. As per official Statement of August 12, 2026 the constellation is to be developed and operationalised by 2029.PDF p. 124
    • The constellation will deliver Analysis Ready Data (ARD) and Value-Added Services (VAS) for applications in climate change monitoring, disaster management.PDF p. 124
    • EO-PPP programmePDF p. 124
    • EO-PPP programme is aimed at building a reliable national EO data backbone, reducing dependence on foreign satellite data and strengthening India’s geospatial and space-based services ecosystem through structured public-private collaboration.PDF p. 124

    ISRO’s LVM3 M6 MissionPDF p. 124

    • India’s heavy-lift launcher LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-3) has been increasingly used for high-value national missions as well as international commerci al launches. In the LVM3M6 mission, ISRO/NSIL launched the BlueBird Block-2 communications satellite ofPDF p. 124

    AST SpaceMobilePDF p. 124

    • (USA) and successfully placed it into the intended orbit.PDF p. 124
    • The Indian Space Research Organisation’s (ISRO) Launch Vehicle Mark-3 (LVM3) on December 24, 2025 and successfully placed the BlueBird Block-2 satellite in its intended low Earth orbit.PDF p. 124
    • ISRO accomplished two milestones with this mission as it was able to deploy the largest commercial communications satellite in low Earth orbit and also the BlueBird Block-2 satellite became the heaviest payload (6,100 kg.) to be launched by LVM3 from Indian soil.PDF p. 124
    • LVM3-M6 mission was the 104 th launch from Sriharikota and also the ninth successful mission of the LVM-3 launch vehicle and the third dedicated commercial mission demonstrating its 100% reliability.PDF p. 124
    • AST SpaceMobilePDF p. 124
    • AST SpaceMobile (AST & Science, LLC) is building the space-based cellular broadband network, which is accessible directly by smartphones and designed for both commercial and government applications.PDF p. 124
    • AST SpaceMobile has launched five satellites — BlueBird 1-5 in September 2024, which enable non- continuous internet coverage across the US and other select countries.PDF p. 124

    The Blue Bird Block-2 satellitePDF p. 125

    • The BlueBird Block-2 satellite features a 223 m2 phased array, making it the largest commercial communication satellite ever deployed into low Earth orbit.PDF p. 125
    • The BlueBird Block-2 mission is part of the global Low Earth Orbit constellation to provide direct-to- mobile connectivity through a satellite.PDF p. 125
    • This constellation would enable 4G and 5G voice and video calls, texts, streaming and data for anyone at any time, ISRO said.PDF p. 125
    • The BlueBird Block-2 spacecraft launched heaviest payload into Low Earth Orbit in the history of the LVM3 rocket on December 24, 2025. B. Recent Science & TechnologiesPDF p. 125

    India Mobile Congress 2026PDF p. 125

    • Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi inaugurated the 10th edition of the India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026, Asia’s leading digital technology and telecommunications forum, on 8 October 2026 at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi. The event, held from October 7 to October 10, 2026, was jointly organised by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Ministry of Communications, and the Cellular Operators Association of India (COAI) under the overarching theme “Scale Without Boundaries”, reflecting India’s ambition to expand digital innovation, connectivity and technology-led growth beyond traditional boundaries.PDF p. 125

    The four key pillars of IMC 2026PDF p. 125

    • Srishti – Building the Future: Promoting innovation, emerging technologies and next-generation digital infrastructure.PDF p. 125
    • Samvardhan – Fueling Growth : Accelerating investment, entrepreneurship, manufacturing and industry-led growth.PDF p. 125
    • Sashakt – Expanding Opportunities: Leveraging digital technologies to create opportunities for citizens, enterprises and communities.PDF p. 125
    • Suraksha – Strengthening Trust: Building secure, resilient and trusted digital networks and technology ecosystems.PDF p. 125
    • AI for Good Build-a-thon 5.0PDF p. 125
    • The Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Ministry of Communications, Government of India, organised the Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Good Build-a-thon 5.0 on October 10, 2026 at the India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026, held at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi.PDF p. 125
    • The event, themed “Creating innovative agents in 5G”, was inaugurated by Dr. Bilel Jamoussi, Deputy Director and Chief, Study Groups and Policy Department, Telecommunication Standardization Bureau, ITU.PDF p. 125
    • The 1st prize went to Team Netaxis, RVCE Bangalore, for “Context Aware Agentic Orchestration of QoS and Adaptive Security in Resource Constrained 5G”.PDF p. 125

    Google’s India-first AI modelsPDF p. 125

    • Google DeepMind’s AnthroKrishi team developed Agricultural Landscape Understanding (ALU) and Agricultural Monitoring and Event Detection (AMED) to turn satellite imagery into useful agricultural information. Initially focused on India, these models now suppor t applications in farming, agricultural credit, water management and policy beyond the country.PDF p. 125

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 125

    How the models workPDF p. 125

    • ALU: Maps agricultural landscapes, including individual field boundaries, trees, woodlands and small irrigation structures such as farm wells and dug ponds.PDF p. 125
    • AMED: Tracks agricultural activity at the field level, including the likely crop and its sowing and harvesting periods.PDF p. 125
    • Access: The model outputs are freely accessible through application programming interfaces (APIs). ALU data is also available as a layer in Google Earth.PDF p. 125

    From mapping fields to supporting farmersPDF p. 125

    • One of the applications is in sustainable rice cultivation. CarbonFarm is using the ALU API alongside Gemini to automate field-level insights, including mapping individual field boundaries, as part of programmes aimed at reducing the environmental impact of rice farming.PDF p. 125

    India’s first LNG-powered trainPDF p. 125

    • On September 27, 2026, Union Home and Cooperation Minister Amit Shah formally flagged off India’s first LNG-powered train from Sabarmati Railway Station in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. The project introduces liquefied natural gas into railway propulsion to reduce diesel consumption and support cleaner, more fuel- efficient operations.PDF p. 125

    Key specificationsPDF p. 125

    • The train is a Diesel Electric Multiple Unit (DEMU). It has two converted Driving Power Cars (DPCs), each rated at 1,400 horsepower (HP).PDF p. 125
    • The fuel system can replace up to around 40 per cent of diesel consumption with LNG.PDF p. 125
    • This figure refers to diesel substitution, rather than a measured 40 per cent reduction in emissions.PDF p. 125
    • Each DPC carries a 2,200-litre LNG tank.PDF p. 125
    • The onboard installation includes LNG receiving, storage and re-gasification equipment.PDF p. 125

    Trials and inaugural routePDF p. 126

    • The converted power cars completed more than 2,000 km of field trials to establish their performance in railway operations.PDF p. 126
    • The inaugural journey on 27 September 2026 ran from Sabarmati to Mahesana Junction in Gujarat.PDF p. 126
    • The September event marked the formal flag-off of a system that had entered passenger service earlier.PDF p. 126

    NIELIT Launches CYBER KUSHTI 2026PDF p. 126

    • On August 15, 2026, the National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT) launched CYBER KUSHTI 2026, a national cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence (AI) hackathon. It is designed to test and recognise human judgment in cybersecurity assessment rather than merely rewarding the speed of vulnerability detection. The hackathon was formally launched by Prof. (Dr.) M. M. Tripathi, Director General of NIELIT and Vice-Chancellor of NIELIT Deemed-to- be University. It is the official parallel technical track of the 3rd National Conference on Cyber Security, Digital Forensics and Intelligence (NCCDFI 2026).PDF p. 126

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 126

    • The competition is being conducted in collaboration with the Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC Foundation) under the National Security Database initiative. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) is its Knowledge Partner.PDF p. 126
    • Final Round – The Kesari: To be held in person in November, 2026 at the Dr. Ambedkar International Centre, New Delhi , where the ten finalist teams will work under supervision before presenting and defending their assessments on the main stage of NCCDFI 2026.PDF p. 126
    • The winning team will be awarded the title “Cyber Kesari 2026” and presented the traditional Gada. The runners-up will be recognised with the titles “Rustam” and “Pahalwan.”PDF p. 126

    AIKosh University Engagement ProgrammePDF p. 126

    • The IndiaAI Mission, under the Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology (MeitY), is strengthening India’s artificial intelligence ecosystem by promoting innovation, responsible AI development and wider access to national AI resources. As part of this effort, the Mission organised thePDF p. 126

    AIKosh University Engagement ProgrammePDF p. 126

    • (UEP) at Chitkara University, Rajpura, on 6 August 2026, with the objective of familiarising students with AIKosh and encouraging practical engagement with India’s national AI infrastructure.PDF p. 126
    • AIKosh University Engagement ProgrammePDF p. 126
    • The programme aimed to increase AI awareness, democratise access to AI resources and equip students with relevant knowledge and tools.PDF p. 126
    • More than 250 students from Chitkara University participated in expert sessions, live demonstrations and hands-on activities.PDF p. 126
    • The programme is part of a nationwide initiative to deepen AI adoption across higher educational institutions.PDF p. 126
    • IndiaAI Mission and AIKosh PlatformPDF p. 126
    • The IndiaAI Mission was approved by the Government of India in March 2024.PDF p. 126
    • AIKosh is a key pillar of the IndiaAI Mission and functions as India’s unified data platform.PDF p. 126
    • It provides access to (as on October 6, 2026) :PDF p. 126
    • 16,000+ datasetsPDF p. 126
    • 350+ AI modelsPDF p. 126

    India’s First Hydrogen-Powered TrainPDF p. 126

    • Indian Railways is entering a new era of clean and sustainable transportation. Hydrogen fuel cell technology has emerged globally as a promising alternative to fossil fuel-based traction systems. India’s first indigenous hydrogen-powered train marks an important step in adopting this next-generation technology. It is a locomotive that generates its own electricity onboa rd using hydrogen. With the inauguration on the Jind- Sonipat section ( Haryana) of the Northern Railway on 17 July 2026 by PM Narendra Modi ,the hydrogen fuel cell-powered train is begin its operations.PDF p. 126
    • The project combines advanced propulsion technology with dedicated hydrogen storage, refuelling and operational infrastructure.PDF p. 126
    • It will demonstrate the feasibility of clean rail transportation in India.PDF p. 126

    Inside India’s First Hydrogen TrainPDF p. 126

    • The hydrogen train project has been developed in accordance with design approval and technical specifications prepared by the Research, Designs & Standards Organisation (RDSO) . Designed and developed entirely in India, the project demonstrates the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat.PDF p. 126

    Key Features of the Hydrogen Powered Train on the Jind- Sonipat Section-PDF p. 126

    • The Train has two 1200 kW power cars, totalling 2400 kW hydrogen fuel cell propulsion system.PDF p. 126
    • Approved to operate at a maximum speed of 75 kmph with a design speed of 110 kmph.PDF p. 126
    • Capacity of Around 2,600 Passengers.PDF p. 126
    • Developed from the design stage through prototype manufacturing.PDF p. 126
    • It will connect Jind Junction, Gohana Junction and Sonipat while serving intermediate stations.PDF p. 126

    Technology Behind the TrainPDF p. 127

    • Hydrogen fuel cell technology produces electricity through a chemical reaction using hydrogen.PDF p. 127
    • The primary energy source is a Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC) . This is a fuel cell that generates electricity by reacting hydrogen and oxygen across a proton-conducting Perfluorosulfonic Acid (PFSA) polymer membrane.PDF p. 127
    • The process produces only water vapour and heat as byproducts. Hydrogen is a high-energy fuel, 120 MJ/Kg (megajoules per kilogram) in comparison to diesel, which is 43 MJ/Kg.PDF p. 127
    • Hydrogen InfrastructurePDF p. 127
    • The country’s largest railway hydrogen storage and refuelling facility has been established at Jind, Haryana.PDF p. 127
    • The indigenous facility stores nearly 3,000 kg of hydrogen at a time. It will support hydrogen-powered train operations.PDF p. 127
    • The train consists of two Hydrogen Driving Power Cars (DPCs) and eight Trailer Coaches (TCs).PDF p. 127
    • Each DPC houses fuel cells, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and hydrogen storage cylinders.PDF p. 127

    JAMA Blood Group in HumansPDF p. 130

    • The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) has recognised JAMA as the 49 th human blood group system, numbered ISBT 049. The discovery followed a joint investigation by researchers in the United Kingdom and Israel into unusual blood samples from a woman and her brother. ISBT ratified the system at its Kuala Lumpur Congress in 2026 and announced it on September 14, 2026. The finding adds to the understanding of rare blood characteristics and the ir possible importance in transfusion medicine.PDF p. 130

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 130

    • Blood plays a vital role in the human body, carrying oxygen and essential nutrients to cells. For years, A, B, AB and O have been the blood groups most familiar to people.PDF p. 130
    • Now, scientists have identified a new blood group system called JAMA, taking the total number of recognised blood group systems to 49.PDF p. 130
    • The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) has officially recognised JAMA as the 49th blood group system.PDF p. 130
    • The discovery came from a joint investigation by researchers from the UK and Israel. It began when scientists examined the blood of an Israeli woman and her brother.PDF p. 130
    • The woman was found to have an antibody that reacted with the red blood cells of most people.PDF p. 130
    • However, the same reaction did not occur with her own red blood cells or those of her brother.PDF p. 130
    • This unusual result caught researchers’ attention because the antibody did not correspond to any previously identified blood group antigen.PDF p. 130
    • JAMA should not be viewed as another category alongside A, B, AB and O. Instead, it is a separate blood group system involving a specific antigen.PDF p. 130
    • This antigen is found on the red blood cells of most people. In the woman and her brother, however, it was absent.PDF p. 130
    • Their blood also contained a corresponding antibody, helping scientists identify the unusual blood group characteristics.PDF p. 130

    • Rabies: Important Scientific FactsPDF p. 131
    • Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal after clinical symptoms appear, but deaths can be prevented through timely treatment.PDF p. 131
    • Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) involves thorough wound washing, human rabies vaccination and rabies immunoglobulins (RIG), when indicated.PDF p. 131
    • Infected dogs account for up to 99% of human rabies transmissions globally.PDF p. 131
    • The Global Strategic Plan to End Human Deaths from Dog-Mediated Rabies by 2030.PDF p. 131

    • An important feature of SAHI is that it is designed to create coordination between healthcare institutions, technology developers, researchers and policymakers.PDF p. 132

    BODH: benchmarking and validation platform for Health AIPDF p. 133

    • BODH has been developed by the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur in collaboration with the National Health Authority.PDF p. 133
    • It is a privacy-preserving benchmarking platform for Health AI. Its main role is to allow rigorous evaluation of AI models on diverse, anonymized real- world health data without sharing the underlying datasets.PDF p. 133

    AI-Preneurs of IndiaPDF p. 133

    • On the same occasion, Atal Innovation Mission under NITI Aayog launched AI-Preneurs of India, a flagship coffee table book on India’s AI startup ecosystem.PDF p. 133
    • The book documents the journeys of 45 AI startups that are working on real-world problems.PDF p. 133

    India’s first state-funded Bio- Safety Level-4 (BSL-4) laboratoryPDF p. 133

    • India is expanding its highest-level bio-containment capacity with a new Bio-Safety Level-4 (BSL-4) Bio- Containment Facility at the Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre (GBRC), Gandhinagar. The foundation stone was laid on 13 January 2026 by Union Home Minister Amit Shah.PDF p. 133
    • The technical term “Bio-Safety Level 4) represents the highest level of biological containment.PDF p. 133
    • BSL-4 (Biosafety Level 4) facility is the maximum containment laboratory designed for studying the world’s most dangerous, often incurable pathogens (e.g., Ebola, Nipah, Marburg).PDF p. 133

    Existing BSL-4 labs in IndiaPDF p. 133

    • Currently, there is only one civilian BSL-4 laboratory functional in India, located at the National Institute of Virology (NIV) in Pune, Maharashtra.PDF p. 133

    WHO Global Tuberculosis (TB) Report 2025PDF p. 133

    • Recently, WHO released the Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 on November 12, 2025, giving an updated assessment of the TB epidemic and response at global, regional and country levels based mainly on data up to 2024. Data from 184 countries and areas cover more than 99% of the world’s population and TB cases, giving the report very strong global representativeness.PDF p. 133
    • Tuberculosis (TB) is described as the world’s leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, and remains among the top 10 causes of death worldwide.PDF p. 133
    • TB is an airborne, contagious disease; since 2000, global efforts to combat TB have saved an estimated 83 million lives.PDF p. 133

    Global TB BurdenPDF p. 133

    • In 2024, an estimated 10.7 million people developed TB, corresponding to 131 new cases per 100,000 population worldwide.PDF p. 133
    • Top eight countries (≈ two-thirds of global TB burden):PDF p. 133
    • India (25%), Indonesia (10%), Philippines (6.8%), China (6.5%), Pakistan (6.3%), Nigeria (4.8%), Democratic Republic of the Congo (3.9%), Bangladesh (3.6%).PDF p. 133

    TB Incidence in IndiaPDF p. 133

    • TB incidence in India has fallen by 21%, from 237 per lakh population in 2015 to 187 per lakh population in 2024 , almost double the global decline of 12%; this is described as one of the highest declines globally among high-burden countries.PDF p. 133
    • TB mortality in India (TB deaths in HIV-negative people) has reduced from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 21 per lakh population in 2024 , with India achieving a higher reduction than the global reduction.PDF p. 133
    • India’s treatment coverage rose from 53% in 2015 to over 92% in 2024 , ahead of global universal health coverage and other high-burden countries.PDF p. 133
    • In 2024, 26.18 lakh TB patients were diagnosed in India, out of an estimated 27 lakh incident cases, reducing the “missing cases” from 15 lakh in 2015 to less than one lakh in 2024, with no significant increase in MDR-TB cases.PDF p. 133

    HPV Vaccination Drive for 14-Year-Old GirlsPDF p. 133

    • India launched the nationwide free HPV vaccination campaign on 28 February 2026 from Ajmer, Rajasthan. It targets 14-year-old girls across all 36 States and Union Territories. After the national launch, States and UTs also held their own rollout events. The campaign is aimed at reducing the future burden of cervical cancer through early prevention. Around 1.2 crore girls are expected to benefit every year.PDF p. 133
    • Cervical cancer remains a major women’s health challenge. WHO says it is largely preventable through HPV vaccination and regular screening.PDF p. 133
    • As per WHO fact sheet dated July 3, 2026 Globally, it was the fifth most common cancer among women in 2024, with about 6,04,000 new cases and 2,80,000 deaths.PDF p. 133
    • In India, IARC-GLOBOCAN 2022 recorded 127,526 new cases and 79,906 deaths, making cervical cancer the second most common cancer among Indian women. GLOBOCAN 2024 India sheet estimates 79,360 new cases and 36,319 death.PDF p. 133

    Target Population and Coverage:PDF p. 133

    • The campaign will cover girls aged 14 years.PDF p. 133
    • As per Registrar General of India (RGI) 2021 estimates, the annual cohort of 14-year-old girls is approximately 1.2 crore, who are expected to benefit from this initiative each year.PDF p. 133

    Key Features:PDF p. 134

    • Vaccination Duration: three months (90 days) in campaign mode (as on September 11, 2026).PDF p. 134
    • After completion of the campaign phase, the HPV vaccine will be available on routine immunization session days.PDF p. 134
    • Dose & Administration: Single dose (0.5 ml) Intramuscular (IM) injection in the left upper armPDF p. 134
    • Vaccination is voluntary, free of cost and will be administered only after parental/guardian consent.PDF p. 134
    • Beneficiaries may pre-register and schedule appointments on the U-WIN digital platform.PDF p. 134
    • The U-WIN platform will be used for session planning, registration, recording and reporting, while the e-VIN portal will manage vaccine stocks and logistics.PDF p. 134

    Malaria Vaccine: AdFalciVaxPDF p. 134

    • The Regional Medical Research Centre (RMRC), Bhubaneswar, of the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), has developed a recombinant multi-stage malaria vaccine candidate named AdFalciVax.PDF p. 134
    • Its objective is to prevent individual infection against Plasmodium falciparum and to reduce community-level transmission.PDF p. 134
    • As of June 17, 2026 , this technology has been licensed to five Indian companies , while it is still in the preclinical stage (TRL 4) and is not approved for clinical use.PDF p. 134
    • This vaccine candidate has not yet been approved for clinical use; hence, the timeline assessment will depend on regulatory progress.PDF p. 134
    • Currently, WHO-recommended vaccines— RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) and R21/Matrix-M— are available for widespread use in children ; both have received WHO prequalification.PDF p. 134
    • AdFalciVax has very high stability . It remains effective for up to 12 months at normal room temperature.PDF p. 134
    • This eliminates the need for expensive cold chain logistics, which is a major challenge for vaccination campaigns in remote and resource-limited areas.PDF p. 134
    • The estimated production cost of this vaccine is only `20 per dose , compared to existing vaccines that cost between `250 and `830 per dose.PDF p. 134
    • This makes it extremely cost-effective for large- scale immunization programs.PDF p. 134
    • India aims to achieve zero indigenous malaria cases by 2027 and full elimination by 2030. D. DefencePDF p. 134

    Ahuti Mk IIPDF p. 134

    • Ahuti Mk II is an electric multirotor interceptor developed by Hyderabad-based Apollyon Dynamics, a defence technology startup from the BITS Pilani Hyderabad Campus ecosystem. It gained national recognition after achieving a recorded test speed of 498 km/h. The development is relevant to India’s indigenous counter-drone capabilities and the role of academic incubation in defence innovation.PDF p. 134
    • The record was confirmed on 29 August 2026; the entry was published on 1 September 2026.PDF p. 134
    • According to Apollyon Dynamics, the speed exceeded the previous recorded benchmark of 325 km/h. The difference is 173 km/h.PDF p. 134
    • The manufacturer distinguishes the 498 km/h speed achieved by its developmental test platform from the approximately 400 km/h operational speed band targeted for production interceptors.PDF p. 134

    Apollyon Dynamics and Its FoundersPDF p. 134

    • Apollyon Dynamics was founded by Jayant Khatri and Sourya Choudhury. The startup’s early development received support through the BITS Pilani SOLVE programme, under which Khatri’s undergraduate work received a prototype grant of ₹2 lakh.PDF p. 134

    DRDO develops indigenous GaN technologyPDF p. 134

    • On May 13, 2026, SAMEER and ISRO’s ISTRAC agreed to develop X-band deep-space communication amplifiers using indigenous GaN chips from GAETEC, DRDO.PDF p. 134
    • Gallium Nitride (GaN) is a semiconductor technology suitable for high-frequency and high- power applications.PDF p. 134
    • A single indigenous GaN chip measuring 3.5 × 3 mm can deliver up to 30 watts of power and reportedly operate at speeds 300 times faster than silicon.PDF p. 134
    • The Solid State Physics Laboratory (SSPL) of DRDO has developed indigenous processes for manufacturing 4-inch Silicon Carbide (SiC) wafers.PDF p. 134
    • SSPL has fabricated GaN HEMTs with power capabilities up to 150 watts and MMICs up to 40 watts for applications up to X-band frequencies.PDF p. 134
    • Limited production capability for indigenous GaN- on-SiC MMICs has been established at GAETEC, Hyderabad.PDF p. 134
    • Under the Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) initiative, a contract was signed with Agnit Semiconductors Private Limited to develop advanced GaN semiconductors for next-generation defence wireless transmitters.PDF p. 134

    Applications and Strategic SignificancePDF p. 135

    • GaN technology is used in radars, electronic warfare systems, communications, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR) and unmanned systems.PDF p. 135
    • Its high power, high frequency and compact size make it suitable for radar transmitters and electronic warfare jammers.PDF p. 135
    • GaN-on-SiC technology offers higher efficiency, reduced size and weight, and improved performance.PDF p. 135
    • Multifunctional MMICs have applications in strategic systems, space, aerospace, 5G and satellite communications.PDF p. 135

    India’s first indigenous long- range attack drone KALPDF p. 135

    • IG Defence, a private defence technology company headquartered in Noida, has announced the successful flight trial of its indigenously developed KAL drone at the Pokhran Field Firing Range in Rajasthan. KAL is a long- range one-way attack system designed for autonomous strike missions. Its development is relevant to Ind ia’s efforts to build domestic capabilities in unmanned defence technology.PDF p. 135

    KAL Technical Specifications and Navigation TermsPDF p. 135

    • Parameter Manufacturer declared specification Range Up to 1,000 km Endurance 7-8 hours Maximum take-off weight 200 kg Payload configuration 50 kg high-explosive warhead Speed Cruise 160 km/h; maximum 200 km/h Operating altitude Up to 5,000 m above mean sea level (AMSL) Operating temperature -20 degrees C to +60 degrees C Launch and deployment Rocket-assisted take-off or vehicle take-offPDF p. 135

    INS MangrolPDF p. 135

    • INS Mangrol, the third Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft (ASW-SWC) built by Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL), Kochi, was commissioned into the Indian Navy on 12 October 2026 at Naval Dockyard, Mumbai. The commissioning ceremony was presided over by Vice Admiral Sanjay Vatsayan, Flag Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Western Naval Command. The vessel is named after Mangrol, a coastal town and fishing harbour in the Junagadh district of Gujarat. It carries forward the legacy of the former INS Mangrol (M85), a minesweeper that served the Indian Navy until April 7, 2004.PDF p. 135

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 135

    Indigenous Development and T echnical FeaturesPDF p. 135

    • Built under the Make in India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiatives, INS Mangrol contains over 80% indigenous content.PDF p. 135
    • The vessel is equipped with advanced weapons and sensors, including:PDF p. 135
    • Abhay Hull-Mounted SonarPDF p. 135
    • Lightweight torpedoesPDF p. 135
    • Indigenous anti-submarine rocket launcherPDF p. 135
    • Maareech Advanced Torpedo Decoy SystemPDF p. 135
    • Powered by three diesel engines with waterjet propulsion, the vessel offers high manoeuvrability in shallow waters.PDF p. 135
    • It is designed for underwater surveillance, anti- submarine warfare, low-intensity maritime operations and mine warfare-related tasks.PDF p. 135

    Mahe Class and the ASW SWC ProgrammePDF p. 135

    • The overall ASW-SWC programme comprises 16 vessels: eight contracted to CSL, Kochi, and eight to Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers (GRSE), Kolkata.PDF p. 135
    • INS Mangrol is the third vessel in CSL’s eight-ship Mahe-class series. INS Mahe and INS Malvan were commissioned before it.PDF p. 135
    • The Mahe class is intended to replace the Abhay- class ASW corvettes.PDF p. 135
    • CSL’s construction contract was signed on 30 April 2019.PDF p. 135
    • The class has a maximum speed of 25 knots and an endurance of 1,800 nautical miles. Order Ship Commissioning Date Location 1st INS Mahe 24 November 2025 Mumbai 2nd INS Malvan 22 July 2026 Karwar 3rd INS Mangrol 12 October 2026 MumbaiPDF p. 135

    India’s First Indigenous 350 kg-Thrust-Class Expendable Turbojet EnginePDF p. 135, 136

    • The first indigenous Expendable Turbo Jet Engine of 350 kg thrust class, designed by DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE), has been successfully developed. GTRE had identified Azad Engineering, Hyderabad as Industry partner for the manufacturing and assembly of the engine. On July 22, 2026, the engine was successfully realised and delivered to GTRE byPDF p. 135
    • Azad Engineering, a landmark achievement for India’s aerospace and defence ecosystem. The delivery marks the culmination of years of precision engineering, advanced manufacturing, and close partnership between India’ s scientific & industrial communities.PDF p. 136

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 136

    • The achievement demonstrates:PDF p. 136
    • Indian capability to manufacture and integrate a complex propulsion system from an indigenous design.PDF p. 136
    • Increasing cooperation between DRDO laboratories and private manufacturers.PDF p. 136
    • Progress in precision engineering, advanced metallurgy and thermal management.PDF p. 136
    • The possibility of reducing dependence on imported compact propulsion systems after successful testing and production approval.PDF p. 136

    IOL launches ‘GARUDPDF p. 136

    • India Optel Limited (IOL), a Mini Ratna Category-I Defence Public Sector Undertaking under the Department of Defence Production, launched the indigenous ‘GARUD’ High Resolution Binoculars for the civilian market on August 13, 2026 at DPSU Bhawan, New Delhi. The product was launched in the presence of Joint Secretary (Land Systems) Dr Garima Bhagat.PDF p. 136

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 136

    • GARUD has been developed and manufactured by Ordnance Factory, Dehradun, a unit of India Optel Limited.PDF p. 136

    Key Features and SpecificationsPDF p. 136

    • GARUD is designed to provide defence-grade optical performance for civilian users. Its major features include:PDF p. 136
    • 8x magnificationPDF p. 136
    • 7.6-degree wide field of viewPDF p. 136
    • ±5 diopter adjustment for different eyesight requirementsPDF p. 136
    • Weight of approximately 610 gramsPDF p. 136

    India’s first privately built FFSC rocket enginePDF p. 136

    • On August 7, 2026, Bengaluru-based Astrobase Space Technologies unveiled EVEREST, which it describes as India’s first fully integrated, privat ely developed Full-Flow Staged Combustion (FFSC) rocket engine. As of August 22, 2026, full-scale integrated hot- fire testing remained pending, so reported performance figures were company-stated design targets.PDF p. 136

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 136

    • High Thrust FFSC Rocket Engines – FFSC engines route fuel and oxidiser through separate pre-burners before the main combustion chamber. Gases produced drive turbines connected to pumps and then enter the chamber, ensuring that propellants contribute to thrust instead of being released into the atmosphere.PDF p. 136
    • Efficiency and Reusability – Unlike conventional engines, which use only part of the propellants to drive turbopumps, FFSC engines improve turbopump and propulsion efficiency. They support precise throttle control and reusable launch systems. LOX-methane propellants provide cleaner combustion, which can simplify refurbishment and support faster turnaround. However, the cycle is complex to design, develop and execute.PDF p. 136
    • Significance of EVEREST – EVEREST is presented as India’s first LOX-methane high- thrust engine and the fourth commercial FFSC development globally, after SpaceX, Stoke Space and LandSpace. It could support reusable launches carrying up to 30 tonnes to low Earth orbit and provide a medium-lift platform for commercial and strategic missions. Advanced manufacturing includes India’s largest industrial 3D printer.PDF p. 136

    The Indian Navy launched MachilipatnamPDF p. 136

    • Cochin Shipyard Limited launched Machilipatnam (BY 529), the seventh vessel in its eight-ship Mahe- class programme, at Kochi on July 29, 2026. An Anti- Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft is a compact warship designed to detect, track and counter underwater threats near the coast. Its small draught and specialised sensors make it suitable for littoral and shallow-water operations.PDF p. 136

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 136

    • Machilipatnam was launched by Mrs Goolrukh Anand in the presence of Vice Admiral Atul Anand, Additional Secretary, Department of Military Affairs.PDF p. 136
    • It is named after Machilipatnam, the historic port city and headquarters of Krishna district in Andhra Pradesh.PDF p. 136
    • Its principal roles will include coastal anti-submarine warfare, underwater surveillance, Low-Intensity Maritime Operations and mine-laying operations.PDF p. 136
    • It will strengthen coastal defence, littoral security and Maritime Domain Awareness after commissioning.PDF p. 136
    • The project incorporates more than 80% indigenous content and supports Aatmanirbhar Bharat in naval shipbuilding.PDF p. 136

    Project BackgroundPDF p. 136, 137

    • The Ministry of Defence and CSL signed the contract for eight vessels on April 30, 2019.PDF p. 136
    • The broader procurement programme consists of 16 ASW SWCs—eight Mahe-class vessels from CSL, Kochi, and eight Arnala-class vessels from GRSE, Kolkata.PDF p. 136
    • Official sources describe the Arnala class as replacing the ageing Abhay-class corvettes and the Mahe class as a parallel CSL-built class. For examinations, it is safest to connect the Abhay-class replacement with the wider 16-vessel ASW-SWC programme.PDF p. 136
    • Mangrol – Delivered on August 21, 2026, commissioned on October 12, 2026.PDF p. 136
    • Machilipatnam – Launched on 29 July 2026; not delivered or commissionedPDF p. 137
    • “Seventh” denotes Machilipatnam’s construction position within CSL’s series. It does not mean that it is the seventh commissioned vessel.PDF p. 137

    INS Malvan commissioned into Indian NavyPDF p. 137

    • INS Malvan, the second of the indigenously designed and built Mahe-class Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft (ASW-SWC), was commissioned at Karwar on July 22, 2026. The ship carries deep historical and cultural significance as it derives its name from the historical coastal town of Malvan in Maharashtra, a region intrinsically linked to the illustrious maritime heritage of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj.PDF p. 137

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 137

    • INS Malvan is the second of eight ASW-SWCs, being indigenously built by CSL, Kochi, and the sixth of 16 ASW-SWCs to be commissioned into Indian Navy.PDF p. 137
    • With over 80 percent indigenous content, the ship reinforces the Government of India’s vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat and India’s expanding ecosystem of naval design, equipment, system integration, and growing self-reliance in defence shipbuilding.PDF p. 137
    • The crest of INS Malvan carries the ‘Bagh Nakha’ (Tiger’s Claw), symbolising bravery, warfare tactics, agility, and audacity, resonating with the ship’s ethos to attack rapidly and strike silently.PDF p. 137
    • The waves surrounding ‘Bagh Nakha’ reflect the vast sea surrounding the coasts and the Indian Navy’s unwavering resolve to remain ever vigilant, ever ready, and steadfast in safeguarding the nation’s seas and sovereignty.PDF p. 137
    • The ship’s motto, ‘Silent Claws’, embodies lethality, stealth, and the ability to strike the adversary swiftly.PDF p. 137

    Garudastra Mortar SystemPDF p. 137

    • Recently on June 17, 2026 , Pune-based defence manufacturer Nibe Limited demonstrated Garudastra, an advanced long-range 120 mm vehicle-mounted mortar and bomb system, to the Indian Army at the Infantry School, Mhow. The demonstration was conducted on a No Cost–No Commitment (NC-NC) basis. According to Nibe’s official stock-exchange filing, the system was presented in technical collaboration with a foreign original equipment manufacturer, or OEM.PDF p. 137

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 137

    ICGS Akshay Commissioned into Bharatiya Tatrakshak FleetPDF p. 137

    • Bharatiya Tatrakshak marked another milestone in its force modernisation with the commissioning of ICGS Akshay, a new-generation Fast Patrol Vessel (FPV), at Goa Shipyard Limited, Goa, on June 27, 2026.Named Akshay, meaning Indestructible, the Fast Patrol Vessel embodies the enduring spirit, resilie nce and unwavering commitment of Bharatiya Tatrakshak towards safeguarding the nation’s maritime interests.PDF p. 137

    I-2SEA Submarine Cable System UnveiledPDF p. 137

    • A consortium comprising Microsoft, Singtel, Tata Communications and AI connectivity platform Lightstorm will build the I-2SEA (“India- Southeast Asia) submarine cable system connecting India, Malaysia and Singapore. Lightstorm announced the signing of contracts to launch the construction of the cabl e system on July 2, 2026. The facility is designed to cater to the rapidly growing demand from hyperscalers, GPU infrastructure providers and enterprises running AI training and inference workloads across the India– Southeast Asia corridor.PDF p. 137

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 137

    • The I-2SEA consortium will operate under a joint build agreement.PDF p. 137
    • NEC Corporation has been appointed as the system supplier and ASEAN Cableship as the marine installation partner. The system is open for capacity commitments.PDF p. 137

    Route, Landing Stations and ConnectivityPDF p. 137, 138

    • I-2SEA will link India’s east coast, which is home to the rapidly growing AI and hyperscaler data centre clusters in Hyderabad and Chennai, directly to Singapore, the region’s cloud interconnect and AI hub, and Malaysia’s emerging data centre corridor in Kuala Lumpur.PDF p. 137
    • The system will have dual landings in India.PDF p. 137
    • The landing at Machilipatnam will provide the shortest subsea access to Hyderabad, while the other landing will be located at a new and diverse location in South Chennai.PDF p. 137
    • The estimated length of the high-capacity cable will be 3,600 km from Singapore to Machilipatnam, with onward connectivity to Hyderabad.PDF p. 138
    • It is expected to deliver the fastest transmission on the Singapore–Malaysia–Hyderabad corridor, which is the most strategically critical city pair for AI workloads in the region.PDF p. 138

    India Becomes World’s Top Ship Recycling Nation in 2025PDF p. 138

    • India emerged as the world’s leading ship-recycling nation in 2025, achieving an important target of th e Maritime India Vision 2030 five years ahead of schedule. According to the latest data of the Unite d Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), cited by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways on 22 June 2026, India accounted for 35.4% of global ship recycling in 2025.PDF p. 138

Indicator 2024 2025 India’s share in global ship recycling 30.1% 35.4% Volume of ships recycled 1.86 million GT 2.99 million GT Annual growth in recycling volume — Nearly 60%PDF p. 138

INS Mahendragiri is the sixth Project 17A stealth frigate commissioned within approximately 1 8 months.
