    Agray: Design and ConstructionPDF p. 139

    • Agray has been indigenously designed and built by GRSE, Kolkata.PDF p. 139
    • The ship is around 77 metres long and belongs to a class of vessels described by the Indian Navy as the largest Indian Naval warships propelled by waterjets.PDF p. 139
    • Sanshodhak — Survey Vessel Large – GRSE also delivered Sanshodhak, the fourth and final Survey Vessel (Large) of its class. It is designed for full- scale coastal and deep-water hydrographic surveys, including surveys of ports, harbour approaches, navigation channels and maritime routes.PDF p. 139

    Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile ‘Agni-III’PDF p. 139

    • Agni-III is an important part of India’s strategic deterrence system. On February 6, 2026, India successfully test-fired Agni-III from the Integrated Test Range, Chandipur, Odisha.PDF p. 139
    • With this test, the Agni series of missiles continues to strengthen India’s strategic capabilities. The series includes Agni-1 with a range of 700 km, Agni-2 with a range of 2,000 km, Agni-3 with a range of 3,000 km, Agni-4 capable of striking targets up to 4,000 km, and Agni-5, which has the longest striking range of 5,000 km.PDF p. 139

    What is Agni 3 and why its success matters for IndiaPDF p. 139

    • The Agni-3 is an indigenous, two-stage, solid-fuelled intermediate-range ballistic missile, featuring a strike range of more than 3000 km and 1.5-tonne payload capacity.PDF p. 139
    • Launch of the First Cadet Training Ship ‘Krishna’PDF p. 139
    • The launch of the first Cadet Training Ship, Krishna, is an important development for the Indian Navy. It strengthens India’s sea-training capacity for future officers and also reflects the wider national push toward indigenous defence production under Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India.PDF p. 139
    • Yard 18003 (Krishna), the first of the three Cadet Training Ships (CTS) under construction at M/s L&T, Kattupalli (Chennai), has been launched on 16 Feb 2026.PDF p. 139

    INS AridamanPDF p. 139, 140

    • India’s reported induction of its third nuclear- powered ballistic missile submarine, INS Aridhaman/PDF p. 139
    • Aridaman , and the official commissioning of the stealth frigate INS Taragiri at Visakhapatnam mark an important step in India’s naval modernisation.PDF p. 140
    • A larger 7,000-tonne vessel, INS Aridaman will carry more K-15 missiles, as well as the intermediate- range K-4 nuclear-capable submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs) – with nearly double the number of VLS tubes than its predecessors – that can hit targets 3,500 km away.PDF p. 140

    Indigenous Pilot trainer Aircraft ‘HANSA-3 NG”,PDF p. 140

    • The CSIR–National Aerospace Laboratories (CSIR- NAL), Bengaluru, showcased a major step from “lab- to-market” by launching the production version of the indigenous HANSA 3 (NG) trainer aircraft, alongside multiple aerospace initiatives aimed at strengtheni ng India’s civil and defence aviation ecosystem.PDF p. 140
    • Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology Dr. Jitendra Singh on November 29, 2025 launched the production version of India’s indigenous HANSA-3 NG pilot trainer aircraft at CSIR–National Aerospace Laboratories (NAL) in Bengaluru.PDF p. 140
    • The Hansa-3 has an all-composite airframe (as opposed to purely metal), and is designed to meet the expanding demand for PPL (Private Pilot Licence) and CPL (Commercial Pilot Licence) training.PDF p. 140
    • First designed and developed by the CSIR-NAL in the early 1990s, the latest iteration of the HANSA-3 has undergone significant upgrades.PDF p. 140

    Dhvani: Hypersonic MissilePDF p. 140

    • India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is developing the ‘Dhvani’ Hypersonic Missile under its advanced hypersonic weapons program. This is a next-generation missile system designed as a Hypersonic Glide Vehicle (HGV), capable of performing sharp maneuvers at high altitudes at speeds exceeding Mach 5 (more than 7,400 km/h).PDF p. 140
    • Dhvani is a Hypersonic Glide Vehicle (HGV) capable of high-speed changes in direction while traveling at hypersonic speeds at high altitudes.PDF p. 140
    • The missile’s potential operational range is 6,000 to 10,000 kilometers , which could nearly double the reach of India’s Agni-V Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM).PDF p. 140
    • The missile’s speed is greater than Mach 5, making its interception by current missile defense systems virtually impossible.PDF p. 140

    ‘Saksham’ Counter-Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) Grid SystemPDF p. 140

    • The Indian Army has initiated the procurement of the indigenously developed ‘Saksham’ Counter Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) Grid System to strengthen its operational readiness against emergi ng aerial threats.PDF p. 140
    • SAKSHAM stands for Situational Awareness for Kinetic Soft and Hard Kill Assets Management.PDF p. 140
    • It is an indigenously developed Counter-Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) grid system, developed by Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL).PDF p. 140
    • Its Objectives are:PDF p. 140
    • To detect, track, identify, and neutralize enemy drones, quadcopter drones, and Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) in real-time in border areas. E. MiscellaneousPDF p. 140

    Global Fintech Fest 2026PDF p. 140

    • India is reshaping the global fintech landscape through scale, innovation and Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI). The introduction of Aadhaar, expansion of internet connectivity and development of Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transformed financial services. These innovations enabled digital identity, instant payments and consent-based data sharing at population scale.PDF p. 140
    • This transformation has positioned India as a global centre for fintech innovation and digital finance. The Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 reflects India’s growing global influence in this sector. The 7th edition of GFF was held in Mumbai from 8 to 11 September 2026. It provides a platform for global dialogue, collaboration and innovation in financial technology.PDF p. 140
    • Since its inception in 2020, GFF has grown into one of the world’s leading fintech gatherings.PDF p. 140

    GFF 2026 - Powering the Next Wave of Financial InnovationPDF p. 140

    • The 7th Global Fintech Fest 2026 is far more than a conference. It is the world’s largest fintech festival, uniting the brightest minds to shape an AI-powered future.PDF p. 140

    Global Fintech Fest - ThemePDF p. 140, 141

    • The theme of GFF 2026 is “ Potential to Impact: Agentic AI | Tokenisation | Quantum: Trusted, Connected, Global Systems for Inclusive Finance.”PDF p. 140
    • It is built upon three foundational technologies that are shifting the landscape of global finance toward autonomous, programmable, and secure ecosystems.PDF p. 140
    • Agentic AI : It enables financial systems to sense, decide, and act in real time within strong governance frameworks.PDF p. 141
    • Tokenisation: It transforms assets into programmable digital units, enabling fractional ownership, instant settlement, and interoperable money.PDF p. 141
    • Quantum: Quantum technologies introduce a foundational shift in computation and security.PDF p. 141

    Understanding FintechPDF p. 141

    • FinTech is generally described as an industry that leverages technology to make financial systems and the delivery of financial services more efficient.PDF p. 141

    Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicator Report 2026PDF p. 141

    • The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) on October 12, 2026 has released the “Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicator Report” for the quarter ending 30th June 2026 details of services in India for the period covering 1st April 2026 to 30th June 2026 compiled mainly on the basis of information furnished by the Service Providers.PDF p. 141

    Internet Access and Data UsePDF p. 141

    • Internet subscriptions rose from 1,092.79 million in March 2026 to 1,114.17 million in June 2026, an increase of 1.96%.PDF p. 141
    • Broadband subscriptions increased by 2.03% to 1,087.50 million, while narrowband subscriptions fell by 0.89% to 26.67 million.PDF p. 141
    • The internet base included 47.73 million wired connections and 1,066.43 million wireless connections. Mobile wireless access accounted for 94.07% of all internet subscriptions.PDF p. 141
    • Mobile data use rose by 8.30% to 84,424 petabytes (PB) during the quarter. Average monthly use per mobile data subscriber increased by 6.32% to 28.39 gigabytes (GB).PDF p. 141
    • Mobile data subscriptions reached 1,045.55 million, compared with 1,026.75 million in March.PDF p. 141
    • These rounded totals imply growth of about 1.83%, although the official summary states 1.86%.PDF p. 141

    Telephone ConnectionsPDF p. 141

    • Total telephone subscriptions increased by 1.31% to 1,348.08 million. They were 10.65% higher than in June 2025.PDF p. 141
    • Overall tele-density rose from 93.26 to 94.31 connections per 100 people. The headline totals include Machine-to-Machine (M2M) cellular connections, which allow devices to communicate. Tele-density excluding M2M was 84.88.PDF p. 141
    • Wireless mobile and Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) connections together reached 1,300.25 million, up by 1.40%. Wireline subscriptions declined by 0.88% to 47.82 million. FWA uses a wireless link to serve a fixed location.PDF p. 141
    • Private operators held 92.50% of all telephone subscriptions, while public sector operators held 7.50%.PDF p. 141

    The Urban and Rural GapPDF p. 141

    • Rural telephone subscriptions increased to 556.01 million, but their share of the national total fell from 41.47% to 41.24%.PDF p. 141
    • Urban subscriptions grew faster. The comparison below shows that the gap remained wide.PDF p. 141

    Revenue and UsagePDF p. 141

    • Monthly wireless Average Revenue per User (ARPU) rose by 1.19% to ₹187.12. Monthly Minutes of Usage (MOU) per subscriber fell by 2.65% to 933 minutes.PDF p. 141
    • Average revenue earned per GB of mobile data fell by 5.07% to ₹7.13. This is an operator revenue indicator, not a universal retail price for one GB.PDF p. 141
    • Access services contributed 83.85% of sector AGR. Licence fees increased by 2.41% to ₹7,103 crore.PDF p. 141

    Indigenous Micro Graphics Processing Unit at IIT DelhiPDF p. 141

    • On September 24, 2026, IIT Delhi announced an indigenous micro-GPU for embedded devices. As of 13 October 2026, it has demonstrated the FPGA design, while ASIC development remains planned. A Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is a specialised processor that renders images and handles many calculations in parallel. A micro-GPU is a compact graphics processor. This project targets embedded devices, which contain computers designed for specific functions.PDF p. 141

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 141

    Development and key featuresPDF p. 141

    • M.Tech students Nammi Akash and M. Ravi Teja led the project under Prof. Jayadeva and Prof. Kaushik Saha of IIT Delhi’s Department of Electrical Engineering.PDF p. 141
    • The team demonstrated programmable graphics rendering using a custom floating-point GPU engine, implemented entirely in Register Transfer Language (RTL).PDF p. 141
    • The design was mapped to a Spartan-7 Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) and demonstrated on a standard development board. An FPGA is a chip whose logic can be programmed after manufacture.PDF p. 141
    • The processor is a scalable, programmable intellectual property (IP) design that can be adapted for different devices. It can run on an FPGA or be made as an Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), a chip designed for a particular task.PDF p. 141

    NFI 2026 & Biovigilance Programme of IndiaPDF p. 142

    • Union Minister of State for Health & Family Welfare and Chemicals & Fertilizers, Smt. Anupriya Patel, on 21 September 2026 launched the 7th Edition of the National Formulary of India (NFI), the Guidance Document for Hospitals in India for Safety Monitoring and Reporting of Medical Device-Related Adverse Events, and the ADR-PvPI 2.0 Mobile App for iOS users at the 6th National Pharmacovigilance Week programme organised by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) at Dr. Ambedkar International Centre, New Delhi. She also announced government approval of the Biovigilance Programme of India, extending safety monitoring to products used in organ and tissue transplantation.PDF p. 142

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 142

    Biovigilance Programme of IndiaPDF p. 142

    • The Government of India has approved the programme to strengthen the reporting, assessment, monitoring and prevention of adverse events associated with medicines and biological products used in organ and tissue transplantation.PDF p. 142
    • Its coverage includes products administered to both donors and recipients.PDF p. 142

    Cabinet approves scheme of Chemical Parks (BHAVYA Rasayan)PDF p. 142

    • The Union Cabinet chaired by the Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi has approved Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana Rasayan or BHAVYA - Rasayan Scheme for establishing three dedicated Chemical Parks in the country. The Scheme was announced in the Union Budget of FY 2026–27.The Scheme will have a total financial outlay of Rs.3,030 crore, with Rs.3,000 crore towards meeting the cost of establishing the Common Infrastructure Facilities and Basic Utilities inside the park and Rs. 30 Crores as administrative expenditure. The scheme would run for a period of 5 years from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31.PDF p. 142

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 142

    Financial Assistance and Economic BenefitsPDF p. 142

    • Under this scheme central government would provide a grant of up to Rs.1,000 crore per park.PDF p. 142
    • This will be subject to minimum contribution of Rs.500 crore by the concerned State Government.PDF p. 142
    • BHAVYA Rasayan Scheme will promote development of the Chemical industry along the whole value chains including upstream, downstream and ancillary industries promoting efficient utilization of resources, leading to lower logistics cost.PDF p. 142

    India commissioned its first and deepest geothermal wellsPDF p. 142

    • The Ladakh administration has commissioned India’s first geothermal wells in the cold desert with two 1000-metre-deep wells at Puga Valley. It is a major step towards setting up India’s first-ever geothermal power plants in the region.PDF p. 142

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 142

    • Established at an altitude of 14,000 feet, the two deep wells are expected to pave the way for a one- megawatt geothermal power plant in Ladakh.PDF p. 142
    • The project was inaugurated by VK Saxena, Lt Governor of Ladakh.PDF p. 142
    • “The two geothermal wells are critical for the successful implementation of the 1 MW pilot geothermal power project at Puga, which will be India’s first demonstration-scale geothermal power project.PDF p. 142
    • The maximum temperature of 135 degrees Celsius was recorded at a depth of 400 metres.PDF p. 142
    • This geothermal power project would act as a catalyst for Ladakh’s holistic development.PDF p. 142

    Bharat Electricity Summit 2026PDF p. 142

    • Over the past decade, India’s power sector has undergone a period of major structural change, transitioning to a system defined by adequacy, expanded capacity, and improved reliability.PDF p. 142
    • Bharat Electricity Summit 2026 was held from 19 to 22 March 2026 at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi.PDF p. 142
    • The Summit was a global conference-cum-exhibition for the power and electricity sector.PDF p. 142
    • It was held under the theme “Electrifying Growth. Empowering Sustainability. Connecting Globally.”PDF p. 142

    The Summit was important for India’s long- term power-sector planning.PDF p. 142

    • Two important reports were released at the Summit: the National Resource Adequacy Plan and the Transmission Plan for Integration of over 900 GW Non-Fossil Fuel Capacity by 2035–36.PDF p. 142
    • Transmission planning is necessary because renewable energy projects are often located far from major demand centres.PDF p. 142

    India recorded major capacity expansion during FY 2025–26.PDF p. 142, 143

    • The figure of 52,537 MW capacity addition belongs to the period up to 31 January 2026.PDF p. 142
    • For the completed FY 2025–26, official MNRE data state that non-fossil capacity addition was 55.29 GW, the highest increase in any year.PDF p. 142
    • In FY 2025–26, solar capacity addition reached 44.61 GW, while wind capacity addition reached 6.05 GW.PDF p. 142
    • As of 31 March 2026, India’s total installed power generation capacity was 5,32,740 MW , or about 532.740 GW.PDF p. 142
    • As of March 31, 2026, India’s total non-fossil capacity was 2,83,468 MW, or about 283.468 GW, forming 53.2% of total installed capacity.PDF p. 143

    The latest official renewable energy data show further growth after March 2026.PDF p. 143

    • As of 31 May 2026, India’s total renewable energy capacity, including large hydro, was 282,745.08 MW.PDF p. 143
    • As of 31 May 2026, India’s total non-fossil capacity was 291,525.08 MW.PDF p. 143
    • Solar power remained the largest renewable segment, with cumulative solar capacity of 157.05 GW as on May 31, 2026.PDF p. 143
    • Wind power capacity stood at 56,807.04 MW as of 31 May 2026.PDF p. 143
    • The National Power Portal dashboard for June 2026 showed India’s total installed capacity at 548,848.48 MW.PDF p. 143
    • In that classification, thermal capacity was 251,489.13 MW, hydro capacity was 52,064.66 MW, RES capacity excluding large hydro was 236,514.69 MW, and nuclear capacity was 8,780 MW.PDF p. 143

    India’s transmission network has also expanded significantlyPDF p. 143

    • In January 2026, India’s national power transmission network crossed 5 lakh circuit kilometres of transmission lines of 220 kV and above.PDF p. 143
    • At that milestone, transformation capacity reached 1,407 GVA.PDF p. 143
    • The Ministry of Power described India’s grid as the world’s largest synchronous national grid.PDF p. 143
    • The milestone was linked to the vision of “One Nation – One Grid – One Frequency.”PDF p. 143
    • As per the National Power Portal data available for June 2026, India’s transmission network reached 509,603 ckm, and transformation capacity reached 14,77,951 MVA, or about 1,477.951 GVA.PDF p. 143
    • Transmission expansion is important because India needs to evacuate and integrate large quantities of solar, wind, hydro and other non-fossil electricity into the national grid.PDF p. 143

    India has moved close to power sufficiency.PDF p. 143

    • In FY 2025–26, the country’s energy requirement was 17,07,493 MU , while energy availability was 17,06,985 MU.PDF p. 143
    • The energy deficit was only 0.03% in FY 2025–26.PDF p. 143
    • The peak demand was 2,45,444 MW , while maximum demand met was 2,45,416 MW.PDF p. 143
    • The peak deficit was only 0.01%, showing a very small gap between demand and supply.PDF p. 143

    Research Station: Approval for the Construction of Maitri IIPDF p. 143

    • India is now set to begin a new chapter on the wor ld’s southernmost continent, Antarctica. According to a press release issued by the Ministry of Finance on October 4, 2025, approval has been granted for the construction of ‘Maitri II’, which will be India’s proposed fourth research station , to be built in East Antarctica. The station is planned to be ready by 2032.PDF p. 143
    • India began research activities in Antarctica in the early 1980s.PDF p. 143
    • The first station, ‘Dakshin Gangotri’, operated for a few years.PDF p. 143
    • Currently, India has two active stations—PDF p. 143
    • Maitri (since 1989),PDF p. 143
    • Bharati (since 2012).PDF p. 143
    • The Maitri station is situated on a 20 km long ice- free stretch of land called the Schirmacher Oasis.PDF p. 143
    • It is located at an altitude of approximately 50 meters above sea level and about 100 km inland from the coast.PDF p. 143
    • It is noteworthy that the project is being executed by the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Re- search (NCPOR), Goa.PDF p. 143

    News in ShortPDF p. 143

    India’s first national ship manufacturing heavy industry parkaPDF p. 143

    • The National Shipbuilding & Heavy Industries Park, Tamil Nadu (NSHIP , TN) has been established as the country’s first Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) dedicated to developing a mega shipbuilding cluster.PDF p. 143

    WAVES Animation Bazaar and 8 th Edition of India Joy 2025PDF p. 143

    • Recently, on November 1, 2025 WAVES Animation Bazaar and 8 th edition of India Joy 2025, a two- day event dedicated to media and entertainment inaugurated in Hyderabad.PDF p. 143
    • The two-day event, being organised with support of Telangana government, the Telangana VFX, Animation and Gaming Association and the Union Ministry of I&B is dedicated to the creative economy across films, e-sports, VFX, animation, OTT, comics and other emerging digital entertainment sectors.PDF p. 143
    • The WAVES Bazaar platform aims to empower creators to monetise their work and accelerate industry growth, thus transforming craft to commerce.PDF p. 143

    India International Science Festival (IISF), 2025PDF p. 143

    • The 11th edition of IISF was held from December 6-9, 2025 in Panchkula, Haryana. This flagship event featured exhibitions, business-to-business meetings, competitions, and cultural programs that bridge the gap between laboratories and society.PDF p. 143
    • The theme of India International Science Festival (IISF) 2025 – “Vigyan Se Samruddhi: for Atmanirbhar Bharat” was to celebrate and advance the spirit of science-led growth for a self-reliant and prosperous India.PDF p. 143

    Chapter 6 · PDF pp. 144-156

    Environmental Affairs

    Environmental reports are easiest to read by separating a measured value, a target and a projection. Always preserve the baseline year, the unit and exclusions. For wetlands, keep the place-state pair and treat the issue's changing tally as dated information.

    1. Climate: actuals, targets, baselines
    2. Wetlands: names and locations
    3. COP outcomes: mitigation, adaptation, finance

    Build the chapter in eight anchors

    A small difference is not proof of a peak

    The issue's Emissions Gap Report article gives global emissions of 58.4 GtCO₂e in 2025 against a revised 58.5 in 2024, but says uncertainty prevents confirmation of a decline or peak.

    PDF p. 144
    Absolute and per-capita emissions

    The same article gives India 4.5 billion tonnes CO₂e in 2025 and 3.1 tonnes per person against a 6.4-tonne global average. Both Indian figures exclude land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF).

    PDF p. 144
    Reductions need a baseline

    The source's pathway requires global reductions of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040 against 2025 levels. These are pathway requirements, not claimed achieved reductions.

    PDF p. 144
    Dated Ramsar tally

    The issue reports Sauj Lake and Sukhna Wetland additions on 15 October 2026 and a total of 103 Indian Ramsar sites. This is the issue's snapshot, not a live total.

    PDF p. 144
    UP wetland pair

    The map places Sauj Lake in Mainpuri and Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary (Surha Tal) in Uttar Pradesh. It lists 14 UP entries; its dates differ from the prose and are flagged.

    PDF p. 145
    Largest, smallest and first

    The map's fact box identifies Sundarbans, West Bengal, as India's largest Ramsar wetland; Vembannur Wetland Complex, Tamil Nadu, as smallest; Chilika and Keoladeo as the first Indian sites in 1981.

    PDF p. 145
    COP30 setting

    COP30 is placed in Belém, Brazil, on 10-22 November 2025. The article describes an implementation focus and a four-step action cycle: Coordinate, Measure, Showcase, Scale.

    PDF p. 156
    A target with two years

    The Belém 4x Pledge described in the article targets quadrupling sustainable-fuel use by 2035 relative to 2024, with progress tracked by the IEA. It is a pledge, not a completed result.

    PDF p. 156
    Actual, target and projection
    Kind of statementExample from the issueReading rule
    Measured/estimated actual58.4 GtCO₂e in 2025Keep uncertainty and revised comparison
    Pathway requirement18% reduction by 2030 from 2025A requirement is not an achievement
    Pledge4x sustainable fuels by 2035 from 2024Keep both target year and baseline
    Dated inventory103 Ramsar sites, October 2026Do not call it today's count
    PDF p. 144, 156
    Learning aid - not from sourceFor a climate number ask 'relative to when?' and 'what is excluded?'. For a wetland, first recall the State, then the date. This is an editorial reading aid.

    Close the notes. Explain it back.

    Why does 58.4 versus 58.5 not establish an emissions peak?

    The source explicitly says uncertainty prevents confirmation of a decline or peak. A tiny difference between estimates is not enough to discard that caveat.PDF p. 144

    Explain how India's large total and lower per-capita figure can coexist.

    Total emissions and emissions per person measure different things. The source gives 4.5 billion tonnes overall and 3.1 tonnes per person, excluding LULUCF; do not compare those numbers without their units.PDF p. 144

    Reconstruct the three global reduction requirements with their baseline.

    18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, all against 2025. They describe a pathway, not cuts already achieved.PDF p. 144

    Recover the COP30 action cycle in order.

    Coordinate → Measure → Showcase → Scale. The source presents this as its implementation activation cycle.PDF p. 156

    What are the target and baseline in the Belém 4x Pledge?

    Quadruple sustainable-fuel use by 2035 relative to 2024. IEA tracking is the monitoring detail, not the baseline year.PDF p. 156

    Source check. The prose says Sauj Lake and Sukhna were added on 15 October 2026, but the map labels Sauj 18 June 2026 and Sukhna 16 March 2026. The map also labels Surha Tal 19 January 2025 while p. 5 describes its 100th-site news in June 2026. These dates are preserved and not used as unqualified test keys.PDF p. 144, 145

    UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026PDF p. 144

    • UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026: 17th edition of the Emissions Gap Report 2026 (titled The Point of Return) was released by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) on October 21, 2026.PDF p. 144
    • Global emissions: Greenhouse gas emissions reached 58.4 gigatonnes of CO 2 equivalent (GtCO2e) in 2025, against a revised 58.5 GtCO2e in 2024; uncertainty prevents confirming a decline or peak.PDF p. 144
    • G20: Excluding the Afrizcan Union, members contributed 76% of global emissions; their emissions excluding land use, land-use change and forestry rose 0.7% in 2025.PDF p. 144
    • National commitments: By 1 September 2026 , 124 Parties, representing 76% of global emissions, had submitted updated nationally determined contributions (NDCs).PDF p. 144
    • Warming threshold: Exceeding 1.5°C above preindustrial levels is unavoidable; stronger mitigation can reduce its magnitude and duration.PDF p. 144
    • Lowest overshoot pathway: Peak warming can be limited to 1.7–1.8°C with 66% probability , with around 50% probability of returning to 1.5°C by 2100.PDF p. 144
    • Required reductions: Against 2025 levels , emissions must fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040.PDF p. 144
    • Commitment shortfall: Full NDC implementation delivers only 5–8% reductions by 2030 and 11–15% by 2035.PDF p. 144
    • Emissions gap: Even with conditional commitments implemented, the gap against the lowest overshoot pathway remains 5 GtCO 2e in 2030 and 16 GtCO2e in 2035.PDF p. 144

    Emissions Gap Report 2026: India-specific factsPDF p. 144

    • Third-largest emitter: India’s greenhouse gas emissions were 4.5 billion tonnes of CO 2 equivalent in 2025, placing it third after China and the United States. This estimate excludes land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF).PDF p. 144
    • Low per capita emissions: India emitted 3.1 tonnes of CO 2 equivalent per person in 2025 , compared with the global average of 6.4 tonnes— the lowest among the six largest emitters assessed. These figures also exclude LULUCF.PDF p. 144
    • Decadal emissions trend: During 2016–2025, India’s total greenhouse gas emissions increased by an annual average of 3.5%, while per capita emissions increased by 2.6% annually.PDF p. 144
    • 2035 emissions-intensity target: India’s updated nationally determined contribution (NDC) seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions per unit of GDP by 47% from 2005 levels by 2035.PDF p. 144
    • 2035 non-fossil electricity target: India aims for about 60% of cumulative installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources by 2035 , conditional on technology transfer and international finance.PDF p. 144
    • 2035 carbon-sink target: India aims for a cumulative increase of 3.5–4 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent in carbon sinks through forest and tree cover , relative to 2005 levels. Emissions- Gap-Report-2026PDF p. 144
    • Progress towards 2030 commitments: India is among six G20 members likely to achieve their unconditional 2030 targets under existing policies, alongside China, Indonesia, Russia, South Africa and Türkiye . The report also projects India to achieve its conditional 2030 target.PDF p. 144
    • Projected emissions under NDCs: Under full implementation of its NDC targets, India’s annual emissions in 2035 are projected to be 1,254 million tonnes of CO 2 equivalent higher than in 2030 , with per capita emissions of 3.6 tonnes. Emissions- Gap-Report-2026PDF p. 144
    • Coal-power construction: India and China together account for 95% of coal-power capacity currently under construction worldwide . This figure concerns construction, rather than existing installed capacity. Emissions-Gap-Report-2026PDF p. 144

    • Interesting FactsPDF p. 145
    • Total Ramsar sites in India at Present: 103PDF p. 145

    Major Ramsar Sites in IndiaPDF p. 145

    • 1. Sukhna Wetland (March 16, 2026)PDF p. 145

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 146

    • BackgroundPDF p. 146
    • The Montreal Protocol (1987) was adopted to phase out CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances.PDF p. 146
    • Countries have since eliminated nearly 99% of controlled ozone-depleting substances, helping the ozone layer recover.PDF p. 146
    • HFCs became widely used in refrigeration and air- conditioning because they do not damage the ozone layer.PDF p. 146
    • However, many HFCs have hundreds or thousands of times the warming impact of CO 2 over 100 years.PDF p. 146
    • As HFC use expanded, the Federated States of Micronesia and Mauritius proposed bringing them under the Montreal Protocol in 2009.PDF p. 146
    • The Kigali Amendment entered into force in January 2019 . It establishes binding schedules to reduce HFC production and consumption, while developing countries receive longer compliance periods.PDF p. 146
    • Since limited HFC use can continue after reductions, it is called a phase-down rather than a phase-out.PDF p. 146

    India’s Kigali CommitmentsPDF p. 146

    • India ratified the Kigali Amendment in 2021.PDF p. 146
    • 2028: Freeze HFC production and consumption at the agreed baseline.PDF p. 146
    • 2032: Reduce HFCs by 10% below the baseline.PDF p. 146
    • 2047: Achieve an 85% reduction.PDF p. 146
    • The limits are calculated according to the gases’ warming impact.PDF p. 146
    • Equipment purchased before the first reductions may remain in use well into the 2030s.PDF p. 146

    Cabinet approves Green Energy Corridor Phase-III schemePDF p. 146

    • On 30 September 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Green Energy Corridor Phase III to strengthen renewable electricity transmission and add battery storage.PDF p. 146

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 146

    Green Energy CorridorPDF p. 146

    • A Green Energy Corridor is a network of transmission lines and substations that carries electricity from renewable energy plants to the power grid.PDF p. 146
    • Power evacuation means moving the electricity generated at a plant into this network.PDF p. 146
    • Phase III will strengthen the Intra-State Transmission System (InSTS) within States and Union Territories.PDF p. 146

    Objectives and Key FeaturesPDF p. 146

    • It aims to support evacuation of up to 135 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy and deployment of 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) by FY 2032–33.PDF p. 146

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 146

    • 103rd Ramsar Site: Sauj LakePDF p. 146
    • Sauj Lake, located in Mainpuri district of Uttar Pradesh, is a shallow lake surrounded by farmland in the floodplain of the Ganga River.PDF p. 146
    • It forms part of a larger network of wetlands, contributing to ecological connectivity in the wider landscape, and is close to Saman Bird Sanctuary.PDF p. 146
    • 102nd Ramsar Site: Sukhna WetlandPDF p. 146
    • Located at the edge of the city of Chandigarh and at the base of the Outer Himalayas , Sukhna Wetland is a peri-urban reservoir that plays an important role in regulating sediment and water flows from the surrounding catchment.PDF p. 146
    • 101st Ramsar Site: Glaw LakePDF p. 146
    • Glaw Lake in Arunachal Pradesh was announced as India’s 101st Ramsar Site on 3 August 2026.PDF p. 146
    • It became the first wetland from Arunachal Pradesh to be included in the List of Wetlands of International Importance.PDF p. 146
    • Glaw Lake, locally known as Glaw Tuwi, is a natural freshwater wetland in Lohit district.PDF p. 146
    • As of August 2026, India ranked third globally by number of Ramsar Sites, behind the United Kingdom with 176 sites and Mexico with 144 sites.PDF p. 146

    100th Ramsar Site: Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary (Surha Tal)PDF p. 146

    • On 5 June 2026, the Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary, also known as Surha Tal, located in Ballia district of Uttar Pradesh, was recognised as India’s 100th Ramsar Site.PDF p. 146

    India’s first petroglyph conservation park inaugurated in LehPDF p. 146

    • PM Modi inaugurated India’s first Petroglyph Conservation Park on October 15, 2026 at Sindhu Ghat in Leh to protect Ladakh’s ancient rock art and archaeological heritage.PDF p. 146

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 146, 147

    • A petroglyph conservation park is a dedicated open- air facility designed to protect, preserve, and showcase ancient rock carvings (petroglyphs) that are at risk from natural erosion, infrastructure expansion, and unregulated tourism. The Kigali Amendment marked its 10th anniversary The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol marked its 10th anniversary on October 15, 2026 . Adopted in Kigali, Rawanda on October 15, 2016. It seeks to phase down HFCs, which are used in cooling. Full implementation could avoid about 0.3 – 0.5°C global warming by 2100.PDF p. 146
    • The scheme will strengthen transmission networks so that more renewable electricity can reach consumers.PDF p. 147

    Financial Outlay and ImplementationPDF p. 147

    • Target Completion: FY 2032–33.PDF p. 147
    • Total Project Outlay: ₹1,86,405 crore.PDF p. 147
    • Intra-State Transmission System development under GEC-III: ₹1,36,378 crore.PDF p. 147
    • Deployment of 50 GWh of battery storage: ₹50,000 crore.PDF p. 147
    • Total Central Financial Support: ₹54,082 crore.PDF p. 147
    • Central Financial Assistance (CFA) will reduce intra- state transmission charges and help keep electricity costs affordable.PDF p. 147

    Expected Benefits and SignificancePDF p. 147

    • Support India’s target of 900 GW installed non- fossil fuel capacity by 2035.PDF p. 147
    • Enhance national energy security and promote environmentally sustainable development by reducing carbon emissions.PDF p. 147
    • Generate direct and indirect employment in the power, manufacturing, construction and energy storage sectors.PDF p. 147
    • Create long-term skilled jobs in grid management, operation and maintenance.PDF p. 147
    • Improve renewable energy utilisation and ensure reliable, affordable electricity for consumers.PDF p. 147

    India’s Net Zero Portal and the NAPCC DashboardPDF p. 147

    • Union Minister of State for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Kirti Vardhan Singh, on 16 September, 2026 launched India’s Net Zero Portal and the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) Dashboard on the occasion of World Ozone Day 2026 in Mumbai. The two digital initiatives mark an important step towards strengthening transparency, coordination and evidence-based climate action.PDF p. 147

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 147

    • Net Zero emissions refer to a state where anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by an entity (organization / industry / government) over a period of one year are compensated by GHG removals through anthropogenic interventions over the same period of time.PDF p. 147

    The Net Zero PortalPDF p. 147

    • The Net Zero Portal is a centralised digital platform for voluntary registration and disclosure of Net Zero commitments by Indian entities across sectors.PDF p. 147
    • Participating entities can disclose their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, declare Net Zero targets and provide annual progress updates.PDF p. 147

    The NAPCC DashboardPDF p. 147

    • The NAPCC Dashboard provides a consolidated digital view of implementation and progress across the National Missions under the NAPCC.PDF p. 147
    • It brings together mission-related information and identified indicators on a common platform, facilitating systematic monitoring by concerned Ministries and Departments.PDF p. 147

    Indian climate goals in 2015PDF p. 147

    • India’s 2015 Intended Nationally Determined Contribution (INDC) contained eight goals. Three were quantitative targets, shown in the comparison below.PDF p. 147
    • The remaining five concerned sustainable lifestyles, cleaner development, adaptation, finance and technology .PDF p. 147

    NDC updates in 2022 and 2026PDF p. 147

    • A Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) is a country’s climate action plan under the Paris Agreement.PDF p. 147
    • The 2022 Updated First NDC strengthened India’s targets for 2030 and explicitly supported Lifestyle for Environment (LiFE). India submitted its NDC for 2031–2035 on 24 April 2026, raising all three quantitative targets. Quantitative goal 2015 INDC By 2030 2022 update By 2030 2026 NDC By 2035 Reduction in GDP emissions intensity from the 2005 level 33–35% 45% 47% Share of cumulative installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources About 40% About 50% About 60% Forest and tree carbon sink in billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent Additional 2.5–3.0 Additional 2.5–3.0 3.5–4.0 relative to 2005PDF p. 147

    Progress and future milestonesPDF p. 147

    • 2019: The original GDP emissions-intensity goal reached a 33% reduction from 2005, eleven years before the 2030 deadline.PDF p. 147
    • 2021: The original 40% non-fossil installed-capacity target was achieved nine years early.PDF p. 147
    • June 2025: The revised 50% non-fossil installed- capacity target was achieved five years early.PDF p. 147
    • India’s Progress on Climate CommitmentsPDF p. 147
    • India reduced the emissions intensity of GDP by 37.38% in 2022 compared with the 2005 level.PDF p. 147
    • During 2005–2022, India created an additional carbon sink of 2.44 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through increased forest and tree cover.PDF p. 147
    • This reflects India’s continued progress towards achieving its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets.PDF p. 147
    • Expansion of Non-Fossil Electricity CapacityPDF p. 147
    • As of 30 September 2026, non-fossil fuel sources accounted for about 55% of India’s total installed electricity capacity.PDF p. 147
    • India’s total installed electricity capacity stood at 558.8 GW , of which 308 GW came from non-fossil sources.PDF p. 147
    • The growing share of non-fossil capacity highlights India’s transition towards a cleaner and low-carbon energy system.PDF p. 147

    Swachh Sagar Surakshit Sagar 2026PDF p. 148

    • The fifth edition of Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar was held from 12 to 19 September 2026. Launched on 1 September, it brought citizens and institutions together for coastal cleanup and ocean conservation.Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar means Clean Coast, Safe Sea. It is a campaign led by the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) to improve ocean health through public participation. It encourages people to reduce litter and keep beaches clean.PDF p. 148

    Activities in the 2026 editionPDF p. 148

    • Beach cleanup drives were planned at 100-plus locations, with human chains, cycling rallies, marathons and other public activities.PDF p. 148
    • The Ocean Olympiad, described by MoES as the first national Ocean Olympiad, sought to strengthen environmental awareness among students and youth.PDF p. 148
    • Ocean conservation pledges and activities associated with World Ozone Day encouraged environmental awareness.PDF p. 148

    About “Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar/ Clean Coast Safe Sea “campaignPDF p. 148

    • The “Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar/Clean Coast Safe Sea “campaign is a citizen-led campaign for improving ocean health through collective action.PDF p. 148
    • The campaign started on July 5th, 2022 and has 3 strategic underlying goals that target transformation and environmental conservation through behaviour change.PDF p. 148
    • The three underlying goals of the campaign are to 1. Consume Responsibly 2. Segregate waste at home and 3. Dispose Responsibly.PDF p. 148

    Project GIB Adds Three ChicksPDF p. 148

    • Project Great Indian Bustard (GIB) has added three more chicks to the conservation breeding programme in the last couple of days, taking the total number of chicks hatched so far in the fourth year of captive breeding to 26, Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shri Bhupender Yadav said on 14 June 2026 . The captive stock has now grown to 94 birds, with more chicks expected this season.PDF p. 148
    • As per the report in the fourth year of GIB captive breeding, 26 chicks have hatched so far, including 18 through artificial insemination, four through natural breeding and four from wild-collected eggs.PDF p. 148
    • As per the report in exchange for the wild eggs, three chicks have hatched in the wild in Rajasthan through a jumpstart intervention to improve founder genetic diversity and mitigate predation risk.PDF p. 148
    • Project Great Indian Bustard (Project Bustard) was launched by the Chief Minister of Rajasthan on 5 June 2013 to conserve the Critically Endangered Great Indian Bustard ( Godawan; Ardeotis nigriceps), the State Bird of Rajasthan. Rajasthan became the first state to launch a dedicated conservation project for the species, initially in the Desert National Park (DNP), Jaisalmer.PDF p. 148
    • The Great Indian Bustard is a flagship grassland bird and an indicator of healthy grassland ecosystems.PDF p. 148

    WWF Global Conservation Conference at Jaipur (Rajasthan)PDF p. 148

    • Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav, on 21 September 2026 inaugurated the Global Conservation Conference of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) at Jaipur.PDF p. 148

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 148

    Expansion of conservation networks reported at the conferencePDF p. 148

    • Conservation network Earlier figure Figure cited in 2026 Protected areas Around 750 More than 1,000 Tiger reserves 47 58 Elephant reserves 30 33 Ramsar sites 24 103PDF p. 148
    • WWF (World Wide Fund) is an independent global conservation organisation formed in 1961, and is based in Switzerland.PDF p. 148

    Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar YojanaPDF p. 148

    • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY) to accelerate floating solar development. It combines Floating Solar Photovoltaic (FSPV) projects with co-located Energy Storage Systems (ESS) to support land-efficient generation, grid flexibility and peak-demand management.PDF p. 148

    Background and NeedPDF p. 148

    • The National Institute of Solar Energy estimates floating-solar potential at approximately 102.18 GWp across reservoirs and suitable inland water bodies. With only around 700 MW operational when PM-SSY was approved, the scheme seeks to expand generation without increasing competition for scarce land.PDF p. 148

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 148

    • PM-SSY covers all States and Union Territories and seeks to add 5,000 MW of floating-solar capacity. Eligible projects will receive Central Financial Assistance of ₹1 crore per MW after successful commissioning. Feasibility studies, including bathymetry, hydrography and environmental studies, may receive up to ₹50 lakh per project.PDF p. 148
    • The scheme is expected to reduce annual carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 10 million tonnes, create 16,000–17,000 full-time-equivalent employment opportunities and promote domestic flotation-system, solar-PV and storage manufacturing.PDF p. 148

    Solar Growth in IndiaPDF p. 148, 149

    • Installed solar capacity increased more than 58 times, from 2.82 GW in March 2014 to 164.59 GWPDF p. 148
    • on 31 July 2026, making solar the largest individual component of renewable capacity. This included 122.57 GW ground-mounted, 30.74 GW grid- connected rooftop, 4.77 GW in hybrid projects and 6.51 GW off-grid solar.PDF p. 149

    Record Growth in FY 2025 to 2026PDF p. 149

    • India added 44.61 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025–26, compared with 23.83 GW in FY 2024–25. Total non-fossil capacity reached 283.46 GW , including 274.68 GW renewable capacity, following a record annual non-fossil addition of 55.29 GW . Solar-module manufacturing capacity rose from about 2.3 GW in 2014 to around 172 GW by 31 March 2026. On 29 July 2025, renewables met a record 51.5% of electricity demand of 203 GW .PDF p. 149

    Enabling InfrastructurePDF p. 149

    Solar Parks Scheme and Bhadla Solar ParkPDF p. 149

    • The Solar Parks Scheme provides land, transmission connectivity and common infrastructure. Its initial 20 GW target expanded to 40 GW in 2017. By February 2026, 54 parks with 39,188 MW sanctioned capacity had been approved, including an inter-state floating solar park spanning Jharkhand and West Bengal. Rajasthan’s Bhadla Solar Park, developed during 2015–2020, covers nearly 5,700 hectares and has approximately 2,245 MW installed capacity.PDF p. 149

    Production Linked Incentive SchemePDF p. 149

    • The PLI Scheme for High-Efficiency Solar PV Modules began in 2021 with an initial outlay of ₹4,500 crore, followed by a ₹19,500 crore second tranche. By March 2026, reported cumulative investment was approximately ₹64,873 crore and direct employment 14,794. By 10 June 2026, domestic module and cell manufacturing capacities reached about 192 GW and 30 GW respectively. Module capacity enlisted under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) crossed 200 GW in August 2026; this category differs from total manufacturing capacity.PDF p. 149

    Current Solar and Non Fossil Capacity SnapshotPDF p. 149

    • On 31 July 2026, renewable capacity including large hydro was 291.73 GW . Total non-fossil capacity was 300.50 GW , comprising solar 164.59 GW , wind 58.14 GW , large and small hydro 57.24 GW , bio- power 11.75 GW and nuclear 8.78 GW . The nuclear figure excludes 100 MW under prolonged outage, temporarily removed from installed-capacity calculations from 31 May 2025. Non-fossil sources exceeded 54% of approximately 552 GW total capacity. A rounded 27 August update placed non- fossil capacity at 302–303 GW and solar at around 165 GW . The detailed 31 July break-up remains the source-wise statistical reference available up to 30 August 2026.PDF p. 149

    India launched its first-ever Guide to GrasslandsPDF p. 149

    • India launched its first-ever Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs) of India on August 17, 2026 at an official side event of the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia.PDF p. 149

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 149

    • The Guide was launched under the aegis and guidance of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.PDF p. 149
    • Its publication and the launch event were organised by the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE).PDF p. 149
    • The event brought together representatives of the government, research institutions, international organisations and civil society.PDF p. 149

    Need for the GuidePDF p. 149

    • Grasslands, scrublands and ravines have often been assessed mainly on the basis of their lack of dense tree cover and consequently described as “wastelands”.PDF p. 149
    • However, these ecosystems provide habitats to specialised and endemic species and sustain pastoral and livestock-dependent communities.PDF p. 149
    • Major Open Natural Ecosystems covered in the GuidePDF p. 149
    • Himalayan and Terai grasslandsPDF p. 149
    • Thar and Banni landscapesPDF p. 149
    • Deccan savannasPDF p. 149
    • Rocky plateausPDF p. 149
    • Ravines and scrublandsPDF p. 149
    • Coastal ecosystemsPDF p. 149
    • Desert landscapes UNCCD COP17PDF p. 149
    • Mongolia hosted UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar from 17–28 August 2026 under the theme “Restoring Land, Restoring Hope.” International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists 2026PDF p. 149
    • The UN General Assembly proclaimed 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists (IYRP) through Resolution 76/253, adopted on 15 March 2022.PDF p. 149
    • The proposal was spearheaded by Mongolia, while the Food and Agriculture Organization is the lead agency for its implementation.PDF p. 149

    India’s First Dedicated Urban Night SafariPDF p. 149, 150

    • The Supreme Court on 15 July 2026 permitted Uttar Pradesh to proceed with the proposed Kukrail Night Safari and Zoological Park Project in Lucknow.However, this is only conditional prior permission from the Court. It is not a blanket environmental clearance, and every separate statutory approval must be obtained before the related work begins. The order also remains subject to further directions of the Supreme Court.PDF p. 149
    • The project had faced years of scrutiny because it is to come up inside the ecologically sensitive 2,027-hectare Kukrail Reserve Forest on the outskirts of Lucknow, which is also home to Uttar Pradesh’s first gharial rehabilitation centre, established in 1975.PDF p. 150
    • The Rs 1,510-crore project will come up over 855 acres within the Kukrail Reserve Forest and will be developed in two phases:PDF p. 150
    • Phase I: Night Safari and Eco-tourism ZonePDF p. 150
    • Phase II: Day ZooPDF p. 150

    Prakriti CaféPDF p. 150

    • Union Minister Prataprao Jadhav inaugurated Prakriti Café at Ayush Bhawan, New Delhi, on 22 July 2026. Prakriti Café is a workplace food outlet that brings the principles of Ayush Ahaar into everyday meal choices.PDF p. 150

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 150

    • The idea behind Prakriti Café is to bring the principles of Ayush closer to everyday life. A healthy lifestyle is built through simple and consistent choices, and mindful eating is an important part of that journey.PDF p. 150
    • The café offers a range of fresh and wholesome food options inspired by the Ayush Ahaar initiative, which seeks to promote nutritious dietary practices rooted in India’s traditional knowledge systems.PDF p. 150

    Ethanol Blending in IndiaPDF p. 150

    • Ethanol is a renewable alcohol fuel. India’s Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme mixes domestic ethanol with petrol to reduce crude-oil dependence, support farmers and rural industry, and lower road transport’s environmental impact.PDF p. 150

    Meaning and Present StatusPDF p. 150

    • E5, E10 and E20 contain about 5%, 10% and 20% ethanol by volume. E20 combines anhydrous ethanol with 80% petrol. Since November 2023, the Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) runs from 1 November to 31 October. India first achieved 20% blending in 2025; the November 2025 – August 2026 average was 20%. Public-sector outlets normally supply E20; premium grades XP100, poWer100 and Speed100 remain ethanol-free. From 1 April 2026, notified blended petrol requires a minimum Research Octane Number of 95.PDF p. 150

    Evolution of the ProgrammePDF p. 150

    • Pilots began in 2001, and the EBP Programme launched in 2003 in nine States and four Union Territories. The 2018 National Policy on Biofuels targeted E20 by 2030; the 2022 amendment advanced it to ESY 2025–26. E10 was achieved in June 2022, and phased E20 rollout began on 6 February 2023.PDF p. 150

    Scale and Measurable OutcomesPDF p. 150

    • Capacity grew from 421 crore litres in 2014 to about 2,000 crore litres in 2026. Procurement was about 38 crore litres in ESY 2013–14 and was projected to exceed 1,200 crore litres in ESY 2025–26. The 10 July 2026 update reported cumulative gains since ESY 2014–15: foreign-exchange savings exceeding ₹1.97 lakh crore, nearly 316 lakh tonnes of crude substitution, around 952 lakh tonnes of CO 2 reduction and farmer payments exceeding ₹1.66 lakh crore.PDF p. 150
    • Why Ethanol Blending MattersPDF p. 150
    • Energy SecurityPDF p. 150
    • Farm and Rural EconomyPDF p. 150
    • Environment and Fuel QualityPDF p. 150
    • Major Government MeasuresPDF p. 150
    • Vehicle Compatibility and MileagePDF p. 150

    International PerspectivePDF p. 150

    • E10 predominates in the United States; E85 contains about 51–83% ethanol and is intended for flex-fuel vehicles. Brazil mandated E30 from 1 August 2025. Brazil temporarily introduced E32 in ordinary and additivated petrol from August 1, 2026 for 180 days with one possible equal extension. Japan targets direct E10 by FY 2030 and E20 by FY 2040. India helped launch the Global Biofuels Alliance in September 2023 to promote sustainable biofuels, standards and best practices.PDF p. 150

    Tamil Nadu’s 3D-Printed Artificial Reef pilot under PMMSYPDF p. 150

    • Tamil Nadu has begun deploying advanced 3D-printed artificial reef modules off Rameswaram in Ramanathapuram district. The pilot forms part of Phase II of Tamil Nadu’s artificial-reef programme supported under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) . It combines digital manufacturing with marine habitat restoration, fisheries development and coastal-community resilience.PDF p. 150
    • Each module weighs about 1 tonne and has been developed by Chennai-based startup Tvasta, an IIT Madras-incubated company, in collaboration with the Visakhapatnam Regional Centre of the ICAR- Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute.PDF p. 150
    • The project is being led by Principal Scientist and Head Dr Joe K. Kizhakudan.PDF p. 150
    • Unlike conventional artificial reefs made from reinforced concrete structures, these modules feature complex geometries with multiple crevices, folds and attachment surfaces.PDF p. 150
    • The initiative aims to restore fish habitats and strengthen the resilience of coastal communities.PDF p. 150
    • The project is jointly funded by the Central and State governments in a 60:40 ratio.PDF p. 150

    Sustainable Development Report 2026 and SDG Progress in IndiaPDF p. 151

    • The Sustainable Development Report, 2026, released by the Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN) on June 23, 2026, places India 94 th among 169 ranked countries with a score of 68.3 out of 100. On the SDSN scale, a score of 100 would indicate achievement of all the SDGs. India has climbed 18 places, from 112th in 2015 to 94 th in 2026 , making it one of the largest movers since the SDGs were adopted. East and South Asia have recorded the strongest regional progress since 2015. Among major economies, India improved by 18 places, while China improved by 14 places.PDF p. 151

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 151

    • India’s higher score has not yet placed the country on course to meet the 2030 Agenda. According to the 2026 assessment.PDF p. 151
    • A calculation from the official 2026 data set finds trends for 75 available indicators for India :PDF p. 151
    • Of these 25 are on track or maintaining achievement (33.3%).PDF p. 151
    • Eight are moderately improving (10.7%), 33 are stagnating (44.0%) and Nine are decreasing (12.0%)PDF p. 151
    • Thus moderate improvement and stagnation together account for 54.7%.PDF p. 151
    • These are indicator shares, not shares of all 169 targets.PDF p. 151

    Zero Hunger and India’s Double Burden of MalnutritionPDF p. 151

    • SDG 2: Zero Hunger remains one of India’s most serious development challenges. India’s overall performance under this goal is largely stagnating.PDF p. 151
    • Of the 9 indicators assessed under SDG 2, 4 remain in the “significant challenges” or “major challenges” categories.PDF p. 151
    • The only SDG 2 indicator presently on track is cereal yield, which reached 3.6 tonnes per hectare of harvested land in 2023 . Progress on nutrition- related indicators has been much slower.PDF p. 151

    Child stuntingPDF p. 151

    • Stunting, which refers to low height for age and usually reflects long-term undernutrition, declined from 37.9 per cent in 2015 to 35.5 per cent in 2020 in the series used by the SDG report.PDF p. 151

    Child wastingPDF p. 151

    • Wasting, or low weight for height, indicates acute undernutrition.PDF p. 151
    • The series used in the Sustainable Development Report shows that child wasting increased from 16.9 per cent in 2017 to 18.7 per cent in 2020.PDF p. 151

    Undernourishment and obesityPDF p. 151

    • India is also off track in reducing undernourishment. The proportion of undernourished people declined from 12.1 per cent in 2015 to 10.5 per cent in 2018, but subsequently increased to 12 per cent in 2023 . The trend is classified as stagnating.PDF p. 151
    • At the same time, adult obesity increased from 4.91 per cent in 2015 to 7.27 per cent in 2022.PDF p. 151

    Health, Climate and Governance PressuresPDF p. 151

    • India faces major difficulties under SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being . Half of the 14 monitored health indicators are either stagnating or deteriorating.PDF p. 151
    • The death rate associated with air pollution increased marginally from 131.72 deaths per 100,000 population in 2019 to 132 deaths per 100,000 in 2023.PDF p. 151
    • Similarly, the probability of death from heart disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic lung disease among adults aged 30–70 increased from 22.6 per cent in 2015 to 23.6 per cent in 2021.PDF p. 151
    • India’s carbon dioxide emissions from fossil-fuel combustion and cement production also continued to increase. Per capita emissions rose from 1.69 tonnes in 2015 to 2.21 tonnes in 2024.PDF p. 151

    Global SDG Outlook and Why India MattersPDF p. 151

    • The global outlook remains difficult. In SDSN’s goal-level assessment, none of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals is fully on course for achievement by 2030.PDF p. 151
    • Progress has been especially weak in sustainable cities, environmental protection, food systems and peaceful institutions. SDG 11, SDG 14, SDG 15 and SDG 16 are among the goals furthest off track, while some of the most poorly performing indicators are connected with SDG 2 and SDG 16.PDF p. 151
    • Disaster-related deaths fell by 65 per cent when comparing 2015-2024 with 2005-2014 (excluding COVID-19).PDF p. 151
    • In 2025, global temperatures reached 1.43°C above pre-industrial levels , while atmospheric carbon dioxide reached its highest concentration in 2 million years.PDF p. 151

    Centre of Excellence on Human- Wildlife ConflictPDF p. 151

    • Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bhupender Yadav inaugurated the Centre of Excellence (CoE) on Human–Wildlife Conflict at WII– SACON, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, on July 10, 2026.The Minister launched the National Human–Wildlife Conflict Portal and released the first edition of the publication series Current Status of Human–Wildlife Conflict in India: An Overview.PDF p. 151

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 151

    • Wildlife Institute of India’s premier research institute Salim Ali Centre for Ornithology and Natural History (SACON), Coimbatore, got a shot in the arm with the establishment of a national-level Centre of Excellence (CoE) on human - wildlife conflict.PDF p. 151

    Namo Oxygen ParksPDF p. 152

    • Marking World Environment Day 2026, Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav and Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on June 5 , 2026 inaugurated 18 Namo Oxygen Parks across the national capital and launched a series of green initiatives under the nationwide ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’ campaign.PDF p. 152
    • The origin of these parks traces back to an act of environmental vandalism. In 2024, the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) illegally axed over 1,100 mature trees in the Southern Ridge, a protected reserve forest often called the ‘lungs of the capital’.PDF p. 152

    E85 Fuel Rollout in IndiaPDF p. 152

    • India’s launch of E85 fuel marks a shift from ordinary ethanol blending in petrol to a wider flex-fuel mobility ecosystem. The policy is important for energy security, import reduction, farmer income, cleaner mobility and India’s long-term climate commitments.PDF p. 152

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 152

    • Union Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas Shri Hardeep Singh Puri launched E85 fuel at an IndianOil retail outlet in New Delhi on the occasion of World Environment Day 2026 (June 5, 2026).PDF p. 152
    • E85 is a high-ethanol blended fuel comprising 80–85 per cent ethanol and 14–19 per cent petrol, specifically designed for use in flex-fuel vehicles.PDF p. 152
    • The initiative aims to facilitate the adoption of Flex- Fuel Vehicles (FFVs), which are capable of operating on ethanol blends from E20 to E100, without restricting consumers to a single blend.PDF p. 152
    • Ethanol blending has increased from 1.53 per cent in 2014 to 20 per cent as of June 5, 2026, with the target achieved five years ahead of schedule.PDF p. 152

    Benefits of E85:PDF p. 152

    • E85 is priced nearly `20 per litre lower than conventional petrol to ensure that the economic benefits of domestically produced ethanol are passed on to consumers.PDF p. 152

    Flex-fuel vehiclesPDF p. 152

    • operating on E85 can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 61 per cent compared to conventional petrol vehicles.PDF p. 152
    • Flex-fuel vehiclesPDF p. 152
    • A flex-fuel vehicle is typically understood as the one which holds the capability to run on different variants of fuel.PDF p. 152
    • In the present context, the FFVs should be able to run on E20, E85, and E100 types of fuel.PDF p. 152
    • The vehicle’s engine and fuel system automatically detect the ethanol content and adjust fuel injection and ignition timing accordingly.PDF p. 152

    Andaman & Nicobar Islands Set Guinness World RecordsPDF p. 152

    • In May 2026, the Andaman and Nicobar Administration created two underwater Guinness World Records at Swaraj Dweep. The records were linked with the Administration’s larger effort to promote the islands as a global centre for scuba diving, marine tourism and responsible adventure tourism. Guinness World Records lists the Andaman and Nicobar Administration as the record holder for both underwater achievements.PDF p. 152

    Location: Swaraj DweepPDF p. 152

    • Swaraj Dweep, earlier known as Havelock Island, is one of the important tourist destinations of South Andaman.PDF p. 152

    Sequence of the AchievementsPDF p. 152

    • The first achievement was the underwater unfurling of the Indian Tricolour. Guinness World Records records this achievement under the title “Largest flag unfurled underwater.”PDF p. 152
    • The second achievement followed with the creation of the “Tallest human stack underwater” at Swaraj Dweep.PDF p. 152

    First International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil FuelsPDF p. 152

    • The First Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was an important step in global climat e governance because it focused specifically on how countries can reduce their dependence on coal, oil and gas in a just, orderly and equitable manner. The background to the conference lies in the COP28 Global Stocktake decision.PDF p. 152

    Guiding PrinciplesPDF p. 152

    • The Conference was guided by three key principles:PDF p. 152
    • Participation by those ready to move forward.PDF p. 152
    • Implementation as the guiding star, based on the shared scientific certainty.PDF p. 152
    • Focus on solutions that meaningfully support the transition rather than delay it. India’s 1st Satellite-Tagged Ganges Soft-shell Turtle India’s first satellite-tagged Ganges soft-shell turtle, an endangered species, was released in the 1,302 sq. km Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve in Assam on May 15, 2026.PDF p. 152

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 152

    • Assam is one of the world’s top priority areas in freshwater turtle conservation. The soft-shell turtles reported from India, five are known from the Kaziranga landscape.PDF p. 152

    The Ganges soft-shell turtlePDF p. 153

    • The Ganges soft-shell turtle ( Nilssonia gangetica ), a Schedule I animal under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, can be differentiated from other riverine turtles by its distinct arrowhead-shaped markings on the top of the head.PDF p. 153
    • Ganges softshell turtle (Nilssonia gangetica) can be differentiated from other riverine turtles in having distinct arrow head shaped markings on top of head.PDF p. 153

    India Ranks Third Globally in Renewable Energy Installed CapacityPDF p. 153

    • India ranks third in renewable electricity install ed capacity in IRENA ’s end-2025 international comparison, ahead of Brazil and behind China and the United States. The figures below incorporate the July 2026 IRENA revision, the latest verified MNRE capacity snapshot and CEA ’s later generation data, checked on 18 October 2026.PDF p. 153
    • IRENA ’s Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026 originally placed India at 250.52 GW . Its July 2026 Renewable Energy Statistics revised this estimate to 250.50 GW without changing India’s third position.PDF p. 153
    • The revised end-2025 country comparison places China first with 2,258.02 GW and the United States second with 466.45 GW .PDF p. 153
    • Brazil follows India with 228.20 GW , followed by Germany with 200.90 GW , Japan with 134.95 GW and Canada with 110.39 GW .PDF p. 153
    • The revised world renewable capacity total is 5,155.01 GW , compared with 5,149.28 GW in the March edition.PDF p. 153
    • MNRE’s latest verified capacity figures are for 30 September 2026. Renewable capacity stood at 299.247 GW , and nuclear capacity of 8.780 GW raised total non-fossil capacity to 308.027 GW .PDF p. 153
    • Renewable capacity comprised 171.051 GW of solar, 59.201 GW of wind, 11.748 GW of bio- power, 5.182 GW of small hydro and 52.065 GW of large hydro.PDF p. 153
    • At the earlier 31 March 2026 milestone, India had 283.46 GW of non-fossil capacity, comprising 274.68 GW of renewable capacity and 8.78 GW of nuclear capacity.PDF p. 153
    • The renewable component comprised 150.26 GW of solar, 56.09 GW of wind, 11.75 GW of bioenergy, 5.17 GW of small hydro and 51.41 GW of large hydro.PDF p. 153
    • India achieved its 2030 NDC target of about 50% non-fossil share in cumulative installed electric power capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of schedule. This share reached 54.18% on 30 June 2026.PDF p. 153
    • India’s NDC for 2031–2035 raises the capacity-share target to about 60% by 2035, with technology transfer and low-cost international finance. India also targets 500 GW of non-fossil installed capacity by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2070.PDF p. 153
    • CEA ’s March 2026 Executive Summary gives an actual FY 2025–26 generation aggregate of 1,847.941 BU, including 7.831 BU imported from Bhutan. Total generation grew by 1.04%.PDF p. 153
    • Fossil or thermal generation was 1,307.131 BU, accounting for a calculated 70.73% of this aggregate and declining by 4.10% from the preceding year.PDF p. 153
    • Calculated non-fossil generation, including imports, was 540.811 BU or 29.27%; renewable generation including large hydro and imports was 485.620 BU or 26.28%.PDF p. 153
    • Using the previous-year baseline published with the earlier provisional series, these updated totals imply growth of about 16.1% for non-fossil sources and 18.7% for renewables including hydro and imports.PDF p. 153
    • CEA ’s renewable generation report records 310.585 BU from renewables excluding large hydro in FY 2025–26, an increase of 21.79%.PDF p. 153
    • Wind generation reached 106.700 BU, growing by 28.02%, while solar generation reached 174.757 BU, growing by 21.23%.PDF p. 153
    • Together, wind and solar generated a calculated 281.456 BU, equivalent to 15.23% of the Executive Summary aggregate including Bhutan imports.PDF p. 153
    • The 8 April 2026 provisional release reported coal generation of 1,250.189 BU, a 67.7% share and a decline of 3.69%. These coal figures belong to that earlier provisional series and should retain that qualification.PDF p. 153
    • CEA ’s domestic generation series excludes Bhutan imports. On this basis, FY 2025–26 generation was 1,840.110 BU, including 532.980 BU from non-fossil sources and 477.789 BU from renewables.PDF p. 153
    • Installed capacity and electricity generation measure different things. Renewable capacity is part of non- fossil capacity, which also includes nuclear power. Reaching a 50% capacity share therefore does not mean that non-fossil sources generate 50% of annual electricity.PDF p. 153

    COP 15 of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory SpeciesPDF p. 153

    • Migratory species are animals that move across countries, continents, oceans, rivers and skies for food, breeding, climate suitability or survival. Their protection cannot be done by one country alone because their routes cut across political boundaries. This is why the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) , also known as the Bonn Convention, is important for global biodiversity governance.PDF p. 153
    • The 15 th Meeting of the Conference of the Parties to CMS (CMS COP15) was held in Campo Grande, Brazil, from March 23 to March 29, 2026, under the theme “Connecting Nature to Sustain Life.”PDF p. 153

    Major OutcomePDF p. 154

    • The biggest outcome of COP15 was the decision to provide new or upgraded treaty protection to 40 species, subspecies and populations of birds, aquatic wildlife and terrestrial animals.PDF p. 154
    • These were added to or upgraded within CMS Appendices I and II. With this, the Convention now covers over 1,200 unique species.PDF p. 154

    Brazil’s Role and Next COPPDF p. 154

    • With the conclusion of COP15, Brazil holds the CMS COP Presidency for the next three years . The focus during this period will be on implementing the decisions taken in Campo Grande.PDF p. 154
    • The next CMS COP , COP16, will be held in Bonn, Germany, in 2029 . It will coincide with the 50th anniversary of CMS , making it symbolically important because Bonn is the city where the treaty was signed in 1979.PDF p. 154

    Project Him SarovarPDF p. 154

    • Project Him Sarovar is a new water-security initiative of the Ladakh Administration. It has been designed for Ladakh’s cold desert conditions, where water is a lifeline for agriculture, settlements and livelihoods. The project focuses on scientific snow harvesting , conservation of snowmelt and glacial melt , and creation of small water bodies so that seasonal water, which usually flows away, can be stored and used during lean periods.PDF p. 154

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 154

    • Project Him Sarovar was launched on April 10, 2026 by Vinai Kumar Saxena, LG of Ladakh.PDF p. 154
    • Under Phase I, 50 water bodies were proposed with 30 in Leh and 20 in Kargil covering nearly 25% of Ladakh’s villages. As of June 12, 2026. 5 reservoirs had already been completed and the target was to create 100 such water bodies by next year.PDF p. 154

    IQAir World Air Quality Report 2025PDF p. 154

    • Recently on March 24, 2026, IQAir released the 2025 IQAir World Air Quality Report. This 8th edition annual Report provides a comprehensive overview of air quality across the globe for the calendar year 2025. This Report presents PM2.5 air quality data sourced from 9,446 cities spanning 143 countries, regions, and territories.PDF p. 154

    Expansion of Global Air Quality CoveragePDF p. 154

    • Last year’s World Air Quality Report included data from 8,954 cities across 138 countries, regions, and territories.PDF p. 154
    • The current report expanded its coverage to 9,446 cities in 143 countries, regions, and territories.PDF p. 154
    • In 2025, West Asia saw increased data contributions, especially due to the inclusion of Iran, Syria, and Jordan.PDF p. 154
    • This resulted in a 33% increase in the number of cities covered in the region.PDF p. 154
    • Burundi, Turkmenistan, and Togo, which ranked among the top 30 most polluted countries in 2024, are absent from this year’s report due to a lack of available data.PDF p. 154

    Global PM2.5 Trends and WHO Guideline PerformancePDF p. 154

    • Globally, only 13 countries, regions, and territories met the WHO annual PM2.5 guideline of 5 μg/m³.PDF p. 154
    • These included French Polynesia, Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands, Barbados, New Caledonia, Iceland, Bermuda, Réunion, Andorra, Australia, Grenada, Panama, and Estonia.PDF p. 154
    • In 2025, only 14% of global cities met the WHO annual PM2.5 guideline.PDF p. 154
    • This was a decline from 17% in 2024, showing that clean air remains a fragile achievement.
