    India’s National Repository for Deep-Sea FaunaPDF p. 155

    • India has taken an important step in marine biodiversity conservation by designating the “Bhavasagara” Referral Centre at the Centre for Marine Living Resources & Ecology (CMLRE), Kochi, Kerala, as the National Repository for Deep-Sea Fauna on March 24, 2026. The designation was made by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), while CMLRE functions under the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES).PDF p. 155

    About Bhavasagara Referral CentrePDF p. 155

    • The Bhavasagara Referral Centre is a specialised national facility dedicated to deep-sea biodiversity. It acts as a repository for deep-sea faunal collections from India’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).PDF p. 155
    • Bhavasagara maintains over 3560 taxonomically identified and geo-referenced voucher specimens.PDF p. 155
    • The repository will also support capacity building in deep-sea taxonomy.PDF p. 155

    State of India’s Environment (SOE) 2026 ReportPDF p. 155

    • The State of India’s Environment 2026 report was released by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) and Down to Earth Magazine on February 25, 2026 at the Anil Agarwal Dialogue 2026 in Nimli near Alwar Rajasthan. The annual SOE series began in 2014, though CSE’s longer environmental reporting tradition goes back to the 1982 Citizen’s First Report.PDF p. 155

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 155

    • The report states that 2025 recorded the highest rise in the frequency and impact of extreme weather events in India during the last four years.PDF p. 155
    • These events included heatwaves, cold waves, heavy rainfall, and floods.PDF p. 155
    • From January 1 to November 30, 2025 , extreme weather events occurred on 99% of the days in India, causing 4,419 deaths and affecting at least 17.41 million hectares of crop area.PDF p. 155
    • In comparison, 2024 saw such events on 88% of the days, with 3,393 deaths and 3.61 million hectares of crop damage, while 2023 recorded them on 89% of the days , causing 3,208 deaths and affecting 2.09 million hectares.PDF p. 155
    • Among the States, Himachal Pradesh was the worst affected with extreme weather on 267 days, followed by Kerala with 173 days and Madhya Pradesh with 162 days.PDF p. 155

    Air Pollution, Freshwater Stress, and Novel EntitiesPDF p. 155

    • On air pollution, CSE’s analysis shows that only 15% of India’s population, about 200 million people, lives within 10 km of a continuous air quality monitor.PDF p. 155
    • This means that 85% of the population, or over 1.2 billion people, lives beyond 10 km of a continuous monitor in CSE’s February 2026 analysis.PDF p. 155
    • The report notes that ocean acidity has increased by 30–40% since the industrial era , threatening marine ecosystems, including corals and shell- forming organisms , and weakening the ocean’s ability to absorb carbon.PDF p. 155

    International Renewable Energy AgencyPDF p. 155

    • Recently, the Sixteenth Session of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) Assembly concluded on 12 January 2026 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (UAE) , marking a significant milestone in global deliberations on sustainable energy transition. The Assembly was held under the theme “Powering Humanity: Renewable Energy for Shared Prosperity”.PDF p. 155
    • The IRENA Youth Forum, held on the sidelines of the Assembly, brought together young leaders from more than 60 countries to emphasise the role of youth innovation, digital skills and inclusive policy in shaping sustainable energy futures.PDF p. 155

    India’s First Indigenous Designed Pollution Control VesselPDF p. 155

    • Marking a major step forward in India’s pursuit of Aatmanirbharta in shipbuilding and maritime capability development, Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh commissioned Indian Coast Guard Ship (ICGS) ‘Samudra Pratap’, the first of two Pollution Control Vessels built by Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL), in Goa on January 05, 2026.PDF p. 155
    • With over 60% indigenous content, ICGS Samudra Pratap is India’s first indigenously designed pollution control vessel and the largest ship in the ICG fleet to date.PDF p. 155
    • ICGS Samudra Pratap has been specially designed for pollution control, but its role is not limited to this alone.PDF p. 155

    Global Methane Status ReportPDF p. 155, 156

    • The report was launched on 17 November 2025 during COP30 in Belém, Brazil.PDF p. 155
    • UNEP states the GMP includes 159 countries + the European Commission.PDF p. 155
    • The report notes that (as of April 2025) those members covered about 57% of global anthropogenic methane emissions.PDF p. 156
    • Sector shares of global anthropogenic methane are about 42% agriculture, 38% energy, 20% waste.PDF p. 156
    • G20+ countries are responsible for about 65% of total anthropogenic methane emissions and hold 72% of global technicale methane mitigation potential by 2030. 30th Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC: COP30 COP30, held in Belém in the Amazon region, became strongly associated with an “implementation-first” framing. Alongside the political track, COP30 also showcased a large- scale implementation architecture through the COP30 Global Climate Action Agenda (GCAA)—a renewed framework built on the Marrakech Partnership and the Global Stocktake response, organized into six thematic axes and driven by 30 activation groups (482 initiatives).PDF p. 156

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 156

    • COP30 took place in Belem from November 10-22, 2025.PDF p. 156
    • In parallel, the COP30 Global Climate Action Agenda (GCAA) operationalized this “implem- entation turn” through a four-step activation cycle–Coordinate, Measure, Showcase, Scale.PDF p. 156
    • Coordinate: 30 activation groups with 482 initiatives aligned toward 30 key objectives.PDF p. 156

    COP30’s “Implementation Shift” and the Belém PackagePDF p. 156

    • Unlike earlier COPs that leaned heavily toward announcing new pledges, COP30 marked a clear shift toward implementation.PDF p. 156
    • The central political outcome was widely described as the Belém Package —around 29 decisions functioning less as a new “target set” and more as an implementation toolkit to deliver the Paris Agreement.PDF p. 156
    • The package’s conceptual foundation was the Global Mutirão decision.PDF p. 156
    • “Mutirão” (a Brazilian term) implies the community coming together for shared work—similar in spirit to India’s concept of “Shramdaan.”PDF p. 156

    Accelerating Action: Mitigation, Adaptation, and Finance (with Finance the Most Contested)PDF p. 156

    • (1) Climate Finance: reinforcing obligations + tracking and delivery toolsPDF p. 156
    • A major achievement attributed to COP30 was strengthening the interpretation of Paris Agreement Article 9.1 (developed countries “shall provide” financial resources to developing countries).PDF p. 156
    • A two-year “Climate Finance Work Programme” was launched.PDF p. 156
    • Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF): Brazil- led blended finance mechanism targeting USD 125 billion, designed like a “scholarship for forests,” delivering performance-based payments for protecting tropical forests (monitored via satellite data). (2) Adaptation: operationalizing the GGA and scaling resilience deliveryPDF p. 156
    • COP30 decisions treat the Baku Adaptation Road Map as an ongoing work stream with a defined first phase (2026-28). (3) Mitigation & Transition: the Belém 4x Pledge and sectoral scalingPDF p. 156
    • To curb emissions and accelerate system transitions, COP30 advanced the implementation of the Belém 4x Pledge. The pledge was launched at the Pre- COP .PDF p. 156
    • Target: quadruple the use of sustainable fuels by 2035 relative to 2024 (including green hydrogen, advanced biofuels, and e-fuels).PDF p. 156
    • Tracking: IEA to track progress.PDF p. 156
    • 23 countries officially endorsed the pledge, with broad non-state support (including major industry actors).PDF p. 156

    Just TransitionPDF p. 156

    • Belém Action Mechanism (BAM): adopted to support a socially fair transition away from fossil fuels—focused on worker reskilling and social dialogue, though without a large dedicated fund.PDF p. 156
    • The Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative announced its 18th nation-state supporter (Cambodia) and presented a PAS with next steps through the Climate Action Agenda.PDF p. 156

    HealthPDF p. 156

    • Belém Health Action Plan: launched to build climate-resilient health systems to tackle heatwaves and vector-borne diseases.PDF p. 156
    • The Belém Health Action Plan is described as the world’s first international climate adaptation plan dedicated entirely to health , launched with an initial USD 300 million investment from a coalition of 35+ philanthropies, funding research, policy, solutions for extreme heat/air pollution/ infectious diseases, and strengthening health systems via climate-data integration.PDF p. 156
    • COP30 also marked “Race to Zero for health care hits 100”: The campaign has reached 100 institutions representing 14,000+ hospitals/ health centers across 28 countries.PDF p. 156
    • India’s position at COP30 (as reflected in negotiations and blocs)PDF p. 156
    • Finance is an obligation: India emphasized that under Article 9.1, climate finance is a legal obligation, not charity, and demanded USD 1.3 trillion/year.PDF p. 156
    • Opposition to CBAM: India strongly opposed unilateral trade measures like the EU’s CBAM, arguing they violate CBDR-RC and resemble “green protectionism.”PDF p. 156
    • Looking ahead: COP31 (Türkiye, 2026) and the “Belém Mission to 1.5°C”PDF p. 156

    Uttar Pradesh Current Affairs

    Make a UP map in your head: event → district → purpose. Read the state budget separately from the economic survey: a budget proposes future spending, while the survey describes estimates and trends for earlier years.

    Build the chapter in eight anchors

    Place-event pair

    The issue places the Wings Over Ganga air show at Namo Ghat, Varanasi, on 22, 24 and 25 October 2026, and the 50th India Carpet Expo at Bhadohi on 4 October 2026.

    PDF p. 157
    Two paddy grades

    UP's reported FY 2026-27 paddy procurement MSPs are ₹2,441 per quintal for common paddy and ₹2,461 for Grade A. The procurement target is 65 lakh metric tonnes.

    PDF p. 157
    Two procurement windows

    The source gives western UP's paddy window as 12 October 2026-15 February 2027 and eastern UP's as 1 November 2026-28 February 2027, with payment within 48 hours.

    PDF p. 157
    UP-AIM scope

    The reported UP Artificial Intelligence Mission has a proposed ₹2,000 crore outlay for FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, with ₹225 crore for FY 2026-27, district AI centres in all 75 districts and a target to train 5 lakh youth.

    PDF p. 157
    Budget balances

    For FY 2026-27, the budget discussion estimates a revenue surplus of ₹64,458 crore (1.6% of GSDP), a fiscal deficit of ₹1,18,481 crore (3%) and a primary deficit of ₹49,560 crore (1.2%).

    PDF p. 165
    Receipts and State GST

    The budget article estimates revenue receipts of ₹7,28,928 crore and own tax revenue of ₹3,34,491 crore. State GST is its largest own-tax source, budgeted at ₹1,49,956 crore.

    PDF p. 165
    Survey's sector mix

    The economic survey gives the FY 2024-25 primary-secondary-tertiary shares as 25.8%, 27.2% and 47.0%. These are broad sectors, not individual subsectors.

    PDF p. 166
    Income labels matter

    The survey gives FY 2024-25 net per-capita income as ₹1,09,844 and gross per-capita income as ₹1,26,304. Its March 2026 population estimate is 25.19 crore; this is an estimate, not a fresh Census count.

    PDF p. 168
    Reading the state balances
    Measure, FY 2026-27Issue's amount/ratioMeaning in the article
    Revenue surplus₹64,458 crore; 1.6% of GSDPRevenue receipts exceed revenue expenditure
    Fiscal deficit₹1,18,481 crore; 3% of GSDPOverall financing gap
    Primary deficit₹49,560 crore; 1.2% of GSDPGap before interest payments
    PDF p. 165
    Learning aid - not from sourceKeep two notebooks lines for money: 'Budget = plan' and 'Survey = reported economy'. Always add the financial year and estimate status. This is an editorial learning aid.

    Close the notes. Explain it back.

    Reconstruct the two UP paddy MSPs with the unit.

    Common ₹2,441/quintal; Grade A ₹2,461/quintal, for the reported 2026-27 procurement policy. Grade A is ₹20 higher; the unit is per quintal, not per tonne.PDF p. 157

    How do the western and eastern procurement windows differ?

    West starts 12 October 2026 and ends 15 February 2027; east starts 1 November 2026 and ends 28 February 2027. Retain the region with each date pair.PDF p. 157

    Why can a state have a revenue surplus and a fiscal deficit?

    The revenue account can be in surplus while the broader budget still requires financing, including for capital spending. The issue itself reports a revenue surplus and a 3%-of-GSDP fiscal deficit together.PDF p. 165

    Which is the largest broad sector in the survey's 2024-25 mix?

    The tertiary sector at 47.0%, against 27.2% secondary and 25.8% primary. Broad-sector shares should not be substituted for a manufacturing-only share.PDF p. 166

    Which qualifications belong to the population and income figures?

    Population 25.19 crore is a March 2026 estimate. ₹1,09,844 is net per-capita income for FY 2024-25; ₹1,26,304 is the gross figure.PDF p. 168

    IAF Varanasi Air Show 2026PDF p. 157

    • The Indian Air Force (IAF) organised a three-day aerial display over the Ganga at Namo Ghat, Varanasi, on 22, 24 and 25 October, 2026, marking its 94th anniversary.PDF p. 157
    • Theme: The show was titled “Wings Over Ganga.” The broader anniversary celebrations carried the theme “Indian Air Force – Infallible, Impervious and Precise.”PDF p. 157

    India Carpet Expo, BhadohiPDF p. 157

    • Inauguration Date: 4 October 2026; CM Yogi Adityanath inaugurated the 50th (Golden Jubilee) India Carpet Expo at the Carpet Expo Mart, Bhadohi.PDF p. 157
    • Development Projects: The Chief Minister also inaugurated or laid the foundation stones of 112 projects worth over ₹1,340 crore in Bhadohi district.PDF p. 157

    Paddy Procurement Policy, 2026–27PDF p. 157

    • Approval Date: 9 October 2026; the UP Cabinet approved paddy procurement for 2026–27, with an MSP of ₹2,441/quintal for common paddy and ₹2,461/quintal for Grade-A paddy.PDF p. 157
    • Target & Centres: A procurement target of 65 lakh metric tonnes through approximately 4,500 centres, involving eight procurement agencies.PDF p. 157
    • Procurement Period: Western UP: October 12, 2026 – February 15, 2027; Eastern UP: November 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027 , with payments to farmers within 48 hours.PDF p. 157

    Coarse Cereals Procurement Policy, 2026–27PDF p. 157

    • Approval Date: 9 October 2026; the policy was approved for procurement from 1 October to 31 December 2026, with MSPs of maize ₹2,410, bajra ₹2,900, hybrid jowar ₹4,023 and Maldandi jowar ₹4,073 per quintal.PDF p. 157
    • Procurement Targets: 2.20 lakh MT of bajra, 50,000 MT of jowar and 15,000 MT of maize.PDF p. 157
    • Districts & Centres: Bajra in 33 districts (300 centres), jowar in 13 districts (80 centres) and maize in 25 districts (75 centres) , using biometric verification and direct bank payments.PDF p. 157

    Uttar Pradesh Interest Waiver Scheme, 2026PDF p. 157

    • Approval & Notification: Approved on 9 October 2026 and notified on 16 October 2026 , providing relief on eligible outstanding tax demands up to 31 December 2025.PDF p. 157
    • Waiver Structure: A 100% interest waiver on principal dues up to ₹10 lakh; 90% for ₹10 lakh– ₹1 crore, 75% for ₹1–5 crore and 50% for dues above ₹5 crore.PDF p. 157
    • Coverage: Applicable across 75 districts for 3 months from the date of notification; eligible penalties are fully waived, subject to conditions under specified state tax laws.PDF p. 157

    • Status Update: On 14 October 2026 , Defence Minister Rajnath Singh stated that the proposed National Military Drone Technology Hub at IIT Kanpur had made significant progress and its approval process was nearing completion.PDF p. 157

    Reservation for Former AgniveersPDF p. 157

    • Notification Reported: 15 October 2026; amended recruitment rules were reported for former Agniveers in the UP Transport Department. The Cabinet had originally approved the reservation proposal on 15 September 2026.PDF p. 157
    • Reservation & Age Relaxation: A 20% horizontal reservation in Transport Enforcement Constable recruitment for eligible former Agniveers, with 3 years’ age relaxation after completing four years of military service.PDF p. 157

    Uttar Pradesh Artificial Intelligence Mission (UP-AIM)PDF p. 157

    • Approval & Budget: Approved on October 9, 2026, with a proposed outlay of ₹2,000 crore for the period from 2026–27 to 2030–31, including ₹225 crore allocated for 2026–27.PDF p. 157
    • Infrastructure: District AI Centres are proposed in all 75 districts, with one AI Fellow per district receiving ₹40,000 per month for one year. Over 200 AI skill labs are planned, targeting certification of 1 lakh technical learners.PDF p. 157
    • Major Targets: Train 5 lakh youth, develop 50,000 AI professionals, support at least 100 AI startups and develop over 100 AI-based solutions. The mission will operate under the IT & Electronics Department.PDF p. 157

    UP Startup Procurement Scheme, 2026PDF p. 157, 158

    • Approval & Notification: Approved on 9 October 2026; a government order was issued on 12 October 2026. The UP Startup Mission is the nodal agency, with a dedicated startup module linked to the Government e-Marketplace (GeM).PDF p. 157
    • Eligibility: Available to DPIIT-recognised startups registered under the UP Startup Policy, 2026, with headquarters in UP or at least 50% of their workforce or specified operations located in the state.PDF p. 158
    • Procurement & Payments: Single tender procurement is permitted up to ₹50 lakh, extended to ₹1 crore for sunrise sectors; startup-only limited tenders permitted up to ₹1 crore. Payments are structured as 30% up issuance of the on purchase order, 60% after successful supply/installation and 10% after warranty completion.PDF p. 158

    Sustainable Aviation Fuel Manufacturing Promotion Policy, 2026PDF p. 158

    • Approval & Objective: Approved on 9 October 2026 to establish UP as a Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) manufacturing hub using agricultural residues such as rice husk, wheat straw and sugarcane bagasse.PDF p. 158
    • Investment Categories: Manufacturing units are classified as Large ( ₹200–500 crore), Mega ( ₹500– 1,500 crore) and Ultra-Mega (above ₹1,500 crore) based on capital investment.PDF p. 158
    • Incentives & Implementation: The policy includes stamp-duty relief, interest subsidy, SGST reimbursement and 100% electricity-duty exemption for up to 10 years. UPNEDA is the nodal agency; the policy will remain effective for 5 years from promulgation or the until the government promulgates a new policy.PDF p. 158

    Minimum Wage Revision in Uttar PradeshPDF p. 161

    • The Uttar Pradesh Government issued a notification on April 17, regarding revision of minimum wages in the state as an interim step, with retrospective effect from April 1, 2026.PDF p. 161
    • The notification revises existing minimum wage rates under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, using powers under the United Provinces Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.PDF p. 161
    • An important provision is the division of the state into three categories, depending upon geographical and economic factors.PDF p. 161
    • Gautam Buddha Nagar and Ghaziabad are categorised as Category I because of the concentration of industrial activity and the high cost of living in these areas.PDF p. 161
    • Category II encompasses districts with municipal corporations, while Category III overs the rest.PDF p. 161
    • In each case, wages are set based on skill levels — unskilled, semi-skilled, and skilled.PDF p. 161
    • The wage structure comprises a basic amount and a Variable Dearness Allowance (VDA).PDF p. 161
    • In Category I, monthly wages are fixed at `13,690 for unskilled labour, `15,059 for semi-skilled labour, and `16,868 for skilled labour.PDF p. 161

    • The Uttar Pradesh Budget for 2026–27 was presented by Finance Minister Suresh Kumar Khanna on February 11, 2026 . This is a large, expansionary budget with a strong focus on growth, infrastructure, welfare, and technology-led development.PDF p. 164
    • The budget combines higher expenditure , continued revenue surplus , and a fiscal deficit kept at 3% of GSDP, which indicates that the state is trying to balance development spending with fiscal discipline.PDF p. 164

    Economic Background of Uttar PradeshPDF p. 164

    • The Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) of Uttar Pradesh for 2026–27, at current prices, is projected at ₹39.8 lakh crore . This implies a 28% increase over the revised estimate for 2025–26.PDF p. 164
    • In 2024–25, Uttar Pradesh’s GSDP at constant prices is estimated to grow by 9%, which is higher than the estimated 6.5% GDP growth for India in the same year.PDF p. 164
    • The structure of the state’s economy in 2024–25 shows that agriculture contributes 27% , manufacturing contributes 26% , and services contribute 47% of the economy. This means services remain the largest sector, but agriculture continues to hold a very significant share in Uttar Pradesh’s economy.PDF p. 164
    • Uttar Pradesh’s per capita GSDP in 2024–25 is estimated at ₹1,24,366, which is an increase of 11.6% over 2023–24. It is noted that India’s per capita GDP is estimated at ₹2,34,859 in 2024–25.PDF p. 164

    Overall Size of the BudgetPDF p. 164

    • The total expenditure proposed in the budget for 2026–27 is ₹9,12,696 crore . This is 27% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.PDF p. 164
    • Out of this, debt repayment is estimated at ₹61,795 crore. Therefore, net expenditure , which is the more meaningful measure for policy analysis, stands at ₹8,50,901 crore.PDF p. 164
    • Total receipts are budgeted at ₹8,48,233 crore , while net receipts excluding borrowings are estimated at ₹7,32,420 crore. The difference is to be partly met through borrowings.PDF p. 164

    Revenue Surplus, Fiscal Deficit, and Primary DeficitPDF p. 165

    • The budget estimates a revenue surplus of ₹64,458 crore, which is 1.6% of GSDP , in 2026–27. This means the state expects its revenue receipts to exceed its revenue expenditure.PDF p. 165
    • However, this revenue surplus is lower than the revised estimate for 2025–26, when revenue surplus was estimated at ₹74,348 crore, or 2.4% of GSDP. This suggests that while the state remains in surplus on the revenue account, the cushion is becoming smaller.PDF p. 165
    • The fiscal deficit for 2026–27 is budgeted at ₹1,18,481 crore, which is 3% of GSDP. This is the same ratio as the revised estimate for 2025–26 and aligns with the 16th Finance Commission’s recommended annual limit of 3% of GSDP for states for 2026–31.PDF p. 165
    • The primary deficit is estimated at ₹49,560 crore, or 1.2% of GSDP, in 2026–27. This is significantly higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26, indicating a larger gap even before interest payments are considered.PDF p. 165

    Expenditure PatternPDF p. 165

    • Revenue expenditure in 2026–27 is proposed at ₹6,64,471 crore , which is 31% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26. Revenue expenditure mainly includes salaries, pensions, interest payments, grants, and subsidies.PDF p. 165
    • Capital outlay is budgeted at ₹1,77,744 crore , which is an increase of 11% over the revised estimate of 2025–26. Capital outlay is important because it creates assets such as roads, buildings, and infrastructure.PDF p. 165
    • The rise in revenue expenditure is being driven by higher spending on pension, general education , rural development , grants to local bodies and Panchayati Raj institutions, and energy.PDF p. 165

    Receipts StructurePDF p. 165

    • Revenue receipts for 2026–27 are estimated at ₹7,28,928 crore , which is 26% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.PDF p. 165
    • Of the total revenue receipts, roughly 50% will be raised by the state from its own resources and the remaining 50% will come from the Centre , either as the state’s share in central taxes or as grants.PDF p. 165
    • State’s own tax revenue is estimated at ₹3,34,491 crore in 2026–27, which is 48% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.PDF p. 165
    • State’s own non-tax revenue is estimated at ₹26,754 crore , which is almost double the revised estimate for 2025–26. The budget attributes this mainly to increases in concession fees, rent, royalty, share capital receipts from Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation for rural electrification, and interest income.PDF p. 165
    • The state’s share in central taxes is estimated at ₹2,68,911 crore, while grants from the Centre are estimated at ₹98,772 crore.PDF p. 165

    Tax Revenue and Tax TrendsPDF p. 165

    • Among own tax sources, State GST is projected to be the largest source , contributing 45% of the state’s own tax revenue in 2026–27. State GST is budgeted at ₹1,49,956 crore, which is 79% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.PDF p. 165
    • State excise is estimated at ₹71,278 crore, or 17% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.PDF p. 165
    • Sales tax/VAT is projected at ₹48,115 crore , showing a 43% increase over the revised estimate of 2025–26.PDF p. 165
    • Stamp duty and registration fees are estimated at ₹43,802 crore, while taxes on vehicles are budgeted at ₹15,808 crore.PDF p. 165
    • The revised estimates for most own-tax revenue heads in 2025–26 were lower than the original budget estimates, which suggests that revenue projections have recently been difficult to realise fully.PDF p. 165

    Debt, Liabilities, and GuaranteesPDF p. 165, 166

    • At the end of 2026–27, the state’s outstanding liabilities are estimated at 23.1% of GSDP, which is lower than the revised estimate of 27.6% of GSDP for 2025–26. This indicates an expected improvement in the debt burden relative to the size of the economy. Rupee Comes In, 2026-27 (B.E.) Rupee Goes Out, 2026-27 (B.E.)     • It is noted that as of 31 March 2025, Uttar Pradesh’s outstanding government guarantees were estimated at ₹1,71,924 crore , which is 5.8% of GSDP. These are contingent liabilities that may become actual obligations in the future.PDF p. 166

    • The sectors listed account for 60% of the total sectoral expenditure budgeted by the state in 2026–27.PDF p. 166
    • Education, Sports, Arts, and Culture have been allocated ₹1,08,154 crore, which is 28% higher than the revised estimate of 2025–26.PDF p. 166

    • Health and Family Welfare has been allocated ₹53,326 crore, which is 24% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.PDF p. 166
    • Transport has been allocated ₹50,391 crore, while Rural Development receives ₹49,044 crore , with rural development showing a sharp 59% increase over the revised estimate.PDF p. 166
    • Social Welfare and Nutrition has been allocated ₹42,263 crore , Police gets ₹41,898 crore , Agriculture and Allied Activities gets ₹30,938 crore, and Urban Development gets ₹27,532 crore.PDF p. 166

    Important Scheme Allocations by SectorPDF p. 166

    • In education, Rs. 55,792 crore has been allocated towards assistance to non-government primary schools, and ₹7,738 crore has been allocated for primary education under Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan.PDF p. 166
    • In energy, ₹21,500 crore has been allocated towards power subsidy.PDF p. 166
    • In health, ₹5,793 crore is allocated for urban health services (Allopathy) and ₹6,818 crore for rural health services (Allopathy).PDF p. 166
    • In transport, ₹38,592 crore has been allocated towards capital outlay on roads and bridges.PDF p. 166
    • In rural development, ₹6,102 crore is allocated for Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Rural , ₹5,544 crore for MGNREGS, and ₹4,580 crore for Ajeevika Mission.PDF p. 166
    • In social welfare, ₹8,950 crore has been allocated towards old age/farmer pensions , and ₹3,500 crore towards Nirashrit Mahila Pension Yojana.PDF p. 166
    • In agriculture, ₹2,400 crore is allocated for subsidy for power supply to private tubewells , and ₹638 crore for the conversion of diesel pumps to solar pumps.PDF p. 166
    • In urban development, ₹6,842 crore is allocated towards Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban.PDF p. 166
    • In agriculture, the state will launch a programme to encourage agriculture marketing and exports.PDF p. 166
    • For ease of doing business, industrial requirements such as licensing and registration will be simplified in the next phase under the principle of Jan Vishwas.PDF p. 166

    Uttar Pradesh Economic Survey 2025–26PDF p. 166

    • On February 9, 2026 , the Government of Uttar Pradesh presented the Uttar Pradesh Economic Survey 2025–26.PDF p. 166
    • With the vision of rapid development, the state has set a target of becoming a one trillion dollar economy.PDF p. 166
    • According to quick estimates at current prices, the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) of Uttar Pradesh increased from `13.30 lakh crore in 2016– 17 to `26.67 lakh crore in 2023–24.PDF p. 166
    • In 2024–25, advance estimates placed it at `29.62 lakh crore , while revised estimates placed it at `29.78 lakh crore.PDF p. 166
    • With a 13.4% growth over the previous year , the GSDP is estimated at `30.25 lakh crore , higher than both earlier estimates.PDF p. 166
    • In 2025–26, the state economy is estimated to reach approximately `36 lakh crore.PDF p. 166
    • According to the research report ‘Ecowrap’ by State Bank of India , India is moving towards becoming the third-largest economy in the world by 2027, surpassing Japan and Germany, and Uttar Pradesh is expected to play a decisive role in this achievement.PDF p. 166
    • Uttar Pradesh’s GSDP at current prices increased from `13.30 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `30.25 lakh crore in 2024–25 (quick estimates) , registering a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.8% over 8 years.PDF p. 166
    • In 2024–25, the state contributes about 9.1% to India’s GDP.PDF p. 166

    Structural Changes in EconomyPDF p. 166

    • From 2017–18 to 2024–25 , structural changes are visible in the state economy:PDF p. 166
    • The primary sector remained almost stable (from 25.9% to 25.8%).PDF p. 166
    • The secondary sector increased significantly (from 25.4% to 27.2% ), indicating growth in industrial production, manufacturing, and infrastructure.PDF p. 166
    • The tertiary sector declined slightly (from 48.8% to 47.0%), indicating a balanced restructuring of services.PDF p. 166

    Comparison with National EconomyPDF p. 166, 167

    • At the national level:PDF p. 166
    • The Primary sector declined from 20.4% to 19.7%PDF p. 166
    • The Secondary sector declined from 27.0% to 25.3%PDF p. 166
    • The Tertiary sector increased from 52.5% to 54.9%PDF p. 166
    • Sector-wise Contribution in 2024–25 Sub-sector Share Agriculture, forestry and fisheries 24.9% Construction 12.9% Real estate and professional services 13.9% Manufacturing 11.7% Trade and hotels 8.3% Transport and communication 7.4%PDF p. 167

    Agriculture and Allied SectorPDF p. 167

    • The agriculture and allied sector has shown continuous progress.PDF p. 167
    • Its Gross Value Added increased from `2.96 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `6.95 lakh crore in 2024–25 , growing at a CAGR of 11.2% , which is nearly a doubling of value.PDF p. 167
    • Advance estimates placed it at `6.86 lakh crore , while revised estimates placed it at `7.12 lakh crore.PDF p. 167
    • Crops remain the main component , contributing the highest share of 67.4% in the Gross Value Added (GVA) of the agriculture and allied sector.PDF p. 167
    • Livestock contributes 24.7%, forestry contributes 4.5%, and fisheries and aquaculture contribute 3.5%.PDF p. 167
    • In 2024–25, the total foodgrain production in the state increased by 9.9% over the previous year , reaching 737.4 lakh metric tonnes , and the state continues to hold a leading position in the country.PDF p. 167
    • Within this, oilseed production increased by 57.9%, total cereals increase by 11%, including a 23.6% increase in paddy and a 6.3% increase in wheat production.PDF p. 167
    • Milk production increased by 33.6%, placing the state at the first position in the country.PDF p. 167
    • Egg production increased by 167%.PDF p. 167
    • In 2025–26, fish production is estimated to increase further by 15.7%, reflecting efforts towards sustainable agriculture and diversification.PDF p. 167

    Forestry and Land UsePDF p. 167

    • It increased from 23,437.53 sq. km in 2021 to 23,996.72 sq. km in 2023, registering an increase of 559.19 sq. km (2.39%).PDF p. 167
    • Uttar Pradesh ranks second in the country in terms of increase in forest and tree cover.PDF p. 167

    Secondary Sector (Industry and Infrastructure)PDF p. 167

    • The Gross Value Added (GVA) of the secondary sector increased from `3.34 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `7.60 lakh crore in 2024–25, growing at a CAGR of 10.8%.PDF p. 167
    • Within the secondary sector:PDF p. 167
    • The construction sector leads with a 47.4% share, reflecting rapid expansion of infrastructure and urban development.PDF p. 167
    • The manufacturing sector contributes 42.9%, indicating strong industrial capacity and investment.PDF p. 167
    • The electricity sector contributes 9.6%, ensuring energy availability and continuity of industrial activities.PDF p. 167
    • According to the Annual Survey of Industries 2023–24, the Gross Value Added of industries in the state increased by 25% over the previous year, which is the highest among major states and more than double the national growth rate of 11.9%.PDF p. 167

    Infrastructure DevelopmentPDF p. 167

    • In Varanasi, the country’s first urban ropeway project is under construction, which is considered a major step in urban transport.PDF p. 167
    • The state is developing as the capital of expressways, with:PDF p. 167
    • 7 operational expresswaysPDF p. 167
    • 3 expressways under constructionPDF p. 167
    • 12 proposedPDF p. 167
    • At present, the state has 12 domestic and 4 international airports (Lucknow, Varanasi, Kushinagar, and Ayodhya).PDF p. 167
    • With the start of operation at Noida International Airport at Jewar (Gautam Buddha Nagar), the state will become the first in India with 5 international airports.PDF p. 167
    • The total road network includes 12,123 km of National Highways, and 90 National Highways pass through the state.PDF p. 167

    Energy and Digital ConnectivityPDF p. 167

    • Uttar Pradesh achieved a leading position in power generation, producing 126.50 thousand gigawatt- hours by December 2025–26.PDF p. 167
    • The state also ranked first in the country in terms of the number of internet subscribers, with 13.82 crore subscribers as of September 2025–26.PDF p. 167

    Service SectorPDF p. 167

    • The service sector contributes 47.0% to the state economy.PDF p. 167
    • The Gross Value Added (GVA) of the service sector increased from `5.95 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `13.10 lakh crore in 2024–25 (quick estimates) , growing at a CAGR of 10.4%.PDF p. 167
    • The progress of the service sector in Uttar Pradesh has been remarkable in 2024–25 compared to 2016–17, as the Gross Value Added (GVA) of all sub-sectors has almost doubled.PDF p. 167

    State FinancesPDF p. 167, 168

    • The total state budget increased from `3.47 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `8.33 lakh crore in 2025–26 , recording an increase of `4.86 lakh crore over nine years.PDF p. 167
    • The public debt-to-GDP ratio declined from 29.3% in 2016–17 to 28.0% in 2024–25 , which is significantly lower than the national level (81.3%) and the global average (92.8%) , indicating fiscal stability and discipline.PDF p. 168

    Per Capita IncomePDF p. 168

    • The per capita income (net) increased from `54,564 in 2016–17 to `1,09,844 in 2024–25 , growing at a CAGR of about 9.1%.PDF p. 168
    • During the period 2020–21 to 2024–25, the growth rate was higher at 14.7%.PDF p. 168
    • The per capita income (gross) was estimated at `1,26,304 in 2024–25.PDF p. 168

    Population and Demographic TrendsPDF p. 168

    • As per March 2026 estimates, Uttar Pradesh has a population of 25.19 crore, which is:PDF p. 168
    • 17.8% of India’s population (141.51 crore)PDF p. 168
    • 3.0% of the world’s population (830 crore)PDF p. 168
    • India contributes about 17% of the global population.PDF p. 168
    • If Uttar Pradesh were a country, it would rank 5th in the world in population , after India, China, the United States (33.5 crore), and Indonesia (27.7 crore).PDF p. 168

    Population Growth and FertilityPDF p. 168

    • The population growth rate declined from 1.85% per year in 2011 to 1.70% in 2021, and is expected to decline further to 0.58% during 2026–2051.PDF p. 168
    • The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) declined from 2.7 (NFHS-4, 2015–16) to 2.4 (NFHS-5, 2019–21) and is expected to reach the replacement level of 2.1 soon.PDF p. 168

    Life Expectancy and Social IndicatorsPDF p. 168

    • Life expectancy is expected to increase as follows :PDF p. 168
    • Males: from 62.5 years (2011) to 73.2 years (2051)PDF p. 168
    • Females: from 65.0 years (2011) to 77.1 years (2051)PDF p. 168

    Sex Ratio and Age StructurePDF p. 168

    • The sex ratio at birth in Uttar Pradesh was 111 boys per 100 girls in 2011.PDF p. 168
    • The age pyramid shows clear demographic changes:PDF p. 168
    • 2011: wide base (high child population)PDF p. 168
    • 2026: higher proportion of the working-age population (20–34 years)PDF p. 168
    • 2046: decline in the 0–14 age group and an increase in the population aged 40 and above.PDF p. 168

    Dependence on Central TaxesPDF p. 168

    • The state’s dependence on central taxes has been continuously declining.PDF p. 168
    • It was 56.0% in 2016–17, and is estimated to decline to 46.4% in 2025–26.PDF p. 168
    • The State’s Own Tax Revenue increased from `0.86 lakh crore in 2016–17 to `2.09 lakh crore in 2024–25 (advance estimates), which is about 2.5 times growth.PDF p. 168
    • The capital expenditure increased from `69.79 thousand crore in 2016–17 to `147.72 thousand crore in 2024–25 (advance estimates) , reflecting development-oriented priorities.PDF p. 168
    • The public debt-to-GDP ratio declined from 29.3% in 2016–17 to 28.0% in 2024–25 , which is significantly lower than the national level (about 81.3%) and global average (about 92.8%) , indicating fiscal discipline and stability.PDF p. 168

    Budget and ReceiptsPDF p. 168

    • Over the last nine years, the total budget increased at a CAGR of about 10.3%, reaching approximately `8.09 lakh crore in 2025–26.PDF p. 168
    • During the same period, total receipts increased at 10.2% CAGR, reaching about `7.79 lakh crore.PDF p. 168
    • As per the 2025–26 budget:PDF p. 168
    • Revenue expenditure: `5.83 lakh crorePDF p. 168
    • Compared to 2024–25 revised estimates:PDF p. 168
    • Revenue receipts increased by 21.0%PDF p. 168
    • Revenue expenditure increased by 19.2%PDF p. 168
    • Over the last nine years (2016–17 to 2025–26):PDF p. 168
    • Revenue receipts grew at a CAGR of 11.1%PDF p. 168
    • Revenue expenditure grew at a CAGR of 11.9%PDF p. 168
    • The ratio of revenue expenditure to revenue receipts declined from 92% (2016–17) to 89.2% (2024–25) and is estimated at 87.9% in 2025–26.PDF p. 168

    Composition of Revenue ReceiptsPDF p. 168

    • Revenue receipts represent income from regular government operations.PDF p. 168
    • The main components include:PDF p. 168
    • The state’s own resources (tax and non-tax revenue)PDF p. 168
    • Transfers from the Central Government (share in the divisible pool and grants)PDF p. 168
    • Revenue receipts increased from `2.57 lakh crore (2016–17) to `6.63 lakh crore (2025–26 BE).PDF p. 168
    • Over nine years:PDF p. 168
    • State tax and non-tax revenue grew at 12% a CAGRPDF p. 168
    • Central transfers grew at a CAGR of 10.3%.PDF p. 168

    Breakup of RevenuePDF p. 168

    • State Tax RevenuePDF p. 168
    • 2016–17: `0.86 lakh crorePDF p. 168
    • 2025–26: `2.95 lakh crorePDF p. 168
    • Growth rate: CAGR of 14.7%PDF p. 168
    • Share in Central TaxesPDF p. 168
    • Estimated at `2.55 lakh crore in 2025–26PDF p. 168
    • Growth rate: 9.9%PDF p. 168
    • Non-Tax RevenuePDF p. 168
    • State non-tax revenue: `0.25 lakh crore (2025–26)PDF p. 168
    • Grants from the Centre: increased at a CAGR of 11.7% to about `0.88 lakh crore (2025–26).PDF p. 168

    Chapter 8 · PDF pp. 169-177

    Bihar Current Affairs

    Bihar remains in the supplied book even for a UPPSC reader. Use it for State-to-State comparisons, but keep proposed investments, July draft incentives and actual budget figures in separate boxes.

    1. Digital infrastructure: existing and proposed
    2. Budget: size and financing
    3. Survey: growth and district economy

    Build the chapter in eight anchors

    Data centre versus AI factory

    The issue reports a ₹400 crore CtrlS data centre at Patliputra, Patna, with initial IT load of 12 MW, inaugurated on 13 October 2026. A separate LoI concerns a proposed ₹10,000 crore, 150 MW AI factory in Bodh Gaya.

    PDF p. 169
    A dashboard's scope

    The Sankalp Dashboard, launched alongside the Samanvay Portal on 13 October 2026, is described as bringing work of all 48 Bihar departments onto one platform.

    PDF p. 169
    MSME draft qualifier

    The chapter's MSME targets and detailed subsidies are explicitly from the July 2026 draft: formalise 1 crore MSMEs, generate over 1 crore jobs and train 1 lakh MSMEs annually. Do not silently call all draft incentives final.

    PDF p. 169
    Budget size has boundaries

    The FY 2026-27 budget discussion gives ₹3,47,589.76 crore including debt repayment, versus about ₹3,24,925 crore excluding it. The separate Appropriation Bill gross figure is ₹3,53,045.15 crore.

    PDF p. 174
    Fiscal balance

    The issue's Bihar FY 2026-27 target is a ₹1,143.19 crore revenue surplus and ₹39,111.80 crore fiscal deficit, or 2.99% of GSDP. Projected current-price GSDP is ₹13.09 lakh crore.

    PDF p. 174
    Saat Nischay-3 period

    The development roadmap is for 2025-2030. The agriculture roadmap discussed separately is the Fourth Agriculture Roadmap, 2023-2028.

    PDF p. 175
    Same year, two growth rates

    For FY 2024-25 quick estimates, the Bihar survey reports 8.6% constant-price GSDP growth and 13.1% current-price growth; the constant-price series uses base year 2011-12.

    PDF p. 176
    Per-capita and district comparisons

    FY 2024-25 per-capita GSDP at current prices is ₹76,490, while per-capita NSDP is ₹69,321. The survey names Patna, Begusarai and Munger as the top three GDDP districts in that order.

    PDF p. 174, 175, 176

    Learning aid - not from sourcePlace each policy number under 'operational', 'proposed' or 'draft'. An investment letter of intent is not installed capacity. This is an editorial learning aid.

    Close the notes. Explain it back.

    Why must the two CtrlS capacities be kept separate?

    12 MW is the Patna data centre's initial IT load. 150 MW is the proposed Bodh Gaya AI factory under an LoI. Different projects and stages cannot be merged.PDF p. 169

    What qualification belongs to the MSME incentive list?

    The source explicitly says those details come from the July 2026 draft. A policy launch paragraph does not make every draft detail an enacted rule.PDF p. 169

    Explain the three budget totals without choosing one as the only correct number.

    ₹3,47,589.76 crore includes debt repayment; about ₹3,24,925 crore excludes it; ₹3,53,045.15 crore is gross appropriation. They use different coverage.PDF p. 174

    Separate the periods of Saat Nischay-3 and the agriculture roadmap.

    Saat Nischay-3 covers 2025-2030; the Fourth Agriculture Roadmap covers 2023-2028. Similar roadmap language does not mean the same dates.PDF p. 175

    Why are Bihar's 8.6% and 13.1% not conflicting here?

    They refer to constant-price and current-price GSDP growth respectively for FY 2024-25 quick estimates. The price basis changes the measure.PDF p. 176

    Source check. MSME incentive details retain the source's 'July 2026 draft' label. Bihar budget totals retain their including/excluding debt-repayment and gross-appropriation definitions; they are not treated as interchangeable totals.PDF p. 169, 174

    Bihar’s First AI-Ready Data CenterPDF p. 169

    • Chief minister Samrat Choudhary on October 13,2026 inaugurated a Rs 400-crore data centre of CtrlS Data centers Ltd in Patliputra industrial area in Patna with an initial IT load capacity of 12 MW .PDF p. 169
    • Along with it CtrlS Data Centers has also signed a letter of intent (LoI) with the Bihar government to invest ₹10,000 crore in a proposed 150 MW hyper- scale AI factory in Bodh Gaya.PDF p. 169

    Sankalp Dashboard and Samanvay PortalPDF p. 169

    • Recently on October 13,2026, Bihar chief minister launched the Sankalp Dashboard and Samanvay Portal.PDF p. 169
    • The Sankalp dashboard brings the work of all 48 state departments onto one digital platform to improve transparency and accountability.PDF p. 169

    Cabinet clears Bihar’s first tech park at Gardanibagh, PatnaPDF p. 169

    • The state cabinet on 12 October ,2026 approved Bihar’s first tech park at Gardanibagh in Patna, to anchor an IT and IT-enabled services (ITES) ecosystem in the capital.PDF p. 169
    • NBCC (India) Ltd, a central public sector enterprise, will build it, and the state is authorised to sign an MoU with it.PDF p. 169

    Bihar MSME Policy, 2026PDF p. 169

    • The policy was unveiled on 8 October 2026 , alongside the inauguration of MSME centres in all districts to support entrepreneurs.PDF p. 169
    • It aims to promote industrialisation, investment and employment, and develop Bihar as a manufacturing hub of Eastern India.PDF p. 169
    • Major Targets in the Draft-PDF p. 169
    • Formalise 1 crore MSMEs across manufacturing and services.PDF p. 169
    • Generate over 1 crore direct and indirect jobs.PDF p. 169
    • Integrate 500-plus MSMEs into Global Value Chains (GVCs).PDF p. 169
    • Train 1 lakh MSMEs annually in Industry 4.0 and sector-specific skills.PDF p. 169
    • Establish four Technology/Extension Centres in Kosi, Bhagalpur, Munger and Purnea.PDF p. 169
    • Incentives Proposed in the Draft-PDF p. 169
    • Capital subsidy: Provide 25% in Category A districts and 30% in Category B districts, capped at ₹25 lakh, ₹1.5 crore and ₹5 crore for micro, small and medium enterprises, respectively.PDF p. 169
    • Additional support: Provide 10% additional capital subsidy to women, SC, ST, BC, Divyang and transgender entrepreneurs.PDF p. 169
    • Employment support: Reimburse employers’ EPF contributions for three years, capped at ₹24,000 per employee annually, subject to employment thresholds.PDF p. 169
    • Electricity subsidy: Reimburse 20% of eligible low- tension power charges for three years.PDF p. 169
    • Rooftop solar subsidy: Provide 25% of installation cost, capped at ₹5 lakh, for systems up to 300 kW .PDF p. 169
    • Stamp duty: Provide 100% reimbursement on land purchases by new manufacturing enterprises. Note: These detailed targets and incentives are from the July 2026 draft.PDF p. 169

    Rising Bihar - Investor Summit 2026PDF p. 169

    • Rising Bihar - Investor Summit 2026 was organised on the theme Bihar – The Emerging Investment Destination of India on 1st October 2026 at Hotel Taj City Centre, Patna.PDF p. 169
    • The summit served as a premier platform to showcase the Government of Bihar’s vision for industrial growth.PDF p. 169

    Vinay Kumar appointed as the Chief Information CommissionerPDF p. 169

    • 1991-batch IPS officer Vinay Kumar has taken Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) from the post of Bihar Director General of Police (DGP) and has been appointed as the Chief Information Commissioner (CIC) of Bihar.PDF p. 169

    Bihar Cabinet gives nod to Bihar Green Hydrogen Policy, 2026PDF p. 169

    • Intended to reduce carbon emissions, the Bihar cabinet on September 30, 2026 gave its nod to the draft “Bihar Green Hydrogen Policy, 2026” to promote renewable energy and reduce dependence on imports of natural gas.PDF p. 169
    • A target has been set to produce 0.10 million metric tonnes, or 1,00,000 tonnes of green hydrogen per year by 2031.PDF p. 169
    • The vision is to establish 1 GW of electrolyser capacity and achieve approximately 2.5 GW of renewable energy capacity through green hydrogen and its derivative projects.PDF p. 169

    PM Modi’s Silicon Statue Installed in MotihariPDF p. 170

    • On the occasion of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday on 17 September, 2026 , a silicon statue of PM Modi was installed at the newly constructed Deendayal Bhawan in Motihari, Bihar.PDF p. 170

    Surbhi Sundaram Wins ‘Miss Beautiful Smile’ TitlePDF p. 170

    • Surbhi Sundaram, a resident of Kishanganj, won the ‘Miss Beautiful Smile’ title at the Jewel of South 2026 competition held in Bengaluru.PDF p. 170

    Darbhanga Scientist Imtiaz Ahmed Leads ISRO’s EOS-05 MissionPDF p. 170

    • Imtiaz Ahmed, a scientist from Revada village in Jale block, Darbhanga, has brought recognition to Darbhanga and the Mithila region by serving as the Project Director of ISRO’s EOS-05 mission.PDF p. 170

    Bihar Partners with Google India for AI Teacher TrainingPDF p. 170

    • The Government of Bihar signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Google India to train school teachers across the state in Artificial Intelligence (AI) skills and practical tools.PDF p. 170

    Bihar Launches ‘Bihar Vidya Saathi’ for 24- Hour Online Learning SupportPDF p. 170

    • The Bihar Government launched ‘Bihar Vidya Saathi’, a 24×7 one-on-one interactive learning platform for eligible students in approximately 700 designated model school across Bihar, covering classes 9-10 and the science stream in classes 11-12, integrating teacher support, digital study resources and AI-powered learning tools.PDF p. 170
    • Students can connect with teachers based on their academic needs and queries at any time.PDF p. 170

    Bihar Approves Incentive for Creators Promoting Government SchemesPDF p. 170

    • The Bihar Cabinet, chaired by Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, approved amendments to the Bihar Social Media and Other Online Media Rules, 2024 through the 2026 amendment rules.PDF p. 170
    • Financial Incentive: Eligible creators will receive Rs. 10,000 per one lakh views for qualifying videos.PDF p. 170

    • Bihar’s Budget for 2026–27 was presented by Finance Minister Bijendra Prasad Yadav on February 3, 2026.PDF p. 174

    Key HighlightsPDF p. 174

    • The size of Bihar’s budget has increased from `23,885 crore in 2004–05 to `3,47,589.76 crore (including debt repayment) in 2026–27.PDF p. 174
    • This reflects the state government’s increased fiscal capacity to spend on social sectors, infrastructure and welfare schemes.PDF p. 174
    • After Saat Nischay-1 and Saat Nischay-2 , the government has now framed Saat Nischay-3 for 2025–2030, with the aim of taking Bihar towards the category of developed states.PDF p. 174

    Overall Budget Size and Fiscal FrameworkPDF p. 174

    • For 2026–27, Bihar’s net budget expenditure is estimated at `3,47,589.76 crore, which is `30,694.74 crore higher than the Budget Estimate of `3,16,895.02 crore for 2025–26.PDF p. 174
    • The annual scheme outlay is `1,22,155.42 crore , while establishment and committed expenditure is `2,25,434.34 crore.PDF p. 174
    • Thus, scheme expenditure forms 35.14% of total expenditure and establishment/committed expenditure forms 64.86%.PDF p. 174
    • The Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) for 2026–27 is projected at about `13.09 lakh crore, showing an estimated growth of about 15% over 2025–26.PDF p. 174
    • The Budget targets a revenue surplus of `1,143.19 crore and a fiscal deficit of `39,111.80 crore, equal to 2.99% of GSDP, which is within the 3% limit set under the Bihar Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management framework.PDF p. 174
    • The expenditure excluding debt repayment is estimated at `3,24,925 crore, while debt repayment is about `22,665 crore.PDF p. 174
    • In the Appropriation Bill, the state proposes gross expenditure of `3,53,045.15 crore, out of which `3,02,242.13 crore is voted expenditure and `50,803.02 crore is charged expenditure.PDF p. 174
    • The net expenditure figure used in the budget summary is `3,47,589.76 crore.PDF p. 174

    Revenue Receipts and BorrowingsPDF p. 174

    • Total revenue receipts for 2026–27 are estimated at `2,85,277.12 crore. Of this, the state is expected to raise `75,202.99 crore from its own tax and non-tax sources, while about `2,10,074 crore will come from the Centre through tax devolution and grants.PDF p. 174
    • This shows Bihar’s continuing dependence on central transfers.PDF p. 174
    • The state’s own tax revenue is estimated at `65,800 crore.PDF p. 174
    • Important components include commercial taxes of `50,000 crore, stamp and registration fees of `10,000 crore, transport tax of `5,000 crore, and land revenue of `800 crore.PDF p. 174
    • State GST as the largest source of Bihar’s own tax revenue, with an estimated `38,000 crore in 2026–27.PDF p. 174
    • The state’s own non-tax revenue is estimated at `9,402.99 crore , including `4,200 crore from mining and `2,570.08 crore from interest receipts.PDF p. 174
    • Bihar’s share in central taxes is estimated at `1,58,178.32 crore , while grants-in-aid from the Centre are estimated at `51,895.81 crore.PDF p. 174
    • These grants include `44,002.81 crore for Centrally Sponsored Schemes and `7,893 crore linked to Finance Commission-related grants , including disaster response and local body grants.PDF p. 174
    • Borrowing of `61,939.48 crore is proposed for 2026–27.PDF p. 174
    • The state also proposes to provide loans and advances of `1,413.94 crore.PDF p. 174
    • Debt repayment is estimated at `22,664.83 crore , including repayment of loans taken earlier from the Centre and internal loans.PDF p. 174

    Capital and Revenue ExpenditurePDF p. 174

    • Total capital expenditure is estimated at `63,455.84 crore, which is 18.26% of total expenditure.PDF p. 174
    • This includes capital outlay of `39,377.06 crore , with `6,117.30 crore for general services, `7,434.80 crore for social services and `25,824.96 crore for economic services.PDF p. 174
    • Total revenue expenditure is estimated at `2,84,133.92 crore, or 81.74% of total expenditure.PDF p. 174
    • This includes expenditure on salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, grants and welfare schemes.PDF p. 174
    • Under the state’s broader budget classification, spending on salaries, pensions, interest payments and debt repayment together is estimated at `1,79,327.48 crore.PDF p. 174
    • Using the comparable committed-expenditure classification of salaries, pensions and interest payments, estimates committed expenditure at `1,33,494 crore, or 47% of revenue receipts.PDF p. 174

    Bihar’s Economy: Key IndicatorsPDF p. 174

    • Bihar’s economy is projected to grow strongly in nominal terms. For 2026–27, GSDP at current prices is projected at `13.09 lakh crore.PDF p. 174
    • In 2024–25, Bihar’s GSDP at constant prices is estimated to have grown by 8.6%, compared to India’s GDP growth of 6.5%.PDF p. 174
    • At current prices, agriculture, manufacturing and services are estimated to contribute 22.37%, 23.57% and 54.07% respectively to Bihar’s economy in 2024–25.PDF p. 174
    • Bihar’s per capita GSDP at current prices for 2024– 25 is estimated at `76,490, while India’s per capita GDP is estimated at `2,34,859.PDF p. 174

    Bihar Budget 2026–27PDF p. 174, 175

    • The state’s per capita NSDP for 2024–25 is estimated at `69,321, showing an increase of 11.45% over the previous year.PDF p. 175

    Saat Nischay-3: Main Development Roadmap for 2025–2030PDF p. 175

    • The Budget gives major importance to Saat Nischay-3, which is planned for the period 2025–2030.PDF p. 175
    • Its main objective is to accelerate income growth, employment, social welfare, education, health and infrastructure.PDF p. 175

    Progress in AgriculturePDF p. 175

    • Three roadmaps have already been implemented, and work on the Fourth Agriculture Roadmap, 2023–2028 will be accelerated.PDF p. 175
    • A new state scheme, Jannayak Karpoori Thakur Kisan Samman Nidhi, will provide farmers `3,000 per year in addition to the `6,000 per year provided under the central PM-Kisan Samman Nidhi.PDF p. 175
    • Foodgrain production has increased more than three times since 2005. According to the final estimates for 2024–25, total foodgrain production reached 326.62 lakh metric tonnes, the highest ever for the state.PDF p. 175
    • Bihar holds an important position in several agricultural products. In 2024–25, it ranked first in makhana and litchi production , second in maize, fourth in honey, fifth in rice and sixth in wheat.PDF p. 175
    • The state produces about 85% of India’s makhana and 23% of India’s litchi.PDF p. 175
    • The Government of India has also established a National Makhana Board in Bihar to support makhana farmers and improve production.PDF p. 175
    • Bihar is also a leading state in mushroom production, with current production of about 44,000 metric tonnes.PDF p. 175
    • The government is working on an AI-enabled Mechanised Agriculture Mission , a Bihar Agri Infrastructure Mission with an initial investment vision of `1 lakh crore , and a Bihar Agriculture Acceleration Mission to promote agri-startups, GI-tagged products and rural agricultural markets.PDF p. 175
    • In allied sectors, Bihar’s per capita annual fish availability is 12.21 kg , calculated on the basis of 60% population coverage.PDF p. 175
    • Women’s empowerment is one of the central themes of the Budget. Under Jeevika, about 1.40 crore families have been connected through 11.45 lakh self-help groups , and 91 lakh members have received insurance coverage. At present, 31.71 lakh Jeevika Didis have been declared Lakhpati Didis.PDF p. 175
    • The Mukhyamantri Mahila Rojgar Yojana has been one of the most important welfare-cum- employment measures.PDF p. 175
    • It aims to support self-employment among women, with initial financial help of `10,000 and further assistance of up to `2 lakh for enterprise expansion.PDF p. 175
    • Under the Chief Minister Divyangjan Entrepreneur Scheme, approved beneficiaries will receive loans and grants in a 50:50 ratio up to a maximum project cost of `10 lakh per unit.PDF p. 175
    • For social justice, `19,603.02 crore has been allocated for Scheduled Castes and `1,648.42 crore for Scheduled Tribes in 2026–27.PDF p. 175
    • According to Sample Registration System data, Bihar’s Maternal Mortality Ratio for 2021–23 is 104.PDF p. 175
    • In child health indicators, Bihar’s Infant Mortality Rate is 23, Neonatal Mortality Rate is 18, and Under-5 Mortality Rate is 27.PDF p. 175
    • Bihar’s IMR, NMR and Under-5 mortality rate are better than the national averages of 25, 19 and 29 respectively, though its MMR remains above the national figure of 88. These are based on the SRS 2023 values.PDF p. 175
    • Bihar has maintained the first position on the Government of India’s DVDMS Central Dashboard for supply and distribution of medicines since September 2024.PDF p. 175
    • Bihar has made major progress in basic infrastructure. The length of rural roads increased from 64,205 km in 2015–16 to about 1.19 lakh km in 2025–26 , making Bihar one of the states with high road density.PDF p. 175
    • Per capita electricity consumption increased from 203 kWh in 2015 to 374 kWh in 2025.PDF p. 175

    Sector-wise High-Yield FactsPDF p. 175

    • Sector Important Fact for Exam Education Bihar allocated 21.7% of its sectoral expenditure to education, higher than the 31-state and UT (including Bihar) average of 14.5%. Rural development Bihar allocated 9.4% of sectoral expenditure to rural development, higher than the state average of 4.9%. Health Bihar allocated 6.3% to health, slightly above the state average of 6.2%. Police Bihar allocated 5.2% to police, above the state average of 4.0%. Roads and bridges Bihar allocated 2.9%, lower than the state average of 4.3%. Agriculture Bihar allocated 2.6%, lower than the state average of 5.7%.PDF p. 175

    Bihar Economic Survey, 2025–26PDF p. 176

    • According to the Bihar Economic Survey, 2025–26, Bihar’s Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) at constant (2011–12) prices grew by 8.6 percent in 2024–25 (Q.E.), and at current prices by 13.1 percent, reaching `5,31,372 crore and `9,91,997 crore respectively.PDF p. 176
    • In the last three years, Bihar’s economic growth rate, both at constant and current prices, has been higher than the Gross Domestic Product growth rate of India.PDF p. 176
    • At current prices, Bihar’s GSDP growth rates were 17.9 percent in 2022–23 and 14.9 percent in 2023– 24, compared to 14.0 percent and 12.0 percent respectively for the country.PDF p. 176
    • The quick estimates for 2024–25 show that Bihar’s GSDP growth rate at current prices is estimated at 13.1 percent compared to 9.8 percent for India. At constant (2011–12) prices, Bihar’s growth rate is estimated at 8.6 percent, which is higher than India’s 6.5 percent. These figures place Bihar among the fastest-growing states in the country.PDF p. 176
    • For 2024–25, quick estimates show that the Gross State Value Added (GSVA) of the secondary sector grew by 11.1 percent at constant (2011–12) prices and 15.5 percent at current prices.PDF p. 176
    • In 2024–25, the tertiary sector grew by 8.9 percent at constant prices and 13.5 percent at current prices, while the primary sector recorded growth of 4.1 percent at constant prices and 9.6 percent at current prices.PDF p. 176
    • Between 2020–21 and 2024–25, the share of the secondary sector in GSVA increased significantly from 21.1 percent to 26.8 percent at constant (2011– 12) prices, mainly due to growth in construction and manufacturing.PDF p. 176
    • In contrast, the share of the primary sector declined from 21.9 percent to 18.3 percent, and the share of the tertiary sector also declined from 57.0 percent to 54.8 percent, indicating increasing diversification in the state’s economic activities.PDF p. 176
    • Per capita GSDP at current prices increased from `46,412 in 2020–21 to `76,490 in 2024–25, indicating a consistent upward trend.PDF p. 176
    • At constant (2011–12) prices, per capita GSDP increased from `30,159 in 2020–21 to `40,973 in 2024–25.PDF p. 176
    • Within Bihar, Patna district recorded the highest Gross District Domestic Product (GDDP), followed by Begusarai and Munger districts.PDF p. 176
    • At current prices, per capita GDDP was `2,41,220 for Patna, `1,05,600 for Begusarai, and `93,921 for Munger.PDF p. 176

    Public Financial ManagementPDF p. 176, 177

    • Bihar’s fiscal development path reflects disciplined financial management, as the state government’s total expenditure increased from `1.66 lakh crore in 2020–21 to `2.82 lakh crore in 2024–25. The state government maintained fiscal prudence through moderate borrowing and effective debt servicing while consistently prioritising developmental expenditure in sectors such as education, health, energy, transport, irrigation, and agriculture.PDF p. 176
    • This structural change reflects the government’s focus on long-term investment, infrastructure development, and asset creation.PDF p. 176
    • Revenue receipts of the state government increased from `1.28 lakh crore in 2020–21 to `2.18 lakh crore in 2024–25, with tax revenue as the main source. The share of tax revenue increased from 70 percent to 84 percent, while the share of non-tax revenue declined from 5 percent to 2 percent and the share of grants-in-aid declined from 25 percent to 14 percent.PDF p. 176
    • The structure of revenue expenditure remained largely stable over the last five years, with social services having the highest share at 46 percent. The share of economic services increased slightly from 21 percent in 2020-21 to 22 percent in 2024-25, while the share of general services declined slightly from 33 percent in 2020-21 to 32 percent in 2024- 25.PDF p. 176
    • This distribution reflects the government’s commitment to both welfare expansion and strengthening productive sectors.PDF p. 176
    • The share of plan expenditure in total expenditure increased from 38.3 percent in 2020–21 to 39.9 percent in 2024–25, while the share of establishment and committed expenditure declined from 61.7 percent to 60.1 percent.PDF p. 176
    • This trend indicates a gradual shift towards welfare- oriented activities and policy-driven development priorities.PDF p. 176
    • Developmental expenditure remained around two- thirds of the total budget, reaching 67.4 percent in 2024–25. It increased from `1,12,122 crore in 2020– 21 to `1,89,892 crore in 2024–25, indicating a stronger focus on development and welfare expenditure.PDF p. 176
    • Receipts from the central government increased from `91,625 crore in 2020–21 to `1,59,298 crore in 2024–25, mainly due to transfers from the divisible tax pool, which increased from `59,861 crore in 2020-21 to `1,29,435 crore in 2024-25.PDF p. 176
    • In 2024–25, grants-in-aid from the central government amounted to `29,863 crore.PDF p. 176
    • The state’s own revenue increased from `36,543 crore in 2020–21 to `59,360 crore in 2024–25, with tax revenue as the major contributor.PDF p. 176
    • As of 31 March 2025, the outstanding debt of the state government was `3,74,134 crore, which was 37.7 percent of the GSDP .PDF p. 176
    • At the end of 2024–25, 84.6 percent of the total outstanding debt consisted of public debt. Out of total public debt, 83.8 percent came from internal borrowings, while 16.2 percent came from loans and advances from the central government.PDF p. 176
    • Market loans and loans from financial institutions are the main components of internal debt.PDF p. 177

    Agriculture and Allied SectorPDF p. 177

    • According to provisional estimates released by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics for 2023– 24, agriculture, forestry, and fisheries together accounted for 23.1 percent of GSVA. Within this, crop production contributed 11.5 percent and livestock contributed 8.1 percent.PDF p. 177
    • In 2023–24, rice, wheat, and maize together contributed 99.9 percent of total cereal production in Bihar. In 2024–25, rice accounted for 40.7 percent, wheat for 32.1 percent, and maize for 27.1 percent of total cereal production.PDF p. 177
    • Between 2023–24 and 2024–25, production of rice increased by 4.3 percent, wheat by 7.1 percent, and maize by 12.6 percent.PDF p. 177
    • Bihar is among the leading fruit and vegetable producing states in the country and is a major producer of litchi, makhana, and mushrooms. In 2023–24, total horticulture production in the state was estimated at about 230 lakh tonnes, which is higher than 206 lakh tonnes in 2019–20, with a major share coming from fruits and vegetables.PDF p. 177
    • Between 2023–24 and 2024–25, milk production increased by 4.2 percent, egg production by 10.0 percent, and fish production by 9.9 percent.PDF p. 177
    • The share of electricity consumption in agriculture increased significantly from 5.3 percent in 2020–21 to 14.9 percent in 2024–25.PDF p. 177
    • In 2024–25, the number of Kisan Credit Card holders increased by 16.3 percent compared to 2023–24, while total credit disbursed increased by 32.8 percent from `7,080.07 crore in 2023–24 to `9,399.24 crore in 2024–25.PDF p. 177
    • Total expenditure on irrigation in 2024–25 was `2,729.83 crore, of which 74.3 percent was capital expenditure. Between 2023–24 and 2024–25, total irrigation expenditure increased by 63.1 percent. This increase in public expenditure is reflected in the extensive expansion of major, medium, and minor irrigation projects.PDF p. 177

    Enterprise SectorPDF p. 177

    • Bihar’s secondary sector has experienced fluctuations over the past five years. After a sharp decline in 2020–21 due to the pandemic, it recovered in 2021– 22 and recorded rapid growth in 2022–23, mainly driven by mining, utilities, and construction.PDF p. 177
    • In 2024–25, 37.8 lakh tourists visited 28 eco-tourism sites, which is 24.0 percent higher than the previous year. Total outlay for eco-tourism and park development in 2024–25 was `100.00 crore.PDF p. 177

    Human DevelopmentPDF p. 177

    • Over the past 19 years, expenditure on social services has increased rapidly, rising fivefold in the first decade and 15-fold between 2005–06 and 2024–25. Expenditure on health and education increased by 14.8 times and 13.2 times respectively.PDF p. 177
    • Life expectancy at birth (LEB) in Bihar during 2019–2023 was 68.9 years for males and 69.7 years for females.PDF p. 177
    • It is also notable that between 2017 and 2023, the infant mortality rate (IMR) declined by 12 points from 35 to 23.PDF p. 177
    • Significant progress has been made in reducing maternal mortality Ratio (MMR), which declined from 312 deaths per lakh live births in 2004–2006 by 208 points to 104 in 2021–2023. Under the Janani Suraksha Yojana, institutional deliveries increased from 15.77 lakh in 2020–21 to 16.17 lakh in 2024–25 (an increase of 2.54 percent).PDF p. 177
    • In 2024–25, total enrolment at the elementary level school is 159.22 lakh, including 80.87 lakh boys and 78.35 lakh girls. Total enrolment was 27.54 lakh at the secondary level and 20.33 lakh at the higher secondary level.PDF p. 177

    Environment, Climate Change and Disaster ManagementPDF p. 177

    • Between 2011–12 and 2024–25, Bihar’s forestry and logging sector achieved a compound annual growth rate of 10.4 percent at current prices. The total value increased from `4,187 crore to `15,139 crore during this period.PDF p. 177
    • By 2024–25, this sector accounted for 7.0 percent of GSVA in agriculture and 2.0 percent of the state’s total GSVA.PDF p. 177
    • Since 2011, Bihar’s ecological footprint has expanded significantly. The total area under forest and tree cover increased by 689 sq km from 9,214 sq km to 9,903 sq km by 2023.PDF p. 177
    • The total forest cover increased from 6,845 sq km to 7,532 sq km during this period. Notably, the area under very dense forests (VDF) increased significantly from 231 sq km to 387 sq km, indicating successful conservation within protected areas.PDF p. 177
    • Bihar’s commissioned power capacity is 11,764 MW , with the major share coming from thermal power (7,743 MW). Solar energy is the largest renewable source with a contribution of 1,922 MW , followed by hydropower at 1,356 MW and wind energy at 699 MW .PDF p. 177
    • In 2024–25, the total budget allocation for the Urban Development and Housing Department was `5,274.9 crore and total expenditure was `3,613.8 crore, with a utilisation rate of 68.5 percent.PDF p. 177
    • The credit-to-GSDP ratio in Bihar increased steadily over the last five years from 30.9 percent in 2020–21 to 37.9 percent in 2024–25, indicating increased availability of credit in the state’s economy.PDF p. 177
    • The percentage of non-performing assets (NPAs) in banks in Bihar declined significantly over the last five years from 11.8 percent in 2020–21 to 7.6 percent in 2024–25.PDF p. 177

    Short News, Awards and Persons

    Short news is best learned in pairs: person-post, book-author, exercise-partner and day-theme. Keep only one kind of pair on each flashcard so neighbouring table rows do not get mixed.

    2. Awards, books and creators

    Build the chapter in eight anchors

    PMO's author

    PMO: Prime Minister's Office Through the Years is attributed to Himanshu Roy. Match the full title to the author.

    PDF p. 220
    An autobiography pair

    Triumph of the Indian Republic: My Life, My Struggles is Ram Nath Kovind's autobiography; the page also lists the Hindi title Bharatiya Ganatantra Ki Vijaygatha, Mera Jeevan, Mera Sangharsh.

    PDF p. 220
    A judicial succession

    The issue dates Surya Kant's oath as the 53rd Chief Justice of India to 24 November 2025, succeeding B.R. Gavai. It lists 9 February 2027 as his due retirement date; these are the issue's dated office entries.

    PDF p. 182
    Compassion and murals

    Karuna: The Power of Compassion is attributed to Kailash Satyarthi; Tides of Time: Bharat's History through Murals in Parliament to Sudha Murty.

    PDF p. 220
    Audit and biography

    When Audit Matters: CAG Interventions That Made a Difference is edited by Vinod Rai; The Library Man of India: The Story of P.N. Panicker is by P.P. Sathyan.

    PDF p. 220
    A named appointment

    The issue reports Sudhakar Dalela as India's next Ambassador to Nepal on 16 October 2026. This is a dated appointment item rather than a claim about today's incumbent.

    PDF p. 178
    An award and a field

    The issue names Toby Kiers for the Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement in January 2026, for research on underground fungal networks. It separately lists Graça Machel for the Indira Gandhi Prize for Peace, Disarmament and Development 2025.

    PDF p. 203
    Naval exercise partners

    The exercise table pairs SIMBEX with Singapore-India at Visakhapatnam, VARUNA with India-France at Toulon, and SLINEX with India-Sri Lanka at Visakhapatnam. Keep the exercise, partners and location together.

    Who wrote PMO, and who edited When Audit Matters?

    Himanshu Roy is listed as author of PMO: Prime Minister's Office Through the Years; Vinod Rai as editor of When Audit Matters. The role is part of the match.PDF p. 220

    Match SIMBEX, VARUNA and SLINEX to India's partners.

    SIMBEX - Singapore; VARUNA - France; SLINEX - Sri Lanka. The source places SIMBEX and SLINEX at Visakhapatnam, and VARUNA at Toulon in France.PDF p. 213

    Which pair separates Kovind's autobiography and Sonia Gandhi's memoir?

    Kovind: Triumph of the Indian Republic: My Life, My Struggles. Sonia Gandhi: Belonging: A Journey of Love. The subtitles belong to different books.PDF p. 220

    Distinguish the Tyler Prize and Indira Gandhi Prize entries.

    Toby Kiers - Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement, research on underground fungal networks; Graça Machel - Indira Gandhi Prize for Peace, Disarmament and Development 2025. Keep the award's year with its name.PDF p. 203

    How should an appointment flashcard be qualified?

    Attach post, person and source date. Here it is Sudhakar Dalela, next Ambassador to Nepal, 16 October 2026; this does not independently verify the current office-holder.PDF p. 178

    Narendra ModiPDF p. 178

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi completed 25 continuous years as the head of a government on October 7, 2026.PDF p. 178
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi was conferred with the “Oliy Darajali Do’stlik” Order (Order of Highest Friendship) by the President of Uzbekistan, Shavkat Mirziyoyev on August 30, 2026.This is Uzbekistan’s highest honour for foreign leaders. The award was conferred for his contribution to the strengthening of friendship between the two countries. Awards to PM Narendra Modi Awards Country Date Remarks ‘Bintang Adipurna of the Republic of Indonesia’ Indonesia July 7, 2026 Highest civilian honour of Indonesia ‘Guardian of the Blue Horizon’ Seychelles June 28, 2026 This was the first time that this honour was bestowed “The Order of the White Double Cross, First Class” Slovakia June 15, 2026 Slovakia’s highest State honour Agricola Medal Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) May 20, 2026 Award conferred by Dr. Qu Dongyu, Director General of FAO Royal Norwegian Order of Merit Norway May 18, 2026 Norway’s highest honour bestowed on foreign Heads of Government Royal Order of the Polar, Star, Degree Commander Grand Cross Sweden May 17, 2026 Sweden’s highest honour conferred on foreign Heads of Government Medal of the Knesset Israel February 25, 2026 Highest honour of the Knesset, the Israeli Parliament Order of Oman (First Class) Oman December 18, 2025 Highest civilian honour of Oman Great Honour Nishan of Ethiopia Ethiopia December 16, 2025 Highest civilian honour of EthiopiaPDF p. 178
    • He became the Chief Minister of Gujarat on October 7, 2001 and then became Prime Minister in 2014.PDF p. 178
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi has become the longest-serving elected the Prime Minister of India for consecutive terms on June 10, 2026.PDF p. 178
    • He has surpassed the record of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, who first took the oath as an elected Prime Minister on May 13, 1952, and served until May 27, 1964.PDF p. 178
    • From May 26, 2014 to June 10, 2026, Prime Minister Modi’s continuous tenure is 4399 days.PDF p. 178
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi has achieved a historic milestone in Indian politics by becoming the longest-serving head of an elected government in the country on March 22, 2026.PDF p. 178
    • He has now completed 8, 931 days (as of March 22, 2026) as head of government, combining his tenure as Chief Minister of Gujarat and as Prime Minister.PDF p. 178

    • 36th Ig Nobel AwardsPDF p. 201

Talbot, and Stuart West They defined kissing comparatively by studying mouth-to- mouth contact across species. Economics Paul Piff, Daniel Stancato, Stéphane Côté, Rodolfo Mendoza-Denton, and Dacher Keltner They found that higher social class was associated with some unethical behaviours. Chemistry Sanchari Banerjee and 10 international colleagues They studied nutrient-rich protein crystals produced after Pacific beetle cockroach embryos consume a milk-like secretion. Medicine Tokuji Unno (posthumous) His 1977 study examined airflow and pressure during nose- blowing. Biology João Miguel Alves-Nunes and five colleagues They carefully stepped on venomous snakes to identify conditions provoking bites. Physics Randy Hurd, Zhao Pan, Tadd Truscott, and Kaveeshan Thurairajah They applied physics, geometry, and equations to design splash-free urinals. Technology Justin Puma and 11 colleagues They created “necroprinting” by incorporating a real mosquito proboscis into a 3D-printing nozzle. Olfaction Ilona Croy, Tomasz Frackowiak, Thomas Hummel, and Agnieszka Sorokowska They found that parents rated babies’ odour more favourably than teenagers’ odour. Peace Jaimie Arona Krems and four colleagues They found that people may prefer friends who are kind to them but hostile toward their enemies. Soil Science Franz Bender, Marcel G. A. van der Heijden, Atlant Bieri, and Pia Viviani They buried 1,000 pairs of cotton underpants across over 25 countries to measure soil biological activity through decomposition.PDF p. 201

    Sports News

    Start every sports note with the competition, edition and category. Men's and women's tournaments, T20 and ODI formats, and winners versus individual awards are different rows. Use the issue's result tables as dated source claims.

    1. Competition, edition and host
    2. Champion and runner-up
    3. Individual awards and future hosts

    Build the chapter in eight anchors

    Men's T20 World Cup

    The issue's 10th ICC Men's T20 World Cup is co-hosted by India and Sri Lanka from 7 February to 8 March 2026, with 20 teams and 55 matches; it reports India as champion and Sanju Samson as Player of the Tournament.

    PDF p. 222
    Women's T20 World Cup

    The source places the 10th ICC Women's T20 World Cup in England and Wales, 12 June-5 July 2026, expanded to 12 teams and 33 matches; it reports Australia champion and Beth Mooney Player of the Tournament.

    PDF p. 221
    A different women's World Cup

    The 2025 ICC Women's Cricket World Cup article reports India champion and South Africa runner-up, with the final at DY Patil Stadium, Navi Mumbai. Do not merge this with the 2026 T20 event.

    PDF p. 222
    Two Indian youth/tournament results

    The source reports India as U-19 World Cup 2026 champion (record sixth title), with Vaibhav Suryavanshi Player of the Series; WPL 2026 champion is Royal Challengers Bengaluru, runner-up Delhi Capitals.

    PDF p. 222
    Asian Games identity

    The 20th Asian Games are placed at Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, 19 September-4 October 2026. The mascot is Honohon and slogan Imagine One Asia; the issue reports India fourth with 85 medals, including 21 gold.

    PDF p. 237
    Commonwealth identity

    The issue's Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games use the unicorn mascot Finnie and a compact 10-sport model. It reports India fourth with 39 medals: 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.

    PDF p. 237, 238
    Expanded FIFA format

    The 2026 men's FIFA World Cup is described as co-hosted by Canada, Mexico and the USA, with 48 teams and 104 matches across 16 host cities. Mascots are Maple (Canada), Zayu (Mexico) and Clutch (USA).

    PDF p. 238
    Future host pairs

    The issue lists the 2028 Olympics at Los Angeles, the 2032 Olympics at Brisbane, the 2030 Asian Games at Doha and the 2034 Asian Games at Riyadh. These remain the issue's future-host entries.

    PDF p. 239

    Close the notes. Explain it back.

    Reconstruct the men's T20 event without borrowing a women's-event detail.

    India and Sri Lanka; 7 February-8 March 2026; 20 teams and 55 matches; reported champion India; Player of the Tournament Sanju Samson.PDF p. 222

    Why do India and Australia both appear as women's World Cup champions in these pages?

    They are different competitions and years: India is the source's 2025 Women's Cricket World Cup champion, while Australia is its 2026 Women's T20 World Cup champion.PDF p. 221, 222

    Distinguish Honohon from Finnie.

    Honohon is the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games mascot; Finnie is the Glasgow Commonwealth Games unicorn. Attach the event and host to each name.PDF p. 237

    Recover the three FIFA host-mascot pairs.

    Canada - Maple; Mexico - Zayu; USA - Clutch. The source also gives 48 teams and 104 matches, a separate format fact.PDF p. 238

    Pair the next two Olympic host cities listed in the issue with their years.

    Los Angeles - 2028; Brisbane - 2032. Keep these future-host listings separate from Asian Games hosts Doha 2030 and Riyadh 2034.PDF p. 239

    Source check. The Messi item reports an international-retirement announcement on 31 August 2026 and a last match in October 2026. Both source statements are retained; the guide does not turn them into a single independently verified retirement date.PDF p. 239
